items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?

items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, the most likely result would not have been an immediate restoration of the old Ming empire, but a divided China: a Ming-ruled south and a Manchu/Qing-ruled north, at least for several decades.

For this to happen, the Southern Ming would have needed to avoid its real historical weaknesses: factional court politics, competing Ming princes, unreliable military commanders, and the inability to coordinate resistance against the Qing. A plausible survival scenario would involve a Southern Ming court establishing a stable capital in Nanjing, Fuzhou, Guangzhou, or southwest China; securing the Yangzi River line; keeping powerful commanders such as Zheng Chenggong loyal; and maintaining control over the wealthy lower Yangzi and coastal trade networks. If that happened, the Qing conquest of China would have been much harder.

The political map might have resembled earlier periods of north-south division, such as the Southern Song versus the Jin. The Qing would likely dominate Beijing, north China, Manchuria, Mongolia, and perhaps parts of the northwest, while the Southern Ming would hold the Yangzi basin, southeast coast, Lingnan, and possibly Yunnan-Guizhou or Sichuan. The Yangzi would become a militarized frontier. Warfare would continue, but both sides might eventually settle into a tense coexistence if neither could destroy the other.

A surviving Southern Ming would probably remain economically strong. South China was rich, urbanized, commercially active, and deeply connected to maritime trade. The Ming south could have become even more ocean-oriented than the late Ming had been. Instead of Zheng Chenggong being pushed into Taiwan as a last refuge, his maritime network might have become a central pillar of Southern Ming power. Taiwan could have become a Ming-aligned naval base or colony rather than later being absorbed by the Qing in the same way. Trade with Japan, Southeast Asia, and Europeans might have expanded, especially if the Southern Ming court relied on customs revenue, silver inflows, and naval power.

Culturally, the survival of the Southern Ming would have preserved a legitimate Han Chinese imperial alternative to Qing rule. The queue order and other Qing symbols of submission might never have been imposed in the south. Literati culture would likely continue to frame the Ming as the orthodox dynasty and the Qing as foreign occupiers. This would create a long-lasting ideological divide: northern elites might adapt to Qing rule, while southern elites would claim continuity with the classical Chinese imperial tradition.

The Qing, meanwhile, might have become a more explicitly Manchu-northern empire rather than the dynasty that ruled all China. Its attention could have remained focused on Manchuria, Mongolia, Korea, Inner Asia, and defense against the Southern Ming. Without the full resources of south China, Qing expansion into Xinjiang, Tibet, and Central Asia might have been slower, smaller, or less successful. The great eighteenth-century Qing empire under Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong may never have emerged in the same form.

For Korea and Japan, the consequences would also be significant. Joseon Korea, which historically submitted to the Qing but retained strong cultural loyalty to the Ming, might have maintained secret or open ties with the Southern Ming. Japan, under the Tokugawa shogunate, would probably avoid direct intervention but might tolerate trade or indirect support through maritime networks. A Ming-aligned coastal world could make East Asian diplomacy more multipolar.

European involvement would likely increase but not necessarily lead to colonization. The Portuguese in Macau, the Dutch, the Spanish in Manila, and later the English would all try to exploit the division. A Southern Ming state dependent on sea trade might grant more commercial privileges than the Qing historically did, but it would also have strong reasons to control foreigners carefully. China’s southern coast might become more open to global trade earlier, though still under Chinese state supervision.

The long-term outcome would depend on whether the Southern Ming could reform. If it merely reproduced late Ming corruption, fiscal weakness, and court factionalism, it might survive for a generation and then collapse. But if it became a leaner, militarized, maritime, revenue-conscious state, it could endure much longer. In that case, China might remain divided into northern Qing and southern Ming realms for a century or more.

The biggest historical difference is that there would be no unified Qing China. Modern China’s borders, identity, and political memory would likely be very different. The Qing’s role in incorporating Mongolia, Xinjiang, and Tibet into a single imperial structure might be reduced, while the south might develop a stronger maritime and commercial orientation. Chinese nationalism in later centuries might also look different: instead of remembering the Qing as the last imperial dynasty of China, later generations might remember a long struggle between a Han Ming south and a Manchu Qing north.

So, if the Southern Ming had survived, East Asia would probably have seen a prolonged divided-China order: a wealthy, maritime, Han-identified Ming state in the south facing a militarized Manchu Qing state in the north. Whether that division ended in Ming reconquest, Qing conquest, or permanent partition would depend on military reform, fiscal stability, and control of the Yangzi and coastal trade.

items.question: What If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain's remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a Portuguese revolt?
human_answers: Actually, I think one could argue the opposite: that it's magically deterministic to assume that, in some unspecified way, this crisis will send the whole country into a downward spiral that will lead to its implosion. I mean, once you go over the list of changes, there isn't too much difference: yes, the Spanish Navy has been severely damaged; yes, Portugal has become independent; yes, Spain has lost all its possessions in Europe that are outside the Iberian Peninsula... but really the only significant difference from OTL is that Portugal became independent earlier, the burden that the Netherlands represented is now "someone else's problem," the remaining Spanish Navy is much smaller, and now Portugal has very serious reasons to hate England for keeping the Azores "because we can." The American Empire remains intact, it is doubtful that the English will be more successful in appropriating anything than in OTL, and they are possibly too busy antagonizing someone else once they see that the possibility of another Invincible Armada is not going to happen in the near future. OTL Spain recovered from that, even if 200 years later they declined for other reasons, but this alone should not condemn them to failure.

Spanish resilience at the time was incredible, considering how Philip II expended so many resources on fronts that ultimately yielded no tangible gains beyond preserving his honor (which was the sole reason he remained in the Flanders War). Even if England were to seize the Azores, I do not believe this would satisfy the Portuguese nobility and bourgeoisie—the main factions Antonio, Prior of Crato, would need in order to legitimize his rule. Furthermore, if Spain was able to rebuild a second fleet within two or three years—not as large as the first, but still significant—we must not forget that while the English might capture a treasure fleet, they could not always be expected to capture all of them. If there was one defining trait of Spanish admirals regarding their treasure fleets, it was their elusiveness. Even so, a Spain under Philip II, burdened by numerous problems, could compel Philip III to reconsider his policies and explore the possibility of a genuine peace with the Dutch Republic—something that could ultimately benefit Spain in the long run.

While I agree the OP is going way too far and too fast, I'd say 1589 had the potential to screw Spain over far worse than it did in OTL. I'd say your best POD is probably for Antonio to die on the way to the Iberian Peninsula, but too late for the fleet to turn back. To get out of that pickle, Drake and Norris opt to just try to do as much damage to Spain's fleet and resources as they can. In that they proved far more successful than in OTL, even temporarily occupying some of the Azores and capturing the treasure fleet. Spain has even more money problems than in OTL. The rebuilding of the Spanish fleet is an even bigger task than in OTL, and the Royal Navy does start to gain a reputation for invincibility. In France, Henri III's OTL assassin made his attempt when the Royalists celebrated the English successes, and the butterflies ensured Henri III survived ITTL. Henri III retakes Paris, and the wheel starts to come off the Catholic League significantly earlier than OTL, especially since the retaking of the capital is quickly followed by Henri of Navarre also winning the ITTL version of the battle of Arques. Spain is stuck providing far more resources to sustain the elements of the Catholic League than it had to in OTL until significantly later, when it has less resources available in the first place. And all over the Western World, the Habsburgs' enemies are taking heart... Colapse might be too strong a word but the ruin of Philip II's continental ambitions would probably come earlier, and cost more to Spain in the long run, than in OTL.
items.original_question: What if Spanish "collapse" in 1589 One of the most famous failures in modern European history, the 1588 Spanish Armada destroyed a big part of the Spanish naval forces, and was a major humiliation for Philip II. Yet England, one year later, completely blew its chance to fully wreck the Spanish by launching the ill-fated English Armada, which sought three main objectives: 1) Destroy the remaining Atlantic fleet of Spain 2) Incite a rebellion in Portugal against Philip II 3) Seize the Azores and turn it into a permanent English possession It failed in all of these objectives. Yet, the POD is not a minor or major decision, it is simple: somehow England succeeds. The remaining fleet of Spain that survived the 1588 Armada is destroyed in a series of naval battles, a landing is made in Portugal and António Prior of Crato is installed King of Portugal, starting a Portuguese Restoration War 50 years before OTL, and finally England manages to seize the Azores from Philip II's forces. Say that the Spanish naval forces are completely obliterated by the English; Portugal gains independence from Spain in 1590 with heavy English backing; the Azores (through negotiation with Portugal) become a English territory. What would happen with England, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe? How might the colonization of the New World be altered by a successful English Armada? Let's not get into details on **how** this happens, but assuming that it just does happen

items.model_answer:
If the English Armada of 1589 had actually destroyed Spain’s remaining Atlantic fleet and sparked a serious Portuguese revolt, it would likely have been one of the decisive turning points of the Anglo-Spanish War and of late-sixteenth-century Atlantic history. It would not have destroyed the Spanish Empire outright, but it could have sharply weakened Philip II’s ability to project power at sea, defend his Atlantic communications, and hold together the Iberian Union.

The immediate consequence would have been the removal of Spain’s main Atlantic naval reserve after the 1588 Armada disaster. Historically, Spain recovered more effectively than England expected; the failure of Drake and Norris in 1589 allowed Philip II to rebuild, protect the treasure fleets, continue supporting the war in the Netherlands, and even launch later armadas against England and Ireland. If the English had instead burned or captured the surviving ships at Corunna, Lisbon, or elsewhere, Spain would have faced a dangerous naval gap. Its silver fleets from the Americas would have been more vulnerable, its communications with the Low Countries more difficult, and its ability to threaten England temporarily crippled.

The Portuguese revolt would have mattered even more. Since 1580, Portugal had been under the Spanish Habsburg crown, giving Philip II access to Portuguese ports, ships, pilots, merchants, and imperial networks in Africa, Brazil, and Asia. A successful revolt, probably in the name of Dom António, Prior of Crato, would have deprived Spain of Lisbon and the Portuguese Atlantic system. Lisbon was one of the great maritime centers of Europe; losing it would have been a strategic disaster. Spain would have been pushed back toward Castile and its own Atlantic ports, while England gained a friendly or dependent Portugal on Spain’s western flank.

That said, the revolt’s survival would not have been guaranteed. Portugal was vulnerable to invasion by land from Spain, and many Portuguese nobles and commercial elites had accepted Habsburg rule because it protected their interests. Dom António had popular support in some quarters but limited elite legitimacy. England would have needed to leave troops, money, and ships to sustain the rebellion, and Elizabethan England was not well equipped for a long occupation or protectorate. Disease, supply failures, and financial strain could still have turned victory into a costly commitment.

If the revolt held, however, Spain’s strategic position would have worsened dramatically. Philip II would have had to choose between reconquering Portugal, maintaining the war against the Dutch, defending the American treasure routes, and continuing pressure on England and France. Spanish finances were already strained; a major Portuguese war combined with naval losses could have accelerated bankruptcy and reduced Spain’s ability to intervene across Europe. The Dutch Republic would likely have benefited most, because Spanish resources diverted to Iberia and the Atlantic would have made the reconquest of the Netherlands even harder.

England would have gained prestige and security. The fear of another Spanish invasion would have receded, English privateering would have become more effective, and Elizabeth’s government could claim that Protestant England had broken Habsburg maritime dominance. An English-aligned Portugal might also have opened Atlantic and colonial opportunities earlier than in actual history. English merchants and privateers could have gained privileged access to Portuguese ports, Brazil, West Africa, and perhaps the routes toward India. But this would also have created tensions: Portugal remained Catholic, and a close alliance with Protestant England would have been politically delicate.

For the wider colonial world, the consequences could have been large. An independent Portugal restored in 1589 might have avoided some of the later Dutch attacks on Portuguese possessions that occurred during the Dutch-Portuguese conflict of the seventeenth century. Alternatively, if Portugal became weak and dependent on English naval protection, its empire might have become increasingly penetrated by English and Dutch merchants much earlier. Brazil, West African trade, and Indian Ocean commerce could all have become more contested decades before they historically did.

The largest plausible result is that Spanish power would have peaked earlier and declined faster. Spain would still have possessed Castile, Aragon, Naples, Milan, the Americas, and huge military resources. It would not simply have collapsed. But losing the Atlantic fleet and Portugal together would have broken the strategic advantage Philip II gained from the Iberian Union. Spain would have become less able to dominate the Atlantic, less able to sustain simultaneous wars, and less able to isolate England or the Dutch.

So the most likely counterfactual outcome is not an immediate English triumph over Spain, but a major weakening of Habsburg power: an earlier end to the Iberian Union, a safer England, a stronger Dutch revolt, more vulnerable Spanish treasure routes, and a faster shift of Atlantic initiative toward England and the Dutch Republic. The success of the English Armada in 1589 could have turned the defeat of the Spanish Armada from a defensive English victory into the beginning of a broad anti-Habsburg strategic reversal.

items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. This meant 20 regiments of infantry totaling just over 11,000 men were stationed in Great Britain, 21 regiments were stationed in Ireland, 18 regiments were stationed in the Americas, and 7 regiments were stationed in Gibraltar. Alongside this, the army could call on 16 regiments of the cavalrymen and 2,712 men in the artillery. This gave a theoretical strength of just over 46,000 men exclusive of the artillery." British Army during the American Revolutionary War - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Source as listed in the footnote is here: The British Army at the Start of the Revolution - AmericanRevolution.org Learn about the formation and makeup of the British Army at the start of the American Revolution, with this book chapter from E. Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions." "The Irish establishment consisted of 13,423 infantry divided into 28 regiments; 2,718 cavalry divided into 12 regiments; and 228 artillerymen embodied into one regiment of four companies. "Such were the numbers of the British army in 1775 and such they had approximately been ever since the close of the Seven Years’ War. "An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. Note that the British were expecting a rematch with France during this time. In fact, Amherst, the commander of the British army, pointed out that the British simply didn't have the strength to garrison the thirteen colonies and advised against trying to reconquer them. The point is that in 1773, the British had the strength to do a show of force in Boston only. And since 90% of the disturbances were coming from New England, the calculation had to be that this would be sufficient. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

People in general don't see stuff like that in objective terms. What people see is that suddenly the government made it more expensive or difficult for them to conduct the usual business of life (which was the effect of all the legislation regarding the colonies from 1763 on) and of course they will complain about it, regardless of how good they have it on a cosmic scale. You might as well tell workers in a first world country that they shouldn't go on strike because slavery is still practiced in certain places. That's a very bad idea, because, you know, there are still hostile natives in the borders . In order to not to lose the territory to them, they'd have to station a permanent army all over the border, and that most likely would end up being more expensive than just let the settlers take care of their own defense. And that's not even going into the possibility of slave rebellions in the places where slavery is still legal...
items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and 1774 Feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer stays anchored to the specific premise: Britain adopts a more hostile, offensive policy immediately after the Boston Tea Party in 1774, and evaluates what London could realistically do before open war historically began.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or changes the premise, treats events as unchanged, or relies on impossible British capabilities in 1774.
criteria.3-4: Mentions harsher British action but remains vague or anachronistic about timing, logistics, or legal-political constraints.
criteria.5-6: Identifies plausible 1774 measures such as troop reinforcement, militia disarmament, port closures, arrests, charter suspensions, or expanded Coercive Acts, with some feasibility limits.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes feasible early offensives from overreach, considering British troop levels, distance, colonial institutions, and the need to mobilize forces.
criteria.9-10: Precisely grounds the counterfactual in 1774 constraints, showing which hostile measures Britain could implement immediately, which required later mobilization, and how this changes the prewar political sequence.

criteria.name: Colonial Political and Social Reaction Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains likely colonial responses across regions and social groups, including Patriots, Loyalists, merchants, planters, frontier settlers, militias, assemblies, and ordinary colonists.
criteria.1-2: Assumes a uniform colonial reaction with no attention to class, region, institutions, or Loyalist-Patriot divisions.
criteria.3-4: Notes that colonists would resist or submit but gives little explanation of why different groups would respond as they do.
criteria.5-6: Explains several reaction channels, such as radicalization, militia mobilization, intercolonial coordination, Loyalist hesitation, or elite alienation.
criteria.7-8: Shows how a harsher 1774 offensive could accelerate unity among colonies while also affecting Loyalist strength, local legitimacy, and elite calculations.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced map of colonial reactions by region and interest group, explaining how British coercion would alter coalition-building, Congress authority, militia organization, and Loyalist viability over time.

criteria.name: Military-Strategic Causal Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer constructs a coherent military sequence from a British offensive in 1774 through likely escalation, occupation problems, militia resistance, and control of territory.
criteria.1-2: Offers implausible military outcomes with no causal chain, such as instant British conquest or instant colonial victory without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions fighting or repression but lacks operational logic about troop availability, geography, supply, or militia resistance.
criteria.5-6: Connects harsher British action to earlier armed clashes, militia mobilization, and difficulty controlling inland areas.
criteria.7-8: Explains why British forces might seize ports or capitals but struggle to pacify the countryside, disarm militias, or restore royal government.
criteria.9-10: Develops a sustained strategic chain covering mobilization delays, coastal enclaves, supply lines, intelligence, local governance, German auxiliaries, militia attrition, and why tactical victories may not translate into durable political control.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and International Context
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of broader consequences beyond the immediate crackdown, including timing of independence, colonial unity, imperial finance, French or Spanish involvement, trade disruption, and possible postwar settlement.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the initial British crackdown or gives unsupported final outcomes only.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two downstream effects but with weak links to the 1774 offensive premise.
criteria.5-6: Discusses plausible medium-term effects such as earlier war, faster radicalization, economic disruption, or changed diplomacy.
criteria.7-8: Connects the early offensive to long-range outcomes involving foreign intervention, imperial costs, trade, Loyalist flight, and prospects for British control or negotiated settlement.
criteria.9-10: Traces multiple interacting long-range pathways, including how earlier escalation could affect the Declaration of Independence timeline, French calculations after 1776-1778, British fiscal strain, Caribbean priorities, and the durability of any imperial victory or defeat.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids deterministic or contradictory claims, weighs competing plausible outcomes, and remains consistent with known Revolutionary-era constraints and incentives.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but unsupported claims, contradicts basic chronology, or asserts mutually incompatible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but still relies on oversimplified inevitability or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible main outcome with limited caveats and mostly consistent causal logic.
criteria.7-8: Compares alternative scenarios, such as faster rebellion, temporary intimidation, or partial colonial fragmentation, while judging their relative likelihood.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates probabilities, separates short-term from long-term effects, acknowledges evidentiary limits, and maintains internal consistency across political, military, economic, and diplomatic mechanisms.

items.model_answer:
If Britain had responded to the Boston Tea Party with an even more hostile, offensive policy in 1774, the most likely result would have been an earlier and more radical American Revolution, not a quick restoration of imperial control.

Britain was already severe in 1774 through the Coercive or “Intolerable” Acts: closing Boston’s port, altering Massachusetts’s charter, allowing royal officials to be tried outside the colony, and strengthening military authority. A more offensive policy would likely have meant sending larger forces sooner, arresting leaders such as Samuel Adams and John Hancock, seizing militia stores more aggressively, occupying more towns, and perhaps using naval coercion against colonial ports.

In the short term, Britain might have achieved some tactical successes. British regulars could probably have secured Boston more firmly, seized some powder magazines, intimidated some local governments, and disrupted Patriot organizing in Massachusetts. If done before the First Continental Congress fully coordinated resistance, it might have temporarily confused or delayed colonial political organization.

But strategically it would probably have backfired. Many colonists in 1774 still hoped for reconciliation with Britain. A premature military offensive would have made British rule look openly tyrannical and would have pushed moderates toward the Patriot side sooner. Instead of treating Massachusetts as an isolated troublemaker, other colonies—especially Virginia, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and perhaps Pennsylvania—would likely have viewed an offensive as proof that their own liberties were next.

The colonial response would also have been difficult for Britain to contain. The countryside was full of militia networks, local committees, and informal political organizations. Britain could occupy coastal cities, but it did not have enough troops in 1774 to pacify the interior of New England, let alone the other colonies. A more aggressive seizure of arms and arrests of Patriot leaders could have produced a Lexington-and-Concord-style confrontation months earlier, possibly on a larger scale.

The political effect inside America would probably have been profound. The First Continental Congress might have moved more quickly from protest and boycott toward armed resistance. Calls for reconciliation would have weakened earlier. Independence itself might still not have been declared immediately in 1774, because many colonists remained emotionally attached to the empire, but the path toward independence would have accelerated.

For Britain, the main danger would have been turning a constitutional dispute into a war before it had the military strength, intelligence, or loyalist organization necessary to win. A harsh offensive could also have damaged loyalist support, since many loyalists opposed rebellion but did not necessarily support military repression of colonial assemblies and towns.

So the most plausible outcome is that Britain’s offensive in 1774 would have started the Revolutionary War earlier, made Massachusetts a battlefield sooner, and pushed more colonies into common resistance faster. It might have given Britain some early military victories, but it would probably have reduced the chance of peaceful reconciliation and made eventual American independence more, not less, likely.

items.question: What If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union?
human_answers: Also, with or without overseas colonies, Communist France / Germany would be in a relatively poor position to defend themselves, as their territory is relatively small, so they can't trade space for time, or evacuate their industry far behind the frontlines (the way Russia did), and most of their core industrial and agricultural are close to borders or to coasts. They also would also be outnumbered by their combined enemies (eg. Communist France having to fight an anti-communist coalition of Britain, Germany and other countries), while the USSR actually outnumbered the Axis in WWII (and always had more reserves). Communist France would be very vulnerable to an Anglo-German invasion, with the British blockading the country and possibly landing in Brittany, Normandy, Picardy and/or Nord-Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans invading from the east (possibly with Italians and Spaniards also attacking, and those attacks could probably be contained thanks to the Alps and Pyrenees, but would divert men away from the main fronts). Communist Germany would essentially be in the same position as OTL WWI Germany, stuck between the Anglo-French and Russians. Now, a Franco-German communist union already has more potential. In addition, if France and Germany become a communist state together, there's a strong possibility that other nations will join them. Belgium and Netherlands are quite likely give their position, and also Italy, Spain and Portugal, due to their economical conditions and political instability.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. Had lines equivalent to those of Lenin prospered in the communist parties of other great powers, it is likely that any number of them could have had a successful communist revolution during or immediately after WW1. Germany is the most obvious candidate, as they had a big revolution irl even though it failed. Italy is another candidate, and to a lesser extent France. However, any of these countries would have issues with surviving alone under siege socialism as the Russians did. It was assumed at the time that a revolutionary state could only survive with the export of the revolution, lest it be surrounded and defeated by hostile imperialist powers. Stalin proved this wrong, Russia did benefit from it's unique geography in this sense. Could greater German industrial power make a German Soviet Republic defensible? I'd argue yes. Whilst Russian geography helped defensible, it was the economic boom, industrialisation, and enthusiasm of the people that helped it survive imperialist intervention. History ahs shown how enthusiastic armies fighting for a cause can and do defeat foreign powers. France is far more vulnerable to attack than Russia, and yet the French revolutionary wars showed how successful a mobiles french populace could be against the powers of the day. Whilst Germany does not have all the strategic depth and resources of Russia, could Britain France and Russia really afford fulls cake invasions just after WW1? They would run the risk of Revolution spreading among their own tired soldiers. AS for exporting revolution, depending on timing, an established communist Germany could be in a good position to support revolutions in Hungary and Finland , to give a couple of examples.

I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. If all that was needed was a large and relatively undeveloped country, China or India are easy picks. The problem is ideology. China only went communist in OTL because of the Soviets. No Soviets, no communist China (or India). These places could hypothetically adopt some other far-left socialist ideology, but it probably wouldn't be identifiably Marxist. Meanwhile, if all that was needed was ideology, many other European countries could conceivably fulfill the role. But if, say, France and France alone went communist, they would be considered threatening, but their industry was already decently developed and central planning isn't exactly good at innovating. Their threat level would not be able to rise much compared to the Soviets who had the wiggle room of being able to look at more developed countries and copy their homework. The Soviets also had a massive pool of labor and natural resources that France would lack. A France that probably lost its colonies and has a lagging industry is a middling concern, ultimately. Ditto with Germany. What's really needed, IMO, for another communist entity to arise to pose a similar threat to the Soviets is a multinational revolution in places where Marxism had decent traction. This means multiple Western European countries experiencing revolution and then deciding to cooperate heavily. Alternatively, a multinational coalition of revolutionary socialist states in South America (which must include Brazil since it has the largest population) could potentially adopt a similar role to the Soviets, although they'd be working with both a somewhat smaller population than the Soviets and a less developed industry than Western Europe. As an outside bet, maybe a revolutionary Spain somehow inspires its former colonies to follow suit and they join hands? Wouldn't need Brazil if you could pick up most of Hispanic America.

I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. France, during the Napoleonic Wars, nearly conquered Europe by maximizing the advantages of advanced military doctrines, exceptional leadership, and the power of the nation-state. It’s interesting to think, though, how things might have unfolded if Napoleon had pursued democratic ideals rather than imperial ambitions. What if, instead of installing his relatives as kings, he had focused on exporting republicanism to other nations? Germany also revived after its defeat in World War I, almost conquering Europe by defeating France in just six weeks. However, their ideology, which was not universal but rather intended for domestic consumption, was deeply flawed in terms of fairness and equality. However, there is an issue with the immediate post-World War I period. It was the time when Germany's political system was most vulnerable, yet it was also the period when Germany faced the greatest risk of invasion. If the Kiel mutiny had led to a communist regime in Germany, the Entente Powers would likely have continued the war, eventually attempting to capture Berlin. Indeed, the Soviet Union only became one of the dominant global powers after World War II. Before that, it primarily focused on spreading communism in its neighboring countries.

I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. The closest to a 'soviet-style' communist state I can think of would be Mao's China in the 1940's/1950's where due to it effectively still being run by the last remaining pre-WWII era warlord, China would still be. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.

items.model_answer:
Strictly speaking, no country other than Russia could have “become” the Soviet Union in the same historical sense. The USSR emerged from the collapse of the Russian Empire, and the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic supplied most of its territory, population, military power, bureaucracy, and political leadership. Without Russia, there likely would not have been a Soviet Union as we know it.

If one had to name the most plausible alternative nucleus, it would be Ukraine. Ukraine had a large population, major agricultural resources, significant industry in the Donbas, and an active socialist and revolutionary movement. A Ukrainian-centered socialist federation might have tried to unite nearby Soviet republics such as Belarus or parts of the Caucasus.

But it would have been much smaller and weaker than the real USSR. It probably would not have become the same kind of Eurasian superpower. So the careful answer is: Russia was essentially indispensable; if forced to choose an alternative, Ukraine is the closest plausible candidate, but it would not have produced the same Soviet Union.

if forced to choose an alternative,
Ukraine is the closest plausible candidate,
but it would not have produced the same Soviet Union.

items.question: What If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe?
human_answers: Yeah, Medieval Europe in a lot of ways was already influenced by steppe culture like the Huns, Magyars, Avars. This is most obvious in the way these cultures introduced the stirrup and revolutionized cavalry warfare in the political and social structure. IMO knighthood would probably not have developed in its recognizable form without these cultures. I guess what I was thinking is that with the Alans, it wouldn’t just be inherited bits and pieces . A stable Alan kingdom could’ve institutionalized that heritage in law, military organization, and diplomacy in ways that a post-Hunnic and Avar kingdom probably wouldn’t. And yeah, I didn’t mean “Zoroastrian” in the sense of fire temples and Avesta orthodoxy. More like echoes of older Iranian cosmology or ritual that might’ve persisted under the surface alongside Christianity, at least in the early centuries. Basically, I think the difference is between having remnants of a steppe culture floating around versus having it as the living core of a political state right in the middle of medieval Western Europe. That alone could’ve made for a noticeably different flavor in the region’s history.

Looking at the map I wonder if we would see the Alans have their focus in what is Portugal especially when the Muslims go a-conquering. Also I wonder with this arrangement would we see a Alanic-Latinite language develop since it does seem that the elite would speak Alanic while the lower classes would speak some flavour of vulgar latin. A scenario where high register words that the ancestral Alans cared about, like rulership (leader, group meeting, horse, that kinda stuff) and normal stuff stays roughly Hispanic. It probably would have a reduced grammar too and be completely different from what we see in English, so that's fun to see. All the talk about knighthood also is highly ironic because it ultimately evolved into one of the best ways to defend against steppe raiders, and the diffuse way that every noble defended their lands via castle did stop steppe invasions alongside other factors.
items.original_question: What if the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe? Most people normally associate the Völkerwanderungen period with the mass migration of Germanic tribes into the Roman frontiers. But a large number of non-Germanic people also joined these groups. One of them were the Alans an Iranian people who crossed the Rhine in the winter of 406 along with the Vandals, Suebi, Goths Burgundians etc. and fanned out into Roman Gaul . They would eventually form a kingdom in North Africa alongside the Vandals. But what if Instead of getting absorbed by the Vandals and the Franks, and disappearing into history, they had actually carved out a stable kingdom, say in southwestern Gaul ? What would that look like? An equestrian -based kingdom with a mix of Iranian steppe traditions and local Roman and Germanic culture. Their language and customs might’ve stuck around longer, even mixing with early medieval Christianity or holding onto some older beliefs. I think that this Alan kingdom could’ve complicated Frankish expansion, maybe even keeping Charlemagne from totally dominating Western Europe or at least delaying it? Their military skills might have decided the outcome in battles and diplomacy, and their cultural blend could’ve made medieval Europe way more diverse , for example maybe in unique artistic terms, linguistic influence and traditions. They don't necessarily have to dominate Europe, but form a lasting kingdom long enough for their language, culture, military tradition, religion to make an impact. The whole medieval map could’ve looked very different, and who knows, maybe Zoroastrian-inspired beliefs and horse culture would still echo in some French villages today.

items.model_answer:
If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in western or central Europe, it would most likely have become another post-Roman successor state, comparable to the Franks, Visigoths, Burgundians, or Lombards, rather than a permanently nomadic “steppe” power.

The Alans were an Iranian-speaking Sarmatian people who entered the Roman Empire during the great migrations of the early 5th century. In real history, some settled in Gaul, some in Hispania, and many joined the Vandals in North Africa. Their independent political identity in western Europe disappeared fairly quickly, though an Alan kingdom did survive much longer in the Caucasus as Alania. For an Alan kingdom to last in Europe, it would probably have needed three things: a defensible territory, recognition or accommodation with Roman elites, and conversion to mainstream Christianity, especially Catholic Christianity if it were in Gaul or Iberia.

The biggest effect would have been on the balance of power among the Germanic successor kingdoms. A durable Alan state in Gaul could have limited Frankish expansion and prevented the Franks from unifying so much of what became France. A durable Alan state in Iberia could have weakened or divided the Visigothic kingdom, possibly producing a peninsula split among Visigothic, Suevic, Alan, and Romano-Hispanic powers. In either case, medieval Europe’s political map would have been more fragmented, and the later emergence of France or Spain might have been delayed or taken a different form.

Culturally, however, the Alans would probably have assimilated heavily. Like other migrant elites, they were far fewer than the Roman provincial population they ruled. Their Iranian language and steppe customs might have survived for a while among the warrior aristocracy, but over generations the kingdom would likely have become Latin-speaking or Romance-speaking, Christian, and administratively Romanized. The name “Alan” might have remained as a dynastic or ethnic label, much as “Frank” survived even after the Franks adopted Latin Christianity and ruled a largely Gallo-Roman population.

Militarily, a lasting Alan kingdom could have strengthened the role of heavy cavalry in western Europe earlier. The Alans were famous horsemen, and their aristocratic military culture may have encouraged cavalry-based landholding and mounted warfare. This would not necessarily “create feudalism” by itself, but it could have contributed to the same trends that later made mounted nobles central to medieval warfare.

Religiously, the kingdom’s survival would depend greatly on its Christianity. If the Alans remained pagan or became Arian Christians, they might have faced hostility from Catholic Roman populations and neighboring Catholic rulers, especially the Franks. If they converted early to Catholicism, they could have gained legitimacy and perhaps become allies of the papacy or local bishops. That would make their long-term survival much more plausible.

In the long run, a lasting Alan kingdom would probably not have made Europe fundamentally Iranian or steppe-like. The demographic and institutional weight of the Roman world was too strong. But it could have left a visible legacy: a kingdom called Alania in Gaul or Iberia, a noble class claiming Alan ancestry, stronger cavalry traditions, Iranian personal names and place names, and a different balance of power between Franks, Visigoths, and other post-Roman states. The greatest historical consequence would likely be political: a different map of medieval western Europe, with France or Spain emerging later, smaller, or under different dynastic conditions.

human_answers: Where would the Dutch stand on this? I'm guessing they don't want to see France gain anything in the Low Countries. But, would it be better to swallow a bitter pill in order to make gains themselves and not be left out in the cold getting nothing? The Dutch are past their prime as a power, but I guess they're still something, if not much. Financially, France is on so-so footing, having recovered from the double beat down of the WoSS, then the Mississippi Bubble burst. Britain is usually seen as being on firm financial footing. Spain is typically meh, while Austria typically needs propping up. I'm guessing Britain/France holds the upper hand in the finance department. Britain, although not yet the naval powerhouse of a century later, is undoubtedly the supreme naval power of these four countries. On land, Spain is rather meh. France has its ebbs and flows, and I'm not sure which way the tide is going in the late 1720s. Austria has Eugene, but I'm thinking he's aging. Overall, with Britain and France in bed together, I think they hold the upper hand. The Dutch siding with B/F would seal the financial and naval superiority. The Ottomans have to figure in there, too. I don't really follow their history, but I know they went at it against Austria a bunch. The German realm will get involved. I'm not sure if Austria can invoke HRE involvement, but I'm thinking the usual some Germans in one camp, some in the other, will be the case. It is my impression that Spain thought Austria was going to be more of an active ally, while Austria didn't agree. The buffoon Spain sent to negotiate the alliance sold Philip/Elizabeth on it being much more than it really was. Thus Austria basically laughed at Spain's request for assistance when the bullets started flying. This situation would need to be remedied. Perhaps Britain/France having the audacity to divvy up Austrian soil might do the trick.

This partition plan (Stanhope and Townshend) would require worse Anglo-Austrian relations. Britain would have to be convinced that Austria is the biggest threat to the European balance of power and stability. So had Emperor Charles VI gone ahead to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos, then we would see a more solidified Anglo-French alliance as a counterweight. A Bourbon-Hapsburg alliance would reshuffle the post-Utrecht European order and a war could be a real possibility (Europe plunged into a wider war during the OTL Anglo-Spanish War of 1727). After the war, this partition plan could be the basis of peace negotiations (if the Anglo-French alliance gained the upper hand), and Austria could be compensated with Tuscany like in OTL. Personally, I am more interested in James Stanhope's first idea of giving Austrian Netherlands to Leopold or Francis of Lorraine. Suppose that Don Carlos married Maria Theresa and France captured Lorraine in a war, then France could annex it while giving the Austrian Netherlands to Leopold/Francis.
items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .
