items.question: What If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II?
human_answers: "All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed?" ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)[/QUOTE] Thank-you, I wasn't aware that this investigation into the P-38 compressibility problem had been conducted. It would have been a very productive and effective modification and I'm inclined to agree if the NACA mod had been developed earlier then it would have made it into production. After Pearl Harbor the pressure to produce what ever was available delayed OTL improvements to the P-38 like for example the high-activity propellers as you mentioned. I haven't finished reading the 1942 document yet so I have some questions for you. After the NACA mod had been developed the engineers still thought that dive recovery flaps would be required? Also with the relocation of the Prestone radiators and oil coolers to the new leading edge did the designers consider the Meredith effect when designing the new installation? Making the assumption they were aware of it at the time. The P-38's OTL canopy was one of its' poorer features. If they were redesigning the canopy contours could that also mean replacing it with a bubble type sliding canopy?

1) There is no explicit mention of the Dive Recovery Flaps in the NACA report, however the information about the airflow under the wing at different flap possitions is what ultimately led to their development so it is possible that they could have still been developed although they would have been by no means neccesary (assuming the NACA estimates are accurate). 2) I haven't read any specific refereces to it but it is possible they were aware of the Meredith effect. However, if memory serves, the radiator installations in the P-38 were not well suited or designed for it producing more drag than thrust. The NACA installation would likely also be poor canidatea for Meredith thrust so it is likely a dead end for the sake of this exploration. 3) Indeed the canopy was junk. While it never happened OTL I may explore better canopy options in the ATL. I think this is likely the direction I would go anyway. Some narrative, some ATL technical evaluation reports, maybe even some Encounter Reports when the shooting starts. Yeah, several of the British twin wing designs could be good but are beyond the scope of the PoD and this ATL. The issue with the dive flaps was that the first shipment in a C-54 was shot down by the British and they never bothered sending replacements. Then they didn't want to slow down production to integrate them into the line until all the planned blocks werw complete which meant they weren't factory installed until the P-38J-25 starting June 6, 1944...what a day! And yes, the treatment of the P-38 in the 8th AF was criminal because their disdain led directly to lost aircrew. Edit: sorry for all the typoes...I am on my phone instead computer at the moment.

As a lover of the P-38, a believer in its unrealized superior potential, a person saddened that it was not properly appreciated and thus its potential to escort early US bomber raids and save the lives of countless bomber crew members (not to mention recovering and reusing their OTL shot-down planes)--let me play a bit of Devil's Advocate here. I've seen some of the online wars between P-38 fans and their detractors, and come away more convinced by the former, especially after this most informative OP! But one simple point the naysayers have is clearly true...P-38 was a two-engine plane, while its eventual successor (if we assume the -38 were improved and permitted to do the escort mission) the P-51 was single engine. Thus Lightnings were inherently more costly than any single engine plane, good, bad or mediocre. If the choice was between an excellent two engine job and terrible to mediocre single engine, we just pay the higher price as part of the necessary cost of doing business with the best--except that in Jan 1942, the USAAF needed aircraft in numbers, and soon. If single engine alternatives existed that would be cost-effective, then clearly the Army would prefer that. I don't mean to mention this as some sort of trump card killing the -38's prospects, just as pointing out a factor that was relevant in decision making. The fact is I believe the P-38 was originally authorized under the impression it would be a superstar, just as the B-17 was hoped to be a super bomber the P-38 was to be the star fighter. But that was when war was hypothetical; once it started a panic for sheer numbers set in, and the question of whether one P-38 was worth 2 of another type--or less than 2, or more--was not transparent. One big advantage the P-38 offered, especially if it had indeed been modified to remove its worst drawbacks, and more appreciated hence ordered in more numbers, is that though it used twin engines, those engines were not Merlins! Not to say anything was wrong with Merlins, quite the contrary--though I do seem to recall some comparisons over ranges of altitude wherein the Allison engines, due to being turbosupercharged, had superior perfomance, while the Merlins had a mechanical supercharger. But the point here is, Merlins were good--but in severe demand therefore, so it was most excellent that the Lightning did not require them. I particularly like the way the twin engine layout leaves the central command nacelle to be loaded with heavy and reconfigurable arms.

TTL, it seems likely the dive-recovery spoiler (even assuming it takes OTL's duration to find the answer, which seems less probable; IMO, it'd be quicker TTL) would be on a different C-54, so not shot down. (Might be soon enough to get to production directly, in the *P-38E or -F TTL.) Other improvements? Turbos are hard, but without new materials, there's still reducing the rotating mass (drill the blades, so they look a bit like Swiss cheese), & (possibly) sizing issues (boost lag). Direct improvements to the aircraft itself? Cockpit heat is a must. Adding the wing leading-edge fuel tanks sooner would be good, but TTL, better fuel economy might butterfly them away... Flipside, tho: more P-38s means more headaches, with pilots who don't like twins & aren't trained in them correctly getting themselves in trouble. There was a myth going around England: if a P-38 lost an engine on takeoff, it'd kill you. It would--because the pilots weren't trained how to recover. Tony LeVier showed 'em: kill one engine, boot the rudder hard over against the dead one, crank on full power to the other & climb out to go around...

The 1944 Report clarifies some things I'd heard elsewhere. Thanks for that. All I have for the 1940-41 period is Dolittles commentary, but since he had worked some years as a aircraft engineer for a fuel manufactor his account has some small weight. The short version is through the 1930s commercially available gasoline fuels had a very low octane rating by post WWII standards. 65 Octane is the number I recall. Dolittle & his peers were trying to persuade the corporate suits to develop and market higher octane fuels, up into the 80 & possiblly 90 octane range. The refusal was based on the lack of market since the engine manufactors provided nothing that could use such fuels. To complete the circle the motors that could use high octane fuel were not built because the fuels were not being made. Dolittle did make clear that custom built engines were common for fuels in the 70 to 90 and higher octane ranges. Additives and custom fuel mixes were available in small batches to those who could pay. Dolittle like other knowledgeable pilots carried a witches brew of additives in his aircraft for boosting the commercial fuels of the aircraft he used. Later in 1940-41 Dolittle observed the same problem in plotting the development of the Army Air Corps engines beyond 41. At one point the head of the Quartermasters Corps informed the Air Corps that only 65 octane fuel would be provided across the board to simplify logisitcs. Fortunately the reorganization of early 1942 gave the Army Air force control of its own material supply & development went ahead.
items.original_question: What if NACA Modified P-38 What if NACA Modified P-38 fighter ------------------------------------------------------- Notice to Readers: This TL is still alive but only occasionally updated at this time (Summer 2021). Real life and the greatly expanded scope of detail required to continue advancing the TL at this point (including a fair share of original design and research) has kept me from more regular postings. But, Please, follow along and keep your eyes open for updates when they occur. I really value everyone's input and often the discussion around specific developments has been key to finalizing the next development. Cheers! E Jul. 2021 ------------------------------------------------------- (This was something I had planned to post after being on the board longer but a discussion in another thread prompted some discussion of P-38 development so I thought I would go ahead with this for the sake of discussion.) I know there have been several discussions over the years surrounding the Lockheed P-38 American Twin-Engine fighter/interceptor of WWII but one part of the equation that I have never heard discussed is the “What If…” the NACA recommended modifications to the airplane had been implemented, especially at or near the beginning of P-38 operations. OTL Background : Without re-hashing the origin and initial development history of the Lockheed Model 22 / P-38 (all of that information is readily available on numerous on-line sources) I will focus on what led to the NACA studies of the airframe, their proposed solution to the problems encountered, and why these solutions weren’t put in place. A record-breaking cross-country flight in early 1939 (which resulted in the loss of the only XP-38) garnered enough attention and excitement that the US Army Air Corp (USAAC) placed orders for pre-production (YP-38) and production (P-38) aircraft in numbers greater than Lockheed had anticipated for the entire Model 22 life. This necessitated a rushed production development and major reconfiguration to accommodate the unintended mass-production. Tests in early 1941 of the first pre-production YP-38’s quickly ran into issues when at high speed (around Mach 0.68), especially in dive, where the nose of the aircraft would drop--locking into an often un-recoverable dive accompanied by “buffeting.” The problems getting the production line up and fully operational prevented Lockheed from directing any engineering resources to these problems until November 1941, but they were unable to identify the cause or provide any solutions until Gen. Hap Arnold, head of the by then renamed Army Air Forces (USAAF), ordered the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA—predecessor of NASA) to analyze the YP-38 in their full-scale wind-tunnel in December 1941 – January 1942 which resulted in the report “ Full-Scale Wind-Tunnel Investigation of Buffeting and Diving Tendencies of the YP-38 Airplane .” [EDIT: NASA reorganized its online archives in 2020 so this link is no longer functioning. The upload size limitations on this site prevent me from dropping the file here, but you can find a copy I uploaded at another site, Here ] This report was finally able to identify that the control lock and diving difficulties were the result of a high-speed pressure wake developing over the wing and fuselage resulting is loss of lift to the central wing and buffeting of the tail as the turbulent wake passes over it, a phenomenon just recently discovered at the time which led the idea of the “sound barrier.” This is often referred to a “Compressibility” problem as it related the change of aerodynamics at high speed from a traditional non-compressible fluid to a compressible one. The specific behavior of the P-38 is now better known as “Mach Tuck.” NACA tested several solutions to the problem including wing filleting, partial flap deployment, three different inboard (between the engine booms and the center gondola) wing designs, two revised canopy designs, and an extension to the trailing edge of the gondola. They found the best performance gain (delay of up to 64 mph in the formation of the shock-wave) resulted from a simple 0.2c (20% of chord) leading edge extension to the center wing section and using their second canopy revision. They also noted that although the gondola extension did not increase the Critical Mach number, it did reduce the turbulence of the wake re-joining the airstream and smoothed out the air flow over the tail surfaces. One aspect which I find very interesting with these design modifications was that the extended leading edge moved the center of lift forward causing the plane to become unbalanced. They recommended moving the coolant radiators from the mid-boom into the extended leading edge of the wing to rebalance the aircraft with the added benefit of reducing drag and further streamlining the aircraft. I will address this again in the ATL discussion to follow. The problem is that the report wasn’t completed until March 31, 1942, by which time the US was at war and Lockheed was ramping up to start production on the combat-ready P-38F (beginning in April 1942) at war-time production rates. With the P-38 the most capable fighter then in inventory there simply was not the opportunity to re-design and re-tool for the modifications NACA recommended and the P-38 was sent into combat while still suffering numerous problems, not least of which was the issues with compressibility. The results are well known and documented: the P-38 in the ETO struggled the first 18 months of combat prompting 8th Fighter Command to pre-emptively phase them out in favor of the new P-51 as they became available at the end of 1943 and through the first half of 1944 which prevented Lockheed and the USAAF from implementing a number of fixes for the problems and delayed others until it was too late to have much impact in the reputation of the P-38 in Europe. It was not until the P-38J-25-LO and P-38L-5-LO/VN the airplane really came into its own and that was realized almost entirely in the Pacific. ATL Discussion : For this examination of a “What If…” I have decided to place the POD with the NACA study. Specifically, that Gen. Arnold did not wait for Lockheed to tackle the dive issues first and instead ordered the NACA study to take place in June-July of 1941 with the final report completed September 30, 1941 (six months earlier than OTL). This updated timeline would allow Lockheed engineers to immediately go to work implementing the NACA design changes in fall 1941 prior to US entry into the War and the corresponding production pressures which prevented it from happening in OTL. The first production P-38’s with the NACA modifications would then roll out either as late block P-38E’s in early ’42 or, more likely, as the finalized P-38F in April 1942. OTL, the P-38F/G/H continued to use the enclosed intercooler in the leading edge of the outboard wings, which provided adequate cooling for the early model engines and low-boost ratings but which, by the P-38G and even more so the P-38H, limited engine power to lower settings due to in-adequate cooling. This was a problem that was not anticipated so it wasn’t until the P-38J in August 1943 that the intercoolers were switched to the core-type, chin-mounted position—squeezed between and behind the oil radiators. However, in my ATL, with the oil radiators moved adjacent the coolant radiators in the leading edge extension the space in the chin of the nacelles is completely freed up which allows the core-type intercoolers to be installed in the space previously occupied by the oil radiators as soon as it becomes apparent it is needed without re-designing the nacelles themselves. This means that the engine power limitations of the G either never occurs (because the intercoolers have already been moved) or are quickly overcome by sending field modification kits in early 1943 with full integration on the assembly line taking place with the P-38H in the spring of 1943. Additionally, moving the intercoolers in these earlier models (G or H) would allow a matching earlier installation of the leading edge fuel tanks in the outer wings, increasing the range and combat radius in 1943 sufficient to provide full escort coverage to 8th AF Bombers even to deep penetration targets. Another advantage of moving the Prestone (engine coolant) radiators to the inboard position in the extended leading edge is that the heated coolant can be run through a heater core close to the cockpit cupola, increasing available cockpit heat as soon as it becomes apparent the existing heat is insufficient for high-altitude or cold weather operations. Again, this is something I expect would be utilized no later than early-mid 1943. One final advantage of this layout is that frees up a large amount of space in the tail booms which could be utilized in later production models. With engine weight increases in the F/G and again in the H/J models the Center of Gravity could potentially have been moved forward enough to justify installation of either additional small fuel tanks in the booms where the radiators used to be, or—perhaps a better option—small water/alcohol tanks which would permit the use the Water Injection under War Emergency Power, further increasing performances and reducing the risks of detonation under high manifold pressure (> 60 in/Hg). The estimated (conservative according to NACA documents) dive performance gains of this P-38 redesign are impressive: To put this in perspective, the P-51D had an absolute Critical Mach of around 0.80, depending on the source, but was normally limited to less than 0.73 because of extreme vibrations beyond those speeds. Even if pushing the ’51 to Mach 0.8 or beyond is considered acceptable these NACA estimates for the modified ’38 show a similar diving capability considering a margin for error of the conservative estimate, especially if using Dive Recovery Flaps in addition to the NACA modifications. In these cases the P-38 would be favorable because it can accelerate to max speed faster than the P-51 allowing to either pull-away faster or to gain faster on a diving E/A. Combine that with the faster climb of the P-38, higher peak turning rate, and—in later airplanes—faster roll, there would be nothing that the P-51 could do that the P-38 couldn’t do better. All while bringing a heavier weight of fire on target (128 oz/sec vs 111 oz/sec). Here are some roughly done drawings of how these modifications would appear (done in MS Paint): All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed? ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)

items.model_answer:
If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II, the main effect would probably have been to make the Lightning a much more valuable long-range escort fighter in 1942–43, especially before the P-51 Mustang became available in large numbers.

The most important improvements would have been fixes to the P-38’s real historical weaknesses: high-speed compressibility in dives, poor roll response at high speed, engine and turbo-supercharger reliability problems in cold European conditions, inadequate cockpit heating, and some cooling/intercooler difficulties. Historically, many of these were solved only gradually. If NACA wind-tunnel work and engineering changes had produced dive-recovery flaps, better control behavior, improved engine installations, and better cold-weather reliability much earlier, the P-38 would have been a far more dependable aircraft in the European theater.

That could have mattered a great deal. In 1943, the U.S. daylight bombing campaign suffered heavily because bombers often had to fly beyond the range of effective escorts. The P-47 was rugged and excellent but initially lacked the range for deep penetration missions. The P-51 later solved the problem. A better early P-38 might have partly filled that gap. It had long range, heavy armament, high-altitude performance, and twin-engine safety over water. If it had been reliable and tactically competitive over Germany earlier, U.S. bombers might have suffered fewer losses in raids like those against Schweinfurt and Regensburg, and the Luftwaffe fighter force might have been worn down sooner.

The effect would probably have been strongest in Europe and the Mediterranean. In the Pacific, the P-38 was already highly successful because its range and twin engines were ideal for vast ocean distances; an improved version would have made it even more dominant. Pilots would have had better odds in high-speed combat, fewer mechanical failures, and more confidence diving away or pursuing Japanese aircraft. It might have increased the effectiveness of long-range interception and escort missions, including the kind of operation that killed Admiral Yamamoto.

But it probably would not have completely replaced the P-51 or dramatically changed the outcome of the war by itself. The P-38 was expensive, complex, and maintenance-heavy compared with single-engine fighters. It required two engines, two turbochargers, and more logistical support. Even if improved, it would still have been harder to produce and maintain in huge numbers than the Mustang. The P-51’s combination of range, speed, handling, simplicity, and cost would still have made it the preferred mass escort fighter once available.

So the most likely counterfactual result is not that the P-38 becomes the single decisive Allied fighter, but that the Allies get an effective long-range escort earlier. That could have reduced bomber losses in 1943, increased pressure on the Luftwaffe sooner, improved Allied air superiority in the Mediterranean and Pacific, and perhaps accelerated some aspects of the air war. The war’s final outcome would almost certainly remain the same, but the path to Allied air superiority might have been less costly and somewhat faster.

human_answers: The problem with keeping "TOS" on the air is its consistently poor ratings. In third season, it never got out of the bottom 50 (&, IIRC, was #52 when cancelled). NBC recognizing the better demos early enough might save it in spite of that, much the same way golf gets broadcast despite poor numbers: it attracts a desirable audience. They had two great opportunities to set up a continuing villain, undermined (I suspect) by inability to cast the same actor each time: "Tribbles" & "Day of the Dove". It would have taken more forethought about what Klingons would be like to achieve it, but I'd have loved "DotD" to end with Kirk saying, "Die well, Kang.", & a surprised Kang to say, "Die well, Kirk."--in essence, to be forced to acknowledge UFP as peers. (I know, I know, they didn't even have the concept for the bat'leth , yet...) Depressingly, the writing would have to get a lot better. Even if you take out "Spock's Brain", you've already been saddled with "Errand of Mercy" (the Organian Treaty) in S.1 & "Omega Glory" in S.2. About half of S.3 is pretty awful. Even Dorothy's "Enterprise Incident" has a major flaw, one that would recur for the rest of the franchise: doesn't Starfleet Intelligence have it's own f*ng operatives? You've also got two big issues: personality conflict between Shat's ego & just about everybody, & Leonard being really sick of playing Spock. That said, I'll be watching to see how you save the show, & what butterflies that has down the road.

NBC CONDUCTS STUDY ON TREK: NIELSEN RATINGS NOT FULLY ACCURATE? NBC is unsure of how to handle Star Trek, the big hit with younger American television viewers but a ratings laggard with the general public. The network conducted a study to determine exactly what it has with the science fiction series and its findings were surprising. They determined that younger Americans often watched Star Trek in groups, and it was one of the most popular shows among the age 20-30 and age 30-40 brackets. They also determined that Captain Kirk, Mr. Spock, and the rest of the characters were extremely popular with young kids, who often wanted to stay up past their bedtimes on Friday night to see where they and the Enterprise would go next. However, NBC found a significant decline in popularity among viewers older than 50. Due to this wide age disparity, NBC is mulling over whether they will place Star Trek on Mondays in The Man From U.N.C.L.E.'s old time slot at 8 PM; U.N.C.L.E. was pulled in January and is unlikely to return to television. The Monday 8 PM time slot is often popular with younger audiences, but comes with great competition as is well known in the industry. NBC contacted Gene Roddenberry, the show's creator, Herb Solow, the showrunner at Paramount, who recently acquired Desilu Studios, and Robert Justman, one of the show's producers, for a planning session to widen the show's popularity for a general audience. Roddenberry objected to NBC's proposal to make Star Trek a show with a more pragmatic, less optimistic future. He also objected to the idea that the show had to appeal to older audiences, arguing that the strength of the show was rooted in the creative storytelling that attracted younger adults and children. Solow and Justman also disagreed to an extent but determined that parts of the show had to be remodeled in order to make it a wider hit. Ideas for the third season were pitched to the network; one was rumored to involve Mr. Spock's brain being removed from his body, while another was rumored to have the Enterprise enter Romulan space unprovoked in order to spy on them, a major diversion from the normal behavior of the Enterprise crew.
items.original_question: What if The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons) One of the worst decisions ever made by a television network was NBC's cancellation of Star Trek (the Original Series) after its third season in 1969. After two years of middling ratings placed Star Trek in the Friday Night death time slot, at 10:00 PM, so fewer fans would be able to watch the series. In our timeline, NBC killed off Star Trek, but it went to syndication where it became more popular than ever in the 1970s. NBC knew of the depth of Star Trek fandom but had no idea how deep it ran until they no longer made the show. So here we go...the divergence point. NBC REEVALUATING ITS PRIMETIME LINEUP March 1, 1968 NBC, having finished a distant second in the ratings battle with CBS, was forced to reevaluate its primetime lineup to see where they could find potential strength for the fall 1968 television season. Two shows which faced the chopping block this season were The Man From U.N.C.L.E., on Mondays from 8:00 to 9:00 PM, and Star Trek, on Fridays from 8:30 PM to 9:30 PM. The Man From U.N.C.L.E faced a lot of turbulence when showrunners decided to turn the spy show into a comedy. Its ratings, formerly very competitive with CBS, dropped dramatically in the 1967-68 season; NBC is pondering what direction the show can turn to next. Star Trek was rumored to be cancelled because it rated poorly with an audience of older Americans, but its largely young fanbase swarmed NBC with tens of thousands of letters demanding its renewal. NBC is undecided at this point about U.N.C.L.E.'s fate but is bringing Star Trek back for a third season. However, the suits at the Peacock Network are uncertain about which timeslot to place Star Trek in. Could it replace U.N.C.L.E. on Monday or will NBC try to move it later to Friday night, where its chances of survival are slim?

If *Star Trek* had survived for five seasons, the most immediate effect is that the original series would have matched its own premise: the Enterprise’s “five-year mission” would have ended on television around 1971 instead of being cut short in 1969. That would have changed the shape of the franchise, but probably not eliminated the later *Star Trek* phenomenon.

A five-season *Star Trek* would likely have had more uneven episodes, especially because budgets and network pressure were already problems by the third season. NBC had moved the show into a poor time slot, Gene Roddenberry had stepped back from day-to-day production, and the writing quality had become inconsistent. Two extra seasons might have produced some excellent stories, but also more rushed, cheaper, or repetitive ones. The show may have become more conventional network science fiction rather than the compact, cult object it became in real history.

The biggest difference would be syndication. In reality, *Star Trek*’s three seasons gave it enough episodes to rerun widely, and its cancellation helped turn it into a cause for fans. With five seasons, there would have been many more episodes for local stations to air, which could have made it even more visible in the 1970s. On the other hand, the sense of injustice around its cancellation might have been weaker. The fan campaign to save the show, the conventions, and the “cancelled too soon” mythology were major parts of its early cult identity. A completed five-year run would have made *Star Trek* feel less like a martyr and more like a successful but niche 1960s series.

The cast’s careers would also have shifted. William Shatner, Leonard Nimoy, DeForest Kelley, and the rest would have been tied to the roles longer, possibly deepening audience identification with them but also increasing typecasting. Nimoy in particular had already felt constrained by Spock, so two more years may have intensified tensions. Some actors might have pushed for better contracts or more character focus, especially Nichelle Nichols, George Takei, James Doohan, and Walter Koenig, whose characters often had limited development.

The later film franchise might have emerged differently. In real history, the combination of 1970s syndication popularity, fan activism, and the success of *Star Wars* helped revive *Star Trek* as a movie property, leading to *Star Trek: The Motion Picture* in 1979. If the original series had ended in 1971 after a proper five-year run, Paramount might still have revived it, especially after *Star Wars*, but the pitch would have been different: not “bring back the cancelled cult classic,” but “continue the completed classic series.” The first movie might have been less burdened with reintroducing the crew after a short original run, but it might also have seemed less urgent.

A longer original series could have delayed or altered *The Animated Series*. That show existed partly because the live-action series had ended and there was still demand for more. If live-action *Star Trek* ran until 1971, an animated continuation in 1973 might not have happened, or it might have been framed as a cheaper sixth “season” rather than a revival.

Creatively, two more seasons could have expanded the canon substantially. More alien civilizations, more Federation politics, more Klingon and Romulan stories, and more character backstory would probably have become part of the foundation later series inherited. The original series might have answered questions that later shows eventually explored, such as the structure of Starfleet, the limits of the Prime Directive, Vulcan culture, and the Federation’s relationship with rival powers. Depending on the writing, this could have enriched the universe—or locked later writers into more awkward 1960s-era continuity.

The cultural impact of *Star Trek* would probably still have been significant. Its multiracial bridge crew, optimistic future, Cold War allegories, and humanist themes already distinguished it. More seasons would have given it more chances to address late-1960s and early-1970s issues: Vietnam, civil rights, feminism, environmentalism, student protest, automation, and government distrust. But network television constraints would still have limited how radical it could be.

The most plausible overall outcome is that *Star Trek* becomes a somewhat bigger television property in the short term but a slightly less mythic one in the long term. It would have had more episodes, more canon, and perhaps a more satisfying ending, but it might not have benefited as much from the legend of being a brilliant show cancelled before its time. The franchise would probably still return in the late 1970s or 1980s, because syndication, fan loyalty, and the science-fiction boom would still favor it. But the emotional story around *Star Trek* would be different: not the resurrection of a prematurely cancelled cult classic, but the continuation of a completed 1960s landmark.

items.model_answer:
Assuming Germany invaded the Netherlands during World War I, the most likely result is that Germany would have made its own strategic position worse, not better.

Germany deliberately did not invade the Netherlands in 1914 because Dutch neutrality was useful. The Netherlands gave Germany a neutral border for trade, communications, diplomacy, and limited access to overseas goods despite the British blockade. It also avoided giving Britain another moral and strategic reason to expand the war.

If Germany had invaded the Netherlands along with Belgium, the Dutch army probably could not have defeated Germany in open battle, but the conquest would not have been effortless. The Dutch had prepared defensive flooding systems, especially the “Holland Water Line,” which could protect the core western region around Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and Utrecht. Germany might have occupied parts of the country quickly, especially in the east and south, but taking the main urban and coastal areas could have required time, troops, and engineering effort.

The invasion would almost certainly have pushed the Netherlands into the Allied camp. Britain would have tightened the blockade even more and would likely have treated Dutch ports, shipping, and colonies as part of the enemy system. Dutch overseas possessions, especially the Dutch East Indies, would have become vulnerable to British, French, Australian, or Japanese pressure. Germany would gain Dutch territory, but it would lose the benefits of Dutch neutrality.

Strategically, Germany might have gained access to Dutch ports such as Rotterdam, but this would not have solved its naval problem. The Royal Navy dominated the North Sea, so German use of Dutch ports would have been dangerous and limited. Britain would probably mine and blockade the Dutch coast heavily. Germany would also have had to defend a longer coastline and occupy another hostile country, increasing the burden on its army.

For Belgium and the Western Front, invading the Netherlands might have allowed Germany to maneuver even farther north around Belgian defenses, but it would also have widened the front and created more occupation duties. The German advance through Belgium was already slowed enough to affect the Schlieffen Plan; adding the Netherlands could have delayed Germany further unless the invasion was very limited.

Politically, the effect would have been damaging to Germany. The invasion of neutral Belgium already helped bring Britain into the war and shaped Allied propaganda. Invading a second small neutral country would have strengthened the image of Germany as an aggressor. It might also have increased sympathy for the Allies in the United States, though probably not by itself enough to bring America into the war immediately.

Overall, a German invasion of the Netherlands in WW1 would likely have produced a larger Allied coalition, a harsher blockade, more occupation problems, and little decisive military gain. Germany might still occupy much of the Netherlands, but it would probably be a strategic liability rather than a war-winning move.

items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?

rubrics.question_focus: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Anchoring and Victory Pathway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines a plausible Axis victory scenario and carries its implications forward to 2001 without relying on vague alternate-history spectacle.
criteria.1-2: Gives an unsupported or fantasy premise; ignores how Germany/Italy won and what constraints followed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Axis victory but leaves the war outcome, Soviet fate, Britain/US role, or territorial settlement unclear.
criteria.5-6: Provides a workable victory setup with some implications, but skips key constraints such as occupation capacity, economics, or US neutrality/war status.
criteria.7-8: Clearly specifies the victory path and derives several 2001 conditions from it, including Soviet collapse/containment, Britain, and US non-conquest.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly constrained premise where the exact victory path explains later borders, institutions, rival blocs, economic ties, and ideological evolution by 2001.

criteria.name: German-Dominated Europe and Internal Axis Evolution
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses depth and plausibility in describing what Europe itself looks like in 2001 under a victorious European Axis, including German hegemony, client regimes, occupation zones, Italy, collaborators, and post-Hitler institutional change.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Europe as a static Nazi caricature or total SS empire with no institutional or generational change.
criteria.3-4: Identifies German dominance but gives little detail on administration, client states, Italy, or postwar political development.
criteria.5-6: Describes a recognizable German-led Europe with some client regimes or racial hierarchy, but limited explanation of durability or reform.
criteria.7-8: Explains a layered continental order: German core, eastern colonial zone, client parties, Italy’s sphere, repression, economic integration, and post-Hitler succession.
criteria.9-10: Plausibly models Europe in 2001 as an evolved racist continental system, balancing Germanization, client-state federalism, industrial interests, SS/counterelite tensions, and regime aging.

criteria.name: Global Power Balance, US Response, and Economic Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the long-run interaction between an Axis Europe and the United States, including trade, Cold War-like rivalry, domestic politics, nuclear deterrence, and market realignment.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the United States or assumes simple total war/conquest with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions US-German rivalry but treats it as a generic Cold War without economic or domestic-political detail.
criteria.5-6: Covers US containment, trade friction, or nuclear competition, but misses how no US-German war changes business, politics, and alliance formation.
criteria.7-8: Shows how the US remains a major industrial rival, debates normalization versus anti-fascism, builds non-European markets, and manages nuclear/geopolitical deterrence.
criteria.9-10: Integrates US domestic partisan conflict, corporate pressure for European access, hemispheric policy, nuclear strategy, and bloc economics into a coherent 2001 world order.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Downstream Regions and Decolonization Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses treatment of non-European consequences by 2001, especially the USSR/Russia, Middle East, China, colonies, Latin America, and Japan/Asia where relevant.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on Germany and gives no credible account of the rest of the world.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few regions but mostly as unsupported map changes or stereotypes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major regions with partial mechanisms, such as a weakened USSR, altered Middle East, or US-led Americas.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple regional trajectories: eastern Europe/Russia, colonial empires, Arab politics/Zionism, KMT or Asian alignment, Latin American balancing, and Japan’s fate.
criteria.9-10: Provides an interconnected global 2001, showing how Axis victory reshapes decolonization, nationalism, anti-communism, Baathism/corporatism, Chinese modernization, and regional hedging.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains coherent cause-and-effect over six decades, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids contradictions with the premise or historical constraints.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, deterministic claims, or impossible leaps from 1940s events to 2001.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but frequent causal gaps, timeline confusion, or unqualified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent timeline but underexplains several transitions or treats uncertain outcomes as fixed.
criteria.7-8: Uses conditional reasoning, flags uncertainty, and keeps institutions, demographics, technology, economics, and ideology broadly consistent over time.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a disciplined long-range chain from victory to 2001, with explicit contingencies, competing pressures, no internal contradictions, and well-calibrated confidence.

items.model_answer:
In a plausible “European Axis wins” world, 2001 would probably not look like a sleek Nazi science-fiction utopia. It would look like a harsher, poorer, more militarized, more racially stratified version of the modern world, with a German-dominated Europe at its center and much of the twentieth century’s liberal-democratic order never having formed.

Assume the Axis “win” means Nazi Germany defeats the USSR, forces Britain into a settlement or subordinate neutrality, and the United States never successfully liberates Europe. By 2001, Hitler would be long dead, and the original revolutionary Nazi generation would have passed from power. Germany would likely be ruled by a successor authoritarian regime: still nationalist, racist, militarized, and police-heavy, but perhaps more bureaucratic and less charismatic than under Hitler. It might resemble a fusion of apartheid South Africa, Stalinist surveillance, imperial Japan’s subject hierarchy, and a militarized one-party state.

Europe itself would be radically different. There would be no European Union as we know it, no NATO, no postwar West German democracy, no broadly liberal postwar human-rights order. Germany would dominate the continent through annexed territories, puppet states, client monarchies, military governors, and economic dependencies. France, the Low Countries, Scandinavia, the Balkans, and perhaps Britain would exist in varying degrees of subordination. Italy would likely be a junior imperial partner or, more likely by 2001, a weakened client whose fascist prestige had faded under German dominance.

The most horrific difference would be demographic. Jewish life in Europe would have been almost entirely destroyed. Roma communities would also have been devastated. Large parts of Eastern Europe would have undergone ethnic cleansing, forced German settlement, mass famine, deportation, enslavement, and “Germanization” programs. Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, the Baltic region, and western Russia would not be normal nation-states. They would be colonial zones: some areas settled by Germans, others emptied, others reduced to pools of coerced labor. Slavic populations would be impoverished, controlled, and politically voiceless unless partially assimilated or useful to the regime.

By 2001, German cities might have impressive infrastructure, monumental government architecture, advanced transportation, and strong heavy industry. Berlin might have been rebuilt as a gigantic imperial capital. Elite German districts would likely be clean, orderly, surveilled, and technologically modern. But outside the privileged core, especially in the eastern colonies, the landscape would be bleak: military roads, garrison towns, labor settlements, extractive agriculture, mines, guarded industrial zones, and impoverished subject populations.

Technology would not necessarily be more advanced. The Axis had strong military engineering in some areas, but Nazi science was distorted by ideology, purges, racism, secrecy, and inefficient rival bureaucracies. Without the postwar American-led scientific order, open universities, mass consumer markets, and international collaboration, progress in computers, medicine, aviation, and communications might be slower or more uneven. There might still be nuclear weapons, satellites, jet aircraft, television, computers, and some form of internet-like network by 2001, but access would be tightly controlled. The German bloc might have a censored state intranet, advanced surveillance databases, and military computing, while ordinary citizens would experience restricted media and constant propaganda.

The world economy would be less globalized and less open. Instead of a U.S.-led liberal capitalist order, there would likely be competing imperial blocs. One bloc would be German Europe and its colonies. Another might be the United States and the Americas, assuming the U.S. survived as an independent great power. A third could be a Japanese-dominated East Asia if Japan also avoided defeat, though your question specifies the European Axis, so Japan’s position could vary. Britain’s empire might either have collapsed more slowly, been carved up, or survived in reduced form under German pressure. Decolonization in Africa and Asia would be delayed, bloodier, or redirected into fascist and anti-fascist insurgencies rather than postwar nationalist movements shaped by the UN order.

There probably would be no United Nations in its familiar form, no Universal Declaration of Human Rights with real prestige, no Holocaust memory culture as we know it, and no Israel in its historical form. Anti-colonial and resistance movements would still exist, but they would be framed as terrorism, banditry, communist remnants, or racial rebellion by the Axis powers. Much of global politics in 2001 would revolve around insurgency, border militarization, underground exile movements, and nuclear deterrence between rival blocs.

Everyday life would depend heavily on where one was born. A politically loyal ethnic German in Munich, Hamburg, Vienna, or Berlin might have a stable job, modern appliances, state holidays, subsidized family policies, and carefully curated media telling him he lived in the most advanced civilization on earth. A subject worker in occupied Ukraine or Poland might live under curfews, travel permits, forced labor obligations, and arbitrary police violence. A dissident intellectual in France or the Netherlands might live under censorship and informant networks. A Black African in a German or Italian colonial zone would likely live under explicit racial law and economic exploitation. A surviving Jew in hiding or exile would live in extreme precarity.

So 2001 in an Axis-victory world would likely look modern on the surface but morally and politically archaic: highways, jets, computers, nuclear weapons, television, and skyscrapers alongside colonial rule, racial law, secret police, forced labor, censorship, and official myth-making. The defining feature would not be technological backwardness or futuristic grandeur, but the absence of the post-1945 liberal settlement and the normalization of empire, hierarchy, and state violence.

edus.text: In a plausible “European Axis wins” world, 2001 would probably not look like a sleek Nazi science-fiction utopia.

It would look like a harsher, poorer, more militarized, more racially stratified version of the modern world, with a German-dominated Europe at its center and much of the twentieth century’s liberal-democratic order never having formed.
Assume the Axis “win” means Nazi Germany defeats the USSR, forces Britain into a settlement or subordinate neutrality, and the United States never successfully liberates Europe.
By 2001, Hitler would be long dead, and the original revolutionary Nazi generation would have passed from power.
Germany would likely be ruled by a successor authoritarian regime: still nationalist, racist, militarized, and police-heavy, but perhaps more bureaucratic and less charismatic than under Hitler.
It might resemble a fusion of apartheid South Africa, Stalinist surveillance, imperial Japan’s subject hierarchy, and a militarized one-party state.
Europe itself would be radically different.
There would be no European Union as we know it, no NATO, no postwar West German democracy, no broadly liberal postwar human-rights order.
Germany would dominate the continent through annexed territories, puppet states, client monarchies, military governors, and economic dependencies.
France, the Low Countries, Scandinavia, the Balkans, and perhaps Britain would exist in varying degrees of subordination.
Italy would likely be a junior imperial partner or, more likely by 2001, a weakened client whose fascist prestige had faded under German dominance.
The most horrific difference would be demographic.
Jewish life in Europe would have been almost entirely destroyed.
Roma communities would also have been devastated.
Large parts of Eastern Europe would have undergone ethnic cleansing, forced German settlement, mass famine, deportation, enslavement, and “Germanization” programs.
Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, the Baltic region, and western Russia would not be normal nation-states.
They would be colonial zones: some areas settled by Germans, others emptied, others reduced to pools of coerced labor.
Slavic populations would be impoverished, controlled, and politically voiceless unless partially assimilated or useful to the regime.
By 2001, German cities might have impressive infrastructure, monumental government architecture, advanced transportation, and strong heavy industry.
Berlin might have been rebuilt as a gigantic imperial capital.
Elite German districts would likely be clean, orderly, surveilled, and technologically modern.

But outside the privileged core, especially in the eastern colonies, the landscape would be bleak: military roads, garrison towns, labor settlements, extractive agriculture, mines, guarded industrial zones, and impoverished subject populations.
Technology would not necessarily be more advanced.
The Axis had strong military engineering in some areas,
but Nazi science was distorted by ideology, purges, racism, secrecy, and inefficient rival bureaucracies.

Without the postwar American-led scientific order, open universities, mass consumer markets, and international collaboration, progress in computers, medicine, aviation, and communications might be slower or more uneven.
There might still be nuclear weapons, satellites, jet aircraft, television, computers, and some form of internet-like network by 2001, but access would be tightly controlled.
The German bloc might have a censored state intranet, advanced surveillance databases, and military computing, while ordinary citizens would experience restricted media and constant propaganda.
The world economy would be less globalized and less open.
Instead of a U.S.-led liberal capitalist order, there would likely be competing imperial blocs.
One bloc would be German Europe and its colonies.
Another might be the United States and the Americas, assuming the U.S. survived as an independent great power.
A third could be a Japanese-dominated East Asia if Japan also avoided defeat, though the question specifies the European Axis, so Japan’s position could vary.
Britain’s empire might either have collapsed more slowly, been carved up, or survived in reduced form under German pressure.
Decolonization in Africa and Asia would be delayed, bloodier, or redirected into fascist and anti-fascist insurgencies rather than postwar nationalist movements shaped by the UN order.

There probably would be no United Nations in its familiar form, no Universal Declaration of Human Rights with real prestige, no Holocaust memory culture as we know it, and no Israel in its historical form.
Anti-colonial and resistance movements would still exist, but they would be framed as terrorism, banditry, communist remnants, or racial rebellion by the Axis powers.
Much of global politics in 2001 would revolve around insurgency, border militarization, underground exile movements, and nuclear deterrence between rival blocs.
Everyday life would depend heavily on where one was born.

A politically loyal ethnic German in Munich, Hamburg, Vienna, or Berlin might have a stable job, modern appliances, state holidays, subsidized family policies, and carefully curated media telling him he lived in the most advanced civilization on earth.
A subject worker in occupied Ukraine or Poland might live under curfews, travel permits, forced labor obligations, and arbitrary police violence.
A dissident intellectual in France or the Netherlands might live under censorship and informant networks.
A Black African in a German or Italian colonial zone would likely live under explicit racial law and economic exploitation.
A surviving Jew in hiding or exile would live in extreme precarity.

So 2001 in an Axis-victory world would likely look modern on the surface but morally and politically archaic: highways, jets, computers, nuclear weapons, television, and skyscrapers alongside colonial rule, racial law, secret police, forced labor, censorship, and official myth-making.

The defining feature would not be technological backwardness or futuristic grandeur, but the absence of the post-1945 liberal settlement and the normalization of empire, hierarchy, and state violence.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?

items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in South Dakota in 2004, the immediate national effect would have been limited but real: Republicans would still have controlled the Senate, but by 54–45–1 instead of 55–44–1. George W. Bush’s second-term agenda would still have faced a Republican majority, so Daschle’s victory would not by itself have stopped Bush’s judicial nominees, tax policy, Iraq policy, or the broader direction of the Senate.

The bigger change is that Daschle likely would have remained Senate Democratic leader. Harry Reid became Democratic leader only because Daschle lost; with Daschle still in office, Reid probably stays in a secondary leadership role. Daschle was more publicly identified with the Clinton-era Democratic establishment and with health-care policy, and he was also a careful institutionalist. Democratic opposition to Bush’s Social Security privatization plan, judicial nominations, and Iraq policy would probably have looked broadly similar, though Daschle’s tone and tactics might have differed from Reid’s.

The 2006 midterms become more favorable for Democrats. In real life Democrats won a narrow Senate majority after picking up six Republican seats. With Daschle already holding South Dakota, the same results would have given Democrats a slightly larger majority, roughly a 52-seat Democratic caucus instead of 51. That would have made the new Democratic majority less dependent on every single moderate or independent senator.

The most important downstream effect would likely come in 2009–2010 during the Obama presidency. Daschle was deeply interested in health-care reform and in real life was originally Obama’s choice for secretary of Health and Human Services before withdrawing over tax issues. If he were still a senator—possibly Senate majority leader—he probably would not have been nominated for HHS, but he would have been a major Senate architect of health-care legislation.

With one additional Democratic senator, Obama’s Senate majority would have had more room to maneuver. In real history, Democrats briefly reached 60 votes in 2009 and then lost that margin when Scott Brown won the Massachusetts special election in early 2010. In this counterfactual, Daschle’s seat could have meant Democrats still had 60 votes even after Brown’s win, assuming all other elections and party switches stayed the same. That might have made passage of the Affordable Care Act smoother and possibly allowed a somewhat different final bill. A public option would still not be guaranteed, because several moderate Democrats were skeptical, but the leverage of any single holdout such as Joe Lieberman or Ben Nelson would have been reduced.

John Thune’s career would be dramatically altered. Losing to Daschle in 2004 might have delayed or derailed his rise as a major Republican senator. He likely would not become the national GOP figure he later became, including his eventual role in Senate Republican leadership. He might have run again in 2010, especially if Daschle were tied to Obama and health-care reform in a Republican wave year, but his path would be much less certain.

Long-term, South Dakota was trending Republican, so Daschle would still have faced a difficult future. If he ran again in 2010, he could easily have been vulnerable in the Tea Party wave, particularly if he were Senate majority leader and associated with Obamacare. So the seat might eventually have flipped Republican anyway.

In short, Daschle winning in 2004 would not have changed control of the Senate immediately, but it likely would have kept him as Democratic leader, weakened Harry Reid’s rise, made the 2006 Democratic Senate majority stronger, given Obama an extra crucial vote in 2009–2010, and possibly made health-care reform easier to pass. The biggest individual loser would have been John Thune; the biggest policy effect would likely have been on the politics and mechanics of the Affordable Care Act.

items.question: What If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade in World War II?
human_answers: The RN and other allies can only block the marine trade, so the first thing is to look at who Germany has land borders with. Then, which of those countries might have food or other essentials that Germany needs. If these are willing and able to trade [1], then Germany can maybe get by but if not then they either make do or try to take things by force. Nazi Germany chose force instead of negotiation and trade to try to beak the blockade. Why? because their leaders were mad bastards who were completely untrustworthy to trade with, thought they were better than everyone else, thought that violent conflict was good and who wanted to take over Russian lands for themselves: it ended badly. [1] Italy, for example, might have been willing to trade with Germany, but getting goods into Italy by sea is difficult with the British blocking imports intended for or suspected to be intended for Germany.

Yes its difficult to imagine it now but in 1939 the British had a near monopoly on merchant shipping and many nations merchant ships and their cargos would be 'under written' that is insured by British firms. And much of a nations cargos would likely travel on British ships or ships owned by British firms. In WW1 the blockade of Germany had been part physical i.e. warships stopping ships and inspecting cargos and manifests etc and part commercial pressure. Indeed it was discovered that many of the cargos that had been going to Germany pre war were instead going to Neutral nations like the Netherlands and Denmark and simply continuing on to Germany overland. By 1915 this 'loop hole' was effectively stopped using the commercial apparatus to quite simply restrict goods to no more than had been going to those neutral nations before the war meaning that very little would be left to sell on to Germany.
