items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. Rating Indicator ​ Rating Description ​ G ​ General Audiences - All Ages Admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children whether viewing together with parents or by themselves. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. R ​ Restricted - Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them with proper legal identification at the box office. NC-17 ​ Adults Only - No One 17 Years And Under Admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not legally admitted and all adults must have legal identification at the box office. With the Film Rating System in place to ensure film producers and film distributors have the creative freedom to pursue the projects they want to make, there could be other ways for the Legion of Decency and various religion and social rights groups could clean up Hollywood for film, radio and eventually television without hampering creative freedom. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. Entertainment, education and information fit for religious viewers. They would take in the various technological and artistic talents and know-how from the secular Hollywood studios and apply them towards delivering motion pictures (narrative feature and even the documentaries) with high production standards and quality to deliver their messages to the masses while showing religion on the side of freedom versus tyranny. This would also filter down to local radio stations (and eventually television stations starting in the late 1940s) that would choose to become affiliates of the religious non-denominational Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) which would be listener and eventually viewer-supported to broadcast religious services, national and international news along with news analysis and commentary, local community sports highlights and commentary, charity events, and even motion pictures from the Holy Light library after they finish their original theatrical runs come the advent of television. Local, state and federal non-partisan movements and educational institutions such as colleges, universities, trade schools and public schools would take advantage of the creative and editorial freedoms to organize radio (and eventually television) stations under one coast-to-coast network to provide listener/viewer-supported entertainment/culture, public affairs, educational and community outreach programming for the masses. National Public Radio (NPR) and the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) would both provide alternatives to the commercial broadcast radio (and eventually television) networks found in the American Broadcasting Company (ABC - formerly NBC Blue), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC - formerly NBC Red). All of them would agree, however, that their news reporting standards were to be "factual, fair and without bias" and any commentary and analysis from a partisan political viewpoint should be "clearly defined as such". While NPR and TBN were listener and eventually viewer-supported from the beginning; ABC, CBS and NBC would ensure that commercial time would be limited during hours when children and teenagers would be most likely to be tuning in. The commercial networks would choose to give fair and equal time, coverage and analysis of viewpoints and educational/informative programs to keep up with NPR and TBN's higher standards. However, there was another effect of the Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio decision - the major movie studios could not buy and own the cinema companies that their films would be released to. This would be an antitrust compromise with the governments so that no corporate body could block the release of a film in a release slot that could pose a risk to another company's releases. What would the ripple effects of all this combined be on the motion picture and radio studios and distributors of the time (20th Century-Fox, Columbia, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Paramount, RKO, Republic, United Artists, Universal, Walt Disney and Warner Brothers) on the content in the films they would release to the public? How might some of your favorite films and other pop culture installments from the early 20th Century and beyond have gone if all their makers and distributors were given maximum creative freedom within reason to make what they wanted to? Feel free to discuss this entire ATL in the comments.

items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting had received strong First Amendment protection and effective union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American popular culture would probably have become more politically open, more formally experimental, and more professionally organized decades sooner. But it would not simply have become “free.” Market pressure, racism, sexism, advertiser control, studio ownership, and public moral campaigns would still have shaped what audiences saw and heard.

For film, the biggest change would have been the weakening or possible nonexistence of the Hollywood Production Code system as it actually operated from the mid-1930s to the 1960s. In real history, movies were long treated as a business subject to censorship rather than as protected expression; the Supreme Court did not clearly recognize film as First Amendment speech until 1952. If that recognition had come in the 1910s or 1920s, state and local censorship boards would have had less power, and studios would have had less incentive to accept strict self-censorship under the Hays Code. American cinema might have retained more of the frankness associated with “pre-Code” films: more open treatment of sexuality, crime, labor conflict, corruption, interracial life, gender nonconformity, and political radicalism. Social-problem films, anti-lynching films, pro-labor films, and films critical of capitalism or militarism might have been more visible earlier.

Earlier union protections would also have changed Hollywood from the inside. Actors, writers, directors, animators, technicians, and below-the-line workers would likely have gained better wages, safer hours, clearer screen credit, grievance procedures, and bargaining power sooner. The studio system might still have existed, but its most coercive features—long-term contracts, blacklisting threats, exploitative schedules, and control over artists’ public lives—would have been harder to maintain. Residuals and reuse payments might have emerged earlier, especially once television began recycling films. On the other hand, stronger unions could have raised production costs and reduced the studios’ ability to churn out large numbers of low-budget films, so the industry might have become somewhat smaller, more negotiated, and more strike-prone.

The blacklist era would likely have been less devastating if both expressive and labor protections had been stronger. First Amendment doctrine alone would not have stopped private studios from refusing to hire suspected communists, but stronger unions with enforceable protections against political retaliation could have made mass blacklisting harder. The careers of many writers, actors, directors, and composers might not have been destroyed, and American film and television might have had a more continuous left-liberal, socialist, and anti-fascist tradition after World War II.

Comics would probably have developed as a more adult and diverse medium much earlier. In real history, the 1950s moral panic over juvenile delinquency led to the Comics Code Authority, which severely restricted crime, horror, sexuality, political ambiguity, and social criticism. If comics had been treated clearly as protected speech, and if comics writers and artists had had stronger labor organizations, publishers would have had more room to resist censorship campaigns and distributors. Horror, crime, romance, satire, and political comics might have survived as mainstream genres instead of being pushed underground or sanitized. The American “graphic novel” tradition could have emerged earlier, not waiting as long for underground comix, alternative comics, and later literary comics to legitimize the form.

Labor protections in comics would have had especially large consequences. Many creators in the early comic-book industry lost ownership, credit, and profits from characters that became extremely valuable. Stronger unions or guilds might have produced better contracts, creator royalties, health benefits, and rights reversion. The superhero genre might still have become dominant, but its economic structure would have been different: characters like Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Captain America, and later Marvel heroes might have generated more income and control for their creators. This could have encouraged more experimentation, because artists and writers would have had a better chance of benefiting from original work.

Broadcasting is more complicated because radio and television use the public spectrum, and the government would still have had a licensing role. Even with earlier First Amendment protection, courts might have allowed more regulation of broadcasting than of print because of spectrum scarcity and the perceived public-interest obligations of licensees. Still, stronger constitutional protection would have limited government pressure over political content, indecency, and controversial speech. Radio in the 1920s and 1930s, and television after World War II, might have included more radical politics, more labor voices, more minority programming, and more open criticism of government and corporate power.

Unions in broadcasting would also have mattered. Performers, writers, journalists, technicians, and musicians could have secured better wages, working conditions, authorship credit, and reuse payments earlier. Newsrooms might have been more insulated from owner and sponsor pressure if journalists had stronger collective rights. Entertainment workers would have had more leverage as radio programs moved into television and as recorded broadcasts, syndication, and reruns became profitable.

The broader cultural effect would likely have been an earlier breakdown of the sharp division between “respectable” high culture and “suspect” mass culture. Film, comics, radio, and television would have gained legitimacy sooner as forms of art, journalism, and political expression. American audiences might have encountered mature themes, anti-racist arguments, sexual frankness, labor politics, and formal experimentation earlier and more regularly.

But the change would not have eliminated censorship-like forces. Advertisers could still refuse sponsorship. Theater chains and distributors could still avoid controversial work. Religious groups, parent groups, and patriotic organizations could still organize boycotts. Southern segregationists could still pressure studios and broadcasters over racial content. Corporate owners could still prefer safe, profitable entertainment. Unions themselves might also have reflected the exclusions of their time, including racial and gender discrimination.

So the most likely result is not a fully liberated media landscape, but a less timid and less centralized one. American mass media would probably have become more adult, more politically varied, and more creator-conscious by the 1930s or 1940s rather than by the 1960s and after. The Production Code, the Comics Code, and the blacklist would either have been weaker or harder to enforce. Creators would have had more bargaining power, audiences would have seen a wider range of stories earlier, and the United States would have developed a more robust culture of popular artistic freedom well before the late twentieth century.

items.question: What If the Haber process is never invented?
human_answers: there are very very very few inventions that are so dependent on one person or group or situation that they wont get invented without them. Frankly i am not sure i can think of any. Yes it may get delayed but never invented? seams doubtful Now this isn't my area of expertise but. Usually when it is time to railroad you can pretty much count n somene inventing and building a railroad. This is why we often get similar inventions in multiple locations. Even back in the day a lot of inventions that get credited to one country and that other counties then “stole them” probably had more then a few cases of contry B finally get to the same level of knowledge in that area and this leads to someone figuring it out. The differencecis that as we get to more modern times the knowledges of 1st world countries gets closer and closer and spreads thoughout . This is why things like nuclear science, jet engines and radar were all “sort of” being looked at in multiple countries with a relatively short time span. So unless there are some very unusual circumstances odds are someone will eventually figure it out.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.

items.model_answer:
If the Haber process were never invented, the modern world would likely be far less populous, less agriculturally productive, and differently organized around food, land, and strategic resources.

The Haber process, later scaled industrially as Haber-Bosch, made it possible to synthesize ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen. Its most important consequence was artificial nitrogen fertilizer. Without it, humanity would remain much more dependent on natural nitrogen sources: manure, compost, crop rotation with legumes, guano, Chilean nitrate deposits, and smaller-scale industrial methods such as electric-arc nitrogen fixation or calcium cyanamide. These alternatives existed, but they were more limited, more expensive, more geographically constrained, or much less energy-efficient.

The largest effect would be on agriculture. Modern high-yield farming depends heavily on synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. Without Haber-Bosch ammonia, crop yields would be significantly lower unless far more land, labor, and organic inputs were used. The Green Revolution of the mid-20th century would be much weaker or delayed, because improved wheat, rice, and maize varieties require abundant fertilizer to reach their potential. Food would be more expensive, famines would be more frequent, and many countries that became food self-sufficient through fertilizer-intensive agriculture would remain dependent on imports or suffer chronic shortages.

As a result, global population would almost certainly be much lower. Estimates vary, but a large fraction of the world’s current population is supported by synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. Without it, the planet might sustain billions fewer people, or sustain them only with much more land converted to agriculture and much lower average diets. Urbanization and industrialization in many regions would also slow, because a larger share of the population would need to remain tied to food production.

Geopolitically, natural nitrate deposits would become far more important. Before Haber-Bosch, Chilean nitrate was a strategic resource. If synthetic ammonia never became available, countries controlling nitrate, guano, or other nitrogen sources would gain great leverage. Wars, colonial competition, and trade rivalries over fertilizer resources would likely intensify. Food security would become even more central to state power.

The two World Wars would also be affected, especially the First World War. Germany used Haber-Bosch ammonia not only for fertilizer but also for explosives after access to Chilean nitrates was cut off by the British blockade. Without domestic synthetic ammonia, Germany’s ability to sustain a long war would be reduced. World War I might have been shorter, or Germany might have been forced to adopt different military and diplomatic strategies. However, explosives could still be produced from other nitrogen sources, so war would not disappear; it would simply be constrained by supply.

There would also be environmental differences. On one hand, the world would avoid much of the nitrogen pollution caused by synthetic fertilizers: eutrophication of rivers and seas, nitrous oxide emissions, groundwater contamination, and disruption of the global nitrogen cycle. On the other hand, lower yields would push societies to cultivate more land, causing greater deforestation, habitat loss, and pressure on wildlife. The environmental outcome is therefore mixed: less chemical nitrogen pollution, but potentially more land conversion and scarcity-driven ecological damage.

Societies might adapt by developing agriculture differently. Organic recycling of human and animal waste would be far more important. Legume rotations, mixed farming, and nitrogen-fixing crops would be central to food systems. Meat consumption would probably be lower, because feeding livestock requires large amounts of crop production. Diets would be more seasonal, local, and plant-based in many regions. Scientific effort might also shift toward biological nitrogen fixation, crop breeding for low-nitrogen conditions, or alternative industrial fixation methods, though none may match Haber-Bosch in scale and efficiency.

In short, without the Haber process, the 20th and 21st centuries would be marked by tighter food limits. The world would likely have fewer people, more expensive food, slower development in many regions, greater strategic competition over natural fertilizer sources, and a very different agricultural landscape. It might be less polluted by reactive nitrogen, but it would also be more vulnerable to famine and land scarcity.

items.question: What If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset?
human_answers: That would fall under the bad economics heading. Germany and Italy might well have a good aircraft industry but for something of the Tornado's complexity and expense, they would need partners to spread the burden. Germany previously partnered with Fairchild-Hiller-Republic prior to Panavian efforts and as much as I like the G.91, it isn't really in the Tornado's league. In terms of a precedent for an Italian combat twin, the closest I can get is the PD.808GE which was of course originally a joint-venture between Piaggio and Douglas. If a number of nearby industrial/aerospace powerhouse nations have approximately compatible requirements, not to mention nations that you have other economic partnerships with in mind, why on earth wouldn't you consortium-up? Germany would not be so fiscally inept as to squander the opportunity and go it alone. Why would they choose to build an inferior type that their singular budget would necessitate? I know the popular narrative has Germany as the unwilling partner but much like the recent-ish Typhoon discussion, the narrative isn't bone out by the facts. The reality was Germany studied cheaper, less capable alternatives such as single-seat, fixed wing etc. and then ploughed right on with the full capability. Eminently logical and seemingly blown out of proportion by two generations of media. A simple question. If Germany were errmming and ahhhing so, why is it Panavia GmbH ? I realise that this thread is probably designed to engender responses like: RAF F-15Bs! Yeah, man, cool! Fine as far as it goes but not very probable. From my perspective, the premise is more like what if money, industry and defence stop mattering in Europe in the 1970s and my response is

The Marineflieger simply wanted a replacement for the F-104 but that doesn't matter because as OTL showed, whatever the airforce (both branches) wanted it didn't matter because the politicians decided. As an example of this look at the text below: Spoiler: text At least the VAK 191 would fulfill some of the requirements of the Luftwaffe and the Marineflieger. Both coming in single and two-seat variants, fighter/interceptor configuration and nuclear capable strike bomber. Supersonic and subsonic variants. And if the German aerospace industry lobbies enough, they might see one variant put into production as they actually have an existing product that consumed tons of R&D funds and ended up flying. Well, conventional wisdom showed that the single-seat, single-engine, fixed-wing design ended up outliving the variable-geometry twin-engined two-seater one. Yeah I doubt they were happy with their low-level supersonic strike F-104s and F-4s... The VAK 191 could fulfill the low-level supersonic strike-aircraft role.

IIRC the British Taxpayer paid 48% of the R&D cost of the Tornado IDS and I definitely remember that it paid 100% of the ADV's R&D cost. I don't know if HM Treasury could have paid the other 52% of the R&D cost of the IDS and that's the expensive one because it includes the cost of developing the engines and airframe. If that's correct which defence projects have to be cancelled to pay the difference? Then there's the cost of building them. My guess is that the assembly cost of the aircraft would be the same because they were made in three different factories and the same number of RAF aircraft are built in the same factory IOTL and ITTL. The British factory also built all the IDS and ADV that were exported too. However, the economies of scale for the engines, avionics and the "bits" of the airframe will be lost because the number built will be cut from nearly 1,000 to about 550. A lot fewer aircraft to support may put the operating cost up too by increasing the price of spares. Also the British defence industry may not have enough scientists and engineers to do the R&D on its own. Which may mean it takes longer and costs more. Or other defence projects have to be cancelled so the scientists and engineers can be concentrated on the Tornado IDS. OTOH I've heard people say that collaborative projects cost more and take longer than national projects. That's partially because of the extra layer of bureaucracy and mainly for political reasons. Each nation (naturally) wants its share of the work to be the same as the amount as it pays. That produces a less than optimal distribution of the R&D and production contracts. Or at least a worse distribution than a purely national distribution, as national politics means the best firm for the job doesn't necessarily get the contract either. Is there any truth to that? Or is it a false memory?

items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the most likely result is that the Tornado would not have been built in anything like its historical form. The program depended on the combined orders, funding, industrial workshare, and political commitment of Britain, West Germany, and Italy. West Germany in particular was essential: it was the largest customer and a major industrial partner. Without German and Italian participation, Britain would have faced the full cost of developing a complex variable-geometry, low-level strike aircraft just after cancelling TSR-2 and the F-111K for financial reasons. A purely British “Tornado” would probably have been judged unaffordable.

Britain’s likely response would have been to stretch existing aircraft and then buy or co-develop an alternative. In the short term the RAF would probably have relied more heavily on Buccaneers, Jaguars, Phantoms, and remaining V-bomber-derived capabilities for strike and reconnaissance. For a true deep-strike aircraft, Britain might have reconsidered an American purchase, perhaps some version of the F-111, despite the earlier cancellation. If that remained too expensive, the RAF would have accepted a less capable mix until a later aircraft became available. The Tornado ADV interceptor also would not have existed, so Britain might have kept Phantoms longer and eventually looked harder at aircraft such as the F-15 or a later European fighter solution.

West Germany and Italy would also have had to replace or supplement their F-104 Starfighters by other means. Germany might have bought more F-4 Phantoms in the 1970s and then moved toward F-16s, F/A-18s, or another NATO-standard aircraft in the 1980s. Italy likely would have done something similar, possibly combining upgraded F-104s, more imported fighters, and later a larger role for the AMX or another light strike aircraft. But neither country would have received a direct equivalent to the Tornado IDS: a long-range, all-weather, low-level interdiction aircraft with strong nuclear and conventional strike credentials.

The broader NATO effect would have been a capability gap in European deep strike. Historically, the Tornado gave Britain, West Germany, and Italy a common aircraft for low-level penetration, reconnaissance, maritime strike, and later electronic combat roles. Without it, NATO’s European air forces would have depended more on American F-111s and other U.S. assets for the most demanding interdiction missions. European forces would still have been capable, but less standardized and probably less effective in the specific Cold War role of high-speed, low-altitude attacks against Warsaw Pact targets.

The industrial consequences would have been large. PANAVIA and the Turbo-Union RB199 engine consortium probably would not have developed as they did. British Aerospace, MBB, Aeritalia, Rolls-Royce, MTU, and Fiat/Avio would have lost a major collaborative project. That would have weakened Europe’s experience in managing large multinational combat-aircraft programs. Later cooperation on the Eurofighter Typhoon might still have happened, because the strategic need for a European fighter remained, but it would likely have been harder, slower, or more dependent on U.S. technology and aircraft purchases.

So the central answer is: without West Germany and Italy, the Tornado program almost certainly collapses or becomes a much smaller British project that is cancelled or radically redesigned. Britain, Germany, and Italy would then fill the gap with a mixture of upgraded existing aircraft and American imports. NATO would retain air power, but Europe would lose one of its most important Cold War strike aircraft and one of its most important aerospace cooperation projects.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. If nuclear weapons had never existed, the world would likely have been less threatened by sudden civilization-ending catastrophe, but not necessarily more peaceful.

The most immediate change would have been the end of World War II. Without atomic bombs, Japan probably would still have been defeated, but the route might have been bloodier: continued firebombing, blockade, Soviet entry into the war, and possibly an Allied invasion of the Japanese home islands. Japan may have surrendered after Soviet intervention and economic collapse, but the timing and casualty levels are uncertain.

The Cold War would also have looked very different. Nuclear weapons created “mutually assured destruction,” which made direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union extremely dangerous. Without them, the superpowers might have been more willing to fight directly, especially in crises over Berlin, Korea, Cuba, or Europe. A large conventional World War III would have been more plausible. On the other hand, the absence of nuclear terror would have removed the risk of accidental or intentional nuclear annihilation.

Military strategy would have remained centered on conventional forces: armies, navies, air power, missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and later cyber and space systems. The United States and Soviet Union would probably have spent even more on conventional militaries. Europe might have been heavily militarized, because NATO could not rely on nuclear deterrence to offset Soviet conventional strength.

Decolonization and regional wars might also have changed. Nuclear weapons helped major powers avoid direct clashes but did not stop proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, the Middle East, and elsewhere. Without nuclear weapons, some of these conflicts might have escalated further. States such as Israel, India, Pakistan, and North Korea would lack nuclear deterrents, possibly making some regional wars more likely, though also less catastrophic in worst-case terms.

International politics would be less dominated by nuclear nonproliferation. There would be no Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, no nuclear arms race, no Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it, and no fear of nuclear terrorism. But great-power rivalry would remain, driven by ideology, territory, resources, alliances, and prestige.

Scientific and energy history might also differ. Nuclear physics would still exist, and nuclear power might still be developed if fission were usable for energy but not weapons. If the counterfactual means no usable nuclear chain reactions at all, then nuclear power, nuclear medicine, and parts of modern physics and engineering would be much less developed.

Overall, a world without nuclear weapons would be safer in one enormous sense: no risk of nuclear war. But it would not automatically be a peaceful world. Nuclear weapons have both endangered humanity and restrained some great-power conflicts. Their absence would likely mean fewer existential risks from sudden annihilation, but a greater possibility of large conventional wars between major powers.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

I don't think there's an obvious way for the USSR to react to knowing war is coming. The Germans were much more ready for war. The USSR reaction will probably be a more planned withdrawal in the earliest days of the conflict, blowing some bridges behind their retreat, getting troops out of the pockets where they were surrounded and surrendered. Also less of the air force blown up on the ground in the opening days of the war. A better USSR reaction to Barbarossa might mean, 5,000 planes destroyed on the ground, 500,000 less troops taken as prisoners of war and a German advance that is stopped 100 miles from Moscow. That would probably look disasterous to the USSR and to historians looking backwards but would be a massive improvement over our time line. That said I've no idea how things would progress through the war. There's a lot of decisions to be made. I suspect the Germans might balance a stronger Soviet advance by putting more troops on that front which might make things easier on the Western front. No one really knows. Theres a long war and its all possibilities only.

As noted this ultimately may be worse for the USSR (but probably not) As Stalin had pretty well decimated his military command, So you have a lot of folks that either are no good at the job or have to little experience at the job or both. And if they know it is coming they may as noted by others be more forward deployed and more “aggressive” so they may not fall back as much. A good part of the beginning of the war for the USSR was the learning curve and while they were getting their butt kicked early on this did give them practice that they slowly implemented. In effect trading territory for “reduced” casualties. Compared to how bad they would have been clobbered if the tried to hold the liner harder the OTL. This is obviously exchanged for not getting surprised in this timeline. The question is which did more damage to the USSR the poor leadership needing time to find better officers or to at least get some learning in or the surprise? I tend to think it is a very minor advantage to the USSR to know ahead of time. But I think the poor leadership will mean that 90% of the advantages they get from not being surprised is tossed out the window by leadership that doesn’t know what it is doing. I suspect you will see more troops over run or surrender or otherwise forced to surrender as the order to not retreat will comedown and that there will be bigger battles sooner and closer to Germanies support system any anything that results in Germany have a shorter support line while still getting yo fight big battle vs the zuSSR is probably an improvement for Germany. Plus the war will be fought “faster” if the USSR is less inclined to pull back so the two don’t spend as much time traveling (retreating/advancing). So they are probably bigger battles sooner and more troops committed vs falling back so Germany by should able to kill more Russians faster. That being said it still ultimately sees Germany grind to a halt and it will see the USSR build enough troops and equipment and what have you to stop Germany so Germany will ultimately do better in terms of inflicting casualties on the USSR but they won’t get as far into the USSR. One thing I don’t know is if this fighting closer to the border will result in the German advance stoping before it gets so close that the USSR has to move its factories. Not moving a factory or two could make a big difference.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. Germany will not wait until June 22nd to attack because reality is not Hearts of Iron 4 game on a historical rails. Germans will simply attack in May before Soviet mobilization finishes. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. P.S. And no, Stalin will not give orders to pre-emptive attack against Germany for the very same reasons. Red Army was not in the position to attack anyone and everyone in Soviet leadership, including Stalin knew about that.

items.model_answer:
If the USSR received a credible leak about Operation Barbarossa shortly before 22 June 1941 and actually acted competently on it, but did not launch a preemptive strike, the most likely result is not that Germany is stopped at the frontier. The Wehrmacht probably still breaks into Soviet territory. But the catastrophic scale of the 1941 Soviet collapse would be greatly reduced.

Historically, the USSR did receive many warnings, but Stalin distrusted them, feared provoking Hitler, and the Red Army was in the middle of chaotic reorganization. The key counterfactual is not merely “Moscow knows,” but “Moscow believes the warning and uses it well.”

A better-prepared Soviet response would likely include putting border units on full alert, dispersing aircraft from exposed airfields, camouflaging and hardening depots, preparing bridges for demolition, allowing commanders to return fire immediately, improving communications, and pulling the most exposed formations out of vulnerable forward salients such as Białystok. The Soviet Air Force would not lose thousands of aircraft on the ground in the first days. Fuel, ammunition, and command posts would be less easily overrun. The first German attacks would still succeed tactically, but they would face a Red Army that was awake rather than paralyzed.

The biggest change would be fewer gigantic encirclements. In reality, Germany’s 1941 success depended on destroying huge Soviet armies at Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, Kiev, and Vyazma-Bryansk. If Soviet commanders are allowed to withdraw earlier and avoid holding doomed salients for political reasons, many more troops escape. The Germans still advance, but more slowly, with heavier losses, and with less complete destruction of Soviet forces.

Army Group Centre would probably still take Minsk and push toward Smolensk, but later and at greater cost. The drive on Moscow would be delayed and weakened. In this scenario, Operation Typhoon either begins later, with less strength, or reaches a much more prepared Soviet defense. Moscow is much less likely to be seriously threatened in the same way it was historically.

In the south, the Kiev disaster might be avoided or greatly reduced if Soviet leadership withdraws from Ukraine in time. That alone would be enormous: historically the Kiev encirclement cost the Red Army hundreds of thousands of men. Avoiding it would leave the USSR with a much stronger field army going into autumn 1941.

Leningrad might still be threatened because geography favored the Germans and Finns, but a better initial Soviet response could make its encirclement harder or less complete. The city might still suffer siege conditions, but perhaps with stronger defenses and better supply preparation.

The overall strategic effect is that Barbarossa fails even more clearly and earlier. Germany’s only plausible path to victory was a rapid destruction of Soviet military power in 1941. If the Red Army preserves more of its forces, keeps more aircraft, and retreats in better order, Germany loses that chance. The Wehrmacht becomes stuck in an attritional war sooner, while Soviet mobilization, industrial evacuation, and manpower reserves begin to tell.

So the likely outcome is: Germany still invades successfully and takes large territories, but the Soviet disaster of summer 1941 is much less severe. Moscow probably does not come as close to falling. The Red Army enters winter 1941 in far better shape. The war in the east is still brutal, but Germany is strategically doomed earlier, and the USSR may begin pushing back sooner. The final defeat of Germany could plausibly come earlier than May 1945, though not necessarily by a huge margin, because logistics, Allied operations, Soviet rebuilding, and the scale of the war would still take time.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?

rubrics.question_focus: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity: removing Elvis and The Beatles without erasing broader preconditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that Elvis Presley and The Beatles do not exist or do not become musical actors, while preserving the wider historical conditions that produced modern popular music.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise inconsistently, erases unrelated history, or assumes modern music simply stops developing.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the absence of Elvis and The Beatles but makes broad unsupported changes to unrelated social, technological, or musical conditions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves key background forces such as Black American musical roots, postwar youth culture, radio, labels, and recording technology, with some overreach.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates the missing artists from continuing structural drivers and avoids most butterfly-effect exaggeration.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the historical baseline except where causally affected, distinguishing performer loss, songwriter loss, market niches, and institutional continuity.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage across musical, commercial, and social drivers
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the main mechanisms by which Elvis and The Beatles did or did not shape modern music, including genre development, songwriting, performance, markets, technology, and youth culture.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only fame or personal taste with no causal mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as popularity or chart success, but neglects most music-industry and cultural drivers.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several relevant mechanisms, including rock and roll, British Invasion, singer-songwriters, or recording innovation, but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple interacting mechanisms: covers versus songwriting, Black R&B roots, guitar bands, labels, radio, youth markets, and studio experimentation.
criteria.9-10: Integrates performer, composer, producer, industry, technological, racial, transatlantic, and generational mechanisms into a coherent account of likely musical change.

criteria.name: Differentiation of Elvis’s and The Beatles’ causal roles
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes Elvis Presley’s role as a performer and cultural popularizer from The Beatles’ role as songwriters, studio innovators, and catalysts for later rock and pop developments.
criteria.1-2: Treats Elvis and The Beatles as interchangeable celebrities or ignores one of them.
criteria.3-4: Notes that both were influential but gives little distinction between their types of influence.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes basic differences, such as Elvis popularizing rock and The Beatles writing songs, but does not trace implications far.
criteria.7-8: Explains why Elvis’s repertoire and image may be more replaceable while The Beatles’ compositions, albums, and British Invasion effects have deeper knock-on consequences.
criteria.9-10: Nuances both cases: Elvis’s racialized mainstreaming, performance style, and market role; The Beatles’ songwriting, album form, studio practice, peer competition, and global cultural signaling.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream coherence for modern music
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces consequences from the 1950s and 1960s through later genres, industry norms, and global pop without relying on disconnected speculation.
criteria.1-2: Provides scattered claims about later music with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Offers a simple linear story, such as one replacement artist changing everything, with weak links to later outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible downstream effects, such as delayed British breakthrough, altered rock canon, or different singer-songwriter norms, but chains are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Builds credible medium- and long-range chains linking substitute artists, genre niches, album culture, radio formats, counterculture, and later rock/pop evolution.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust long-range scenario in which specific altered nodes are traced through later music while preserving broad continuity where structural forces dominate.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately signals uncertainty in an open counterfactual, avoids overconfident exact predictions, and remains internally consistent.
criteria.1-2: Makes dogmatic predictions, contradicts itself, or invents precise outcomes without justification.
criteria.3-4: Uses some hedging but still asserts implausibly specific charts, elections, genres, or artists as certain.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids certainty and acknowledges replacement effects, but contains some unsupported or inconsistent claims.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely structural continuities from speculative aesthetic changes and flags unknowable substitutions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence throughout, presents alternatives where appropriate, and maintains strict consistency about what follows from the missing artists.

items.model_answer:
Without The Beatles and Elvis Presley, modern popular music would still exist, but it would probably have developed more slowly, less globally, and with different symbols of rebellion, youth culture, and artistic ambition.

Elvis Presley was crucial in bringing rock and roll into the mainstream in the 1950s. He did not invent rock and roll—Black artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, and others had already shaped its sound—but Elvis helped make it commercially acceptable to a large white American audience. Without him, rock and roll might still have become popular, but its crossover into the mainstream may have been slower or led by different figures. The racial politics of American music would also have looked different: Elvis’s career exposed white audiences to sounds rooted in Black blues, gospel, and rhythm and blues, though it also reflected the unequal system in which white performers often received more recognition and profit than Black innovators.

Without The Beatles, the 1960s pop and rock landscape would have changed even more dramatically. They helped transform the pop group from entertainers into self-contained artists who wrote their own songs, experimented in the studio, and treated albums as serious artistic statements. If they had not existed, other musicians—such as The Beach Boys, Bob Dylan, The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, Motown artists, or later psychedelic and progressive bands—would still have pushed music forward. But the speed and scale of change might have been different. The album era, studio experimentation, British Invasion, and idea of the band as a creative unit would likely have emerged in some form, but perhaps with less unity and less worldwide impact.

Modern music would also have different business and cultural patterns. Elvis helped create the model of the pop superstar as a mass-media figure, combining music, image, television, film, and controversy. The Beatles helped create the model of the globally dominant band whose artistic evolution shaped fashion, politics, youth identity, and recording technology. Without them, record companies might have invested differently, youth culture might have had different icons, and later genres—from hard rock and punk to indie, pop, and alternative rock—would have drawn from other influences.

Still, it would be wrong to imagine a world with no rock, no pop innovation, or no youth-driven music revolution. The forces behind modern music were larger than two acts: urbanization, radio, television, postwar youth markets, Black musical traditions, new recording technology, and global media all pushed popular music toward change. But without Elvis and The Beatles, the history of modern music would likely be less centered on rock as we know it, less dominated by the Anglo-American pop model, and shaped more visibly by the many artists and traditions that their fame partly overshadowed.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
