items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded genuinely carrier-capable Sea Beaufort torpedo bombers and Sea Beaufighter heavy fighters from 1940 onward, the Fleet Air Arm would have been significantly stronger in 1940–42, especially in the Mediterranean. But it would not have transformed the naval war by itself, because the Royal Navy’s limiting factors were not only aircraft performance; they also included carrier numbers, deck capacity, fighter direction, training, radar integration, and the difficulty of operating large twin-engine aircraft from relatively small British carriers.

The biggest immediate effect would have been replacing or supplementing the Fairey Swordfish and early Fulmars with faster, harder-hitting aircraft. A naval Beaufort would have given the RN a modern torpedo bomber earlier than the Barracuda and with much better speed than the Swordfish. A naval Beaufighter would have offered long range, heavy cannon armament, radar potential, and strong anti-shipping ability. In 1940–41, that would have been a major improvement over much of what the Fleet Air Arm actually had.

In the Mediterranean, the effect could have been substantial. British carriers operating around Malta, Crete, and Alexandria often faced intense Axis air attack while also trying to strike Italian fleet units and convoys. Sea Beauforts would have made carrier torpedo strikes faster and less vulnerable than Swordfish attacks in daylight. Sea Beaufighters could have provided long-range combat air patrols, bomber interception, night fighting, and heavy anti-shipping strikes. Italian cruisers, destroyers, and convoy escorts would have faced a more dangerous opponent earlier. Axis supply lines to North Africa might have suffered more heavily in 1941, possibly worsening Rommel’s logistics sooner.

However, the Swordfish should not be dismissed too quickly. At Taranto, for example, the Swordfish was actually well suited to the mission: it could fly slowly at night, launch from short carrier decks, carry a torpedo reliably, and operate in poor conditions. A Sea Beaufort might have been faster and more modern, but it would also have been heavier, more demanding to launch and recover, and less forgiving on small decks. Taranto probably still succeeds, but not necessarily more spectacularly. In some night and bad-weather attacks, the Swordfish’s simplicity was an advantage.

Against the Bismarck in 1941, Sea Beauforts might have given Ark Royal a faster and potentially more survivable torpedo-strike force. They might have attacked with less exposure to flak and weather than Swordfish. But the historical Swordfish attack succeeded precisely because the aircraft could operate in appalling conditions and because one torpedo jammed Bismarck’s rudder. A Sea Beaufort force might have improved the odds, but it would not guarantee a better result. It might even have been harder to operate in that particular weather.

The Sea Beaufighter would have been most valuable as an early long-range carrier fighter and strike aircraft, but it would not have been an ideal fleet fighter. It was large, heavy, and less maneuverable than single-engine fighters. Carrier decks could carry only a limited number of them, and each one would occupy space that could otherwise hold several smaller aircraft. Against nimble enemy fighters, especially Japanese Zeros, it would have struggled if used as a conventional dogfighter. Its real value would have been as a bomber destroyer, night fighter, reconnaissance fighter, and anti-shipping aircraft.

This could have reduced some British carrier losses or damage. For example, Illustrious in 1941 suffered badly from German dive-bombing in the Mediterranean. Better carrier fighters and radar-directed interception might have helped blunt such attacks, though not necessarily prevent damage entirely. The problem was not merely lack of firepower; it was also that early-war carriers often had too few fighters aloft, imperfect fighter control, and limited warning time. Sea Beaufighters would help most if paired with improved radar direction and enough deck capacity to keep them airborne.

In the Indian Ocean in 1942, they might have improved British chances against Japanese air power, but they would not have reversed the balance. Japanese carrier aviation was highly trained, numerous, and tactically mature. A handful of Sea Beaufighters on British carriers would not have made the Eastern Fleet equal to Nagumo’s carrier force. They might have shot down more Japanese bombers, protected reconnaissance better, or made raids riskier, but they would not have saved an exposed ship like Hermes if she were caught without fighter cover.

In the Atlantic, the effect would be more limited. Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would have been too large for most escort carriers, and escort carriers became the key naval aviation tool against U-boats. The Beaufighter was already valuable from land bases for anti-shipping and coastal strike missions. Carrier capability would add flexibility, but it would not solve the mid-Atlantic air gap as effectively as escort carriers with smaller aircraft, long-range patrol bombers, and improved anti-submarine weapons.

There would also be serious practical costs. Navalizing the Beaufort and Beaufighter would require strengthened landing gear, arrestor hooks, corrosion protection, folding wings or deck-handling compromises, and extensive carrier trials. These changes would add weight and complexity. Production capacity would be diverted from RAF Coastal Command and Fighter Command uses. The Royal Navy might gain better carrier aircraft, but Britain might lose some land-based Beauforts and Beaufighters that were historically important in other theaters.

The most plausible overall result is that the Royal Navy performs better in the 1940–42 period, especially in the Mediterranean. Italian naval movements become more dangerous, Axis convoys to North Africa suffer somewhat heavier losses, and British carriers gain a better chance of defending themselves against bombers. Some operations might be less costly; a few ships damaged historically might survive, or survive with less damage. British carrier aviation’s reputation and tactical confidence would improve earlier.

But it probably does not change the outcome of the war in a dramatic way. Britain still lacks the large carrier air groups, production depth, and specialized naval aircraft pipeline of the later United States Navy. The Sea Beaufort would be a useful but imperfect torpedo bomber, and the Sea Beaufighter would be a powerful but bulky carrier aircraft, not a true replacement for a modern single-seat fighter. By 1943–44, American types such as the Avenger, Hellcat, Corsair, and Wildcat/Martlet would still become more important for British carrier operations.

So the counterfactual answer is: early Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would have made the Fleet Air Arm noticeably more dangerous and better defended in the critical early-war years, likely improving British results in the Mediterranean and perhaps reducing some carrier losses. But they would not have made the Royal Navy dominant in carrier warfare from 1940, nor would they have fundamentally altered the strategic course of the Second World War.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. items.model_answer:
If FDR had chosen an openly segregationist vice president in 1944, that person would almost certainly have become president in April 1945 when Roosevelt died. The most plausible historical version is someone like James F. Byrnes of South Carolina: experienced, acceptable to many party conservatives, but strongly tied to the Jim Crow South.

The biggest change would not be the end of World War II. Germany’s defeat was already imminent, Japan’s defeat was approaching, and the military and diplomatic machinery was already in motion. A segregationist president probably still would have approved use of the atomic bomb, especially if the VP were Byrnes-like; in real history Byrnes was one of the strongest advocates of using the bomb and of taking a hard line with the Soviets. The United Nations, occupation of Germany and Japan, and the broad move toward postwar American global leadership would probably still happen.

The largest domestic change would be civil rights. Truman, despite his own racial prejudices, took several important federal steps: he created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, endorsed a civil-rights program in 1948, and desegregated the armed forces by executive order. A segregationist president almost certainly would not have done those things. The Fair Employment Practices Committee would likely have died more quietly, federal civil-rights enforcement would have weakened, and the military would probably have remained officially segregated longer.

That would have changed the Democratic Party’s postwar trajectory. In real history, Truman’s civil-rights moves caused the Dixiecrat revolt in 1948, but they also helped bind Black voters and northern liberals more firmly to the Democratic Party. With a segregationist president, there might be no Dixiecrat walkout, because the Southern wing would already control the White House. But the party would likely lose support from northern liberals, labor activists, Black voters, and anti-racist Democrats. Henry Wallace or another progressive figure could have gained more support, and the Republicans would have had a better chance of winning in 1948.

So the likely political result is that the Democrats become more visibly dominated by their conservative Southern wing in the late 1940s, but at the cost of alienating the emerging urban, Black, and liberal coalition that later became central to Democratic success. A Republican victory in 1948 would become more likely than in real history.

On the Cold War, the difference would probably be smaller. A Byrnes-like president might even be more confrontational toward the Soviet Union than Truman was. The Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin airlift, and NATO might still emerge in some form because they were driven by broad strategic pressures, not just Truman personally. The tone could be harsher, and domestic anti-communism might blend even more strongly with conservative Southern politics.

The long-term civil-rights consequences could be substantial. Without Truman’s executive order desegregating the armed forces, military integration might be delayed until the Korean War or later. Federal moral pressure against Jim Crow would be weaker. Supreme Court appointments might also differ, which could affect the timing or unanimity of Brown v. Board of Education. The civil-rights movement would still arise because the underlying forces—Black migration, NAACP litigation, wartime service, Cold War hypocrisy, and grassroots activism—would remain. But federal support would likely arrive later and with more resistance.

In short: FDR choosing a segregationist VP in 1944 would probably not dramatically alter the military outcome of World War II, but it could significantly delay federal civil-rights progress, reshape the Democratic Party, make a Republican 1948 victory more likely, and leave Jim Crow with stronger protection from the White House during a crucial postwar moment.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.

If the Allies lost the Salonica front, the result would probably not by itself make Germany win World War I, but it would significantly change the Balkans and could prolong the war.

The Salonica front mattered because it kept Bulgaria and some Central Powers forces tied down and, in 1918, the Allied breakthrough there knocked Bulgaria out of the war. Bulgaria’s collapse opened the Balkans to the Entente, threatened Austria-Hungary from the south, endangered Constantinople, and helped trigger the wider Central Powers collapse. So an Allied defeat at Salonica would remove one of the key late-war dominoes.

If the defeat happened early, for example in 1916–1917, the consequences would be serious. Serbia would remain fully occupied with little hope of liberation. Bulgaria would be strengthened and might consolidate its gains in Macedonia. Greece might be intimidated into remaining neutral or leaning toward the Central Powers, especially if King Constantine’s pro-German faction stayed dominant. Romania, already geographically exposed, would be even more isolated; if it had not yet entered the war, it might hesitate or stay out, and if it had entered, its defeat would come even faster.

The Ottoman Empire would also benefit. A secure Balkan corridor from Germany and Austria-Hungary through Bulgaria to Constantinople would make it easier to move supplies and advisers. The British campaigns in Palestine and Mesopotamia would still matter, but the Ottomans would face less strategic pressure from the European side. Constantinople would feel safer, and Bulgaria would no longer fear an Allied army advancing from Macedonia.

If the Allied defeat happened in 1918, after Germany’s spring offensives had failed and the Western Front was turning against the Central Powers, the larger outcome would probably still be an Allied victory. The United States was arriving in strength, Germany was exhausted, the blockade was biting, and the German army was being pushed back in France and Belgium. But without the Salonica breakthrough, Bulgaria would not collapse in September 1918, and the chain reaction against Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire would be slower. The war might last weeks or months longer, and the Central Powers might seek armistices under somewhat less chaotic conditions.

The postwar Balkans would likely look different. Serbia’s position would be weaker, and the creation of Yugoslavia might be delayed, altered, or less favorable to Serbian ambitions. Greece, if it had not clearly joined the victorious Entente, would probably receive fewer rewards; it might not get Smyrna or Eastern Thrace, which could also reduce or avoid the later Greco-Turkish War. Bulgaria, even if still ultimately on the losing side, might negotiate from a less desperate position and perhaps avoid some of the harsher territorial losses it suffered after the war.

So the short answer is: an Allied loss at Salonica would most likely not save Germany from defeat if it occurred late, but it would delay the Central Powers’ collapse and greatly strengthen Bulgaria, weaken Serbia and Greece, and change the postwar settlement in the Balkans. If it occurred early enough and combined with other Central Powers successes, it could make the war longer and more politically favorable to the Central Powers, though a full Central Powers victory would still be unlikely without a major change on the Western Front.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.

items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin from the start, it would probably have been a better high-altitude fighter than the historical Allison-powered P-40, but it would not have become a “P-51 before the P-51.”

The biggest benefit would have been altitude performance. The real P-40’s Allison V-1710 was rugged and reliable, but most early versions lacked an effective two-speed or two-stage supercharger. As a result, the P-40 was strongest at low and medium altitude and lost performance badly above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet. A Merlin-powered P-40, especially one using a Merlin XX-type two-speed supercharger or later Packard Merlin, would have climbed better and retained power higher up. It would have been more useful in European air combat, where high-altitude interception and escort mattered more than in North Africa, China, or the Southwest Pacific.

A Merlin-optimized P-40 would likely have had a cleaner nose, better radiator arrangement, and improved cooling compared with the actual Merlin P-40F/L, which was an adaptation rather than a clean-sheet design. The historical P-40F did receive a Merlin and did improve at altitude, but it was not dramatically faster because the P-40 airframe itself had limitations: it was derived from the P-36, had a relatively thick wing, moderate drag, and limited development margin. A purpose-designed Merlin installation might have produced a fighter somewhat closer to the Hurricane or early Spitfire in engine performance, but still heavier and draggier than the Spitfire and much less aerodynamically efficient than the later P-51.

Operationally, such an aircraft would have been more attractive to the RAF and USAAF in 1941–42. It might have reduced some of the P-40’s reputation as a low-altitude-only fighter and made it more viable in the Mediterranean and perhaps for home-defense or offensive sweeps. It could have been a better match against early Bf 109E/F models than the Allison P-40, though probably still inferior to the best German fighters at altitude.

However, the main problem would have been engine supply. In 1939–41, Merlins were desperately needed for Spitfires, Hurricanes, Lancasters, Mosquitos, and other British aircraft. The United States had the Allison available domestically, while Packard Merlin production did not become significant until later. If Curtiss had committed the P-40 to the Merlin too early, production might have been delayed or limited. That could have been a serious disadvantage, because one of the P-40’s real historical strengths was that it was available in large numbers when the Allies badly needed fighters.

It also probably would not have prevented the rise of the P-51. The Mustang’s success was not just the Merlin engine; it combined the Merlin with a cleaner airframe, better range, lower drag, and excellent high-altitude performance. A Merlin P-40 would have been an improved stopgap fighter, not a long-range escort fighter capable of transforming the air war over Germany.

So the most likely outcome is this: a Merlin-designed P-40 would have been a more capable and more respected early-war fighter, especially above medium altitude, but it would still have been limited by the basic Curtiss airframe and by Merlin production constraints. It might have narrowed the gap between the P-40 and top-line European fighters in 1941–42, but it would not have changed the overall trajectory of Allied fighter development or replaced the P-51 as the decisive Merlin-powered American fighter.

nodes.text: If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin from the start, it would probably have been a better high-altitude fighter than the historical Allison-powered P-40, but it would not have become a “P-51 before the P-51.”
The biggest benefit would have been altitude performance.
The real P-40’s Allison V-1710 was rugged and reliable, but most early versions lacked an effective two-speed or two-stage supercharger.
As a result, the P-40 was strongest at low and medium altitude and lost performance badly above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet.
A Merlin-powered P-40, especially one using a Merlin XX-type two-speed supercharger or later Packard Merlin, would have climbed better and retained power higher up.
It would have been more useful in European air combat, where high-altitude interception and escort mattered more than in North Africa, China, or the Southwest Pacific.

A Merlin-optimized P-40 would likely have had a cleaner nose, better radiator arrangement, and improved cooling compared with the actual Merlin P-40F/L, which was an adaptation rather than a clean-sheet design.

The historical P-40F did receive a Merlin and did improve at altitude, but it was not dramatically faster because the P-40 airframe itself had limitations: it was derived from the P-36, had a relatively thick wing, moderate drag, and limited development margin.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

items.model_answer:
Assuming you mean the PT-109 sinking, the date was August 2, 1943, not July 2. If John F. Kennedy had died then, the largest effect would be the disappearance of the specific Kennedy presidency, not simply a different wartime casualty story.

Immediately, JFK would probably have become a posthumous Navy hero rather than a living one. His survival and rescue of his crew became central to his political image: courage under fire, physical endurance, calm leadership, and wartime legitimacy. Without that living hero narrative, he would not run for Congress in 1946, would not defeat Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. for the Senate in 1952, and would not be the Democratic nominee in 1960.

The Kennedy family’s ambitions would likely shift first to Joseph Kennedy Jr., the eldest son. This is an important wrinkle: Joe Jr. died in 1944 on a dangerous aviation mission, and part of his drive may have been intensified by Jack’s sudden fame as a war hero. If Jack had died in 1943, Joseph Kennedy Sr. might have pushed harder to keep Joe Jr. alive and preserve him as the family’s political heir. If Joe Jr. survived, he might have taken the Massachusetts congressional path that JFK later took. But he probably would not have duplicated JFK exactly: he was more conventionally ambitious, less politically supple, and less likely to create the same 1960 national appeal.

If Joe Jr. still died in 1944, the Kennedy dynasty as Americans know it would be delayed or drastically reduced. Robert Kennedy was too young and initially too tied to his brother’s career to become a national figure on the same timetable. Ted Kennedy might eventually enter politics, but without JFK’s presidency and RFK’s prominence, the family would not have had the same national machine.

The most likely national political consequence is that Richard Nixon wins the 1960 presidential election. Without JFK, the Democrats might nominate Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Adlai Stevenson, or Stuart Symington, but none would clearly reproduce Kennedy’s narrow winning coalition. Nixon only lost by a razor-thin margin in the actual 1960 election, so removing JFK probably tips the presidency to Nixon.

That changes the 1960s sharply. There is probably no “Camelot,” no JFK assassination in 1963, no President Johnson taking power under martyrdom conditions, and therefore no Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act on exactly the same timetable. Civil rights reform would still be pushed by the movement itself, but without JFK’s death and LBJ’s legislative mastery from the presidency, major federal action might be delayed, weaker, or politically differently packaged.

Foreign policy also changes. A Nixon administration in 1961 would likely be more openly anti-communist on Cuba. The Bay of Pigs might be handled with more air support, cancelled, or escalated; in any case, the exact Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 may not occur in the same form. Vietnam remains a major danger because both parties were committed to containment, but the path to escalation would differ from the JFK-to-LBJ sequence. Nixon might intensify pressure earlier, though whether he would commit large ground forces as Johnson did is uncertain.

The space program would likely be less dramatic. JFK’s 1961 pledge to land a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was tied to Cold War prestige after Soviet successes and Kennedy’s own political style. Under Nixon or another president, Apollo might still happen, but probably with less urgency, a later landing, or a smaller program.

So the direct answer is: if JFK died on PT-109, the United States probably never gets President John F. Kennedy; Nixon is the likeliest 1960 winner; the Kennedy dynasty is weakened unless Joe Jr. survives to replace him; civil rights, Vietnam, Cuba, and the Moon race all unfold differently; and the symbolic politics of the 1960s—Camelot, JFK’s assassination, RFK’s rise, and LBJ’s Great Society—are either absent or profoundly altered.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing would almost certainly still have grown, but it would have grown more slowly, less uniformly, and under different corporate winners.

The IBM PC mattered less because it was technically revolutionary than because IBM gave the microcomputer legitimacy. Before 1981, machines from Apple, Commodore, Tandy, Atari, and others already existed, but many large businesses saw them as hobbyist or departmental tools. IBM’s entry told corporate buyers that personal computers were now safe, respectable, and compatible with office computing. Without that signal, many companies would probably have stayed longer with terminals connected to minicomputers and mainframes, while adopting personal computers more cautiously.

The biggest difference would have been the absence of the IBM-compatible clone standard. IBM’s relatively open architecture allowed firms such as Compaq, Dell, AST, and many others to build compatible machines. That created a huge standardized hardware market, drove prices down, and made software developers focus on one dominant platform. Without the IBM PC, the early 1980s computer market would likely have remained fragmented among Apple II, CP/M machines, Commodore systems, Tandy machines, and emerging 16-bit platforms. Software would have been more platform-specific, compatibility would have been weaker, and business adoption would have been messier.

Microsoft’s rise would also have been very different. MS-DOS became powerful because IBM chose it and because IBM-compatible clones spread it everywhere. Without that deal, Microsoft might still have become an important software company through BASIC, applications, and perhaps operating systems for other machines, but it probably would not have achieved the same near-monopoly in PC operating systems so quickly. Digital Research’s CP/M-86, Unix variants such as Xenix, Apple’s systems, or other proprietary operating systems might have had a larger role. The “Wintel” alliance of Microsoft Windows plus Intel processors might never have become so dominant, or it might have emerged later in a weaker form.

Apple might have benefited, but not automatically. In a world without the IBM PC, Apple would have had more room to sell into business and education, especially if the Apple II line and later the Macintosh faced less pressure from IBM-compatible machines. However, Apple’s closed hardware model and higher prices would still have limited its ability to become the universal business standard. It might have become larger and more influential, but not necessarily the single dominant platform.

Intel’s dominance would also have been less secure. The IBM PC helped make the Intel x86 architecture the center of personal computing. Without it, Motorola 68000-based machines, Zilog systems, or later RISC-based designs might have gained more ground. The technical path of desktop computing could have been cleaner in some ways, since x86 survived partly because of compatibility rather than elegance.

The broader social effects would likely have included a slower standardization of office software, delayed spread of interchangeable PC components, and a different geography of tech wealth. Companies built around IBM-compatible hardware and software—especially Microsoft, Intel, Compaq, and Dell—would have been smaller or different. Meanwhile Apple, Digital Research, Commodore, Tandy, Sun, or other workstation and microcomputer firms might have played larger roles.

But the personal computer itself would not have disappeared. Falling chip prices, demand for spreadsheets and word processing, video games, education markets, and office automation were already pushing society toward personal computing. By the late 1980s or early 1990s, some dominant standard would probably have emerged. The main difference is that it might not have been IBM-compatible, Microsoft-controlled, or Intel-based.

So the likely answer is: without the IBM PC in 1981, the PC revolution still happens, but it is slower, more fragmented, and less centered on Microsoft and Intel. IBM’s absence would not stop personal computing, but it would profoundly change who controlled it and how quickly it became standardized.

human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.

criteria.9-10: Develops a detailed, temporally coherent chain with feedback loops: altered target selection, escort availability, German fighter concentration, attrition rates, bomber-force morale/replacement pressures, and likely delays or adaptations in Allied air dominance.

items.model_answer:
If there had been no P-51 Mustang or equivalent long-range fighter escort for Allied bombers over Germany, the Allied strategic bombing campaign would have been much less effective and far more costly.

Before long-range escort became available, U.S. daylight bombing raids suffered severe losses. The raids on Schweinfurt and Regensburg in 1943 showed the problem clearly: unescorted or poorly escorted B-17 and B-24 formations could fight their way in, but German fighters inflicted losses at a rate the U.S. Army Air Forces could not sustain indefinitely. Without the P-51, deep daylight raids into Germany would likely have been reduced, postponed, or shifted more heavily toward night bombing like the RAF campaign.

The biggest effect would have been on air superiority. The P-51 did not merely protect bombers; it helped destroy the Luftwaffe. By escorting bombers deep into Germany and then aggressively engaging German fighters, P-51 units forced the Luftwaffe into battles it could not afford. This attrition weakened German fighter strength before D-Day. Without that pressure, the Luftwaffe might have remained stronger in 1944, making the Normandy invasion more dangerous and increasing Allied losses.

German industry would also have faced less disruption. Oil plants, aircraft factories, transportation networks, and other key targets would still have been attacked, but probably less consistently and with heavier Allied losses. The campaign against German fuel production in particular might have been delayed or weakened, allowing the German military somewhat greater mobility and training capacity in 1944–45.

However, the absence of the P-51 probably would not have changed the final outcome of the war by itself. Germany was already under enormous pressure from the Soviet Union in the east, the British and Americans in the west and Mediterranean, naval blockade, fuel shortages, and overwhelming Allied industrial capacity. Other fighters such as the P-47 and P-38 could provide some escort with drop tanks, though not as effectively. The Allies might also have adapted by emphasizing night bombing, tactical air power, or developing another long-range escort solution.

So the most likely result is not a German victory, but a longer and bloodier air war, higher bomber losses, slower destruction of the Luftwaffe, a riskier D-Day, and possibly a delayed Allied victory in Europe.

nodes.text: If there had been no P-51 Mustang or equivalent long-range fighter escort for Allied bombers over Germany,
the Allied strategic bombing campaign would have been much less effective and far more costly.
Before long-range escort became available, U.S. daylight bombing raids suffered severe losses.
The raids on Schweinfurt and Regensburg in 1943 showed the problem clearly:
unescorted or poorly escorted B-17 and B-24 formations could fight their way in,
but German fighters inflicted losses at a rate the U.S. Army Air Forces could not sustain indefinitely.
Without the P-51, deep daylight raids into Germany would likely have been reduced, postponed, or shifted more heavily toward night bombing like the RAF campaign.
The biggest effect would have been on air superiority.
The P-51 did not merely protect bombers;
it helped destroy the Luftwaffe.
By escorting bombers deep into Germany and then aggressively engaging German fighters,
P-51 units forced the Luftwaffe into battles it could not afford.
This attrition weakened German fighter strength before D-Day.
Without that pressure, the Luftwaffe might have remained stronger in 1944,
making the Normandy invasion more dangerous and increasing Allied losses.
German industry would also have faced less disruption.
Oil plants, aircraft factories, transportation networks, and other key targets would still have been attacked,
but probably less consistently and with heavier Allied losses.
The campaign against German fuel production in particular might have been delayed or weakened,
allowing the German military somewhat greater mobility and training capacity in 1944–45.
However, the absence of the P-51 probably would not have changed the final outcome of the war by itself.

Germany was already under enormous pressure from the Soviet Union in the east, the British and Americans in the west and Mediterranean, naval blockade, fuel shortages, and overwhelming Allied industrial capacity.
Other fighters such as the P-47 and P-38 could provide some escort with drop tanks,
though not as effectively.
The Allies might also have adapted by emphasizing night bombing, tactical air power, or developing another long-range escort solution.
So the most likely result is not a German victory,
but a longer and bloodier air war, higher bomber losses, slower destruction of the Luftwaffe, a riskier D-Day, and possibly a delayed Allied victory in Europe.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.

items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won in 1982, the Falkland Islanders would probably not have been physically expelled or massacred as a matter of policy, but they would almost certainly have lost the political status and protections they valued as a British community.

Argentina regarded the islands as the Malvinas and treated the islanders not as a people entitled to self-determination, but largely as a British-descended settler population living on Argentine territory. A victorious Argentine government would likely have imposed Argentine sovereignty, law, administration, currency, schooling, and Spanish-language public authority. The islands would probably have been governed at first by a military administration, especially given that Argentina was then ruled by a repressive junta.

In the short term, the islanders would likely have faced curfews, censorship, surveillance, restrictions on movement, and pressure to cooperate with Argentine authorities. Prominent pro-British islanders might have been detained, deported, or encouraged to leave. Property would probably not have been confiscated wholesale, but homes, farms, and public buildings could have been requisitioned, and Argentine settlers or officials might have been introduced over time.

In the longer term, Argentina would likely have tried to “Argentinize” the islands while allowing many islanders to remain if they accepted Argentine rule. They might have been offered Argentine citizenship or resident status, but their wish to remain British would not have been allowed to determine sovereignty. Those unwilling to live under Argentine authority would probably have emigrated to Britain or elsewhere.

So the most likely outcome is not mass violence, but political subordination, cultural pressure, and gradual demographic and administrative absorption into Argentina, with serious restrictions at least initially under the military regime. The islanders’ own preferences would have counted for very little.

items.question: What If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank?
human_answers: Let’s first think about the hypothetical scenarios that fit the “conditions” you mentioned. 1. Joseon modernizes before or at the same time as Japan. The relationship between Korea and Japan isn’t bad, but Japan is unable to colonize Korea because Korea becomes strong enough to resist. 2. Japan loses the First Sino-Japanese War or the Russo-Japanese War, and therefore fails to expand into Korea. For each of these conditions, Japan’s situation would be drastically different. In particular, if Japan were to lose a war, the "extent of its defeat" would make a huge difference. However, in my view, if Japan had developed in this way, there’s a high chance that the "Pacific War and other major conflicts" would never have occurred. There wouldn’t have been such "dramatic growth" as in real history—but there also wouldn’t have been such "catastrophic destruction" either. Ultimately, this is something that depends on the imagination of whoever envisions it. Honestly, I think it’s quite possible that Japan could still have developed to the level of a "modern G7 nation". Of course, it’s not inevitable.

East Asia would be completely different without Japanese expansion. Just to keep this in 1900 let's say they beat China but lose to Russia in 1905. I think that a Japan that doesnt even fight the 1894 war with China would be in too alien a modern world for a comparison with OTL to be very useful (mainly since no Chinese defeat in the 1894 war could lead to among other things a surviving Qing dynasty IMO). The Japanese public is highly demoralized by the loss against Russia, Korea remains an idependent country playing off Russian and Japanese influence, and Japan maintains an alliance with the UK and US. Japan not getting militarily or colonially involved in mainland Asia probably reduces the level of overall "momentum" that Japan is able to sustain as a growing world power. Many types of industries go hand in hand in their development and a Japan that does not pursue a world-class navy is probably also not going to be able to justify a world-class heavy industry to go with it. A weaker Japan is also taken less seriously and most importantly takes itself less seriously. I believe they would be somewhat simil啊r to Thailand or the modern day Philippines. Maybe they'd end up like OTL Taiwan and get really deep into some high tech sectors like semiconductors.
