items.question: What If the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out?
human_answers: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? The Holy Roman Empire was the legacy of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire (as opposed to the HOLY Roman Empire) plunged Western Europe into the Middle Ages, from 476 CE (the razing of Rome by the Goths/ the collapse of Rome/ the retrenchment of Rome) to 1266 CE Marco Polo (goes to China) to 1492 CE (the discovery of the Americas by Spain/ starting Mercantilism & Colonialism). It is hard to put a firm date on the latter time when the Middle Ages ended. The role of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire provided a conduit for a Pax Romana, that, in turn, provided for a common culture and trade from Wales in the West to Asia Minor in the East. From Germania in the North to Numidia in the South. The Roman Empire essentially lined the Mediterranian Sea. When the Roman Empire came apart, we saw the balkanization of Europe, EXCEPT for the Holy Roman Empire. We see the various raiding groups causing the fortification and (for the Roman Catholic Church the Monasticism, of Europe, as the social order broke down and people’s view of their then-world became increasingly insular! The exception of the Holy Roman Empire and the Church of Rome were the phoenix that arose out of ashes of the Roman Empire and that was the Roman Catholic Church, aka The Vatican, and that formed the Holy Roman Empire (the geopolitical extension of the Catholic Church.) Which was basically Italy and Germany. There will those who will bring up the Byzantine Empire. You are right but let’s keep this simple, shall we? I believe the questioner was asking about Western Europe and it is that, to which I am addressing my comments. You are free to write your own answer for the Moorish perspective. The Vatican itself had a bigger, but weaker, hold over Western Europe. in contrast to the Holy Roman Empire. In large part, that is that a King needed the Pope’s support & backing to rule. Excommunication was a death sentence to a King’s reign. Power flowed from the Vatican to the King and down thru the nobles. Less is Moor! It is at this point, that I must bring in the Moors, so I might mention that the Middle East was blockaded, as a route to the Orient. Columbus was hired to find a western route to the Orient, by the Spanish royal couple, Ferdinand & Isabella, to end-run that blockade of the Middle East, the Moors having just expelled from Spain! Columbus’s success drew the rulers and merchant of many West Europeans outlook of the world into a more colonial view of the world. Mercantilism & Colonialism. Mercantilism is the economic view of getting resources from colonies and selling finished goods to those colonies. Colonies are a political view of establishing colonies. This race for territory caused a lot, A LOT, of tensions between the nations of Western Europe, not to mention the colony and mother country. The land grab leads to navies, armies, and the settlements to protect trade routes and exploit the resources of those colonies in the Americas, Africa, and Asia. This leads, in turn, to mutual defense treaties (the bifurcation of us vs them. In 1517 CE, Martin Luther & his 95 Thesis’s which begins the beginning of the Reformation. The Vatican begins to lose its grip over Western Europe. Competing Churches no longer recognize the Pope as the supreme authority and Governments rapidly follow suit, leading to even more tension. In 1806 CE, Napolean puts an end to the Holy Roman Empire. Italy and Germany split into principalities, that eventually evolved into modern nations of Italy and Germany. Nationalism took root! The modern era summarized. This tensions reached a flashpoint when a Serbian nationalist assassinated the Archduke of Austria and his wife! All those mutual defense treaties came in to play and WW I began. This led to the Czar and his family being overthrown in Russia, leading in turn to communism and the Soviet Union. The land grab and mutual defense treaties, after WW II, which encouraged colonies to break away and assert their independence. The Cold War. The dissolution of the USSR. Modern times. When it is all said and done. How would it be without the Holy Roman Empire? In a word “Different!” The social and historical order would be changed. Like dominos falling into each other into each other, the dominions of Europe would be reprioritized. We got the history we got because things happened as they did. You start to tug on the woof and weave of time, time will unravel like a cheap sweater, and then all bets are off, about how that history evolves. You can hate the Roman Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Vatican, but they got us where we are and none can say if an alternative would be better or worse!

Question: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? Details: Would Europe perhaps have had 1 or 2 Super States comparable to China in the Middle East? I’m not sure I ‘get’ the question. Charlemagne’s empire, often regarded as the origin of the Holy Roman Empire, was the nearest Western Europe came to a super state. If the Pope had not decided to crown Charlemagne Emperor in 800, so he continued as King of the Franks, as he had been since 774, I can’t really see that would have made much difference. The break-up, shortly after Charlemagne’s death, had nothing to do with his title of Emperor. Partible inheritance had a lot to do with, but even with primogeniture, the Empire might not have been very stable. We know, from the Oaths of Strasbourg (842) that France and Germany already had well established separate languages by then, even though the ruling classes were all of German origin. They also had very distinct cultural histories, with France’s institutions inherited from the old Roman Empire, which Germany had always stood outside. The Holy Roman Empire was refounded as a powerful state by Otto the Great in 962. This incarnation never included France, but did include Germany (plus some surrounding lands) and what contemporaries called Italy (the northern half of what we call Italy). This empire held together as a powerful and, by the standards of the day, quite co-ordinated entity, until the fall of the Hohenstaufen in 1254. I can see how, had the Hohenstaufen not fallen, there was a potential for it to develop into a superstate bestriding much of Western Europe, perhaps by conquest, but more likely by inheritance. Something like Charles V’s empire, but sooner, and based on a much more powerful and united Germany. Its contemporaries could see that potential too, especially when it inherited and took over Sicily (including the southern half of today’s Italy). That is one reason why some of them combined to bring it down when the opportunity presented itself. How the Empire not existing could help that process, though, I’m really not sure. Eastern Europe, of course, had and has its superstate, Russia.

Counterfactual premise A world without the Holy Roman Empire (HRE) means removing a political entity that, from roughly 800–1806, linked a patchwork of central European duchies, bishoprics, free cities and principalities under an elective imperial crown claiming Roman continuity. “Never existed” can be interpreted in two ways: (A) Charlemagne never unified Francian/German lands into an empire in 800, so no imperial tradition develops; or (B) a united central-imperial polity is attempted but fails early and never reconstitutes. Both lead to similar broad consequences: a much weaker supra‑regional institution in Central Europe, earlier fragmentation or alternative unifiers, different church–state relations, altered balance among France, Poland, Italy, the Baltic and the Ottoman frontier, and big effects on state formation, law, religion and culture. Core structural consequences (high level) Greater political fragmentation in the German-speaking lands for longer, accelerating emergence of numerous small sovereign states or city-states with stronger local sovereignty. Without an imperial crown as a focal institution, imperial law, imperial diets and the symbolic framework that mediated overlordship are gone. Earlier consolidation by other regional powers. France would face a more fragmented eastern neighbor; Brandenburg/Prussia, Poland, Bavaria, and Austria would compete to fill the power vacuum. That competition would likely produce a different map: some larger territorial states (Prussia or Poland–Lithuania) could expand sooner and further; alternatively, many microstates persist under shifting suzerainties. Different Church–state dynamics. The HRE’s peculiar relationship with the papacy (lay investiture conflict, imperial coronations, imperial protection of papal interests at times) disappears, changing ecclesiastical politics in Italy and Central Europe. Local princes may gain ecclesiastical autonomy faster; church reform movements and the timing/location of conflicts with Rome shift. Italy’s fragmentation intensifies long-term. The HRE historically provided a counterweight to papal and northern Italian city ambitions. Without imperial intervention, northern Italian communes and the papacy consolidate power in different patterns; the peninsula could see an earlier and more decisive rise of maritime republics or stronger papal states. The map of colonization, warfare and alliances in the later early modern period shifts, because a major central European diplomatic player is missing. European coalitions against France, the Ottomans, or in colonial rivalry form differently. Political and military consequences Rise of alternative hegemonies: Brandenburg/Prussia or Austria might either not arise as single hegemonic states or would develop different identities. If no imperial legitimacy constrains them, dynasties could centralize quicker or be absorbed by neighbors. A strong Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth could expand west into Silesia and Bohemia absent imperial claims, creating a large Poland-centered bloc. The balance against the Ottomans alters: the HRE’s patchwork provided troops, fortresses and political organization to resist Ottoman expansion in Hungary and the Balkans. Without a coordinating imperial structure, response to Ottoman advance could be slower and more regionally uneven; the Ottomans might consolidate greater gains in Central Europe earlier, or conversely local powers could carve defensive coalitions independent of an emperor. Warfare and military innovation diffuse differently. Habsburg dynastic networks that used imperial offices to bind Central Europe would be less effective; their dynastic power would need other bases (landed holdings, marriage alliances), shifting the locus of Habsburg power possibly more toward Spain/Italy earlier or less central in German lands. Religion and the Reformation Protestant Reformation dynamics change substantially. In the historical HRE, the refusal or acceptance of imperial enforcement, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) and the Thirty Years’ War (1618–48) were mediated by imperial institutions. Without an empire: Local rulers might adopt confessional changes with fewer supra‑regional constraints, producing a more mosaic religious map more quickly. Continental confessional wars might be less sweeping but more localized; or they might be replaced by prolonged border conflicts between rising states (e.g., Sweden, Poland, France) rather than an empire-centered Thirty Years’ War. The Peace of Westphalia’s state-sovereignty principles would arise differently or later; the concept of sovereign territorial states might develop earlier as local rulers assert final authority over religion and law. Legal, economic and cultural effects Legal fragmentation and local autonomy accelerate. The imperial legal framework (Imperial Chamber Court, Reichstag) that moderated disputes and preserved rights for imperial estates is absent, so legal pluralism strengthens and regional customary law matters more. Urban and mercantile development. Free imperial cities were historically important nodes. Without imperial status, some cities either fall under territorial princes faster (reducing urban autonomy) or secure different international protections (alliances with Venice, Hanseatic League, or France). The Hanseatic League and Italian maritime republics may gain or lose relative influence depending on territorial pressure from expanded states. Cultural and intellectual flows persist but different patronage networks emerge. Universities, monastic orders and the printing press continue to diffuse ideas; without imperial patronage, cultural centers may cluster more strongly in distinct courts (Prussia, France, Poland, Italian states) and in free cities that find other patrons. Colonial and global consequences Central European absence as a unified actor likely does not dramatically alter early Iberian and later British/Dutch colonization because those were maritime powers. However: A weaker or more fragmented Habsburg base could reduce Spanish/Habsburg coordination across Europe, affecting Habsburg capacities in the 16th–17th centuries. Migration patterns to the Americas and colonies may change: German-speaking emigration might be more regionally driven by small principalities rather than imperial policy, altering settlement patterns in North America and the Caribbean. Military manpower supply for colonial wars differs; mercenary markets in Central Europe could expand, influencing wars abroad. Long-term nation-building and modern map (plausible scenarios) Scenario A — Early microstate Europe Persistent extreme fragmentation: dozens of sovereign German-speaking principalities and city-states survive into the 19th century. France and a stronger Prussia (or a stronger Austria that never consolidated imperial claims) dominate; German unification is delayed or takes a different form (confederation under French or Austrian influence, or a northern confederation led by Prussia emerges later as in real history but with different borders). Industrialization in German lands is uneven; some city-states industrialize quickly, others lag. Scenario B — Alternative unifier rises Prussia (Brandenburg) or a Polish–Silesian union becomes the dominant central European state earlier. If Prussia unifies German lands sooner without an imperial counterweight, a unified German nation-state might appear before 1871, changing the Napoleonic era and the 19th-century balance. If Poland expands west, a large Central European Commonwealth alters Russo‑Prussian dynamics. Scenario C — Stronger regional empires elsewhere Without imperial symbolic legitimacy in Central Europe, dynasties like the Habsburgs pivot toward Italy/Spain and build more coherent maritime/peninsular empires, or they lose ground to France and the Ottomans. The Ottoman Empire may hold more territory in Hungary and the Balkans for longer. Effects on modern Europe (concise) Germany’s path to nationhood changes: the German Empire of 1871 might not exist as known; German-speaking unity could be delayed, achieved under different leadership, or remain fragmented into smaller states in the 20th century. Borders of modern states shift: Poland, Czech lands (Bohemia), Silesia, Bavaria and the Austrian core could belong to different polities or be partitioned differently in the 18th–19th centuries. The ideological legacy of the HRE (mixed sovereignty, legal pluralism, imperial law) that influenced Western legal thought is weaker; the Westphalian state system might crystallize differently, potentially strengthening territorial sovereignty earlier. European wars of the 17th–19th centuries reconfigure: alliances without an imperial center produce different coalition patterns against France, Britain, and the Ottomans, producing alternative outcomes in the Napoleonic and world wars. Key takeaway Removing the Holy Roman Empire shifts Europe from a semi‑centralized, symbolic imperial order to a more fragmented or differently united Central Europe. The most probable outcomes are stronger competition among regional powers (Prussia, Austria, Poland, France, the Ottomans), earlier and deeper political fragmentation in German lands, altered religious and legal settlements, and a different timeline for European state consolidation and balance of power. Exact borders and events are highly sensitive to contingent decisions—small dynastic marriages, battles, or success of a single ambitious ruler could produce radically different maps—so the counterfactual space is wide, but the themes above are robust across plausible variants.

There is no such thing as a total polity vacuum. As an example: defeated Germany in 1945 was occupied, divided and ruled by the victors in specific zones. Lower level German administration (in villages, cities) and courts of justice, never ceased to exist. Similarly, without the Holy Roman Empire, another polity would have taken the place. A confederation of German states, perhaps, with or without a loose central authority. Nothing really different from the HRE, except for one point: there would be much less friction with the East Roman Empire (Constantinople), which always claimed exclusivity in the use of “Roman” and supremacy in title and political protocol. Could such a better understanding between Byzantium and Central Europe have avoided the Schism of the Church in 1054 ? Probably. A united Christianity, under increased influence of the Byzantine ecclesiastic model, might have avoided the struggle between Papacy and European kings, might also have avoided the Protestant Reformation. Last but not least, crusades in much better coordination with Constantinople, better and lasting results. And no Turks in Europe , not even in Asia Minor…

items.model_answer:
If the Holy Roman Empire had never existed, Europe would probably have become more clearly divided into separate regional states earlier, especially in Germany and northern Italy. But it would not necessarily have become simpler or more peaceful. The Empire was weak compared with later centralized monarchies, yet it provided a loose constitutional framework that shaped European politics for almost a thousand years.

The biggest difference would likely have been in Germany. Without the imperial title and institutions linking the German duchies, bishoprics, free cities, and princes, the eastern Frankish lands might have developed in one of two directions: either a stronger German kingdom could have emerged without the distraction of Italian and imperial politics, or, more likely, the region would have fragmented into several medium-sized kingdoms and duchies. Bavaria, Saxony, Swabia, Franconia, and later Austria/Bohemia might have become separate states comparable to France, Poland, or Denmark. There might never have been a single “German” political identity in the same form, and the eventual unification of Germany in the nineteenth century might have been delayed, altered, or never happened.

Italy would also have changed significantly. In real history, northern and central Italy were repeatedly drawn into imperial politics: emperors claimed authority there, cities resisted them, and the papacy maneuvered between imperial and local powers. Without the Empire, northern Italy might have developed even earlier into a system of independent city-states, principalities, and papal territories. Venice, Milan, Florence, Genoa, and other powers might still have flourished, but without the recurring imperial claim over Italy. Alternatively, France or a German-speaking kingdom such as Bavaria or Austria might have intervened sooner, because the absence of imperial authority would have left Italy more open to outside competition.

The papacy would probably have been stronger in some ways and weaker in others. The medieval pope often defined his authority in relation to the emperor: sometimes cooperating with him, sometimes fighting him, as in the Investiture Controversy. Without a Holy Roman Emperor, the pope would have lacked a universal secular counterpart. This could have made the papacy more politically independent, especially in central Italy. But it might also have made the pope more dependent on nearby powers such as the Franks, Normans, French kings, or Italian city-states. The medieval idea of Christendom as a single community under pope and emperor would have been much less powerful.

France might have benefited. In real history, France expanded partly because the Empire was decentralized and unable to hold its western borderlands firmly. Without the Empire, France could have expanded eastward even earlier into Burgundy, Lorraine, Alsace, or the Low Countries—unless strong local successor states blocked it. A Europe without the Empire might therefore have seen a larger France, or alternatively a belt of independent states between France and the Slavic and German lands.

Central Europe would have looked different as well. The Habsburgs rose within the structures of the Empire, using imperial elections, dynastic marriages, and Austrian lands to become a major European house. Without the Empire, the Habsburg monarchy might still have emerged from Austria, but it would have lacked the prestige and mechanisms of imperial office. Bohemia, Austria, Hungary, and the German principalities might have followed more separate paths. The balance against the Ottoman Empire in southeastern Europe could have been weaker or organized differently, perhaps around Hungary, Poland-Lithuania, Venice, or a non-imperial Austrian state.

The Reformation would probably have unfolded very differently. The political fragmentation of the Holy Roman Empire gave Protestantism room to survive: Lutheran princes could protect reformers against both emperor and pope. Without the Empire, Protestantism might either have spread through several independent German states or been suppressed more effectively by stronger monarchies. If Germany had fragmented into many states anyway, the Reformation might still have succeeded. If a centralized German kingdom had formed, the religious outcome would have depended heavily on that monarchy’s policy—more like England, France, or Spain.

The Thirty Years’ War, as we know it, would not have happened, because it was deeply tied to the Empire’s religious and constitutional structure. But that does not mean Europe would have avoided major wars. Conflicts among France, German successor states, Poland, Denmark, Sweden, Austria, and Italy could still have produced large religious and dynastic wars. The Empire often failed to prevent war, but it also provided legal mechanisms that sometimes contained disputes.

In the long run, Europe without the Holy Roman Empire would likely have had fewer tiny principalities and imperial free cities, less of the peculiar German federal tradition, and a weaker medieval ideal of universal Christian empire. Germany and Italy might have consolidated earlier, or they might have fragmented into durable regional states without ever unifying in the modern sense. France might have become stronger earlier. The papacy’s political role would have changed profoundly. The Habsburgs might have been less dominant, and the map of central Europe would have been far less recognizable.

So the most likely outcome is not a Europe without empire, war, or hierarchy, but a Europe in which the German and Italian worlds were organized around regional kingdoms, city-states, and dynastic blocs rather than a loose imperial framework. The Holy Roman Empire did not make Europe centralized; it did almost the opposite. But by holding central Europe together loosely, it delayed and reshaped the emergence of modern nation-states. Without it, European state formation would probably have happened earlier in some places, more unevenly in others, and with a very different balance of power.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?
human_answers: Note: Parts of this answer will be copied from this one . However, this is a different scenario than that one. Note: I do not claim that this answer is realistic, nor that everything would happen the way I say it would. This is, of course, impossible to predict. Anyway, the point of divergence here is 378 AD, with the battle of Adrianople. Battle of Adrianople You see, Rome could have won this battle quite decisively. They had numerical parity, if not superiority, to the Gothic forces. They had great heavy cavalry. Valens had a large amount of additional reinforcements marching in from the west as well. They likely would have arrived within the next few days. Had the two forces linked up, they would have likely beaten the Goths. Why did I have the Romans win at Adrianople? The Roman defeat at Adrianople and the resulting Gothic invasions devastated the Balkans, to the point where they were somewhat depopulated. This is avoided in this timeline. This also avoids the Goths rising up in revolt within the Empire later on. With the Balkans in a much better position, the Romans are able to largely keep the Huns at bay, forcing them west. The Huns were defeated in battle by the Western Romans and their allies in 451 AD, so I could see the Eastern Romans doing the same here. Next, Theodosius the Great recognizes Eunegius as Emperor in 394, rather than killing and deposing him. This avoids the problem of Honorius becoming Emperor and also doesn’t kill over a third of the western army. Eunegius agrees to let Flavius Stilicho become Magister Militum of the west in exchange for being recognized as Emperor. Stilicho would survive longer in this timeline due to Honorius not rising to power, allowing him to better contain the barbarians invading the Empire. He would represent a bridge between the barbarians living within the Empire, allowing them to be more easily assimalated and showing that the two could coexist. Flavius Aetius would also survive longer, giving Rome a strong military leader to hold the Empire together. Next, Majorian is not betrayed in 460 AD, and his fleet is not destroyed. This allows him to retake North Africa, giving Western Rome fresh sources of manpower, taxes, food, and resources. Majorian finds out about Ricimier’s plots and has him executed. His replacement would be loyal and competent. Majorian would stabalize Italy and North Africa, and implement his reforms to the imperial administration. This would make the Empire more stable. Majorian would implement laws to whip the decedant and lazy upper class back into shape, reinvigorate pride in the Roman state, and reintroduce native Italians into the army. Majorian’s successor, likely Julius Nepos, would continue his reforms, enforcing and expanding upon them. Roman Empire in 460 AD. In this timeline, Carthage is under Roman rule as well. Under Majorian’s successors, Gaul and most of Hispania would still be lost, but the Empire would survive. Julius Nepos comes to power in the mid-late 470s, continuing the reforms of Majorian and strengthening the Empire. He would fortify the borders and choose a competent successor, who would continue the reforms of Majorian and Nepos. Majorian, Nepos, and their successors would recognize that the Empire could not rely on slavery, and that it needed to bolster its population in order to survive. Therefore, they would implement more efficient farming practices and the use of technology such as water wheels and mills in order to make the production of flour more efficient. They would also update architectural codes and improve living standards in order to increase stability and keep more people alive and healthy. They would massively revamp sanitation systems to reduce the risk of disease and improve healthcare for pregnant mothers in order to bolster the population further. They would also choose a competent successor, who would likely free most remaining slaves to increase the conscriptable, taxable population. Barbagel water mill complex During this time monuments and architecture would be restored. Propaganda would hearken back to the old days and the resilience of the Roman people, reinvigorating pride in the Empire. Leo I in the East would die a few years later than in our timeline, helping out the West. The West largely goes on as a regional power until Justinian comes along. He would officially reunify the East and West, although there would still be two emperors. Without Italy being devastated by the Gothic wars, its population thrives, and the Roman spirit is reignited in the East as well. Justinian implements the reforms of the West all across the Empire, and Rome reaches a new technological golden age. Hispania and southern Gaul are retaken for the Empire, and the whole of North Africa up to the Atlantic is under Roman control as well. The Justinian Plague is still devastating, but with the improved sanitation and without the devastation of the Gothic wars, Rome is still going strong. The Plague would drive demand for labor up as the population declines, allowing the middle class to grow and seeing the further implementation of technology into the everyday lives of Romans. Women would be allowed to hold more jobs and to work in factories, and would slowly gain more power and rights in society from there. In this timeline, with the Balkans secured and giving Rome much greater manpower than it had in our world, Germanus would be able to destroy the Persians at Antioch, making Persia rethink Rome’s weakness. The Persians would sue for peace, restoring the “Eternal Peace” they had signed with Rome not long before. They would have to make several concessions, allowing Rome to fortify the border. In this timeline, Germanus would not have to fight the Ostrogoths in Italy, and would thus not fall ill. He would become Emperor after Justinian, and after him would be Justin Germanus, who would be another competent ruler. These two would further expand on the reforms of their predecessors, upholding them and giving them time to stick. IRL Rome under Justinian With large sources of manpower from North Africa, the Balkans, and Italy, Rome is not percieved as weak by Persia. In this timeline, Phokas would not rise to power and severely weaken the Empire, as Justin Germanus would not order him to camp north of the Danube for the winter. Maurice would still rise to power after Justin, and would be a fairly competent Emperor as he was in our timeline. After Maurice, Heraclius would not want to see the Empire split between Maurice’s sons and would rise to power. Heraclius was also fairly competent. Without Phokas, and with Persia having been stopped by Germanus decades earlier, the Persians wouldn’t attack the Romans. When the Arabs explode out of the Arabian peninsula, Rome would abandon Gaul and lose Hispania and parts of North Africa. However, they would still hold Carthage, Egypt, and the Levant. They’d also lose bits of the northern Balkans to the Slavs and Avars. However, they’d still hold much of the Balkans. Persia, due to not being exhausted by fighting Rome, would be in a stronger position, and would survive the Arab invasions, though with a loss of territory. In the same way Rome was Europe’s shield during the middle ages, Persia would be Rome’s shield, taking blow after blow and lessening the effects of these invasions on the Roman Empire. The balance of power within the Empire would still shift east, with Constantinople being the capital. The Empire would closely resemble the Eastern Roman/Byzantine Empire of our timeline, but with more Latin influence. During this time, northern Europe still largely develops as it did in our timeline, with the Kingdom of the Franks still emerging and splitting. Hispania is still slowly reconquered by the Europeans, but this time the Romans would participate. Eventually they’d end up with what would be Aragon in our timeline. Much of the middle ages in Europe would be Roman tributary states paying the Romans in exchange for protection. The Pope, chafing under Roman rule, would flee and set up a new branch of Christianity, namely Catholicism. The Romans are able to hold back the Turks as well, keeping them out of the Empire. They win at Manzikert. Rome has entered a period of slow but steady decline, as it did in our timeline. It’s still surviving and prospering, but beginning to rot from the inside. The Great Schism never happens, and neither do the Crusades. Rome is one of the most technologically advanced nations on the planet, being near a state of industrialization. They would have rudimentary air conditioning, sanitation, advanded plumbing and running water, all in every apartment building. They would have hospitals and universities. Their military would be formidable. Factory-like complexes would be common, using water power to produce flour and goods. Slavery would come to be regarded as the mark of a less advanced civilization. Basil II would reinvigorate the Empire, bringing back Roman pride and defeating the Bulgars. He would reform the Empire, and leave it in a much stronger position than it was before his reign. In this timeline, he would choose a competent successor, similarly to Germanus and Justinian. Europe and the Middle East in 1025 AD In 1190, the Romans beat the Bulgarians at the battle of Trinova. This leads to Isaac II not being deposed and the Roman army not being demoralized like in our timeline. Alexios III does not rise to power, and the 4th Crusade never happens, as Alexios IV never needs to contact the crusaders to depose Alexios III. The Romans would have good relations with Hungary to the north. In the 1200s, the Mongol invasions would happen. Whatever Persion/Turkish state that would exists east of Rome would take the brunt of the blow, but Rome would still be hit fairly hard. They wouldn’t be devastated, but they wouldn’t be able to brush it off either. The Black Death would also be devastating, but experience with plagues and sanitation would somewhat mitigate the effects. Like the Justinian Plague before, the Black Death would again grow the middle class, increasing their power within society. The Romans would recover. Mongol expansion The world in 1250 The Turks would still carve out an Empire like they did in our timeline, leading to several wars with the Romans. They would very nearly succeed in taking Constantinople in 1453, but Rome would be able to drive them back. Roman propaganda would once again hearken back to the determination of the Roman people and the strength and culture of classical Rome. There would be a resurgance in classical ideas, innovation, and technology and philosophy, as well as the arts. This would spread throughout Europe, sparking the Renaissance. Rome would reconquer what territory it lost to the Turks, and even expand in some places. Constantine XI and his successor would implement broad reforms to protect from invasions and to make it so that the internal rot that had weakened Rome would not happen again. The 100 Years War ends the way it did in our timeline, and Poland-Lithuania still emerges, as does something like the Tutonic Order. In this timeline, they would fight in the Reconquista before eventually getting evicted and moving up to the Baltic region to stamp out paganism there. Europe in 1450 Rome for centuries would dominate East-West trade, leading the Iberian kingdoms impoverished. They would search for new trade routes, and would travel around Africa and eventually find the Americas. Now the race is on to colonize the New World. In the early 16th century, Rome would conquer down to the Horn of Africa and set up client kingdoms. This would give them access to the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Rome at this point would be incredibly advanced, rich, and prosperous. Huge factory complexes and industrial scale agricultural and mining operations would exist. Roman towns and cities would be among the cleanest in the world. By now almost every building would have a flush toilet and sink. Plumbing would be common in towns as well as cities. Gunpowder weapons would be appearing. Analog computers would be used. The printing press would allow ideas to spread rapidly, spreading technology. The world in 1550 Protestantism would be spreading throughout the northern lands of Europe, and in the early 1610s Germany would be ripped apart by religous war. The Hapsburgs would control Austria, Germany, and Spain, and in a bid to exploit the Hapsburg’s weakness, the French, Romans, and Russians would fight them. The Romans and Russians in particular would support the Protestants against the Catholics, who were enemies of Roman Orthodoxy. The war would end with Germany and Spain crippled, the former of which would be reduced to a messy confederation of states. The Romans would annex Hungary. Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Prussia would come to dominate Germany. Meanwhile, for the past few centuries England, Spain, Portugal, Rome, France, and Holland have been setting up colonies in the Americas. The Romans would not partake in the Atlantic Slave Trade, viewing slavery as the mark of a less advanced civilization. The Portugese would colonize Brazil. The French and British colonies would grow fast in the Americas. Meanwhile, Brandenburg would become a dominant power in Germany alongside Bavaria and Prussia. The three would become close allies, hoping to unite Germany. They would attempt to annex Transnistria, leading to the Seven Years War. The world at the start of the Seven Years War The British side of the war would be: Prussia Brandenburg Bavaria Britain Portugal Rome Russia The French side of the war would be: Austria France Spain Persia Poland Holland The war would be even larger here than in our timeline. Russia would move into Poland-Lithuania, gaining territory until the Polish stop them with a defensive trench line. The Romans would move against the Persians/Turks, pushing them back and taking Armenia. They would advance into Arabia. The British and French would fight in the Americas, and the Romans would advance against the Spanish in both the New World and Old World. The British would seize Spanish islands in the Carribean. The armies of Prussia, Bavaria, and Brandenburg initially push the Austrians back, but get bogged down. After the first winter in Europe, spring offensives begin. criteria.3-4: Shows occasional caution but includes many deterministic claims, inconsistent borders/events, or real-world events that occur without plausible causes.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent and acknowledges uncertainty, though some events are too conveniently preserved or contradicted by earlier assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, flags alternative possibilities, and keeps most claims internally consistent with the altered Roman geopolitical landscape.
criteria.9-10: Consistently distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradiction; explains why familiar events would change or persist; and treats long-range history as contingent rather than inevitable.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire had never fallen and survived as a continuous state until 2020, it would almost certainly not look like the ancient empire of Augustus or Constantine. To survive for that long, it would have had to transform repeatedly: politically, militarily, economically, religiously, and culturally. It would be “Roman” in the way modern China is linked to ancient Chinese states: continuous in identity and institutions, but radically changed in practice.

The most likely version is a Roman state that gradually became a constitutional, bureaucratic, multiethnic empire or federation. Latin might have remained a major administrative and scholarly language, though local languages would still evolve. Romance languages such as Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian might be closer to one another, or Latin might function like a stronger version of English today: a common language of law, government, science, and diplomacy across much of Europe and the Mediterranean.

Christianity would probably still become central, since the historical Roman Empire had already Christianized before the western half collapsed. But the religious map could be very different. If Rome remained politically unified, the split between Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy might not occur in the same way, or it might become an internal church dispute managed by imperial institutions. Islam would still likely arise in Arabia, but its expansion into the Levant, North Africa, and Spain would depend heavily on whether Rome remained militarily strong. A more resilient Roman Empire might prevent or limit the early Islamic conquests, producing a Mediterranean world more dominated by Christian Roman institutions. Alternatively, if Rome survived by compromise, it might include large Muslim populations and become religiously pluralistic.

Europe’s political development would be completely altered. There might be no medieval patchwork of kingdoms in the same form, no Holy Roman Empire as a separate project, and perhaps no France, Spain, Italy, or Germany as we know them. Feudalism might be weaker if Roman taxation, roads, law courts, and central administration remained intact. Roman law would likely be even more dominant globally than it already is.

The Renaissance, Reformation, and Enlightenment would also change. Some classical knowledge was preserved historically through Byzantium, the Islamic world, and medieval monasteries; a surviving Roman Empire might preserve more ancient infrastructure and learning continuously. That could lead to earlier scientific and technological development, but not necessarily. Large stable empires can preserve knowledge, but they can also suppress disruptive innovation. The timing of industrialization might be earlier, later, or centered in different regions depending on whether the Roman state encouraged merchants, engineers, banking, and private enterprise.

Colonialism would probably look very different. If a Roman Empire controlled the Mediterranean and much of western Europe, overseas expansion might be conducted by imperial Roman fleets rather than by separate Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British empires. The Americas might be colonized by a single Roman-led imperial system, or exploration might be slower if the empire remained focused on Eurasia and Africa. Modern borders in the Americas, Africa, and Asia could be almost unrecognizable.

By 2020, a surviving Roman Empire would likely be one of the world’s great powers, perhaps comparable to a combination of the European Union, the United States, and a Mediterranean superstate. Its capital might still be Rome, or it might have shifted to Constantinople, Ravenna, Milan, or another administrative center. It would probably have a senate or parliament, a professional civil service, codified law, a vast military tradition, and a strong imperial identity binding many ethnic groups together.

However, it is unlikely that a single autocratic emperor could rule unchanged into the modern age. To survive nationalism, industrialization, mass literacy, democratic movements, and modern war, Rome would probably have become either a constitutional monarchy, a republic retaining Roman imperial symbolism, or a federal empire with autonomous provinces. If it failed to adapt, it would eventually fracture.

So the direct answer is: if the Roman Empire never fell and reached 2020, the modern world would probably be far more politically unified around the Mediterranean and Europe, with stronger continuity of Roman law, language, infrastructure, and identity. Many modern nation-states might not exist in their current form. Christianity, Islam, colonialism, science, and global politics would all develop differently. But the empire itself would not be an ancient slave-based military monarchy frozen in time; it would have to evolve into a modern, bureaucratic, multiethnic superstate in order to survive.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell? How would this change most of our history today?
human_answers: The problem with the previous answer is that it is ahistorical. The Roman Empire did not fall until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople. Emperor Constantine had moved the capitol to the Greek city of Byzantium because of its excellent geographic, strategic, and central location, calling it New Rome, although at that point the empire was then split between eastern and western halves until the west collapsed in the fifth century. Subsequently renamed Constantinople, it then became the center of the world and continued long after the city of Rome itself declined sharply as the locus of empire shifted. Attempts, sometimes successful, were made to reclaim parts of the west. Indeed the name of the city itself continued until the cataclysm of World War I. In addition, Justinian was the last Emperor to use Latin rather than Greek, which prevailed for another eight centuries, or far longer than Rome itself. There was never a “Byzantine Empire.” That was a far later German concoction in order to legitimate their own “Holy Roman Empire, which, as Voltaire once said, was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, What actually existed, as I have suggested elsewhere, was not something “Byzantine,” but rather a Greco-Roman Empire that lasted for a millennium. This is still confused and not well known due to the ignorance and prejudice of northwestern Europeans towards the south. Thus, the Roman Empire did not fall or disappear the way you have been led to believe. In fact, if the empire began with Augustus, the Rome-based portion only lasted for a bit more than four centuries, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued for another thousand years, and all the people in the empire, including the Greeks, referred to and considered themselves Romans until the very end. The empire itself was polyglot as it always was, but the dominant language was Greek. Thus, while the “Middle Ages” or medieval period happened in the west, which was still backward, that was not the case in the east, in what in fact was the bulk of the empire, which continued a thriving, but heavily Christianized civilization. Thus, in the year 1000 Constantinople had a population of over a million people. The original Roman Empire was far better at practical things, particularly organization, administration, functional engineering, etc. than the quarrelsome Greeks, who otherwise brilliantly developed and dominated culture, art, science, philosophy, etc. Romans provided the critical stability, legal and social infrastructure that was previously lacking in an otherwise largely Greek world that had been established by Alexander and his successors. As a result, Roman law, justice and organization provided the framework which sustained an otherwise largely Greek cultural entity. The empire would not have fallen had it not been for the Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) which, instead of going to Jerusalem to fight Muslims attacked other Christians via Venetian ships and encouragement. The barbarian Knights/Crusaders literally destroyed the city of Constantinople, pillaging and worse, burning down much of the city while the Venetians, at least having some artistic sense, carted off a lot of treasures that you still see in St. Marks to this day. The crusaders took over what was left of the city setting up their own “empire” for a few decades until the Romans finally reclaimed it, but in a much-weakened state. Thus, by the time the Turks finally conquered the city in 1453 with new long-range cannons, there were only about 50,000 people left there. That is when the Roman Empire finally fell, in its Greco-Roman-Christian incarnation. Given true history then, if the empire hadn’t fallen it is quite possible that Greek would still be the common language, you might be speaking it, and the European world would be very different. The “old” nations of Europe after all, have only existed for around five centuries. They really ascended after the fall of the City and the “renaissance” that followed, (another retroactively coined term), instilled to a considerable extent by Greek refugee scholars who fled to the Italian city-states, which welcomed then as teachers, given their thirst for knowledge and ancient manuscripts. Many other things would be different, starting with religion. In the empire the church was subordinate to the Emperor, and less powerful than in the west, where given the power vacuum, the Bishop of Rome, or Pope, was able to claim supremacy. Consequently, if the empire had continued the church would not have had so much power, and it is likely there would never have been a Protestant Reformation. Regions would have had their own Patriarchs. There is no way to know how geography would have taken shape, given uncertainty as to how far the empire might have reached, or how competent it would have been, but at its maximum it could have stretched over all of Europe. Alternatively, it could have been smaller, as it continued to fend of endless barbarian invasions from the east, allowing other powers to emerge in the west anyway, but possibly without the virulent nationalism that eventually developed and led to catastrophic wars and mass murder in the last century. Much would depend on whether the empire could regain Italy, which was essential to the emergence of modern Europe. (In 1500 Italy was richer than all of western Europe combined and more culturally advanced). Since it was then divided into competing city-states in the fashion of ancient Greece, that might have transpired if the empire was relatively free from barbarian invasions. Slavs, at least in the south were already being absorbed before the fall of the empire and thus would likely still be integrated. Unknowns are how the Russians, or more importantly the Germans might have emerged. But generally, the empire had always done a great job of absorbing and integrating other peoples, until the rise of Islam. If the empire had remained strong it is unlikely that the Arabs would have conquered what was then European Christian north Africa and Egypt, or even much of what is now called the “middle east,” which would have remained Christian and Roman, linked to the west via Constantinople. The empire took the brunt of Muslim invasion, thus protecting the west for centuries, and if not for the Fourth Crusade could have grown stronger and more powerful and Europe would not have been threatened or invaded. In addition, Persian culture might still exist, possibly as yet another empire. Greek rationalism did not disappear as the church in the east largely reconciled itself with it and focused on spiritual matters. Consequently, the church would not have been able to significantly thwart scientific progress. Europe, including a good portion of the east would still dominate the world. and remain centered in Constantinople. They would likely still have found the Americas, but development might have been different, possibly without African slavery, among other things. The culture would be more advanced and sophisticated, but economic growth might not be as robust, given a different emphasis and outlook, and without a “Protestant ethic” but rather a sort of merchant mentality. Higher education might not have been found in universities as we know them, but rather closer to the academic format of the ancient world, more focused on the development of the mind and learning. Ultimately we cannot know because of vicissitudes of one-man rule. There can be a great ruler and then a terrible ruler. You can have a Marcus Aurelius or a Caligula. So given different personalities there is no way to know, and that can be precarious and lead to instability or conflict until someone else consolidates power. What we can learn clearly from history is the less power we surrender to others over us the better off we are. Finally, the Fourth Crusade was clearly the worst disaster in western history even beyond World War I if only because the latter might never have happened if the empire hadn’t fallen. Such a general and vague question can lead to endless possibilities and alternatives, but in the end all that is left is what actually happened.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire “never fell,” the biggest change is that Europe would probably have remained under some kind of continuous imperial government instead of breaking into the medieval kingdoms that later became France, England, Spain, Germany, Italy, and others. But it would not mean people today would be living in a frozen version of ancient Rome. A surviving Rome would have changed dramatically over time, likely becoming a Christian, bureaucratic, multilingual empire more like a larger Byzantine Empire than the old pagan empire of Caesar and Augustus.

The most immediate difference would be the absence, or major weakening, of the early medieval “post-Roman” order in western Europe. No collapse of Roman administration in Gaul, Britain, Spain, and Italy would mean no same rise of the Franks, Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Lombards, or Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in the form we know. Feudalism might never develop in the same way, because feudalism grew partly out of the breakdown of centralized authority, local insecurity, and the need for land-based military service. A stronger Roman state could have kept taxation, roads, cities, professional armies, and provincial administration functioning for longer.

Modern national identities would be completely different. France might not exist as “France,” because there may be no Frankish kingdom. England might not exist in its familiar form, because Roman Britain might not be abandoned, and Germanic settlement there would likely be more limited or more assimilated. Germany and Italy as modern nation-states would also have very different histories, since both were shaped by the legacy of Rome’s collapse and the later Holy Roman Empire, papacy, city-states, and dynastic politics.

Language would also change greatly. Latin might have remained a stronger administrative and literary language across western Europe. The Romance languages—French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian—might still emerge as spoken regional forms, but they could be more standardized or more closely tied to official Latin. English as we know it might not exist, because it came from Germanic settlers in post-Roman Britain and was later transformed by Norse and Norman French influence. A continuously Roman Britain may have produced a Latin-Celtic language instead.

Christianity would likely remain central, but the relationship between church and state would be different. In our history, the western Church gained enormous independent power after imperial authority disappeared in the West. If Rome survived, the pope might have been less politically independent, more like the patriarchs in the Eastern Roman Empire who operated under strong imperial influence. This could mean no medieval papacy in the form we know, no same Investiture Controversy, no same Crusades, and possibly no Protestant Reformation as it actually happened.

The Islamic conquests might also unfold differently. A stronger, united Roman Empire could have resisted Arab expansion more effectively in the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, or at least fought it under different conditions. But it is also possible that even a surviving Rome would still lose some provinces, because the seventh-century Arab conquests were driven by powerful religious, military, and political forces. If Rome held North Africa, Egypt, or the Levant, the religious and cultural map of the Mediterranean would be very different.

The Renaissance would not happen in the same way. In real history, the Renaissance involved a “rediscovery” and reinterpretation of ancient Greek and Roman culture after centuries of political fragmentation. If Roman institutions, education, law, and urban culture continued without a sharp break, there may be no Renaissance as a revival of a lost classical world. Instead, classical culture would evolve continuously. This could produce either earlier intellectual development or a more conservative imperial culture that slows some changes.

European exploration and colonization would also be altered. Spain, Portugal, England, France, and the Netherlands led overseas expansion in our timeline because they developed as rival maritime states. A unified Roman superstate might explore more slowly, because it faced less interstate competition, or it might explore earlier if it had the resources and administrative capacity. The colonization of the Americas, the Atlantic slave trade, and the global balance of power would almost certainly be very different.

Modern democracy and nationalism would likely develop differently too. Much of modern political history came from the competition among European states, the growth of parliaments and monarchies, religious wars, revolutions, and nationalist movements. A surviving Roman Empire might preserve a stronger tradition of centralized imperial authority. It could eventually become constitutional, federal, or fragmented by internal pressures, but the path to modern states would not resemble the one we know.

Law and administration might be more Romanized across Europe. Roman law already deeply influenced European legal systems, but in this alternate world its continuity would be even stronger. Property law, citizenship, municipal government, taxation, and military service might all follow Roman models for much longer. Europe might look more like a single civilizational-political zone rather than a continent of competing sovereign states.

The largest overall change is that the world would probably be less shaped by medieval European fragmentation and more shaped by a long-lived Mediterranean empire. There might be no recognizable Middle Ages, no same Catholic Church, no same European kingdoms, no same colonial empires, no same English language, and no same modern nation-state system. However, Rome would still face disease, succession crises, economic problems, military pressure, religious disputes, and regional identities. So the realistic answer is not “ancient Rome continues unchanged,” but rather: world history would be dominated by the evolution, reform, and possible federalization of a surviving Roman state, and almost every later development in Europe and the wider world would follow a different path.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire still existed today, the world would be radically different, but it would not look like ancient Rome frozen in time. To survive for 1,500 more years, it would have had to transform into something more like a federal, bureaucratic, multilingual superstate: partly imperial, partly constitutional, probably Christian in origin, and centered on the Mediterranean.

The biggest difference would be political. Much of Europe, North Africa, and the Near East might be part of one continuous Roman state or at least shaped by it. Countries such as Italy, France, Spain, Greece, and perhaps parts of Britain, Germany, the Balkans, Egypt, Syria, and Turkey might not exist as independent nation-states in the modern sense. They might instead be Roman provinces or autonomous regions within an empire. Modern nationalism would still probably emerge, but it would develop inside an imperial framework, more like regional nationalism within a large federation.

Religion would also be very different. Since the Roman Empire became Christian, a surviving empire would likely have kept tighter control over the Christian Church. The split between Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy might not happen in the same way, or the pope might never become as politically independent as he did in medieval Europe. The Protestant Reformation might also be weaker, delayed, or take a very different form because it was partly a reaction to the medieval Catholic order that emerged after Rome’s western collapse.

The rise of Islam and the history of the Middle East would be one of the biggest uncertainties. If a stronger Roman Empire retained Egypt, Syria, and North Africa, early Islamic expansion might have been slowed or redirected. Islam would probably still arise in Arabia, but the map of the Islamic world could be very different. There might be no Ottoman Empire as we know it, no fall of Constantinople in 1453, and no centuries-long struggle between Ottoman Turkey and Christian Europe in the same form.

European languages and culture would also change. Latin might remain a major administrative or scholarly language much longer, possibly evolving into a standardized modern “Roman” language. The Romance languages—Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Romanian—might be less distinct, or they might exist as regional languages under a common imperial Latin culture. Greek would likely remain important in the eastern provinces. English might not become the dominant global language unless Britain or a Romanized Britain became central to imperial expansion.

The legal and governmental traditions of the world would likely be more Romanized. Roman law already heavily influenced Europe, but in this scenario it might be even more universal. Concepts of citizenship, provincial administration, codified law, public works, and imperial bureaucracy could dominate global political development. Modern democracy might exist, but perhaps inside a Roman constitutional monarchy or imperial republic rather than through separate nation-states.

Economically, the Mediterranean might remain one of the central regions of the world for much longer. In real history, after Rome’s western collapse, political fragmentation shifted power gradually toward northern and Atlantic Europe. If Rome survived, cities like Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Carthage, Antioch, and Athens might remain major global centers. Trade across the Mediterranean would likely be more integrated and stable.

The Age of Exploration and colonialism would also be transformed. Instead of Spain, Portugal, France, Britain, and the Netherlands competing overseas, a surviving Roman Empire might sponsor exploration directly. The Americas might have been colonized by a Roman imperial state rather than by separate European kingdoms. That means countries like the United States, Mexico, Brazil, Canada, and many Caribbean states might have entirely different languages, borders, religions, and political identities. A Roman-dominated Atlantic world might speak Latin-derived languages even more widely than today.

Technological progress is harder to predict. A surviving Rome might preserve infrastructure, literacy, engineering, and urban life better than medieval Europe did, possibly avoiding some periods of economic decline. But large empires can also become conservative and bureaucratic. The intense competition among European states helped drive military, scientific, commercial, and colonial innovation. If Rome reduced that competition, the Industrial Revolution might happen later, or in a different region, or under state direction rather than private capitalist competition.

So the modern world would probably be less divided into the familiar European nation-states and more centered on a massive Roman-descended civilization. Christianity, law, language, borders, colonial history, and global power would all be different. But the empire would not be “ancient Rome with smartphones.” It would likely resemble a long-lived, Roman-branded federation or imperial commonwealth: Christian or post-Christian, multilingual, bureaucratic, legally Roman, and still carrying the prestige of Caesar and the old Mediterranean world.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire survived into the 21st century?
human_answers: A surviving Roman Empire in the 21st century would reshape politics, culture, technology diffusion, religion, law, and global power structures. Below is a compact, structured scenario sketching plausible continuities, ruptures, and systemic consequences while anchoring changes in realistic mechanisms (institutional inertia, technological adoption, conquest limits, cultural assimilation). Core-continuities and institutions Imperial continuity: The Empire preserves imperial institutions—an emperor (or imperial council), provincial administration, legions as core armed forces, and a bureaucratic elite—adapted over centuries into flexible, meritocratic civil service and imperial parliament/assemblies to manage scale. Roman law as global lingua franca: Codified law (an evolved Corpus Juris) becomes the legal foundation across the Empire and, by prestige and trade, a dominant model beyond it; concepts like property rights, contracts, corporate forms, and administrative law are widespread. Urbanism and infrastructure: Roman urban planning, roads, aqueduct successors, ports, and integrated logistics persist and modernize. Dense metropolitan networks across the Mediterranean, Western and parts of Central Europe, North Africa, Anatolia and the Levant remain economic cores. Multilingual administration: Latin remains the imperial legal-administrative language but coexists with vernaculars (Greek, Punic, Syriac, Germanic, Celtic, Berber dialects). A strong tradition of bilingual or trilingual elites exists. Geopolitics and territorial shape Core territories: The Empire holds the Mediterranean rim (Iberia to Levant), much of North Africa, Italy, the Balkans, Anatolia, parts of Central Europe and possibly Britain as a client or integrated province—boundaries adjusted by later contingencies. Successor or extra-European states: Outside the imperial ambit, consolidated polities (a unified Frankish realm, Slavic federations, Islamic caliphates expanded differently, and later colonial states in the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa, and East Asia) create a multipolar world. The Empire competes with and sometimes partners with maritime powers. Imperial fragmentation avoided or mitigated: Rather than a single uninterrupted polity by 2025, the Empire is likely a federated imperial system—suffragan kingdoms, semi-autonomous provinces, and imperial dynasties alternating with elective mechanisms—preventing collapse while allowing regional autonomy. Religion and ideology Religion pluralism anchored in Roman legalism: Early Christianity, or a pluralized Roman state religion that incorporated Christianity, remains influential but subject to imperial regulation. Religious plurality (Judaism, localized pagan survivals, later Islam and Eastern religions) exists with legal frameworks for toleration and civic participation. Secularization pathways: Enlightenment-like movements and commercial modernization produce robust secular administrative norms by the 19th–20th centuries; an imperial secular public sphere coexists with powerful religious institutions. Economy and technology Industrialization: The Empire experiences industrial revolutions driven by integrated markets, stable property law, and urban demand. State investment in infrastructure and military spurs rail, steam, later electric and digital technologies. Industrial centers cluster where Roman urban networks were densest. Trade networks: The Empire’s Mediterranean-centered trade orientation evolves into global commerce via long-distance maritime routes; imperial ports become hubs connecting to Atlantic and Indian Ocean circuits. Maritime technology advances compete with and eventually match Atlantic powers. Banking and corporate forms: Advanced Roman legal corporations (sodalitates, societates) evolve into joint-stock companies, central banking, and imperial-chartered trading companies. Rome-centric financial systems influence global credit norms. Military and diplomacy Professionalized legions: Legions transform into modern, well-funded standing forces with combined-arms doctrine, naval fleets, and expeditionary capabilities; conscription and recruitment adapt to demographic realities. Gunpowder, industrial warfare, nuclear age: The Empire participates fully in the technological military revolution. Its strategic choices (naval investments, alliances, nuclear development) shape 20th-century geopolitics. Balance with other great powers prevents unlimited expansion. Diplomacy: Roman legal diplomacy—treaties, client states, and provincial autonomy—produces layered influence: direct rule where feasible, client kingdoms and protectorates elsewhere, and trade-dominant zones beyond. Culture, identity, and languages Roman identity as civic, not ethnic: Imperial civic identity (civis Romana) emphasizes legal status, obligations, and urban participation rather than ethnicity. Cultural assimilation is patchy; local identities persist under Roman civic frameworks. Latin’s evolution: Vulgar Latin branches into multiple Romance languages with imperial Latin retained for law, liturgy, and academia. Greek remains influential in eastern provinces; multilingualism is common in elites. Arts and sciences: Patronage systems shift from emperors and aristocrats to universities, public institutions, and corporate sponsors. A continuous tradition of Roman engineering and medicine blends with global scientific developments. Colonialism and global expansion Atlantic exploration: Roman maritime institutions and entrepreneurial elites engage in Atlantic exploration. Depending on timing and internal politics, Rome might participate in early colonial ventures or be competed against by independent maritime republics and emergent Atlantic states. Americas and Asia: If Rome delays Atlantic expansion, independent colonial empires arise (Portuguese/Spanish-analogs, Dutch/English-analogs), producing a patchwork of territories. Alternatively, Roman-chartered companies acquire colonies, producing a Roman-speaking settler/merchant presence in the Americas or parts of Africa. Non-European contacts: Sustained contact with Chinese, Indian, and later Pacific polities leads to trade, technology transfer, and complex diplomacy rather than simple conquest. Science, education, and bureaucracy State-sponsored technical education: Roman practicality produces strong engineering schools and imperial academies; public health and civil engineering remain priorities. Literacy rates among urban populations are higher than in many historical analogs. Administrative continuity fosters record-keeping, statistics, and early modern state capacities (census, taxation, public works), accelerating institutional modernization. Possible alternative 20th–21st century dynamics Different alignments in world wars or great-power wars: If imperial fragmentation is limited, large-scale continental wars might occur between the Empire and other consolidated powers. The Empire’s size and resources could prevent dominance by any single non-imperial power, producing a multipolar 20th century with competing blocs. Cold-war analogues: Ideological divides (imperial corporatism vs. revolutionary republics, religious empires vs. secular federations) could create bipolar tensions that include spheres of influence, proxy conflicts, intelligence competition, and arms races including nuclear weapons. European integration replaced by imperial federalization: Instead of EU-style nation-states, regional federal assemblies and an imperial senate coordinate economic policy, standards, and internal mobility at an imperial scale. Society and daily life in 21st-century Roman Empire Urban-rural divide: Highly urbanized imperial cores with advanced services contrast with peripheral provinces with varying development. Provincial capitals are modern metros with Roman street plans, monumental continuity, and modern skyscrapers intermingled with ancient fabric. Civic rituals and symbolism: Imperial ceremonies, legal oaths, and municipal collegia persist as public rituals; imperial monuments and restored ancient sites are central to civic pride and tourism. Social mobility: Legal pathways (citizenship-by-service, trade-based citizenship, imperial grants) enable mobility. Aristocratic families persist but compete with bureaucratic meritocrats and industrial capitalists. Long-term cultural impact beyond the Empire Legal and bureaucratic export: Roman-derived legal codes and administrative practices diffuse globally through trade, education, and colonialism, shaping modern governance worldwide. Architectural and engineering legacy: Roman building methods evolve into modern construction norms in the imperial sphere; global architecture shows stronger classical continuity. Intellectual tradition: A continuous stream of classical scholarship, merged with scientific revolutions, produces different emphases in philosophy, law, and humanistic studies—less romantic nationalism, more civic-universalist discourse. Summary — plausible consequences The 21st-century world would be multipolar but strongly influenced by a Rome-centered legal, administrative, and infrastructural complex. Technological and industrial modernity develops within Roman institutional forms rather than in nation-state molds. Colonial and global expansions produce complex interactions with Americas, Asia, and Africa; outcomes depend crucially on early maritime strategy and whether Rome embraced or ceded Atlantic exploration. Socially and culturally, a Roman civic identity coexists with strong local cultures and multilingualism; legal-civic institutions and urban infrastructure are the Empire’s durable strengths. Global politics would differ in alignments, ideologies, and the balance of maritime vs. continental power, but modern technologies (industrialization, nuclear weapons, digital networks) and economic forces remain drivers—shaping a recognizable but distinct modern world. Examples and analogues Byzantine survival gives a model: An eastern Roman continuity (Byzantium) demonstrates how Roman law, bureaucracy, and urbanism can endure, adapt to new religions and languages, and project power for centuries. Ottoman adaptation shows how a premodern empire modernizes militarily and administratively under internal reform pressures. British imperial experience illustrates how an empire with maritime orientation, legal export, and industrial base shapes world systems—transpose British mechanisms onto Roman institutions for multiple plausible outcomes. This scenario emphasizes institutional adaptability, legal continuity, and urban infrastructure as the key mechanisms enabling a Roman Empire’s survival and modernization, producing a 21st century both recognizably Roman and reshaped by global technological and political currents.
