items.model_answer:
If humanity tried to evacuate the entire Earth with present-day technology, it would fail. Not because launching people into space is impossible, but because moving and sustaining billions of people away from Earth is far beyond our current energy, industrial, biological, and logistical capacity.

There are about 8 billion humans. Even if we imagined transporting only people, not homes, cities, livestock, ecosystems, or most possessions, the launch requirement would be enormous. A human with minimal life-support equipment, food, water, shielding, and habitat mass would likely require many tons of material per person. Modern rockets can place tens to a little over a hundred tons into low Earth orbit per launch. Evacuating billions would therefore require hundreds of millions to billions of heavy launches, depending on assumptions. That is many orders of magnitude beyond the total launch capacity humanity has ever built.

The harder problem is not reaching space; it is surviving there. Earth is not just a place humans stand on. It is our life-support system. It provides air, water cycling, food production, radiation shielding, gravity, waste recycling, and ecological stability. Space provides none of these for free. Any evacuation would need sealed habitats, power systems, agriculture, medical care, manufacturing, spare parts, radiation protection, and governance. We do not currently have even one fully self-sufficient off-world settlement, let alone infrastructure for billions.

Evacuating to another planet would not solve the problem quickly. The Moon has no atmosphere, no liquid water on the surface, no biosphere, low gravity, and high radiation exposure. Mars is more promising than the Moon in some ways, but it is still cold, dry, irradiated, and almost airless from a human perspective. Terraforming Mars, if possible at all, would take centuries to millennia. The nearest potentially habitable exoplanets are many light-years away; with current propulsion, travel times would be thousands to tens of thousands of years.

A total evacuation would also require moving enough of Earth’s biosphere to keep humans alive. That means not just crops and animals, but microbes, pollinators, soil systems, genetic diversity, and vast stores of biological knowledge. A space civilization could rely on artificial ecosystems, hydroponics, and synthetic biology, but building those at planetary scale would be one of the largest engineering projects imaginable.

If humanity had centuries or millennia of preparation, a partial or eventual evacuation becomes more plausible. We could build large orbital habitats, mine asteroids, use solar power, develop closed-loop life support, and move population growth into space gradually. In that scenario, “evacuating Earth” would probably not mean putting everyone on rockets at the last minute. It would mean slowly expanding into a Solar System civilization until most humans lived in artificial habitats, on Mars, in asteroid settlements, or around other planets.

If the evacuation were urgent—say, because of an incoming planet-killing asteroid, runaway solar event, or other near-term catastrophe—only a tiny fraction of humanity could likely be saved with current or near-future systems. The practical response would be to prevent the disaster if possible, not evacuate Earth. For example, deflecting an asteroid is far easier than moving billions of people off-planet.

So the careful answer is: a full evacuation of Earth is not feasible today and would remain impossible in any short emergency. With very long preparation and advanced space industry, humanity might gradually relocate large populations into space, but that would require turning the Solar System into a vast support network of habitats, farms, factories, and transport systems. Earth is not simply our address; it is the infrastructure that keeps us alive. Evacuating it would mean rebuilding much of that infrastructure somewhere else.

items.question: What If Everyone Had Exactly One Soulmate?
human_answers: What a nightmare that would be. There are a lot of problems with the concept of a single random soul mate. As Tim Minchin put it in his song If I Didn’t Have You: (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gaid72fqzNE) Your love is one in a million You couldn’t buy it at any price. But of the 9.999 hundred thousand other loves, Statistically, some of them would be equally nice. But what if we did have one randomly-assigned perfect soul mate, and we couldn’t be happy with anyone else? Would we find each other? We’ll assume your soul mate is set at birth. You know nothing about who or where they are, but—as in the romantic cliché—you’ll recognize each other the moment your eyes meet. Right away, this raises a few questions. For starters, is your soul mate even still alive? A hundred billion or so humans have ever lived, but only seven billion are alive now (which gives the human condition a 93% mortality rate). If we’re all paired up at random, 90% of our soul mates are long dead. [Image: image] That sounds horrible. But wait, it gets worse: A simple argument shows we can’t just limit ourselves to past humans; we have to include an unknown number of future humans as well. See, if it’s possible for your soul mate to be in the distant past, then it also has to be possible for soul mates to be in the distant future. After all, your soul mate’s soul mate is. So let’s assume your soul mate lives at the same time as you. Furthermore, to keep things from getting creepy, we’ll assume they’re within a few years of your age. (This is stricter than the standard age gap creepiness formula (http://xkcd.com/314/), but if we assume a 30-year-old and a 40-year-old can be soul mates, then the creepiness rule is violated if they accidentally meet 15 years earlier.) With the same-age restriction, most of us have a pool of around half a billion potential matches. But what about gender and sexual orientation? And culture? And language? We could keep using demographics to try to break things down further, but we’d be drifting away from the idea of a random soul mate. In our scenario, you don’t know anything about who your soul mate will be until you look into their eyes. Everybody has only one orientation—toward their soul mate. The odds of running into your soul mate are incredibly small. The number of strangers we make eye contact with each day is hard to estimate. It can vary from almost none (shut-ins or people in small towns) to many thousands (a police officer in Times Square). Let’s suppose you lock eyes with an average of a few dozen new strangers each day. (I’m pretty introverted, so for me that’s definitely a generous estimate.) If 10% of them are close to your age, that’s around 50,000 people in a lifetime. Given that you have 500,000,000 potential soul mates, it means you’ll only find true love in one lifetime out of ten thousand. [Image: image] But with the threat of dying alone looming so imminently, society could restructure to try to enable as much eye contact as possible. We could put together massive conveyer belts to move lines of people past each other … [Image: image] ... but if the eye contact effect works over webcams, we could just use a modified version of ChatRoulette. [Image: image] If everyone used the system for eight hours a day, seven days a week, and if it takes you a couple seconds to decide if someone’s your soul mate, this system could—in theory—match everyone up with their soul mates in a few decades. (I modeled a few simple systems to estimate how quickly people would pair off and drop out of the singles pool. If you want to try to work through the math for a particular setup, you might start by looking at derangement problems (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derangement).) In the real world, many people have trouble finding any time at all for romance—few could devote two decades to it. So maybe only rich kids would be able to afford to sit around on SoulMateRoulette. Unfortunately for the proverbial 1%, most of their soul mates are to be found in the other 99%. If only 1% of people use the service, then 1% of that 1% would find their match through this system—one in ten thousand. The other 99% of the 1% (“We are the zero point nine nine percent!”) would have an incentive to get more people into the system. They might sponsor projects akin to One Laptop Per Child (but with a sleazier vibe). Careers like “cashier” and “police officer in Times Square” would become high-status prizes because of the eye contact potential. People would flock to cities and public gathering places to find love—just as they do now. But even if a bunch of us spent years on SoulMateRoulette, another bunch of us managed to hold jobs that offered constant eye contact with strangers, and the rest of us just hoped for luck, only a small minority of us would ever find true love. The rest of us would be out of luck. Given all the stress and pressure, some people would fake it. They’d want to join the club, so they’d get together with another lonely person and stage a fake soul mate encounter. They’d marry, hide their relationship problems, and struggle to present a happy face to their friends and family. (Of course, this never happens in our world.) All in all, the world of random soul mates is an even lonelier one than ours. I prefer Tim Minchin’s take on things: With all my heart and all my mind I know one thing is true: I have just one life and just one love and, my love, that love is you. And if it wasn't for you, baby, I really think that I would have somebody else.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that every person has exactly one soulmate and that this constraint meaningfully changes human mating, search, and social systems.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the premise; treats soulmates as ordinary dating preferences or gives a generic romance answer.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one soulmate but applies the idea inconsistently or relies mostly on vague emotional claims.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the one-soulmate premise in most reasoning, with some attention to exclusivity and rarity.
criteria.7-8: Consistently explores how exclusivity, recognition, and random pairing would affect individuals and society.
criteria.9-10: Fully commits to the premise and derives nuanced consequences from exact one-to-one soulmate assignment across populations and time.

criteria.name: Search Probability and Demographic Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the odds of finding one's soulmate using population size, age cohorts, geography, mortality, future generations, and encounter rates.
criteria.1-2: Provides no quantitative or demographic reasoning; assumes everyone easily finds their soulmate.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes finding a soulmate is hard but gives little support or implausible numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses basic population or probability reasoning, though with gaps or oversimplified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains why random assignment makes discovery unlikely, considering age, location, and encounter frequency.
criteria.9-10: Offers strong probabilistic reasoning, including issues like past/future humans, same-age restrictions, lifetime encounters, and the scale mismatch between candidates and meetings.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Social and Technological Adaptation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream systems society might build or reshape to locate soulmates, such as mass screening, online matching, urbanization, labor incentives, surveillance, or institutional matchmaking.
criteria.1-2: Does not discuss societal or technological adaptation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions dating apps or matchmaking superficially without causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several adaptations but does not explain their feasibility, limits, or incentives.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible systems for increasing encounters and how they would alter behavior, work, status, and infrastructure.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, mechanism-level account of large-scale soulmate search systems, including participation constraints, unequal access, dropout effects, and unintended consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer builds coherent causal chains from the soulmate premise to long-term effects on family formation, inequality, mental health, culture, economics, and institutions.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected effects or makes abrupt unsupported claims.
criteria.3-4: Includes some consequences but weakly links them to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent chain from soulmate scarcity to personal or social outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Connects multiple domains through credible causal pathways over time.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning, tracing feedback loops among search pressure, loneliness, marriage norms, labor markets, inequality, deception, and cultural values.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer states assumptions, acknowledges uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes necessary consequences from speculative ones.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or changes the rules of the scenario without notice.
criteria.3-4: Contains noticeable unsupported certainty or inconsistent assumptions about how soulmates work.
criteria.5-6: States some assumptions and avoids major contradictions, but uncertainty handling is limited.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates assumptions from conclusions and qualifies uncertain social or numerical predictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, keeps all assumptions consistent, and flags alternative outcomes under different soulmate-recognition or assignment rules.

items.model_answer:
If everyone had exactly one soulmate, the world would become a giant matching problem: each person would be paired with one and only one other person. If “soulmate” means a mutual, uniquely compatible romantic partner, then mathematically humanity would have to be divided into pairs. That already creates complications: the number of people would need to be even, and births and deaths would either have to constantly reshuffle soulmates or allow people to have soulmates who are dead, not yet born, or unreachable.

The biggest practical consequence is that most people probably would not find their soulmate by chance. With about 8 billion people alive, the chance that any random person you meet is your one soulmate is roughly 1 in 8 billion. Even if you meaningfully meet 50,000 people in your lifetime, the chance of encountering the one randomly would still be only about 1 in 160,000. Unless there were some strong “fate” mechanism, objective test, or global matchmaking system, soulmates would mostly remain undiscovered.

If soulmates were assigned randomly among all living humans, most people’s soulmates would likely live far away, often in another country, speaking another language, and possibly separated by a large age gap. If soulmates were assigned among all humans who have ever lived, the situation would be worse: since roughly 100+ billion humans have existed and only about 8 billion are alive now, most living people’s soulmates would already be dead or not born yet.

If there were a reliable way to identify soulmates, society would change dramatically. Dating apps, governments, or genetic-style registries could pair people globally. Migration, marriage law, religion, and family planning would all adapt around verified soulmate matches. Long-distance relocation would become normal. Breakups and divorce might decrease if soulmate compatibility truly guaranteed a successful relationship, though people might still face issues of timing, culture, values, health, or choice.

But if there were no way to verify the match, belief in one soulmate could make people less happy. Many would reject good relationships while searching for an almost impossible ideal. Others might leave healthy partnerships because they feared the person was “not the one.” In that case, a one-soulmate universe would not necessarily be romantic; it would make love rarer, more anxious, and much more dependent on luck.

So the direct answer is: if everyone had exactly one soulmate, love would become objectively real but statistically hard to find. Without supernatural guidance or a perfect detection system, most people would never meet their soulmate. With such a system, human society would reorganize around global pairing, but it would raise enormous practical and ethical problems.

items.question: What If Earth's Landmasses Were Rotated by 90 Degrees?
human_answers: It would profoundly alter our biosphere in general and public radio in particular. Socke asks what would happen if the Earth’s surface were slid around by 90 degrees, putting our current North and South Poles on the equator. We’re not changing the tilt of the Earth’s axis; we’re just imagining that the surface were arranged differently. [Image: image] We’ll pick the Greenwich meridian for our new equator, putting the new North and South poles in the Indian ocean (0N, 90E) and off the coast of Ecuador (0N, 90W). India, Indonesia, and Ecuador would become polar, while Europe, Antarctica, and Alaska would become tropical. Where would the deserts and forests be? What areas would get better or worse? This stuff is complicated. In a moment, we'll start using wild speculation to reshape the face of the planet. But first, a brief story to illustrate just how mind-bogglingly complicated this stuff is: In Chad, on the southern outskirts of the Sahara, there’s valley called the Bodélé Depression. It was once a lakebed, and the dry dust in the valley floor is full of nutrient-rich matter from the microorganisms that lived there. From October to March, winds coming in from the east are pinched between two mountain ranges. When the surface winds climb over 20 mph, they start picking up dust from the valley. This dust is blown westward, all the way across Africa, and out over the Atlantic. That dirt—from one small valley in Chad—supplies over 50% of the nutrient-rich dust that helps fertilize the Amazon rainforest (http://iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/1/1/014005). At least, according to that one study. But if it's right, it wouldn’t be a crazy anomaly. This kind of complexity is found everywhere. The basic building blocks of our world are crazy. This is why we can be so certain about large-scale patterns like global warming, where we understand the overall physics pretty well—energy comes in, less energy goes out, so the average temperature rises—but have a harder time predicting how it will affect any particular place or specific species. So even if I were a climate expert—which I’m definitely not—there’d be no way to answer this question with certainty. There are just too many variables. Instead, think of what follows as a rough sketch of some of the things this alternate Earth could contain. To start, here’s a map of our reshuffled world: [Image: image] (An equirectangular projection, by the way. This type of equirectangular projection, centered on a north-south meridian instead of the equator, is specifically called a Cassini projection, so a good name for our alternate Earth might be "Cassini".) Let’s imagine that this alternate Earth develops over millions of years, with ecosystems and climate zones settling out. Then one day we wake up to find our current civilization has been magically transported there—cities and all. What would they find? The climate on the rotated Earth would depend heavily on the details of ocean and atmospheric heat circulation (http://eesc.columbia.edu/courses/ees/climate/lectures/gen_circ/index.html). We'll guess at some of that, but for now, let's assume this world has extremes which are similar to ours. So let's add some ice and permafrost near the poles and in mountainous areas: [Image: image] Next, we should fill in some green areas and deserts. The locations of these depend heavily on rainfall, so we’ll need to sketch out some winds. The main driver of our weather is the sun, which heats air near the equator more than at the poles. Hot air rises at the equator and then flows poleward, and cooler air moves in across the surface toward the equator. This circulation is called a Hadley cell (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_cell). [Image: image] Hadley cells shift north and south of the Equator with the seasons. At this time of year on our Earth, the sun is directly overhead at about 10°N, which is why hurricanes are forming near that latitude right now. Because of the Coriolis effect, the surface winds in a Hadley cell flow from east to west. Further north, for most of the temperate zones, the prevailing surface winds are west to east. (At times, there are also east-to-west winds circulating around the poles.) So let’s fill in some wind patterns—keeping in mind that in reality things would be further complicated by land interactions and the location of persistent high and low pressure systems. [Image: image] Sinking air is cool and dry, so land under the outer edges of the Hadley cells tends to be arid. These regions, lying a bit poleward of 30 degrees, are known as the horse latitudes (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_latitudes). [Image: image] The rising air at the equator carries moisture from the ocean, which then condenses into rain, so tropical areas are usually wet and thick with growth. Areas near the equator are sometimes dominated by a seasonal monsoon cycle (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon). In temperate zones, things are more variable. Weather there is dominated by the movement of jet streams and fronts, and depends heavily on geography. Most of the United States is in this type of region. With all that in mind, let’s fill in some arid and lush areas: [Image: image] (Climates can be hard to predict—for example, in our world, Somalia and French Guiana both sit on the equator, at the eastern coast of a continent, and seem like they should both receive a tropical sea breeze. But coastal French Guiana is dense rain forest while coastal Somalia is an arid desert. The explanation involves the monsoon cycle.) And just for fun, here’s a wild guess as to where the hurricane basins would be: [Image: image] Let’s take a closer look at each continent. North America has a range of climates similar to what it had before, but flipped north-south. The Arctic Canadian provinces are now tropical, while Central America is icy and polar. Hurricanes threaten Greenland, Baffin Island, and the Maritimes. Tropical moisture from Baffin Bay and the northwest (formerly north) Atlantic mixes with cool air flowing down through the US from the Rockies, creating a new Tornado Alley in the prairies inland from Hudson Bay. South America looks sort of like the old Europe. It's cool and temperate along the Brazilian coast, with boreal forests and grasslands across much of its width. In the south, the boreal vegetation gives way to polar tundra, and eventually to the massive icebound Andes, which cut the continent off from the frozen polar waters. The Amazon, which in our world carries more water than the next seven largest rivers put together, is reduced to something akin to the Mississippi. Asia is flipped in the same way North America was, with the Siberian coast facing an enclosed tropical sea. The Indian subcontinent and north (formerly southeast) Asia form the new Siberia. The Gobi Desert is no longer in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, but doesn't exactly become tropical. Europe resembles the old southeast Asia. Great Britain and Ireland look like the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo. Iceland resembles our Philippines. Central Europe is the new New Guinea, with the Alps the only place on the Equator with permanent glaciers. Africa is rotated 90 degrees, with south (formerly west) Africa becoming tropical rainforest and north (formerly east) Africa an arid desert. On our Earth, North America is the only continent where tornadoes are common, but in this world, they're frequent in East Africa as well. Australia is cooler and wetter, with forests across the northern (formerly western) regions. Antarctica is a clear winner. Without its ice cap, it’s a bit smaller than we remember, but most of it is blanketed with highland rainforest. There are alpine zones around the mountains to the south and west. The researchers at McMurdo and Scott Base on Ross Island wake up to a tropical paradise. If any of them find they miss the frozen wastelands, they can always put in for a transfer to Costa Rica. Now, let’s see how the world’s largest cities fare: [Image: image] Some cities get colder. Mexico City, high in the polar mountains, is buried beneath an ice sheet. Jakarta is the new Svalbard—a desolate coastal rock too far north even for most Norwegians. Kolkata and Delhi are icebound, sealed off from the warmer world by the Himalayas. Hong Kong, Manila, Karachi, and Mumbai are similar to our world’s Anchorage or Reykjavik—the ocean isn’t frozen, but it sure is cold. A few cities remain perfectly habitable, albeit with some changes: Seoul, Osaka, Tokyo, Shanghai, and New York City are among the least-affected cities, with climates roughly similar to their previous ones. Shanghai does get colder, but seasonal extremes in all five cities get milder—particularly in Seoul—and substantially wetter. Cairo is moved slightly south. It’s now surrounded by coastal savannah, with spots of rain forest found around the mouth of the Nile. Though it moves closer to the equator, it doesn’t actually get hotter. São Paulo and Buenos Aires cool down a bit. They’re now on the northern coast of a South America, which occupies a Canadalike range of latitudes. Their climate is somewhere between that of our New England and that of our Regular England. Los Angeles is cool and mild. The steady sea breeze carrying moisture up into the San Gabriel mountains makes LA one of the rainiest places in the new US. It closely resembles a wetter version of our Seattle. And a few cities get much hotter. Moscow is extremely hot and very dry, with a climate somewhere between our Phoenix and our Baghdad. Russians, who have been surviving in Russia for centuries, shrug with resignation. London sits in a steamy jungle straddling the equator, with a climate generally resembling Manila's. The food is still bland, the Thames is full of piranha, and it's the only place on Earth where tigers apologize as they attack you. At the beginning, I mentioned the impact on public radio. To explain, let’s consider one more scenario. Namely, what if this change were made on our Earth, over a fairly short time? We’re assuming that all the material is magically shifted around, so there are no massive tsunamis or earthquakes. Even so, it would definitely still be a catastrophe. For starters, the ice caps would melt long before new ones could develop, pushing the ocean up by a few hundred feet. The reshuffling of climate zones would come as a huge shock to the biosphere, leading to collapse of the food chain and eventually to mass extinctions at every level. But if the shift happened just right—and Michael Bay were telling the story—then as the waters of the Gulf of Mexico began to cool and the Mississippi slowed and became an estuary, the region’s wildlife would spread inland. And one morning, Minnesotans would wake up to the sight of floating rafts of fire ants (http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2011/04/pictures/110425-fire-ants-life-rafts-swarms-science-proceedings/), followed by five million lost, hungry alligators … [Image: image] … leading a harrowing, surprisingly bloody “News from Lake Wobegon” segment on what would become the final, fatal broadcast of A Prairie Home Companion.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly applies the specific premise: Earth's landmasses/surface features are rotated 90 degrees relative to the spin axis while axial tilt, solar forcing, rotation, and basic planetary physics remain unchanged.
criteria.1-2: Misunderstands the premise, changes Earth's tilt/orbit/rotation, or treats the scenario as physical tectonic rotation with irrelevant catastrophes only.
criteria.3-4: Partly recognizes land relocation but confuses poles/equator, latitude changes, or rotates only selected continents inconsistently.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the 90-degree landmass relocation and notes latitude shifts, but leaves important geographic implications vague or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Accurately tracks the new polar/equatorial placement of major regions and preserves unchanged planetary drivers with only minor slips.
criteria.9-10: Precisely and consistently applies the rotated-surface premise across continents, oceans, cities, climates, and biosphere without introducing premise-breaking assumptions.

criteria.name: Climate and Geophysical Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the main physical mechanisms determining the rotated Earth's outcomes, including latitude, insolation, atmospheric circulation, ocean currents, mountains, rain shadows, ice, deserts, monsoons, and storms.
criteria.1-2: Gives unsupported guesses about hot/cold regions with little or no climate mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions latitude or temperature but omits most circulation, ocean, precipitation, and topographic effects.
criteria.5-6: Explains several key mechanisms such as equatorial heating, polar ice, and rainfall, but treatment is shallow or misses major interactions.
criteria.7-8: Covers Hadley cells, prevailing winds, ocean moderation, mountains, deserts, forests, ice, and storm zones with generally sound causal links.
criteria.9-10: Integrates atmospheric and ocean circulation, seasonal shifts, topography, hydrology, cryosphere, and ecological feedbacks into a nuanced, question-specific climate sketch.

criteria.name: Regional and Downstream Consequence Specificity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives concrete, plausible consequences for major regions and human/ecological systems affected by the 90-degree rotation.
criteria.1-2: Offers only broad statements such as 'everything changes' without region-specific consequences.

items.model_answer:
If Earth’s landmasses were merely rotated 90 degrees east or west around the spin axis, the result would be surprisingly minor in physical terms: continents would occupy different longitudes, but because longitude has little effect on sunlight, seasons, or climate by itself, Earth would mostly work the same. Time zones, maps, and ocean-current details would change, but the basic climate pattern would remain similar.

If instead the landmasses were rotated 90 degrees relative to the poles and equator, the consequences would be enormous. Latitude is one of the strongest controls on climate, so continents that are now tropical could become temperate or polar, while polar or high-latitude land could move toward the tropics. Antarctica, if moved far from the South Pole, would begin losing much of its ice over time, raising global sea level by tens of meters. Meanwhile, new polar land areas could accumulate ice sheets if they received enough snowfall.

Ocean circulation would be radically reorganized. The positions of continents control where warm and cold currents flow, where deep water forms, and whether ocean basins are open or blocked. A rotated arrangement could shut down something like the modern Atlantic overturning circulation, alter El Niño-like patterns, change sea-ice extent, and produce completely different coastal climates.

Rainfall and deserts would also shift. Mountains rotated into new orientations relative to prevailing winds would create new rain shadows. Monsoons might appear in places that are now dry, while fertile regions could become deserts. The locations of forests, grasslands, tundra, and agricultural zones would be almost entirely rearranged.

For life and human civilization, the short-term result would be catastrophic if the change happened suddenly: earthquakes, tsunamis, crustal disruption, climate shock, ecosystem collapse, and the loss of many coastal cities. Over longer timescales, Earth would settle into a new climate equilibrium, but it would be a very different planet, with new ice caps, new deserts, new ocean currents, and new habitable zones.

So the answer depends on the kind of “90-degree rotation.” A simple rotation in longitude would be mostly cosmetic. A rotation that changes the continents’ latitudes would transform Earth’s climate, oceans, ice sheets, ecosystems, and human geography.

items.question: What If All the Raindrops in a Storm Merged into One Giant Drop?
human_answers: It’s midsummer. The air is hot and heavy. Two old-timers sit on the porch in rocking chairs. [Image: image] On the horizon to the southwest, ominous-looking clouds begin to appear. The towers build as they draw closer, the tops spreading out into an anvil shape. [Image: image] They hear the tinkling of wind chimes as gentle breeze picks up. The sky begins to darken. Air holds water. If you walled off a column of air, from the ground up to the top of the atmosphere, and then cooled the column of air down, the moisture it contained would condense out as rain. If you collected the rain in the bottom of the column, it would fill it to a depth of anywhere between zero and a few dozen centimeters. That depth is what we call the air’s total precipitable water. [Image: image] Normally, the TPW is one or two centimeters. Satellites measure this water vapor content for every point on the globe, producing some truly beautiful maps (http://tropic.ssec.wisc.edu/real-time/mimic-tpw/natl/main.html). We’ll imagine our storm measures 100 kilometers on each side and has a high TPW content of 6 centimeters. This means the water in our rainstorm would have a volume of: \[100\textrm{km}\times100\textrm{km}\times6\textrm{cm}=0.6\textrm{km}^3\] That water would weigh 600 million tons (which happens to be about the current weight of our species). Normally, a portion of this water would fall, scattered, as rain—at most, 6 centimeters of it. In this storm, all that water instead condenses into one giant drop, a sphere of water over a kilometer in diameter. We’ll assume it forms a couple kilometers above the surface, since that’s where most rain condenses (http://rsd.gsfc.nasa.gov/912/edop/misc/1736.pdf). [Image: image] The drop begins to fall. For five or six seconds, nothing is visible. Then, the base of the cloud begins to bulge downward. For a moment, it looks a little like a funnel cloud is forming. Then the bulge widens, and at the ten-second mark, the bottom of the drop emerges from the cloud. [Image: image] The drop is now falling at 90 meters per second (200 mph). The roaring wind whips up the surface of the water into spray. The leading edge of the droplet turns to foam as air is forced into the liquid. If it kept falling for long enough, these forces would gradually disperse the entire droplet into rain. Before that can happen, about 20 seconds after formation, the edge of the droplet hits the ground. The water is now moving at over 200 m/s (450 mph). Right under the point of impact, the air is unable to rush out of the way fast enough, and the compression heats it so quickly that the grass would catch fire if it had time. Fortunately for the grass, this heat lasts only a few milliseconds because it’s doused by the arrival of a lot of cold water. Unfortunately for the grass, the cold water is moving at over half the speed of sound. [Image: image] If you were floating in the center of this sphere during this episode, you wouldn’t have felt anything unusual up until now. It’d be pretty dark in the middle, but if you had enough time (and lung capacity) to swim a few hundred meters out toward the edge, you’d be able to make out the dim glow of daylight. [Image: image] As the raindrop approached the ground, the buildup of air resistance would lead to an increase in pressure that would make your ears pop. But seconds later, when the water contacted the surface, you’d be crushed to death—the shock would briefly create pressures exceeding those at the bottom of the Marianas Trench. The water plows into the ground, but the bedrock is unyielding. The pressure forces the water sideways, creating a supersonic omnidirectional jet that destroys everything in its path. [Image: image] The wall of water expands outward kilometer by kilometer, ripping up trees, houses, and topsoil as it goes. The house, porch, and old-timers are obliterated in an instant. Everything within a few kilometers is completely destroyed, leaving a pool of mud down to bedrock. The splash continues outward, demolishing all structures out to distances of 20 or 30 kilometers. At this distance, areas shielded by mountains or ridges are protected, and the flood begins to flow along natural valleys and waterways. The broader region is largely protected from the effects of the storm, though areas hundreds of kilometers downstream experience flash flooding in the hours after the impact. News trickles out into the world about the inexplicable disaster. There is widespread shock and puzzlement, and for a while, every new cloud in the sky causes mass panic. Fear reigns supreme as the world fears rain supreme, but years pass without any signs of the disaster repeating. Atmospheric scientists try for years to piece together what happened, but no explanation is forthcoming. Eventually, they give up, and the unexplained meteorological phenomenon is simply dubbed a “Skrillex Storm”—because, in the words of one researcher, “It had one hell of a drop.”

items.model_answer:
If all the raindrops in a storm merged into one giant drop, it would not behave like an oversized raindrop for long. It would become a huge falling mass of water, more like a temporary airborne lake than a drop.

The size depends on how much rain the storm contains. For example, if a storm drops 1 cm of rain over 100 km², that is about 1,000,000 m³ of water, with a mass of about 1 billion kg. If gathered into a sphere, it would be roughly 120 m across.

In real physics, such a drop could not stay intact. Normal raindrops larger than about 5–6 mm already become unstable and break apart because air resistance overcomes surface tension. A drop tens or hundreds of meters wide would have essentially no “drop-like” stability. As it fell, air pressure would flatten it, tear it into sheets, and shred it into spray and smaller drops almost immediately. The result would probably be a violent burst of rain, mist, and turbulent water fragments rather than one clean impact.

If, by magic, the giant drop were forced to remain intact until it hit the ground, the impact would be disastrous. Using the example above, a 1-billion-kg water sphere falling from a few kilometers up would carry energy comparable to several kilotons of TNT. It would smash down as a massive water bomb, producing a shock wave, extreme local flooding, destructive water pressure, and possibly a crater or severe ground erosion depending on the terrain.

So the realistic answer is: it would break apart almost instantly and turn back into chaotic rain and spray. The counterfactual “intact giant drop” answer is: it would be a catastrophic concentrated impact, because all the storm’s rainfall energy and water volume would be dumped onto one small area at once.

items.question: What If Everyone on Earth Pointed a Laser Pointer at the Moon?
human_answers: Not if we use regular laser pointers. The first thing to consider is that not everyone can see the Moon at once. We could gather everyone in one spot, but we learned our lesson about that (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/) a few weeks ago. Instead, let’s just pick a time when the Moon is visible to as many people as possible. Since about 75% of the world’s population lives between 0°E and 120°E (http://www.good.is/posts/mapping-the-world-s-population-by-latitude-longitude/), we should try this while the Moon is somewhere over the Arabian Sea. We can try to illuminate either a new moon or a full moon. The new moon is darker, making it easier to see our lasers. But the new moon is a trickier target, because it’s mostly visible during the day—washing out the effect. Brightness aside, an ideal time would probably be 2:00 PM EST on December 27th, 2012, when a full moon will be high in the sky above Mumbai and Islamabad. At that point, the Moon will be visible to approximately five billion people—most of Asia, Europe, and Africa—about as many as can ever see it at one time. But let’s pick a quarter moon instead, so we can see the effect on the dark side. We’ll avoid the December 21st quarter moon to avoid encouraging any Mayan nonsense, and pick the one on January 4th, 2013, half an hour after midnight (GMT). It’ll be day in East Asia but night in Africa and Europe. Here’s our target: [Image: image] The typical red laser pointer is about 5 milliwatts, and a good one has a tight enough beam to actually hit the Moon—though it’d be spread out over a large fraction of the surface when it got there. The atmosphere would distort the beam a bit, and absorb some of it, but most of the light would make it. [Image: image] Let’s assume everyone has steady enough aim to hit the Moon, but no more than that, and the light is spread evenly across the surface. At half an hour after midnight (GMT), everyone aims and presses the button. This is what happens: [Image: image] Well, that’s disappointing. It makes sense, though. Sunlight bathes the Moon in a bit over a kilowatt of energy per square meter. Since the Moon’s cross-sectional area is around 10^13 square meters, it’s bathed in about 10^16 watts of sunlight—ten petawatts, or two megawatts per person—far outshining their five milliwatt laser pointer. There are varying efficiencies in each part of this system, but none of it changes that basic equation. [Image: image] 5 milliwatts is wimpy. We can do better. A 1-watt laser is an extremely dangerous thing. It’s not just powerful enough to blind you—it’s capable of burning skin and setting things on fire. Obviously, they’re not legal for consumer purchase in the US. Just kidding! You can pick one up for $300 (http://www.wickedlasers.com/arctic). So suppose we spend the $2 trillion to buy one-watt green lasers for everyone. (Memo to presidential candidates: this policy would win my vote.) In addition to being more powerful, green laser light is nearer to the middle of the visible spectrum, so the eye is more sensitive to it and it seems brighter. Here’s the effect: [Image: image] Dang. The laser pointers we’re using put out about 150 lumens of light (more than most flashlights) in a beam 5 arc-minutes wide. This lights up the surface of the Moon with about half a lux (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lux) of illumination—compared to about 130,000 lux from the sun. (Even if we aimed them all perfectly, it would only manage half a dozen lux over about 10% of the Moon’s face.) By comparison, the full moon lights up the Earth’s surface with about one lux of illumination—which means that not only would our lasers be too weak to see from Earth, but if you were standing on the Moon, the laser light on the landscape would be fainter than Moonlight is to us on Earth. [Image: image] With advances in lithium batteries and LED technology over the last ten years, the high-performance flashlight market has exploded. But it’s clear that flashlights aren’t gonna cut it. So let’s skip past all of that and give everyone a Nightsun. You may not recognize the name, but chances are you’ve seen one in operation: It’s the searchlight mounted on police and Coast Guard helicopters. With an output on the order of 50,000 lumens, it’s capable of turning a patch ground from night to day. The beam is several degrees wide, we’ll want some focusing lenses to get it down to the half-degree needed to hit the Moon. Here’s the effect: [Image: image] It’s hard to see, but we’re making progress! The beam is providing 20 lux of illumination, outshining the ambient light on the night half by a factor of two! However, it’s quite hard to see, and it certainly hasn’t affected the light half. [Image: image] Let’s swap out each Nightsun for an IMAX projector array—a 30,000-watt pair of water-cooled lamps with a combined output of over over a million lumens. [Image: image] Still barely visible. [Image: image] At the top of the Luxor Hotel in Las Vegas is the most powerful spotlight on Earth. Let’s give one of them to everyone. [Image: image] Oh, and let’s add a lens array to each so the entire beam is focused on the Moon: [Image: image] Our light is definitely visible, so we’ve accomplished our goal! Good job, team. [Image: image] … Well. The Department of Defense has developed megawatt lasers, designed for destroying incoming missiles in mid-flight. The Boeing YAL-1 was a megawatt-class chemical oxygen iodine laser mounted in a 747. It was an infrared laser, so it wasn’t directly visible, but we can imagine building a visible-light laser with similar power. Let’s give one to everyone. [Image: image] Finally, we’ve managed to match the brightness of sunlight! We’re also drawing five petawatts of power, which is double the world’s average electricity consumption. [Image: image] Ok, let’s mount a megawatt laser on every square meter of the surface of Asia. Powering this array of 50 trillion lasers would use up Earth’s oil reserves in approximately two minutes, but for those two minutes, the Moon would look like this: [Image: image] The Moon shines as brightly as the midmorning sun, and by the end of the two minutes, the lunar regolith is heated to a glow. [Image: image] Ok, let’s step even more firmly outside the realm of plausibility. The most powerful laser on Earth is the confinement beam at the National Ignition Facility (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ignition_Facility), a fusion research laboratory. It’s an ultraviolet laser with an output of 500 terawatts. However, it only fires in single pulses lasting a few nanoseconds, so the total energy delivered is about equivalent to a quarter-cup of gasoline. Let’s imagine we somehow found a way to power and fire it continuously, gave one to everyone, and pointed them all at the Moon. Unfortunately, the laser energy flow would turn the atmosphere to plasma, instantly igniting the Earth’s surface and killing us all. But let’s assume that the lasers somehow pass through the atmosphere without interacting. Under those circumstances, it turns out Earth still catches fire. The reflected light from the Moon would be four thousand times brighter than the noonday sun. Moonlight would become bright enough to boil away Earth’s oceans in less than a year. But forget the Earth—what would happen to the Moon? The laser itself would exert enough radiation pressure to accelerate the Moon at about one ten millionth of a gee. This acceleration wouldn’t be noticeable in the short term, but over the years, it adds up to enough to push it free from Earth orbit. … If radiation pressure were the only force involved. 40 megajoules of energy is enough (http://www.psfc.mit.edu/library1/catalog/reports/2000/09rr/09rr011/09rr011_full.pdf) to vaporize a kilogram of rock. Assuming Moon rocks have an average density of about 3 kg/liter, the lasers would pump out enough energy to vaporize four meters of lunar bedrock per second: \[\frac{5\text{ billion people}\times 500\frac{\mathrm{terawatts}}{\text{person}}}{\pi\times\text{Moon radius}^2}\times20\frac{\mathrm{megajoules}}{\mathrm{kilogram}}\times 3\frac{\mathrm{kilograms}}{\mathrm{liter}}\approx4 \frac{\mathrm{meters}}{\text{second}}\] However, the actual lunar rock won’t evaporate that fast—for a reason that turns out to be very important. When a chunk of rock is vaporized, it doesn’t just disappear. The surface layer of the Moon becomes a plasma, but that plasma is still blocking the path of the beam. Our laser keeps pouring more and more energy into the plasma, and the plasma keeps getting hotter and hotter. The particles bounce off each other, slam into the surface of the Moon, and eventually blast away into space at a terrific speed. This flow of material effectively turns the entire surface of the Moon into a rocket engine—and a surprisingly efficient one, too. Using lasers to blast off surface material like this is called laser ablation, and it turns out to be a promising method for spacecraft propulsion (http://materials.web.psi.ch/Publications/Publ_MatDev_files/2010/Claude_JPP_2010.pdf). The Moon is massive, but slowly and surely the rock plasma jet begins to push it away from the Earth. (The jet would also scour clean the face of the Earth and destroy the lasers, but we’re pretending for the moment that they’re invulnerable.) The plasma also physically tears away the lunar surface, a complicated interaction that’s tricky to model. But if we make the wild guess that the particles in the plasma exit at an average speed of 500 kilometers per second, then it will take a few months for the Moon to be pushed out of range of our laser. It will keep most of its mass, but escape Earth’s gravity and enter a lopsided orbit around the sun. Technically, the Moon won’t become a new planet, under the IAU definition of a planet. Since its new orbit crosses Earth’s, it will be considered a dwarf planet like Pluto. This Earth-crossing orbit will lead to periodic unpredictable orbital perturbation. Eventually it will either be slingshotted into the Sun, ejected toward the outer Solar System, or slammed into one of the planets—quite possibly ours. I think we can all agree that in this case, we’d deserve it. Scorecard: [Image: image] And that, at last, is enough power.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone on Earth Pointed a Laser Pointer at the Moon?

criteria.name: Ordinary Laser Pointer Outcome and Scaling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the actual premise of billions of ordinary laser pointers aimed at the Moon, including visibility limits, beam spread, and comparison with solar illumination.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary laser pointers would visibly brighten, damage, move, or significantly heat the Moon with little or no quantitative support.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes the effect is small but gives vague or flawed reasoning, omitting key scale comparisons such as sunlight versus milliwatts per person.
criteria.5-6: Correctly concludes ordinary pointers are not visible from Earth and explains this mainly through total power or beam dilution, with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Uses sound order-of-magnitude reasoning: only part of humanity can see the Moon, beams spread over a large area, and sunlight overwhelms milliwatt lasers.
criteria.9-10: Clearly shows why the effect is negligible using relevant scales such as billions of 5 mW lasers, lunar surface area, atmospheric loss, beam divergence, and solar illumination around kilowatts per square meter.

criteria.name: Geometric and Observational Setup
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of Moon visibility, lunar phase, aiming, atmospheric transmission, and whether the illuminated region could be observed from Earth.
criteria.1-2: Ignores geometry entirely or assumes everyone on Earth can point at the Moon simultaneously without qualification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions visibility or phase but handles it inconsistently, such as placing the Moon overhead for everyone or confusing new, full, and quarter Moon effects.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that only a fraction of people can see the Moon and that lunar phase matters, but gives only a rough setup.
criteria.7-8: Accounts for hemisphere/time-zone constraints, atmospheric distortion or absorption, target phase, and why aiming at the dark portion would matter for detectability.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent observational scenario: maximizes participating population, chooses a phase that aids contrast, distinguishes day/night viewing issues, and keeps beam focus and surface coverage physically plausible.

criteria.name: Power Escalation and Brightness Thresholds
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores how increasingly powerful light sources would change the result, rather than treating all lasers as equivalent.
criteria.1-2: Uses a single unsupported claim for all laser powers or confuses brightness, energy, and visibility.
criteria.3-4: Mentions stronger lasers but gives implausible thresholds or no causal explanation for when the Moon becomes visibly brighter.
criteria.5-6: Explains that higher-power devices would be needed and gives approximate qualitative stages, but lacks clear comparisons to lux, sunlight, or lunar illumination.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes ordinary pointers, watt-class lasers, searchlights/projectors, and megawatt-class lasers, with reasonable visibility and power-demand consequences.
criteria.9-10: Accurately tracks escalating regimes: consumer pointers fail, very bright lamps barely help, massive focused searchlights become visible, and megawatt-per-person lasers approach solar-level lunar illumination while requiring planetary-scale power.

criteria.name: Extreme-Energy Lunar and Terrestrial Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates reasoning about far-counterfactual cases involving enormous lasers, including atmospheric plasma, reflected light, heating, vaporization, ablation, and lunar orbital effects.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to spectacular outcomes such as instant Moon explosion or harmless visibility without mechanisms or scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heating or destruction but misses major processes such as atmosphere interaction, reflected radiation, or ablation.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that extreme lasers could heat or vaporize lunar material and endanger Earth, but gives a short or partially incomplete chain.
criteria.7-8: Explains that sufficiently extreme beams would ionize air, ignite or sterilize Earth, heat lunar regolith, vaporize rock, and produce thrust through ejecta.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent high-energy sequence: atmosphere would become plasma unless assumed transparent, reflected Moonlight could exceed sunlight, lunar surface vaporizes into plasma, laser ablation acts like a rocket, and the Moon could be pushed from Earth orbit over time.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence, Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the counterfactual chain remains internally consistent, appropriately caveated, and calibrated across ordinary, powerful, and impossible laser scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible transitions, or uncaveated certainties that violate earlier assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct pieces but mixes incompatible assumptions, exaggerates precision, or changes the premise without noting it.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with some caveats, but leaves gaps between stages or overstates uncertain long-term outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains consistent assumptions about power, focusing, atmosphere, and duration; marks speculative parts such as ablation efficiency and later orbital evolution.
criteria.9-10: Separates realistic from deliberately impossible cases, states assumptions before using them, avoids false precision, preserves conservation-of-energy intuition, and treats long-term Moon trajectories as uncertain but causally motivated.

items.model_answer:
Almost nothing noticeable would happen.

Assume about 8 billion people each use an ordinary red laser pointer, around 5 milliwatts. That is a total emitted power of roughly 40 megawatts, but only the people on the Moon-facing side of Earth could actually aim at it at once, and clouds/atmosphere would reduce it further.

Even under ideal conditions, the beams would spread enormously. A typical laser pointer beam diverges by about a milliradian, so by the time it reaches the Moon it makes a spot hundreds of kilometers wide. Spread over that area, the combined light is only about \(10^{-4}\ \text{W/m}^2\), while sunlight at the Moon is about \(1{,}360\ \text{W/m}^2\). So the laser illumination would be tens of millions of times dimmer than sunlight.

From Earth, you would not see the Moon turn red or brighten. Against the sunlit Moon it would be utterly invisible. Even on the dark part of the Moon, Earthshine and background glare would swamp it. With sensitive astronomical equipment under carefully chosen conditions, you might be able to detect some tiny red signal, but to human eyes there would be no visible effect.

So the direct answer is: if everyone on Earth pointed a normal laser pointer at the Moon, the Moon would look unchanged. The combined lasers are powerful by human standards, but negligible compared with sunlight and spread far too widely by the time they reach the Moon.

items.question: What If a Giant Water Hose Focused on the Sun?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give short answers to several reader questions. Your brother might be surprised to learn that the water would actually make the Sun hotter! [Image: image] Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, which is fuel for the Sun’s fusion. But more importantly, the extra mass also makes the Sun heavier. This crushes it together more tightly and makes fusion happen faster. This means it will burn more brightly and run through its fuel more quickly. As you keep adding water, the Sun will go through a lot of wacky fusion phases. (During one phase, called a helium flash, the reaction rate is proportional to the 40th power of the temperature—which is probably the largest exponent I’ve ever seen in a physics equation!) But one way or another, eventually the whole thing will collapse in on itself, blow off its outer layers, and become a black hole. This black hole will keep soaking up water, spraying off X-rays in the process, until finally the municipal water department notices what you’ve been doing and shuts off your service. Believe it or not, you’ve been lied to all your life—there’s no such thing as one-way mirror glass. Glass either lets light through or reflects it, but there’s no glass that lets light through one way and reflects it the other way. The glass in police shows is partially reflective (on both sides). The key is that the room on the prisoner’s side is brightly lit, so the reflection washes out the small amount of light from the observers’ side. [Image: image] He’d most likely black out and die somewhere between 100 and 400 meters. [Image: image] The human body handles pressure remarkably well. With the right preparation, we can survive pressures over a dozen atmospheres. Different body systems break down at different depths, but one of the trickiest limits is created by High Pressure Nervous Syndrome (http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/xmlui/handle/123456789/2661). Below about 100 meters, divers become jittery and excitable (especially if the pressure increase is rapid), and at the same time begin slipping in and out of sleep. The reason may be direct pressure on the brain (http://jn.physiology.org/content/92/6/3309.full.pdf). But let’s suppose Michael Phelps were immune to all those things. In that case, it simply becomes a question of speed. There aren’t very many records for underwater swimming, but based on how quickly this guy (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vox9KOxC1ZA) completed the 50m backstroke, it would probably take Michael about ... \[ 2\times\text{Depth of Marianas Trench}\times\frac{23.1\textrm{ seconds}}{50\textrm{ meters}}\approx3\textrm{ hours} \] … to make the trip. Someone recently blew my mind by telling me I’d been misinterpreting that scene all my life. I like their take on it way better: Superman wasn't exerting a force on the Earth. He was just flying fast enough to go back in time. (Faster than light, I guess? Comic book physics.) The Earth changed direction because we were watching time run backward as he traveled. It didn't actually have anything to do with the direction he was flying. Now that I see it, it makes a lot more sense. I mean, as much sense as a red-cape-and-outside-underwear time traveler can make. A discussion of the reversal of the Earth’s spin—and what that even means—will have to wait for another article. \[ \frac{\text{Red light wavelength}}{\text{Green light wavelength}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+\frac{\text{Your speed}}{\text{Speed of light}}}{1-\frac{\text{Car speed}}{\text{Speed of light}}}} \] \[ \textrm{Car speed}=\frac{\textrm{c}\times\left ( \textrm{Red light wavelength}^2-\textrm{Green light wavelength}^2\right )}{\textrm{Green light wavelength}^2+\textrm{Red light wavelength}^2}\approx\frac{1}{6}c \] Bernoulli’s principle (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli's_principle#Incompressible_flow_equation) gives us this estimate of the air flow rate: \[ \text{Flow rate}=\sqrt{2\times\frac{\text{Sea level pressure}-\text{Mexico City pressure}}{\text{Density of air}}}=440\textrm{ mph} \] That’s fast enough to strip up the pavement from a parking lot. I suggest we put it in Kendall Square—the MIT folks are probably used to dealing with this kind of thing. This ... isn’t actually a question. [Image: image] But thank you for sharing!

items.model_answer:
A giant water hose would not put out the Sun. The Sun is not burning by chemical combustion, so it does not need oxygen and cannot be “smothered” by water. Its power comes from nuclear fusion in its core.

If you somehow aimed a magic hose at the Sun, the water would boil, split into hydrogen and oxygen, and then become ionized plasma long before or as it entered the solar atmosphere. The material would simply mix into the outer layers of the Sun. The hydrogen would be additional potential fusion fuel, though it would take a very long time to reach the core, and the oxygen would just be a trace “metal” contaminant in stellar terms.

For any realistic amount of water, the effect would be tiny. All of Earth’s oceans have a mass of about \(1.4\times10^{21}\) kg, while the Sun’s mass is about \(2\times10^{30}\) kg. That is less than one-billionth of the Sun’s mass. Dumping the oceans into the Sun would not cool it; in fact, the infalling water would release a lot of gravitational energy as it fell, briefly adding heat and light. The energy released by dropping all Earth’s oceans onto the Sun is roughly comparable to several days of the Sun’s normal output.

If the hose supplied an absurdly large amount of water, comparable to a significant fraction of the Sun’s mass, then the Sun would become more massive. A more massive Sun would generally burn hotter and brighter and have a shorter lifetime. Add enough mass and you would turn it into a different kind of star; add vastly more and you could eventually create stellar instability or even gravitational collapse.

So the direct answer is: a giant water hose aimed at the Sun would not extinguish it. Small amounts would do essentially nothing; Earth-ocean-sized amounts would make a brief splash energetically but not matter much; truly enormous amounts would make the Sun larger, hotter, and brighter rather than put it out.

edus.text: A giant water hose would not put out the Sun.
The Sun is not burning by chemical combustion,
so it does not need oxygen
and cannot be “smothered” by water.
Its power comes from nuclear fusion in its core.
If you somehow aimed a magic hose at the Sun,
the water would boil, split into hydrogen and oxygen,
and then become ionized plasma long before or as it entered the solar atmosphere.
The material would simply mix into the outer layers of the Sun.
The hydrogen would be additional potential fusion fuel,
though it would take a very long time to reach the core,
and the oxygen would just be a trace “metal” contaminant in stellar terms.
For any realistic amount of water, the effect would be tiny.
All of Earth’s oceans have a mass of about \(1.4\times10^{21}\) kg,
while the Sun’s mass is about \(2\times10^{30}\) kg.
That is less than one-billionth of the Sun’s mass.
Dumping the oceans into the Sun would not cool it;
in fact, the infalling water would release a lot of gravitational energy as it fell,
briefly adding heat and light.
The energy released by dropping all Earth’s oceans onto the Sun is roughly comparable to several days of the Sun’s normal output.
If the hose supplied an absurdly large amount of water, comparable to a significant fraction of the Sun’s mass,
then the Sun would become more massive.
A more massive Sun would generally burn hotter and brighter
and have a shorter lifetime.
Add enough mass
and you would turn it into a different kind of star;
add vastly more
and you could eventually create stellar instability or even gravitational collapse.
So the direct answer is:
a giant water hose aimed at the Sun would not extinguish it.
Small amounts would do essentially nothing;
Earth-ocean-sized amounts would make a brief splash energetically
but not matter much;
truly enormous amounts would make the Sun larger, hotter, and brighter
rather than put it out.

items.question: What If You Detonated a Nuclear Bomb at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: Surprisingly little—especially compared to what would happen if you put it just under the surface. Evin isn’t the first person to think of setting off nuclear weapons underwater. In fact, we’ve actually tried it a bunch of times. This (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ggH-ObiUWEE) is what it looks like. Most of the tests, however, involved either small bombs or shallow water. Evin’s scenario concerns neither. At 53 megatons, the Tsar Bomba was the most powerful nuclear weapon ever detonated, and at 11 kilometers, the Mariana(s) Trench is the deepest part of the ocean. No underwater test has involved bombs anywhere near that size, nor depths anywhere near that deep. In 1962, physicist Freeman Dyson wrote a memo discussing eight possible novel weapon systems, all of which looked like they’d be possible in the near future, and outlined the potential military uses and dangers of each. This memo has been declassified, but was never published. Freeman’s son, science historian George Dyson, got a paper copy of the memo from his father, and was kind enough to show it to me. In the memo, one of the eight ideas Freeman discusses is the use of gigaton nuclear weapons as wave generators. It includes this rather terrifying passage describing the detonation of a submerged gigaton mine off the North American coast: “Quantitative study of the destructive effects has not been made. Rough estimates indicate that the inundation would reach to a height of 200-300 feet above sea level, or a distance of 200-300 miles inland, whichever limit is reached first.” [Image: image] Luckily for the coast, later research paints a less dire picture. The seminal work in the field of nuclear ocean waves is Water Waves Generated By Underwater Explosions (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?Location=U2&doc=GetTRDoc.pdf&AD=ADA304244), a sprawling 400-page report produced for the Department of Defense by Bernard Le Mehaute and Shen Wang. The report, published in 1996, exhaustively examines and summarizes all available research about the ocean waves created by nuclear explosions. The report outlines how when a nuclear weapon goes off underwater, it produces a cavity of hot gasses, which then collapses. If the explosion happens near the surface, it can create some pretty big waves—under some circumstances, they can be hundreds of feet high near ground zero. [Image: image] Or is it ocean zero? Fortunately for the coast, these waves are fundamentally different from tsunamis. It turns out that if the waves are very large, they break early, and expend most of their energy creating a narrow surf zone on the continental shelf. This is potentially hazardous to some ships, but much less catastrophic than a direct nuclear attack. When they reached the coast, the waves would be no worse than those from a bad storm. But those are waves from an explosion close to the surface. A nuke set off deep underwater acts a bit differently. The explosion at the bottom of the Mariana Trench will create a quickly-expanding spherical cavity of hot steam. To figure out how big it gets, we can try a formula from the 1971 paper Evaluation of Various Theoretical Models For Underwater Explosion (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/737271.pdf): \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right )^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx580\text{ meters}\] The bubble grows to about a kilometer across in a couple of seconds. The water above bulges up, though only slightly, over a large area. Then the pressure from that six miles of water overhead causes it to collapse. Within a dozen or so seconds, the bubble shrinks to a minimum size, then ‘bounces’ back, expanding outward again. It goes through three or four cycles of this collapse and expansion before disintegrating into, in the words of the 1996 report, “a mass of turbulent warm water and explosion debris.” According to the report, as a result of such a deep-water closed bubble creation and dissipation, “no wave of any consequence will be generated.” That “turbulent warm water” is actually quite substantial. The rising column of heat creates a hot spot in the ocean—many degrees warmer than the surrounding water—that lingers for some time. [Image: image] Earlier this year, Severe Tropical Storm Sanvu passed over the Mariana Trench. The column of deep, hot water from our nuke could conceivably have been enough to strengthen it into a typhoon, much as the deep warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico’s Loop Current sometimes cause hurricanes to rapidly intensify. In addition to the heat energy from the water, Sanvu could whip up a spray containing fallout from the blast, and approach Iwo Jima as a radioactive whirlwind. Of course, that’s getting a little far-fetched. In the absence of an improbable typhoon interaction, the overall effect of the bomb isn’t quite as dramatic as Evin might have imagined. ... But. All that changes when this cat enters the equation: [Image: image] Literally. Let’s say that when I’m typing the above equation, the cat hops onto my desk and steps on the “0” key, which inserts six extra zeroes: \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right) ^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53000000\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx35\text{ miles}\] If there was enough water, and if the model held up, this blast would expand into a bubble 70 miles across. In reality, the oceans aren’t that deep. Instead, it blows a hole in the Earth’s crust dozens of miles across, leaving a hole through which briefly glows the magma of the mantle. Around the early 1990s, scientists started discovering jumbled fields of petrified wood mixed with sand buried beneath the Louisiana and Texas coast. These turned out to be the remains of North American forests swept out to sea by a massive tsunami. The culprit was a comet or asteroid hitting the Yucatan—the impact that killed most of the dinosaurs. The debris played a key role in identifying the 65-million-year-old Chicxulub impact site—this book (http://www.amazon.com/Crater-Doom-Princeton-Science-Library/dp/0691131031) provides a wonderful account of the unraveling of that mystery. 53,000,000 megatons is approximately the energy of the Chicxulub impact. A blast this size in the Mariana Trench creates kilometer-high waves that engulf the forests of Indonesia, California, and the Pacific Northwest, along with most of coastal China and the rest of the Pacific rim. Huge volumes of rock and water are blasted into space. The debris takes less than an hour to encircle the Earth. As the chunks of rock fall back into the atmosphere, they heat to a glow—like meteors—igniting global firestorms. The hole fills in, with huge columns of steam and great convulsions. The Mariana Trench is gone, and with it Guam and the Mariana Islands. The area is now marked by a 100-kilometer-wide scar of magma sizzling beneath the waters of the Pacific. The majority of the world’s plants die and the food chain collapses completely. Between the famine and the fires, most life on Earth is wiped out. Stupid cat. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
A nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench would produce an enormous but mostly local underwater explosion, not a planet-changing catastrophe.

At about 11 km depth, the pressure is roughly 1,100 atmospheres. If a nuclear weapon actually functioned there, the detonation would instantly vaporize nearby water and seafloor material, forming a superheated gas/plasma bubble. That bubble would expand violently, but the immense surrounding pressure would crush it back down. It would likely go through several expansion-collapse pulses, producing powerful shock waves through the water and into the seabed.

The immediate effects would be severe near the blast: marine life in the region would be killed by shock, heat, and pressure changes; sediment and rock on the trench floor could be blasted into a crater; and radioactive material would contaminate nearby water and seabed sediments. Much of the fallout would likely remain trapped deep in the ocean, diluted and deposited locally rather than spreading immediately into the atmosphere.

It would not “crack the Earth,” trigger global earthquakes, or blow a hole through the ocean. Even a very large nuclear weapon is tiny compared with the energy involved in major tectonic events. A 1-megaton bomb releases about \(4 \times 10^{15}\) joules, comparable to a moderate earthquake in total energy, but it does not couple efficiently into tectonic motion.

It also probably would not create a Hollywood-style mega-tsunami. Deep underwater explosions make intense pressure waves, but tsunamis require large-scale displacement of the ocean surface or seafloor over a broad area. A nuclear blast is too compact and too brief to efficiently push an ocean-wide wave. There might be surface disturbances above the site, depending on yield, but at 11 km depth even a megaton-scale explosion’s bubble would be far too small to reach the surface directly.

So the short answer is: it would make a huge deep-sea shock wave, crater and contaminate the local trench environment, kill nearby life, and be detectable by seismic and hydroacoustic sensors around the world. But it would not destroy the planet, empty the ocean, or create a civilization-ending tsunami.
