rubrics.question_focus: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of the money-printing premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer anchors the counterfactual in realistic order-of-magnitude calculations for a home printer producing usable currency.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful calculation or gives wildly implausible amounts without basis.
criteria.3-4: Attempts arithmetic but misses key factors such as bills per page, duplex printing, print speed, or yearly output.
criteria.5-6: Estimates output in the right broad range but with incomplete assumptions or unclear unit handling.
criteria.7-8: Correctly uses plausible assumptions, such as four $100 bills per sheet and about one duplex page per minute, to estimate hundreds of millions per year.
criteria.9-10: Gives a clear, checked order-of-magnitude calculation and distinguishes bills, face value, print rate, operating time, and annual total.

criteria.name: Macroeconomic scale and inflation reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer compares the printer's output to existing money supply, currency circulation, and economic scale rather than assuming instant economic collapse.
criteria.1-2: Claims global hyperinflation or economic destruction from one printer with no scale comparison.
criteria.3-4: Mentions inflation or money supply but treats the effect qualitatively and exaggeratedly.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that one printer makes the owner rich but likely has limited macroeconomic impact, with weak quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Compares the output to circulation or annual production of high-denomination bills and concludes the macro effect is small.
criteria.9-10: Accurately separates personal wealth effects from aggregate effects, noting that a few million extra $100 bills per year is tiny relative to existing currency and broader money supply.

criteria.name: Causal chain from physical printing to spendable wealth
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms that determine whether printed money actually functions as money, including authenticity, detection, laundering, banking, and spending constraints.
criteria.1-2: Assumes printed pages automatically become usable wealth without considering authentication or circulation.
criteria.3-4: Briefly notes legality or counterfeiting but does not analyze how the bills enter the economy.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some practical constraints such as serial numbers, security features, suspicious deposits, or spending limits.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain from printing to attempted use, including counterfeit detection, banking scrutiny, law enforcement, and transaction bottlenecks.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly explains how physical realism, legal status, traceability, laundering difficulty, and behavioral responses govern the actual outcome under the premise.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and institutional response
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences beyond the immediate windfall, including government, financial, and social responses.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'you get rich' or 'the economy collapses' with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few consequences but as disconnected guesses.
criteria.5-6: Covers likely personal, legal, and economic consequences, though with limited causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Explains escalating effects such as spending patterns, audits, seizure, Secret Service involvement, changes to bill designs, or containment of the anomaly.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-range scenario showing how institutions detect, investigate, adapt to, and likely neutralize or exploit the money-printing capability.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the ambiguous counterfactual consistently and flags uncertainties without undermining its own assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or makes mutually incompatible claims without acknowledgment.
criteria.3-4: Uses inconsistent assumptions about whether the money is real, counterfeit, magical, or legally valid.
criteria.5-6: Mostly maintains a consistent interpretation but leaves important ambiguities unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions, such as whether the bills pass authentication or merely look real, and keeps conclusions aligned with them.
criteria.9-10: Separates multiple plausible interpretations, calibrates confidence in each, and avoids overclaiming while preserving causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If your printer could really print money that was physically indistinguishable from official currency, it would not make you “create wealth” in the broader economic sense. It would let you create claims on existing goods and services. In practice, that would be counterfeiting unless the money were legally issued by the government or central bank.

At first, if you printed a small amount and spent it, you would personally gain purchasing power. The loss would be spread across everyone else using that currency, because you would be adding money without adding any new goods, services, or productive capacity. Economically, it is like secretly taxing everyone by diluting the value of the money supply.

If many people had such printers, prices would rise rapidly. Money works partly because it is scarce, trusted, and difficult to forge. If anyone could print unlimited perfect cash, the supply of money would explode. Sellers would respond by raising prices, demanding alternative payment, or refusing the currency entirely. The currency could collapse into hyperinflation, where money loses value so fast that people rush to spend it immediately or switch to barter, foreign currency, commodities, or digital assets.

If only you had the printer and used it heavily, the effect would depend on scale. Printing a few thousand dollars might have no measurable macroeconomic effect but would still be illegal. Printing billions would noticeably increase the money supply, distort markets, trigger investigations, and likely destabilize parts of the economy. Banks, retailers, and governments track currency flows, serial numbers, deposits, and suspicious transactions, so spending large amounts of “new” cash would be hard to hide.

If the printer were legally authorized, then it would essentially be part of the central bank’s money-creation system. Modern governments already “print money,” mostly digitally rather than as paper cash. They can increase the money supply, but they must manage it carefully. Too little money can contribute to recession or deflation; too much can cause inflation.

So the short answer is: if your printer could print real money, you might become richer briefly, but you would not create real wealth. You would either be committing counterfeiting, or, if everyone could do it, the money would quickly stop being worth much. Real wealth comes from producing valuable goods, services, technology, infrastructure, knowledge, and resources—not from creating more pieces of currency.

nodes.text: If your printer could really print money that was physically indistinguishable from official currency,
it would not make you “create wealth” in the broader economic sense.
It would let you create claims on existing goods and services.
In practice, that would be counterfeiting
unless the money were legally issued by the government or central bank.
At first, if you printed a small amount and spent it,
you would personally gain purchasing power.
The loss would be spread across everyone else using that currency,
because you would be adding money without adding any new goods, services, or productive capacity.
Economically, it is like secretly taxing everyone by diluting the value of the money supply.
If many people had such printers,
prices would rise rapidly.
Money works partly because it is scarce, trusted, and difficult to forge.
If anyone could print unlimited perfect cash,
the supply of money would explode.
Sellers would respond by raising prices, demanding alternative payment, or refusing the currency entirely.
The currency could collapse into hyperinflation,
where money loses value so fast that people rush to spend it immediately or switch to barter, foreign currency, commodities, or digital assets.
If only you had the printer and used it heavily,
the effect would depend on scale.
Printing a few thousand dollars might have no measurable macroeconomic effect
but would still be illegal.
Printing billions would noticeably increase the money supply, distort markets, trigger investigations, and likely destabilize parts of the economy.
Banks, retailers, and governments track currency flows, serial numbers, deposits, and suspicious transactions,
so spending large amounts of “new” cash would be hard to hide.
If the printer were legally authorized,
then it would essentially be part of the central bank’s money-creation system.
Modern governments already “print money,”
mostly digitally rather than as paper cash.
They can increase the money supply,
but they must manage it carefully.
Too little money can contribute to recession or deflation;
too much can cause inflation.
So the short answer is:
if your printer could print real money,
you might become richer briefly,
but you would not create real wealth.
You would either be committing counterfeiting,
or, if everyone could do it,
the money would quickly stop being worth much.
Real wealth comes from producing valuable goods, services, technology, infrastructure, knowledge, and resources—
not from creating more pieces of currency.

items.question: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?
human_answers: About 65,000, give or take a few. You’d have to arrange them like this: [Image: image] The rocket would weigh about as much as a tow truck. There wouldn’t be room for anything except the engines, aerodynamic shell, and minimal staging equipment. Each rocket motor would burn for about three seconds. The layer cake arrangement means that every three seconds, the bottom layer of spent rockets would detaches and the next stage would kick in. It would go through between 25 and 30 of these stages, burning for a total of a minute and a half, after which it would coast upward and just barely brush the edge of space. (For this design, I’m assuming something akin to Estes E9-4 engines, which are on the large end of the common model rocket engines. There are larger ones—the classes go all the way up to O and beyond—but at a certain point, they stop being model rocket engines, and just become rocket engines.) A 30-stage rocket is, to put it lightly, an engineering nightmare. This design assumes the non-engine portion of the vehicle is limited to the weight of a person (60 kg). In effect, the spaceship would be a solid block of rocket engines. They’d need to be insulated from each other so the upper stages didn’t ignite prematurely, and the staging and aerodynamics would both be a challenge. The stack of engines narrows as you go from bottom to top. By the time the top stages are firing, the rocket will have shed most of its mass, so it won’t need as much thrust to get the same acceleration. The reason the engine stack bulges in the middle is so that the acceleration profile will look like this: [Image: image] Rockets work best when their thrust is several times greater than the force of gravity. But you don’t want to accelerate too quickly while you’re low down. Air drag increases with the square of your speed, and if you accelerate too quickly, you’ll find yourself wasting all your fuel just to maintain your speed. You want to accelerate slowly at first, then ramp it up as the air starts getting thinner. [Image: image] Now, as you may have noticed, this rocket will get you into space (for a few seconds, at least), but not orbit. Can you use model rocket engines to dock with the ISS? No. Taking into account atmospheric drag, to get into space, you need a rocket capable of accelerating (in a vacuum) to about 2 kilometers per second. To get to orbit, you need a rocket capable of accelerating to about 10 kilometers per second. If you try to produce an orbital rocket using the same design math we used for the suborbital rocket, it spits out a description of a pancake-shaped mountain of model rocket engines over a mile wide. It would taper to a 10-meter-high spire in the center and would weigh about as much as the Great Pyramid. [Image: image] Not only would this vehicle never get out of the atmosphere, it would probably not stand up under its own weight. Frankly, the word “vehicle” is a bit misleading. Essentially, what you’ve created is an unstable pile of gunpowder the size of Central Park. If it went up in flames—which it would—it would break the record for the largest manmade non-nuclear explosion in history. (Interestingly, the current holder of that dubious record is also a rocket that exploded during launch (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m79UO4HOQmc).) The bottom line is that it would be very difficult, but perhaps not impossible, to launch something up to the edge of space using model rocket engines. However, if you try to build a ship capable of getting to orbit, you will not go to space today.

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?

criteria.name: Quantitative Scaling Under Model-Engine Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer uses plausible order-of-magnitude reasoning for how many model rocket engines, how much mass, burn duration, staging count, and velocity capability would result from trying to launch a real rocket with engines such as large Estes-class motors.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful numbers or relies on wildly impossible claims such as a few engines launching a person to orbit.
criteria.3-4: Includes some quantities but they are mostly unsupported, off by many orders of magnitude, or ignore mass and thrust scaling.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that tens of thousands of engines and many stages are needed, but gives limited or partially inconsistent quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Provides credible estimates for engine count, short burn times, staging, mass, and suborbital velocity needs with minor gaps.
criteria.9-10: Closely captures the scale: roughly 65,000 large model engines, tow-truck-like mass, 25-30 short stages, about 90 seconds burn, and only marginal space-reaching performance.

criteria.name: Propulsion, Staging, and Acceleration Mechanism Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the causal mechanism by which clustered model engines might work: layered staging, dropping spent motors, thrust-to-weight changes, acceleration shaping, and atmospheric drag effects.
criteria.1-2: Treats the engines as if they simply add together without explaining staging, thrust, drag, or mass loss.
criteria.3-4: Mentions clustering or staging but misses why spent engines must be discarded and how drag or acceleration matters.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic staging and thrust-to-weight issues but omits important effects such as drag losses or changing acceleration as mass falls.
criteria.7-8: Covers layered stages, short burns, shedding mass, changing thrust needs, and why acceleration should be moderated in dense air.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent mechanism including layer-cake staging, narrowing/bulging engine stack, gravity and drag tradeoffs, and rising acceleration as atmosphere thins.

criteria.name: Suborbital Space vs Orbit Endpoint Distinction
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly distinguishes briefly reaching the edge of space from achieving orbit or docking with the ISS, including the much larger delta-v requirement for orbit.
criteria.1-2: Confuses reaching space with orbit or claims ISS docking is feasible with model engines.
criteria.3-4: States orbit is harder but gives no clear physical reason or implies the same design could scale straightforwardly.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says suborbital flight might be possible and orbit is not, but gives only vague velocity or energy reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly contrasts about 2 km/s effective suborbital need with about 10 km/s orbital need, and rejects ISS docking.
criteria.9-10: Precisely explains that the model-engine stack might barely brush space briefly but cannot reach orbit; scaling to orbit produces an absurd, atmosphere-bound, structurally untenable mega-pile.

criteria.name: Engineering Failure Modes and Practical Constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream engineering consequences specific to a rocket made almost entirely of model motors, including packaging, insulation, aerodynamics, ignition control, structural integrity, and explosion risk.
criteria.1-2: Ignores practical engineering constraints or assumes the design is straightforward once enough engines are added.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or complexity but does not identify concrete failure modes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several issues such as staging complexity, mass, or premature ignition, but misses major structural or aerodynamic consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers most key constraints: minimal payload room, insulation, ignition sequencing, aerodynamics, structural load, and high explosion risk.
criteria.9-10: Shows how the counterfactual cascades into a near-solid block of motors, severe staging/aero/thermal control problems, structural collapse for orbital scaling, and possible record-scale non-nuclear explosion.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Discipline, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer stays within the premise of using model rocket engines, states assumptions and uncertainty appropriately, and avoids contradictions with rocket physics or its own causal chain.
criteria.1-2: Breaks the premise, invokes non-model engines or magic technology, or contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Mostly follows the premise but makes unsupported leaps, overconfident claims, or inconsistent statements about feasibility.
criteria.5-6: Maintains the premise and basic physics, with some uncertainty acknowledged, but has minor contradictions or vague assumptions.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions about engine class, payload, and idealization; calibrates feasibility as difficult but not impossible for suborbital and impossible for orbit.
criteria.9-10: Consistently reasons from explicit assumptions, separates idealized math from real engineering risk, uses qualified estimates, and avoids conflicting claims about thrust, mass, staging, or orbital feasibility.

items.model_answer:
If “launch” means “make a full-size rocket rise off the pad,” then yes, in principle: enough model rocket engines could produce enough thrust for a few seconds. If “launch” means “send a real rocket to space or orbit,” then no, not in any practical sense.

A typical Estes-style model rocket motor, say a D motor, produces on the order of 10–20 newtons of thrust for about 1–2 seconds, with a total impulse around 20 newton-seconds. A real orbital rocket needs millions of newtons of thrust and billions of newton-seconds of total impulse.

For example, a Falcon 9 produces roughly 7.6 million newtons of thrust at liftoff. Using 10-newton model motors, you would need roughly three-quarters of a million motors just to match liftoff thrust. They would burn out almost immediately, giving the vehicle only a tiny kick upward. It might hop, shake itself apart, or explode, but it would not meaningfully accelerate toward orbit.

The deeper problem is not just thrust; it is efficiency and mass ratio. Model rocket engines have low specific impulse compared with real launch-vehicle engines, and each tiny motor carries its own casing, nozzle, clay, and packaging. That means you are adding huge amounts of dead weight. The rocket equation punishes this severely. Even if you built many stages, each stage would spend most of its effort lifting thousands or millions of little spent motor casings and the next pile of motors.

There are also practical failures: igniting hundreds of thousands of motors simultaneously would be nearly impossible; some would fail, some would ignite late, and uneven thrust would tear the vehicle apart or send it tumbling. The exhaust plumes and heat would damage neighboring motors and structure. The wiring, mounting hardware, and control system would become absurdly heavy.

So the result would be: a spectacular, dangerous, very expensive firework. With enough model engines you could make a large object briefly leave the ground. But launching a real rocket to space, especially to orbit, using only ordinary model rocket engines is effectively impossible in practice.

edus.text: If “launch” means “make a full-size rocket rise off the pad,”
then yes, in principle: enough model rocket engines could produce enough thrust for a few seconds.
If “launch” means “send a real rocket to space or orbit,”
then no, not in any practical sense.
A typical Estes-style model rocket motor, say a D motor, produces on the order of 10–20 newtons of thrust for about 1–2 seconds,
with a total impulse around 20 newton-seconds.
A real orbital rocket needs millions of newtons of thrust
and billions of newton-seconds of total impulse.
For example, a Falcon 9 produces roughly 7.6 million newtons of thrust at liftoff.
Using 10-newton model motors, you would need roughly three-quarters of a million motors just to match liftoff thrust.
They would burn out almost immediately,
giving the vehicle only a tiny kick upward.
It might hop, shake itself apart, or explode,
but it would not meaningfully accelerate toward orbit.
The deeper problem is not just thrust; it is efficiency and mass ratio.
Model rocket engines have low specific impulse compared with real launch-vehicle engines,
and each tiny motor carries its own casing, nozzle, clay, and packaging.
That means you are adding huge amounts of dead weight.
The rocket equation punishes this severely.
Even if you built many stages,
each stage would spend most of its effort lifting thousands or millions of little spent motor casings and the next pile of motors.
There are also practical failures:
igniting hundreds of thousands of motors simultaneously would be nearly impossible;
some would fail, some would ignite late,
and uneven thrust would tear the vehicle apart or send it tumbling.
The exhaust plumes and heat would damage neighboring motors and structure.
The wiring, mounting hardware, and control system would become absurdly heavy.
So the result would be: a spectacular, dangerous, very expensive firework.
With enough model engines you could make a large object briefly leave the ground.
But launching a real rocket to space, especially to orbit, using only ordinary model rocket engines is effectively impossible in practice.

items.question: What If Humanity Sped Up Earth's Rotation to Eliminate Leap Seconds?
human_answers: The Earth’s spin is slowing down. This is annoying. One reason that it’s annoying is that it makes time standards more difficult. We already have way too many time standards (http://tycho.usno.navy.mil/systime.html), including: TAI, time based on an atomic clock, which ignores all motion of the Earth UT0 and UT1, time based on precise measurement of the Earth’s rotation GPS, the time standard used by GPS satellites UTC, the standard used in computing, which is like TAI but with leap seconds to keep it in sync with Earth TDT, TBT, TCB, and TCG, which are all even worse This leads to all kinds of little headaches, particularly for programmers. For example, the clock in your smartphone’s GPS is 16 seconds out of sync with the phone’s system clock. This is because the system clock uses Coordinated Universal Time (which has leap seconds), but GPS time doesn’t. They were in sync in January of 1980 and probably never will be again. Half a billion years ago (when the Earth was 4 billion years old, instead of 4.5), each day was 22 hours long instead of 24. The day has gotten longer because of tidal forces from the Moon. Loosely speaking, here’s how tidal drag works: The Moon’s tides raise bulges in the Earth, but the Earth’s rotation moves those bulges out of line with the Moon. The Moon’s gravity tries to tug the bulges back into line, which exerts a twisting force on the Earth, slowing it down: [Image: image] Strangely, the Earth is actually not slowing down as much as you’d expect from tidal drag. The biggest reason for the discrepancy is that during the last ice age, the continents were pushed down by the weight of the glaciers, and they’re still springing back into place. This has the effect of shifting mass toward the poles, closer to the axis of rotation: [Image: image] This makes us spin faster—or, at least, keeps us from slowing down as quickly. At the moment, each day is about 0.8 milliseconds longer than the 86,400 seconds it needs to be to avoid adding leap seconds. [Image: image] This difference fluctuates over time based on weather and other effects (it’s actually shortened a bit since the early 1990s), although in the long run, it will definitely get larger as the Earth slows. If we wanted to get rid of leap seconds, we’d need to keep the Earth spinning at a more constant rate. This means speeding up the Earth and shortening each day by about 0.8 milliseconds. This is a tough problem. Here are a few things that won’t work: Spinning counterclockwise (http://xkcd.com/162/) in a chair. It temporarily alters the Earth’s rate of rotation, but not enough to matter. Putting rocket engines on the Equator. This won’t work because the exhaust would go into the atmosphere, which transmits the force back to the ground as wind drag—it’d be like making a bike go forward by pushing on the handlebars. If the engines were somehow mounted above the atmosphere, they’d be able to slow the Earth, but not by enough to accomplish our goal. Triggering big earthquakes. This can alter the length of the day (http://www.nasa.gov/topics/earth/features/japanquake/earth20110314.html), but even those aren’t big enough to make a difference. In the end, there’s only one solution: Hitting the Earth with asteroids. Given enough time, we could send a spaceship (captained by an anti-Bruce Willis) to perform repeated flybys of a comet. Over time, the gravitational perturbation could steer the comet into a collision course with Earth. By hitting the Earth at the right angle, we would give it a push: [Image: image] Even if the comet burns up in the atmosphere, its momentum is transmitted to the surface by wind drag (taking a matter of days). It takes about a decade (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/227650235_Topographic_CoreMantle_Coupling_and_Polar_Motion_On_Decadal_TimeScales) for the core to sync up with the crust, so we’d have to plan the impact schedule carefully to avoid overshooting. Here’s the bad news: To get enough spin, we have to hit the Earth with on the order of a billion liters of rock per second (several times the volumetric discharge rate of the Amazon). This adds up to about one six-mile dinosaur-killing asteroid every couple days. Humanity—and life—wouldn’t survive the bombardment long. What about a steady stream of smaller asteroids? [Image: image] If asteroid B-612 in The Little Prince is four meters across and made of rock, we’d need an average of around fifty thousand of them to enter the atmosphere each second to keep up the pressure. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the steady high-altitude meteor shower would deliver just as much energy to the atmosphere that daily giant impacts would, and the eventual death toll would be the same: Seven billion humans, plus four billion Little Princes per day. But at least we could stop worrying about leap seconds.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Target and Timekeeping Framing
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual: eliminating leap seconds by changing Earth’s rotation rather than redefining time standards, and whether it identifies the relevant day-length mismatch and its causes.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise, treats leap seconds as purely administrative, or gives no connection between Earth rotation and timekeeping.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes leap seconds relate to Earth’s rotation but is vague or wrong about whether Earth must speed up or slow down.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says Earth must spin slightly faster to keep days near 86,400 SI seconds, but gives little quantitative context.
criteria.7-8: Accurately explains the current millisecond-scale day excess, tidal slowing, and UTC/leap-second motivation with minor omissions.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the target as shortening the day by about 0.8 ms, distinguishes atomic and rotational time, and notes short-term fluctuations versus long-term tidal slowdown.

criteria.name: Angular Momentum and Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses correct rotational dynamics to reason about how Earth’s spin could be changed under the counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Relies on magical, local, or internally impossible mechanisms with no angular-momentum reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions force or energy but confuses torque, linear momentum, atmospheric coupling, or conservation laws.
criteria.5-6: Applies basic angular-momentum ideas and recognizes that external torque or mass redistribution is needed.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains why many intuitive methods fail, such as ground-based engines or human motion, and why off-world momentum transfer could work.
criteria.9-10: Gives a physically faithful chain involving torque, impact angle, atmospheric momentum transfer, crust-core coupling, and conservation constraints.

criteria.name: Scale, Feasibility, and Quantitative Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer captures the enormous scale required to measurably speed up Earth and avoids implausibly small fixes.

items.model_answer:
If humanity tried to eliminate leap seconds by physically speeding up Earth, the required change in rotation rate would be tiny in everyday terms but enormous in engineering terms.

Leap seconds exist because atomic time counts exact SI seconds, while Earth’s rotation is slightly irregular and, on average, slowly slowing due mainly to lunar tides. Since 1972, UTC has needed 27 positive leap seconds, meaning Earth has lagged atomic time by roughly 27 seconds over about five decades. That corresponds to the mean solar day being about 1–2 milliseconds longer than 86,400 SI seconds.

To stop future leap seconds, humanity would need to shorten Earth’s day by about a millisecond or two. That means increasing Earth’s angular velocity by only about one part in 60–100 million. At the equator, the surface would move only a few micrometers per second faster. People would not feel lighter in any noticeable way, weather and tides would barely change, and the equatorial bulge or sea level redistribution would be tiny if the spin-up were done gently.

But the planetary-scale physics is brutal. Earth’s rotational angular momentum is about \(5.9 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}\). Changing the day length by about 1.4 ms would require adding roughly

\[
10^{26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}
\]

of angular momentum and about

\[
10^{22}\ \mathrm{J}
\]

of rotational energy.

That is on the order of ten years of total current human energy use, and the harder problem is not energy but angular momentum: you cannot just “add spin” to Earth without pushing against something else. You would need to exchange angular momentum with the Moon, asteroids, expelled mass, or some enormous space-based machinery. An impactor could do it in principle, but an impact large enough to matter would be globally catastrophic. A gentle gravitational or mass-driver scheme would be fantastically beyond present engineering.

Also, speeding Earth up once would not permanently solve the problem. Earth’s rotation varies because of tides, atmosphere, oceans, core motion, earthquakes, and long-term tidal braking. You would need continual active control of Earth’s rotation to keep atomic time and Earth-rotation time locked together.

If the goal were to “erase” the existing leap seconds, that is a different problem. You would need Earth to gain about 27 seconds of rotational phase relative to atomic time. A 1 ms/day speed-up would take about 74 years to catch up; a faster catch-up would require much larger torques and energies.

So the direct answer is: in principle, speeding up Earth could reduce or temporarily eliminate the need for leap seconds, and the direct physical effects of the slightly shorter day would be negligible. In practice, it would require absurd planetary-scale angular momentum transfer, would need constant maintenance, and would be vastly harder than simply changing the timekeeping rules. That is why the real-world solution is administrative: stop using leap seconds, or allow UTC to drift slowly from Earth rotation, rather than trying to spin up the planet.

items.question: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?
human_answers: Every second, 1.8 humans die and 4.2 humans are born. Under Mr. Petzall’s plan, the number of deaths would increase to 2.8. This randomized culling would obviously be a big deal—it would be responsible for over a third of all deaths—but, at least for a while, our population would continue to grow. At one death per second, any given person currently has a 0.464% chance of being chosen each year. Put another way, the scenario would result in 4.64 deaths per 1,000 people (or 464 per 100,000). [Image: image] There are about twenty countries with death rates below 4.64 per 1,000. It’s an odd bunch (https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2066rank.html), including the Dominican Republic, Brunei, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Maldives, and Paraguay. These are the countries where Guy’s program would be responsible for the majority of all deaths. The death rate in all of these countries is going to go up. It has to, because of math. It seems intuitively obvious that death rates below 10 per 1,000 are unsustainable. If fewer than one person out of every hundred dies each year (and enough are born to sustain the population) then the average person must have to wait over a hundred years to die—which is clearly not compatible with our current lifespans. In those countries with low single-digit death rates, the rates are guaranteed to rise in the future. This includes the United States, whose death rate is 8.40 per 1,000—a number which will go up substantially as the Baby Boomers age. A rate of one death per second isn’t enough to reverse population growth at present, but it would have been until recently. In 1950, the world’s population was only 2.52 billion. One death per second would mean 12.5 annual deaths per 1,000 people, almost triple the number in 2013. At the start of the early 20th century, this would have been enough to reverse population growth, and within a handful of decades—as population levels off—it will be again. Of course, if people die faster, this in turn has an effect on birth rates—as people change their behavior in response to the change in mortality—so the actual result would be more complicated. [Image: image] In the United States, Guy Petzall would be the leading cause of death for females between the ages of 1 and 55 and for males between the ages of 1 and 48. Currently, about 96% of infants survive to age 40, but in Guy’s scenario, only 80% would. When would these deaths happen? Given the numbers of aircraft in the air at any given time, it’s certain that some pilots would die while flying. This wouldn’t be a disaster, though, since large commercial airliners have multiple crew members who can take over. Cars would be a different story. Since about 10 million Americans are driving (http://what-if.xkcd.com/5/) at any given time, 127 will die behind the wheel each day (plus a smaller but still significant number of passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers). Interestingly, this is only a little larger than the number of Americans who die in car accidents every day already. (This number has been declining, as a percentage of population, since the 1960s, and as a percentage of miles traveled since at at least the 1920s (http://www.saferoads.org/federal/2004/TrafficFatalities1899-2003.pdf).) About 50 million (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr011.pdf) outpatient surgery procedures are performed each year. If they’re primarily performed by one surgeon and each last an average of half an hour, then about 13 surgeons per year will unexpectedly die mid-surgery (as will 13 extra patients). This is a scary thought. But to put it in perspective, that’s about the number of surgeons who will operate on the wrong body part or wrong patient every two days (http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/04/28/ep.wrong.side.surgery/index.html). It’s not that the scenario isn’t scary. It’s just that reality is far more terrifying. Lastly, what about our leaders? Members of Congress die in office at a rate of two or three per year, or about five per Congress. This used to be much higher, as explained in this strangely florid paper (http://home.gwu.edu/~forrest/fmdeathincongressps.pdf). 29 members of Congress died during 1939 and 1940, the two years the 76th Congress was in session. In Guy’s scenario, the current rate would double, leading to a loss of 10 per Congress. This would certainly be tragic, but it would be no higher than the levels seen as recently as the 1960s. All in all, the losses would be dramatic, but not devastating to our species as a whole. And really, in the end, the global death rate is 100%—everyone dies. [Image: image] … or do they? Strictly speaking, the observed death rate for the human condition is something like 93%—that is, around 93% of all humans have died. This means the death rate among humans who were not members of The Beatles is significantly higher than the 50% death rate among humans who were. [Image: image] I expect this significant[dubious–discuss] fact[citation needed] will pave the way[citation needed] for a great deal[dubious–discuss] of important[citation needed][dubious–discuss] research.

criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with occasional unsupported leaps or weak distinction between certain and speculative effects.

items.model_answer:
Assuming the rule is “once per second, one living human is chosen uniformly at random and dies,” the immediate effect would be enormous but not instantly civilization-ending.

One death per second is 86,400 extra deaths per day, or about 31.6 million extra deaths per year. The world currently has roughly 60–70 million deaths per year, so this would increase global mortality by about half. It would become the largest “cause of death” on Earth, exceeding heart disease and cancer individually.

For an individual person, the risk would be small in any given moment but significant over a lifetime. With about 8.1 billion people alive, your chance of being the randomly selected person in any one second would be about 1 in 8.1 billion. Over a year, that becomes roughly:

\[
\frac{31.6\text{ million}}{8.1\text{ billion}} \approx 0.39\%
\]

So each person would face about a 0.4% annual chance of dying from this random process. Over 80 years, assuming population size stayed similar, the cumulative chance would be around 27%. In other words, roughly one in four people would eventually be killed by the random-death mechanism before accounting for normal mortality.

The demographic effect would be severe but not immediately depopulating. Current global births are still far higher than deaths, by roughly 60–70 million per year. Adding 31.6 million deaths per year would reduce population growth sharply, but humanity would likely still grow at today’s birth rates, perhaps by around 30–40 million people per year instead of much more. However, as global fertility continues to fall, this extra mortality could push the world into population decline sooner.

The social effect would be much worse than the raw numbers suggest because the deaths would be random across age, health, location, and social role. Unlike ordinary mortality, which is concentrated among older people, this would kill infants, children, parents, doctors, pilots, teachers, heads of state, engineers, and caregivers in proportion to how many exist. The loss of life-years would be huge: each extra death would often remove decades of expected life. Globally, this could mean over a billion expected life-years lost every year.

There would also be secondary consequences. If deaths are sudden, some people would die while driving, flying, performing surgery, operating machinery, managing power systems, or caring for dependents. That would cause additional accidents and force society to redesign many systems around the assumption that anyone can vanish at any second. Critical roles would need redundancy everywhere.

Psychologically and politically, the world would change dramatically. Every day would bring 86,400 apparently arbitrary deaths. Families, workplaces, schools, militaries, governments, and hospitals would be in constant churn. Insurance, pensions, inheritance law, employment planning, and security systems would all have to adapt. The randomness would make it feel like a universal lottery of death.

So the short answer is: one extra random death per second would not immediately wipe out humanity, and at current birth rates it might not even make the global population decline right away. But it would be one of the greatest disasters in human history: 31.6 million additional deaths per year, a major reduction in life expectancy, vast psychological trauma, and serious disruption to every institution that depends on people reliably being alive tomorrow.

items.question: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?
human_answers: I hope you like your steaks Pittsburgh Rare. And you may need to defrost it after you pick it up. Things get really hot when they come back from space. This isn’t because of air friction, strictly speaking—it’s because of air compression. The air can’t move out of the way fast enough, and gets squished in front of the spaceship/meteor/steak. Compressing air heats it up. As a rule of thumb, you start to notice compressive heating above about Mach 2 (which is why the Concorde had heat-resistant material on the leading edge of its wings). A few months ago, skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from 39 kilometers, and hit Mach 1 around 30 kilometers. This was enough to heat the air by a few degrees, but the air was so far below freezing that it didn’t make a difference. (Early in his jump, it was about minus 40 degrees, which is that magical point where you don’t have to clarify whether you mean Fahrenheit or Celsius—it’s the same in both.) As far as I know, this steak question originally came up in a lengthy 4chan thread (http://m.chanarchive.org/4chan/sci/63224/5209640#p5209833), which quickly disintegrated into poorly-informed physics tirades intermixed with homophobic slurs. There was no clear conclusion. To try to get a better answer, I decided to run a series of simulations of a steak falling from various heights. This involved a lot of research. I used Mathematica models of atmospheric density to generate a set of descent profiles for the plummeting steak. For a nice tutorial on how to do this, see the Wolfram Blog’s analysis of Felix Baumgartner’s jump (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/). An 8 oz. steak is about the size and shape of a hockey puck, so I based my steak’s drag coefficients on those given on page 74 of The Physics of Hockey (which author Alain Haché actually measured personally using some lab equipment). A steak isn’t a hockey puck, but the precise drag coefficient turned out not to make a big difference in the result. I used a handy NASA compressive heating calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html) to determine the temperature of the shock layer in front of the steak. Since this blog tends to wind up looking at unusual objects in extreme physical circumstances, often the only relevant research I can find is US military studies from the Cold War era. (Apparently, the US government was shoveling tons of money at anything even loosely related to weapons research.) To get an idea of how the air would heat the steak, I looked at research papers on the heating of ICBM nose cones as they reenter the atmosphere. Two of the most useful were Predictions of Aerodynamic Heating on Tactical Missile Domes (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA073217) and Calculation of Reentry-Vehicle Temperature History (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a231552.pdf). Lastly, I had to figure out exactly how quickly heat spreads through a steak. I started by looking at some papers from industrial food production which simulated heat flow through various pieces of meat. It took me a while to realize there was a much easier way to learn what combinations of time and temperature will effectively heat the various layers of a steak: Check a cookbook. Jeff Potter’s excellent book Cooking for Geeks (http://www.amazon.com/Cooking-Geeks-Science-Great-Hacks/dp/0596805888) provides a great introduction to the science of cooking meat, and explains what ranges of heat produce what effects in steak and why. Cook’s The Science of Good Cooking (http://www.amazon.com/Science-Cooking-Cooks-Illustrated-Cookbooks/dp/1933615982) was also helpful. Putting it all together, I found that the steak will accelerate quickly until it reaches about an altitude of about 30-50 kilometers, at which point the air gets thick enough to start slowing it back down. The falling steak’s speed drops steadily as the air gets thicker. No matter how fast it’s going when it reaches the lower layers of the atmosphere, it quickly slows down to terminal velocity. It always takes six or seven minutes to drop from 25 kilometers to the ground. For much of those 25 kilometers, the air temperature is below freezing—which means the steak will spend six or seven minutes subjected to a relentless blast of subzero, hurricane-force winds. Even if it is cooked by the fall, you’ll probably have to defrost it when it lands. When the steak does finally hit the ground, no matter the initial height, it will be traveling at about 30 meters per second. To get an idea of what this means, imagine a steak flung at the ground by a major-league pitcher. If the steak is even partially frozen, it could easily shatter. However, if it lands in the water, mud, or leaves, it will probably be fine. (Not clean, but intact.) A steak dropped from 39 kilometers will, unlike Felix, probably not break the sound barrier. It also won’t be appreciably heated. This makes sense—after all, Felix’s suit wasn’t scorched when he landed. [Image: image] Steaks can probably survive breaking the sound barrier. In addition to Felix, pilots have ejected at supersonic speeds (http://www.ejectionsite.com/insaddle/insaddle.htm) and lived to tell about it. To break the sound barrier, you’ll need to drop the steak from about 50 kilometers. But this isn’t enough to cook it. We need to go higher. If dropped from 70 kilometers, the steak will go fast enough to be briefly blasted by 350°F air. Unfortunately, this blast of thin, wispy air barely lasts a minute—and anyone with some basic kitchen experience can tell you that a steak placed in the oven at 350 for 60 seconds isn’t going to be cooked. From 100 kilometers—the formally defined edge of space—the picture’s not much better. The steak spends a minute and a half over Mach 2, and the outer surface will likely be singed, but the heat is too quickly replaced by the icy stratospheric blast for it to actually be cooked. [Image: image] At supersonic and hypersonic speeds, a shockwave forms around the steak which helps protect it from the faster and faster winds. The exact characteristics of this shock front—and thus the mechanical stress on the steak—depend on how an uncooked 8 oz. filet tumbles at hypersonic speeds. I searched the literature, but was unable to find anything to help me estimate this. For the sake of this simulation, I assume that at lower speeds some type of vortex shedding creates a flipping tumble, while at hypersonic speeds it’s squished into a semi-stable spheroid shape. However, this is little more than a wild guess. If anyone puts a steak in a hypersonic wind tunnel to get better data on this, please, send me the video. If you drop the steak from 250 kilometers, things start to heat up. 250 kilometers puts us in the range of low earth orbit. However, the steak, since it’s dropped from a standstill, isn’t moving nearly as fast as an object re-entering from orbit. [Image: image] The steak reaches a top speed of Mach 6, and the outer surface may even get pleasantly seared. The inside, unfortunately, is still uncooked. Unless, that is, it goes into a hypersonic tumble and explodes into chunks. From higher altitudes, the heat starts to get really substantial. The shockwave in front of the steak reaches thousands of degrees (Fahrenheit or Celsius; it’s true in both). The problem with these levels of heat is that it burns the surface layer completely, converting it to little more than carbon. That is, it becomes charred. Charring is a normal consequence of dropping meat in the fire. The problem with charring meat at hypersonic speeds is that the charred layer doesn’t have much structural integrity, and is blasted off by the wind—exposing a new layer to be charred. (If the heat is high enough, it will simply blast the surface layer off as it flash-cooks it. This is referred to in the ICBM papers as the “ablation zone”) Even from those heights, the steak stilldoesn’t spend enough time in the heat to get cooked all the way through. (I know what some of you are probably thinking, and the answer is no—it doesn’t spend enough time in the Van Allen belts to be sterilized by radiation). We can try higher and higher speeds, and we might lengthen the exposure time via dropping it at an angle, from orbit. But if the temperature is high enough or the burn time long enough, the steak will slowly disintegrate as the outer layer is repeatedly charred and blasted off. If most of the steak makes it to the ground, the inside will still be raw. Which is why we should drop the steak over Pittsburgh. As the probably-apocryphal story goes, steel workers in Pittsburgh would cook steaks by slapping them on the glowing metal surfaces coming out of the foundry, searing the outside while leaving the inside raw. This is, supposedly, the origin of the term Pittsburgh Rare (http://www.livestrong.com/article/436635-how-to-cook-pittsburgh-style-steaks/). So drop your steak from a suborbital rocket, send out a collection team to recover it, brush it off, reheat it, cut away any badly charred sections, and dig in. Just watch out for salmonella. And the Andromeda Strain. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
In any realistic Earth-atmosphere scenario, you can’t cook a steak just by dropping it.

A simple energy estimate gives a tempting lower bound: meat has a specific heat of about \(3.5 \text{ kJ/kg·°C}\). To warm a steak from refrigerator temperature, say \(5^\circ\text{C}\), to a cooked internal temperature around \(60^\circ\text{C}\), you need roughly

\[
3.5\times 55 \approx 190 \text{ kJ/kg}.
\]

Gravitational potential energy is \(gh\), so if 100% of the fall energy went into heating the steak,

\[
h \approx \frac{190{,}000}{9.8} \approx 19{,}000 \text{ m},
\]

or about 20 km.

But that is an impossible best case. In reality, almost all the energy from falling through air goes into heating the surrounding air and stirring turbulence, not into the steak. The steak also reaches terminal velocity, probably on the order of tens of meters per second, so the final impact energy is tiny: enough to splatter it, not cook it. At terminal speed, the air friction would warm the air by only a few degrees at most, nowhere near enough to sear or cook meat.

If you dropped it from much higher, like from space, it would not become a nicely cooked steak either. It would freeze, tumble, dry out, char or ablate on the outside during reentry, and likely break apart or splatter on impact while remaining unevenly heated.

So the careful answer is: an idealized calculation says about 15–20 km if all the energy heated the steak, but in the real atmosphere there is no height from which you can drop a steak and have it cook properly.

items.question: What If You Went Swimming in a Spent Fuel Pool?
human_answers: Assuming you’re a reasonably good swimmer, you could probably survive treading water anywhere from 10 to 40 hours. At that point, you would black out from fatigue and drown. This is also true for a pool without nuclear fuel in the bottom. Spent fuel from nuclear reactors is highly radioactive. Water is good for both radiation shielding and cooling, so fuel is stored at the bottom of pools for a couple decades until it’s inert enough to be moved into dry casks. We haven’t really agreed on where to put those dry casks yet. One of these days we should probably figure that out. Here’s the geometry of a typical fuel storage pool: [Image: image] The heat wouldn't be a big problem. The water temperature in a fuel pool can in theory go as high as 50°C, but in practice they're generally between 25°C and 35°C—warmer than most pools but cooler than a hot tub. For the kinds of radiation coming off spent nuclear fuel, every 7 centimeters of water cuts the amount of radiation in half. The most highly radioactive fuel rods are those recently removed from a reactor. Based on the activity levels provided by Ontario Hydro in this report (http://www.osti.gov/energycitations/servlets/purl/7284014-xaMii9/7284014.pdf), this would be the region of danger for fresh fuel rods: [Image: image] Swimming to the bottom, touching your elbows to a fresh fuel canister, and immediately swimming back up would probably be enough to kill you. Yet outside the outer boundary, you could swim around as long as you wanted—the dose from the core would be less than the normal background dose you get walking around. In fact, as long as you were underwater, you would be shielded from most of that normal background dose. You may actually receive a lower dose of radiation treading water in a spent fuel pool than walking around on the street. [Image: image] That’s if everything goes as planned. If there’s corrosion in the spent fuel rod casings, there may be some fission products in the water. They do a pretty good job of keeping the water clean, and it wouldn’t hurt you to swim in it, but it’s radioactive enough that it wouldn’t be legal to sell it as bottled water. (Which is too bad—it’d make a hell of an energy drink). We know spent fuel pools can be safe to swim in because they’re routinely serviced by human divers. However, these divers have to be careful. On August 31st, 2010 (http://www.isoe-network.net/index.php/publications-mainmenu-88/isoe-news/doc_download/1756-ritter2011ppt.html), a diver was servicing the spent fuel pool at the Leibstadt nuclear reactor in Switzerland. He spotted an unidentified length of tubing on the bottom of the pool and radioed his supervisor to ask what to do. He was told to put it in his tool basket, which he did. Due to bubble noise in the pool, he didn’t hear his radiation alarm. When the tool basket was lifted from the water, the room’s radiation alarms went off. The basket was dropped back in the water and the diver left the pool. The diver’s dosimeter badges showed that he’d received a higher-than-normal whole-body dose, and the dose in his right hand was extremely high. The object turned out to be protective tubing from a radiation monitor in the reactor core, made highly radioactive by neutron flux. It had been accidentally sheared off while a capsule was being closed in 2006. It sank to a remote corner of the pool floor, where it sat unnoticed for four years. The tubing was so radioactive that if he’d tucked it into a tool belt or shoulder bag, where it sat close to his body, he could’ve been killed. As it was, the water protected him, and only his hand—a body part more resistant to radiation than the delicate internal organs—received a heavy dose. [Image: image] So, as far as swimming safety goes, the bottom line is that you’d probably be ok, as long as you didn’t dive to the bottom or pick up anything strange. But just to be sure, I got in touch with a friend of mine who works at a research reactor, and asked him what he thought would happen to you if you tried to swim in their radiation containment pool. “In our reactor?” He thought about it for a moment. “You’d die pretty quickly, before reaching the water, from gunshot wounds.”

items.model_answer:
If you went swimming at the surface of a properly maintained spent nuclear fuel pool, the radiation itself would probably not be what kills you.

Spent fuel pools are deep for a reason: several meters of water sit above the fuel assemblies, and water is an excellent radiation shield. The spent fuel at the bottom is intensely radioactive, but the radiation level near the surface of the pool is typically very low because the water absorbs most of the gamma rays and stops beta radiation entirely. In a normal pool, a brief swim near the surface could give you a radiation dose comparable to ordinary background levels, possibly less than many medical X-rays.

The danger changes dramatically if you dive down toward the fuel. Close to the spent fuel assemblies, radiation levels can become extremely high. Near freshly discharged fuel, a lethal dose could be received in a short time, potentially minutes or less depending on distance, fuel age, and shielding. Touching or approaching exposed spent fuel would be extremely dangerous.

Other practical hazards also matter: the water is chemically controlled, often borated, very pure, and not something you should drink; the pool is an industrial nuclear facility with strict security; and disturbing fuel racks or equipment would be a serious safety issue. You also would not “become radioactive” just from swimming in clean pool water, though contamination would be a concern if the pool were damaged or poorly maintained.

So the direct answer is: swimming on the surface of an intact spent fuel pool would likely be surprisingly safe from a radiation standpoint, but diving toward the fuel at the bottom could be fatal, and in real life you would never be allowed to do it.

items.question: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?
human_answers: Here’s our aircraft: [Image: image] The Cessna 172 Skyhawk, probably the most common plane in the world. Here’s our pilot: [Image: image] Here’s what happens when the aircraft is launched above the surface of the 32 largest Solar System bodies: [Image: image] In most cases, there’s no atmosphere, and the plane falls straight to the ground. (If it’s dropped from one kilometer, in a few cases, the crash will be slow enough that the pilot may survive—although the life-support equipment probably won’t.) There are nine Solar System bodies with atmospheres thick enough to matter: Earth—obviously—Mars, Venus, the four gas giants, Saturn’s moon Titan, and the Sun. Let’s take a closer look at what would happen to a plane on each one. The Sun: This works about as well as you'd imagine. If the plane is released close enough to the Sun to feel its atmosphere at all, it's vaporized in less than a second. Mars: To see what happens to aircraft on Mars, we turn to X-Plane (http://www.x-plane.com/desktop/home/?utm_expid=25103718-8). X-Plane is the most advanced flight simulator in the world. The product of 20 years of obsessive labor by a hardcore aeronautics enthusiast who uses capslock a lot when talking about planes, it actually simulates the flow of air over every piece of an aircraft’s body as it flies. This makes it a valuable research tool, since it can accurately simulate entirely new aircraft designs—and new environments. In particular, if you change the X-Plane config file to reduce gravity, thin the atmosphere, and shrink the radius of the planet it can simulate flight on Mars (http://www.x-plane.com/adventures/mars.html). (Note: Thank you to Tom J and the folks in the X-Plane community for their help with aerodynamic calculations in different atmospheres.) X-Plane tells us that flight on Mars is difficult, but not impossible. NASA knows this, and has considered surveying Mars by airplane (http://marsairplane.larc.nasa.gov/). The tricky thing is that with so little atmosphere, to get any lift, you have to go fast. You need to approach Mach 1 just to get off the ground, and once you get moving, you have so much inertia that it’s hard to change course—if you turn, your plane rotates, but keeps moving in the original direction. The X-Plane author compared piloting Martian aircraft to flying a supersonic ocean liner. Our Cessna 172 isn’t up to the challenge. Launched from 1 km, it doesn’t build up enough speed to pull out of a dive, and plows into the Martian terrain at over 60 m/s (135 mph). If dropped from four or five kilometers, it could gain enough speed to pull up into a glide—at over half the speed of sound. The landing would not be survivable. Venus:Unfortunately, X-Plane is not capable of simulating the hellish environment near the surface of Venus. But physics calculations give us an idea of what flight there would be like. The upshot is: Your plane would fly pretty well, except it would be on fire the whole time, and then it would stop flying, and then stop being a plane. The atmosphere on Venus is over 60 times denser than Earth’s, which is thick enough that a Cessna moving at running speed would rise into the air. Unfortunately, the air it’s rising into is hot enough to melt lead. The paint would start melting off in seconds, the plane’s components would fail rapidly, and the plane would glide gently into the ground as it came apart under the heat stress. A much better bet would be to fly above the clouds. While Venus’s surface is awful, its upper atmosphere is surprisingly Earthlike. 55 kilometers up, a human could survive with an oxygen mask and a protective wetsuit; the air is room temperature and the pressure is similar to that on Earth mountains. You need the wetsuit, though, to protect you from the sulfuric acid. (I’m not selling this well, am I?) The acid's no fun, but it turns out the area right above the clouds is a great environment for an airplane (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20030003716_2002108457.pdf), as long as it has no exposed metal to be corroded away by the sulfuric acid. And is capable of flight in constant Category-5-hurricane-level winds, which are another thing I forgot to mention earlier. Venus is a terrible place. Jupiter: Our Cessna can’t fly on Jupiter; the gravity is just too strong. The power needed to maintain level flight is three times greater than that on Earth. Starting from a friendly sea-level pressure, we’d accelerate through the tumbling winds into a 275 m/s (600 mph) downward glide deeper and deeper through the layers of ammonia ice and water ice until we and the aircraft were crushed. There's no surface to hit; Jupiter transitions smoothly from gas to solid as you sink deeper and deeper. Saturn: The picture here is a bit friendlier than on Jupiter. The weaker gravity—close to Earth’s, actually—and slightly denser (but still thin) atmosphere mean that we’d be able to struggle along a bit further before we gave in to either the cold or high winds and descended to the same fate as on Jupiter. Uranus: Uranus is a strange, uniform bluish orb. There are high winds and it’s bitterly cold. It’s the friendliest of the gas giants to our Cessna, and you could probably fly for a little while. But given that it seems to be an almost completely featureless planet, why would you want to? Neptune: If you’re going to fly around one of the ice giants, Neptune (Motto: “The Slightly Bluer One”) is probably a better choice than Uranus. It at least has some clouds to look at before you freeze to death or break apart from the turbulence. Titan: We’ve saved the best for last. When it comes to flying, Titan might be better than Earth. Its atmosphere is thick but its gravity is light, giving it a surface pressure only 50% higher than Earth’s with air four times as dense. Its gravity—lower than that of the Moon—means that flying is easy. Our Cessna could get into the air under pedal power. In fact, humans on Titan could fly by muscle power. A human in a hang glider could comfortably take off and cruise around powered by oversized swim-flipper boots—or even take off by flapping artificial wings. The power requirements are minimal—it would probably take no more effort than walking. The downside (there’s always a downside) is the cold. It’s 72 kelvin on Titan, which is about the temperature of liquid nitrogen. Judging from some numbers on heating requirements for light aircraft, I estimate that the cabin of a Cessna on Titan would probably cool by about two degrees per minute. The batteries would help to keep themselves warm for a little while, but eventually the craft would run out of heat and crash. The Huygens probe, which descended with batteries nearly drained (taking fascinating pictures (http://www.beugungsbild.de/huygens/huygens.html) as it fell), succumbed to the cold after only a few hours on the surface. It had enough time to send back a single photo (http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/New_images_from_Titan) after landing—the only one we have from the surface of a body beyond Mars. If humans put on artificial wings to fly, we might become Titan versions of the Icarus story—our wings could freeze, fall apart, and send us tumbling to our deaths. [Image: image] But I've never seen the Icarus story as a lesson about the limitations of humans. I see it as a lesson about the limitations of wax as an adhesive. The cold of Titan is just an engineering problem. With the right refitting, and the right heat sources, a Cessna 172 could fly on Titan—and so could we.

items.model_answer:
An ordinary airplane would not work as an ordinary airplane anywhere else in the Solar System, mainly because its engine needs oxygen. No other planet or moon has an oxygen-rich atmosphere. But if you supplied power some other way, such as batteries, rockets, or onboard oxidizer, then the answer depends on air density and gravity.

On airless worlds such as the Moon, Mercury, most asteroids, and many moons, wings are useless. There is essentially no atmosphere, so the plane would not “fly”; it would follow a ballistic path and crash unless it had rockets.

On Mars, flight is barely possible but not for an ordinary airplane. Mars has only about 1% of Earth’s atmospheric pressure. Lower gravity helps, but not enough: a normal airplane would need to fly several times faster than on Earth to produce the same lift, often near or above the local speed of sound. Its propeller or jet engine also would not work normally because there is almost no oxygen and very little air to push against. Special aircraft can fly on Mars, but they need very light structures, large wings or rotors, and custom propulsion.

On Venus, aerodynamics would be easy but survival would not. Near the surface the atmosphere is extremely dense, so wings would generate enormous lift at low speed. But the surface is about 465°C, with around 90 times Earth’s pressure and corrosive chemistry, so an ordinary airplane would be crushed, cooked, and chemically attacked. Higher up in Venus’s atmosphere, around 50–60 km altitude, pressure and temperature are more Earthlike, and flight or floating would be quite feasible, but a normal engine still could not breathe the CO₂ atmosphere.

Titan, Saturn’s large moon, is probably the best place in the Solar System for airplane-like flight. It has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and very low gravity. A plane would need much less speed to stay aloft than on Earth; in principle, even human-powered flight would be much easier there. But Titan is extremely cold, about −180°C, and its atmosphere contains no oxygen, so a normal gasoline or jet engine would not run without onboard oxidizer or electric power.

The gas giants—Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—have atmospheres, so winged flight is physically possible in some layers. But there is no solid surface or runway, no oxygen for normal engines, and conditions become rapidly more extreme with depth. Jupiter in particular has high gravity, intense radiation, strong winds, and turbulence. A specially designed powered glider or probe might fly temporarily, but an ordinary airplane would not survive or operate usefully.

Pluto, Triton, and similar icy bodies have atmospheres far too thin for normal flight. They are effectively vacuum from an airplane’s point of view.

So the short answer is: an unmodified ordinary airplane can only really fly on Earth. With a non-air-breathing power source and suitable materials, Titan would be the easiest place to fly, Venus’s upper atmosphere would also be promising, Mars would be difficult, and airless worlds would be impossible for winged flight.

items.question: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?
human_answers: This is a common question. The Hubble operators get it a lot, and their FAQ page answers it (http://hubblesite.org/reference_desk/faq/answer.php.id=78&cat=topten). The problem isn’t—as some people say—that the Earth is too bright. As Phil Plait of Bad Astronomy pointed out (http://www.badastronomy.com/mad/2000/hubbleearth.html), Hubble looks at Earth pretty regularly. The real problem is that Hubble is moving over the surface at over 7 kilometers per second. Even a short exposure would be a blur. That’s no fun. Is there a way we could make it work? I decided to take a closer look. As our picture target, we’ll use this typical desk: [Image: image] The Earth’s atmosphere won’t be a problem. It’s actually much more of a problem for surface-based telescopes looking at space than for space-based telescopes looking at the surface. The reason for this is geometric: [Image: image] Hubble is the best visible-light telescope we have, but its resolution does have limits. Pluto, out in the Kuiper belt, lies right at those limits. The best pictures we have of Pluto (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/solar-system/pluto/2010/06/) come from Hubble, but the ex-planet is still little more than a mysterious blur. At that resolution (about 0.05 arcseconds, give or take) and Hubble’s distance from the desk (about 570 kilometers) the desk would look like this: [Image: image] But that desk is also zooming by, so even a perfect image will be blurred: [Image: image] Combining the two effects gives us an end result that looks like this: [Image: image] That’s no good. Could we rotate Hubble to track the surface, and eliminate the blur? Hubble swivels to follow targets. Usually, they’re far enough away that we can assume they’re at infinite distance. The automatic on-board parallax algorithms can’t handle targets closer than about ten times the distance to the Moon. When astronomers want to use it to take pictures of the Moon, sometimes they send it commands to rotate manually (http://www.stsci.edu/hst/HST_overview/documents/uir/UIR-2007-01.pdf), then turn on the camera mid-maneuver. It doesn’t work very well. Moving Hubble at those speeds is cumbersome with the current guidance package. The resulting photos (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/1999/14) are better than what you can see with the naked eye, but they’re not very good by Hubble standards. Here’s our desk, with the image degraded by a similar amount that the Moon one was: [Image: image] Fortunately, the Moon is bright enough that if you’ll settle for a short exposure, you can avoid the problem. This photo (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/2012/22/fastfacts/) was taken with a half-second exposure, short enough that it didn’t have to do much in the way of tracking. Unfortunately, our desk is moving across the telescope’s field of view about 600 times faster than the Moon. Tracking is unavoidable. The strange thing is, the desk really isn’t moving all that fast. Hubble is just really slow. To track the surface, it would need to rotate less than a degree per second at maximum. But Hubble wasn’t built for surface tracking. The telescope’s top rotational (“slew”) speed is only a few degrees per minute (about the speed of a minute hand on a clock) and even those speeds are fast enough that its gyroscopes cause it to vibrate (http://www.pha.jhu.edu/groups/hst10x/pdffiles/HST10X_Technical.pdf), which destroys the image quality. Clearly, we’d need to disable Hubble’s guidance system and bolt on our own control system. Hubble’s rotational moment of inertia (http://www.dept.aoe.vt.edu/~cdhall/courses/aoe5984/bs.pdf) is similar to that of a small carousel; too hard for the existing gyroscopes to move, but not hard in the absolute sense. With our custom control system, it could be made to track the surface, and get photos pretty close to optimal quality: [Image: image] But this isn’t just a hypothetical situation. Much of the technology in military spy satellites is believed to be similar to that of Hubble. So in a sense, pointing a Hubble-type telescope at the surface is not only possible—it’s what the US government actually does (http://www.onorbit.com/node/3850).

items.model_answer:
If Hubble were simply pointed at Earth, it would not produce a spectacular “Hubble Deep Field of Earth.” In normal operation it probably would not be allowed: Hubble has pointing restrictions to avoid the bright Earth, Sun, and Moon, and its instruments are protected against excessive light and scattered glare.

If those protections were overridden, the main result would be a very bright, rapidly smeared image. Hubble orbits only about 540 km above Earth and moves about 7.6 km/s. A ground scene would race through its field of view; without special ground-tracking and very short exposures, features would blur across the detector. Daylit Earth is also enormously brighter than the faint galaxies Hubble usually observes, so ordinary exposures would saturate the cameras.

In principle, a Hubble-sized telescope looking down could be very sharp. Its diffraction-limited visible-light resolution is about 0.05 arcseconds, which from Hubble’s altitude corresponds to roughly 10–15 cm on the ground. That is in the range of seeing cars and large objects, not reading newspapers or seeing through roofs. Atmospheric turbulence, clouds, haze, focus differences, and motion would degrade that.

So the careful answer is: Hubble is not built or operated as an Earth-imaging spy satellite. If forced to point at Earth, it would likely get overexposed, motion-blurred, operationally unsafe images. If redesigned with proper tracking, filters, fast shutters, and Earth-observation software, a Hubble-class telescope in low Earth orbit could take very high-resolution pictures of small patches of the surface.

edus.text: If Hubble were simply pointed at Earth,
it would not produce a spectacular “Hubble Deep Field of Earth.”
In normal operation it probably would not be allowed:
Hubble has pointing restrictions to avoid the bright Earth, Sun, and Moon,
and its instruments are protected against excessive light and scattered glare.
If those protections were overridden,
the main result would be a very bright, rapidly smeared image.
Hubble orbits only about 540 km above Earth
and moves about 7.6 km/s.
A ground scene would race through its field of view;
without special ground-tracking and very short exposures,
features would blur across the detector.
Daylit Earth is also enormously brighter than the faint galaxies Hubble usually observes,
so ordinary exposures would saturate the cameras.
In principle, a Hubble-sized telescope looking down could be very sharp.
Its diffraction-limited visible-light resolution is about 0.05 arcseconds,
which from Hubble’s altitude corresponds to roughly 10–15 cm on the ground.
That is in the range of seeing cars and large objects,
not reading newspapers or seeing through roofs.
Atmospheric turbulence, clouds, haze, focus differences, and motion would degrade that.
So the careful answer is: Hubble is not built or operated as an Earth-imaging spy satellite.
If forced to point at Earth,
it would likely get overexposed, motion-blurred, operationally unsafe images.
If redesigned with proper tracking, filters, fast shutters, and Earth-observation software,
a Hubble-class telescope in low Earth orbit could take very high-resolution pictures of small patches of the surface.
