items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself. If we can figure out the total weight of all the world’s ships, we can figure out how much water they’re displacing, then divide that volume by the surface area of the ocean to figure out how much the water level would drop. Weighing ships is confusing (http://www.pomorci.com/Zanimljivosti/TONNAGE%20MEASUREMENT%20OF%20SHIPS.pdf). There are a bunch of different measurements of the size of a ship, and many of them, like gross tonnage, are actually measures of the volume of the ship’s rooms and other internal spaces, not its weight. The UN Conference on Trade and Development publishes estimates (http://unctad.org/en/Docs/rmt2011ch2_en.pdf) of the size of the world shipping fleet. What the UNCTD publishes is “deadweight tonnage”, which is the maximum weight of the ship’s fuel, cargo, and crew. What we want is “displacement”. Unfortunately, comprehensive numbers for displacement are harder to find. Fortunately, we can estimate it. Brian Barrass’s book Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates gives a table of ratios of deadweight tonnage to displacement for different types of ships. Extrapolating from the last few years of UNCTD data, and using the coefficients from the book, suggests that the world fleet weighs about 2.15 billion tons when fully loaded. The main component of the fleet by weight is oil tankers and bulk ore-carrying ships, which make up over two-thirds of the total. (The UNCTD data doesn’t include small recreational boats or naval fleets. However, based on some numbers for naval fleets (http://www.csbaonline.org/4Publications/PubLibrary/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti.pdf) and recreational boats (http://nmma.net/assets/cabinets/Cabinet445/2011_abstract_preview.pdf), neither one contributes much to the total.) A ton of water is about a cubic meter. 2.15 billion cubic meters divided by the surface area of the oceans equals about 6 microns (0.006 mm). But you don’t have to worry about that six-micron sea level drop. The oceans are currently rising at about 3.3 millimeters per year due to global warming (through both glacial melting and thermal expansion of seawater). At that rate (normalized for seasonal variation and short-term fluctations), if you removed every ship from the ocean, the water would be back up to its original average level in 16 hours. [Image: image] Sea levels will likely rise a few feet by the year 2100 (https://what-if.xkcd.com/33). Current fish wet biomass is about 2 billion tons (http://phys.org/news151251277.html), so removing them won’t make a dent either. (Marine fish biomass dropped by 80% over the last century (http://news.aaas.org/2011_annual_meeting/0228declining-fisheries.shtml), which—taking into consideration the growth rate of the world’s shipping fleet—leads to an odd conclusion: Sometime in the last few years, we reached a point where there are, by weight, more ships in the ocean than fish.) And what about the old joke about how much deeper the ocean would be without sponges? While estimates of sponge biomass are hard to come by, the answer is probably that if you removed all the sponges, sea level would drop by no more than a few microns ... and much less if you squeezed them out first. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Archimedes-Based Sea-Level Estimate
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response correctly applies buoyancy/displacement reasoning to estimate the immediate global mean sea-level change from removing all ships from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Does not use displacement or buoyancy; predicts a large or directionally wrong sea-level change.
criteria.3-4: Mentions displaced water but confuses ship volume, cargo capacity, or tonnage, leading to an implausible estimate.
criteria.5-6: Uses Archimedes' principle qualitatively and gets the drop direction right, but gives only a rough or poorly supported magnitude.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates displaced mass/volume from world fleet weight and ocean area, yielding a micron-scale sea-level drop.
criteria.9-10: Accurately explains displacement versus tonnage, uses plausible fleet mass and ocean-area assumptions, and arrives near about 6 microns.

criteria.name: Scope of Removed Vessels and Mass Accounting
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the response defines 'every ship' and accounts for commercial, naval, recreational, cargo, fuel, and load-state contributions without overcounting.
criteria.1-2: Treats ships as empty geometric objects or ignores fleet composition entirely.
criteria.3-4: Considers only one class of vessels or relies on arbitrary guesses with no distinction among ship types.
criteria.5-6: Includes major commercial vessels but handles cargo/load state, naval fleets, or small boats vaguely.
criteria.7-8: Identifies commercial shipping as dominant and notes that naval and recreational craft are comparatively minor.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes displacement, deadweight, cargo/fuel load, and vessel categories while explaining why omitted small fleets barely affect the result.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and Relative Scale
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of physical, environmental, and societal consequences after instantaneous ship removal, while keeping them proportional to the tiny water-level effect.
criteria.1-2: Claims catastrophic ocean drainage, tsunamis, climate shifts, or ecosystem collapse from sea-level change alone.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but greatly exaggerates the sea-level, tidal, or geological consequences.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the sea-level effect is tiny but gives limited discussion of other consequences such as transport disruption or pollution changes.
criteria.7-8: Separates negligible ocean-level effects from major human impacts like global trade disruption, stranded cargo, fuel loss, and maritime safety issues.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent hierarchy of downstream effects: micron-scale sea-level change, no meaningful tidal/geophysical impact, but severe logistics, economic, rescue, and possible pollution consequences depending on removal details.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Mechanism Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response maintains a consistent causal chain under the premise that all ships are removed at once from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or contradicts it repeatedly, such as leaving ships in place while analyzing their removal.
criteria.3-4: Applies the premise inconsistently, mixing removal of ships, water, cargo, or marine life without clear rules.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise but leaves ambiguous whether cargo, people, fuel, or displaced water vanish or are relocated.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions about instantaneous removal and consistently traces immediate and later consequences.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly handles alternative interpretations, such as removing vessels only versus ships plus contents, and explains how each changes outcomes without breaking causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether numerical claims and speculative effects are appropriately qualified, internally consistent, and compared to relevant baselines such as modern sea-level rise.
criteria.1-2: Presents unsupported precise claims, contradictions, or physically impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Uses some plausible facts but mixes incompatible numbers or fails to flag major uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty generally but lacks clear bounds or relevant scale comparisons.
criteria.7-8: Uses order-of-magnitude reasoning, avoids false precision, and compares the result to ocean area, fleet mass, or annual sea-level rise.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates all estimates with transparent assumptions, sensible error bars, and comparisons such as millimeters-per-year sea-level rise overwhelming a few-micron drop within hours.

items.model_answer:
If every ship, boat, and vessel were removed from Earth’s waters at the same instant, the biggest immediate physical effect would be surprisingly small globally: sea level would fall by only a few micrometers to perhaps a few tens of micrometers.

That is because floating ships raise sea level only by the volume of water they displace. By Archimedes’ principle, a floating vessel displaces water equal to its own weight plus cargo, fuel, and contents. Even if the total floating mass of the world’s merchant, naval, fishing, and recreational fleets were several billion tonnes, that corresponds to only a few cubic kilometers of displaced seawater. Spread across the oceans’ roughly 361 million square kilometers of surface area, the average sea-level change is tiny: far less than a millimeter.

Locally, however, the effect could be dramatic for a moment. Each removed ship would leave behind a hull-shaped void in the water. Surrounding water would rush in to fill it, creating splashes, turbulence, and waves. In crowded harbors, canals, locks, naval bases, or marinas, the sudden disappearance of many vessels could produce noticeable surges and sloshing. A large ship displaces tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of cubic meters of water, so its instant removal could generate strong local waves, though not an ocean-wide tsunami.

There would be no major change to tides, ocean currents, Earth’s rotation, or climate from the physical removal itself. The mass of all ships is negligible compared with Earth and the oceans.

The real global consequences would be economic and logistical. International trade would be instantly crippled, because most bulk goods—oil, grain, coal, iron ore, manufactured goods, containers—move by sea. Fishing fleets would vanish from the water, naval power projection would stop, ferry routes would cease, and many island and coastal communities would be cut off. Fuel, food, medicine, and industrial supply chains would be heavily disrupted within days to weeks.

Environmentally, the oceans would quickly become quieter and safer for many marine animals. Ship strikes, underwater engine noise, anchor damage, bilge discharge, and shipping-related emissions would drop sharply. Industrial fishing pressure would also collapse if fishing vessels were included. But the human disruption would be enormous.

So the direct ocean-physics answer is: the seas would barely fall globally, but harbors would experience sudden local turbulence. The civilization-level answer is: global maritime trade and naval activity would stop almost instantly, causing severe worldwide disruption.

edus.text: If every ship, boat, and vessel were removed from Earth’s waters at the same instant,
the biggest immediate physical effect would be surprisingly small globally: sea level would fall by only a few micrometers to perhaps a few tens of micrometers.
That is because floating ships raise sea level only by the volume of water they displace.
By Archimedes’ principle,
a floating vessel displaces water equal to its own weight plus cargo, fuel, and contents.
Even if the total floating mass of the world’s merchant, naval, fishing, and recreational fleets were several billion tonnes,
that corresponds to only a few cubic kilometers of displaced seawater.
Spread across the oceans’ roughly 361 million square kilometers of surface area,
the average sea-level change is tiny:
far less than a millimeter.
Locally, however, the effect could be dramatic for a moment.
Each removed ship would leave behind a hull-shaped void in the water.
Surrounding water would rush in to fill it,
creating splashes, turbulence, and waves.
In crowded harbors, canals, locks, naval bases, or marinas,
the sudden disappearance of many vessels could produce noticeable surges and sloshing.
A large ship displaces tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of cubic meters of water,
so its instant removal could generate strong local waves,
though not an ocean-wide tsunami.
There would be no major change to tides, ocean currents, Earth’s rotation, or climate from the physical removal itself.
The mass of all ships is negligible compared with Earth and the oceans.
The real global consequences would be economic and logistical.
International trade would be instantly crippled,
because most bulk goods—oil, grain, coal, iron ore, manufactured goods, containers—move by sea.
Fishing fleets would vanish from the water,
naval power projection would stop,
ferry routes would cease,
and many island and coastal communities would be cut off.
Fuel, food, medicine, and industrial supply chains would be heavily disrupted within days to weeks.
Environmentally, the oceans would quickly become quieter and safer for many marine animals.
Ship strikes, underwater engine noise, anchor damage, bilge discharge, and shipping-related emissions would drop sharply.
Industrial fishing pressure would also collapse if fishing vessels were included.
But the human disruption would be enormous.
So the direct ocean-physics answer is: the seas would barely fall globally,
but harbors would experience sudden local turbulence.
The civilization-level answer is: global maritime trade and naval activity would stop almost instantly,
causing severe worldwide disruption.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere. No matter what happens inside the box, if there’s 1875 watts of power being used, eventually there will be 1875 watts of heat flowing out. This is true of any device that uses power, which is a handy thing to know. For example, people worry about leaving disconnected chargers plugged into the wall for fear that they’re draining power. Are they right? You can use heat flow to come up with simple rule of thumb: If an unused charger isn’t warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny of electricity a day. For a small smartphone charger, if it’s not warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny a year. This is true of almost any powered device (though not necessarily those plugged into a second device. If a charger is connected to something, like a smartphone or laptop, power can be flowing from the wall through the charger into the device.) But back to the box. Heat will flow from the hair dryer out into the box. If we assume the dryer is indestructible, the interior of the box will keep getting hotter until the outer surface reaches about 60°C (140°F). At that temperature, the box will be losing heat to the outside as fast as the hair dryer is adding it inside, and the system will be in equilibrium. [Image: image] The equilibrium temperature will be a bit cooler if there’s a breeze, or if the box is sitting on a wet or metallic surface that conducts away heat quickly. If the box is made of metal, 60°C is hot enough to burn your hand if you touch it (http://www.mascoat.com/assets/files/Insulative_Coating_Evaluation_NACE.pdf) for more than five seconds. If it’s wood, you can probably touch it for a while, but there’s a danger that parts of the box in contact with the mouth of the hair dryer will catch fire. The inside of a box will be like an oven. The temperature it reaches will depend on the thickness of the box wall; the thicker and more insulating the wall, the higher the temperature. It wouldn’t take a very thick box to create temperatures high enough to burn out the hair dryer. But let’s assume an indestructible hair dryer. And if we have something as cool as an indestructible hair dryer, it seems like a shame to limit it. [Image: image] With 18,750 watts flowing out of the hair dryer, the surface of the box reaches over 200°C (475°F), as hot as a skillet on low-medium. [Image: image] I wonder how high this dial goes. [Image: image] The surface of the box is now 600°C, hot enough to glow a dim red. [Image: image] If it’s made of aluminium, the inside is starting to melt. [Image: image] Two megawatts pumped into a laser (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/) is enough to destroy missiles. At 1300°C, the box is now about the temperature of lava. [Image: image] One more notch. If it’s made of something like tungsten, it might conceivably last a little longer. Just one more, then we'll stop. [Image: image] 187 megawatts is enough to make the box glow white. Not a lot of box materials can survive these conditions, so we’ll have to assume the box is indestructible. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the floor isn’t. Before it can burn its way through the floor, someone throws a water balloon under it. The burst of steam launches the box out the front door and onto the sidewalk. (Note: If you’re ever trapped with me in a burning building, and I suggest an idea for how we could escape the situation, it’s probably best to ignore me.) [Image: image] 1.875 gigawatts (I lied about stopping). According to Back to the Future, the hair dryer is now drawing enough power to travel back in time. [Image: image] The box is blindingly bright, and you can’t get closer than a few hundred meters due to the intense heat. It sits in the middle of a growing pool of lava. Anything within 50-100 meters bursts into flame. A column of heat and smoke rise high into the air. Periodic explosions of gas beneath the box launch it into the air, and it starts fires and forms a new lava pool where it lands. [Image: image] 18.7 gigawatts. The conditions around the box are similar to those on the pad during a Space Shuttle launch. The box begins to be tossed around by the powerful updrafts it’s creating. In 1914, H.G. Wells imagined devices like this in his book The World Set Free (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Set_Free). He wrote of a type of bomb that, instead of exploding once, exploded continuously, a slow-burn inferno that started inextinguishable fires in the hearts of cities. The story eerily foreshadowed the development, 30 years later, of nuclear weapons. [Image: image] The box is now soaring through the air. Each time it nears the ground, it superheats the surface, and the plume of expanding air hurls it back into the sky. [Image: image] 1.875 terawatts is like a house-sized stack of TNT going off every second. [Image: image] The box, soaring high above the surface, is putting out energy equivalent to three Trinity tests every second. At this point, the pattern is obvious. items.model_answer:
A running hair dryer in a sealed 1 m × 1 m × 1 m box would turn essentially all of its electrical power into heat inside the box.

The fan would just circulate the same air around; it would not “cool” the box or remove heat, because no air or energy is leaving. A typical hair dryer uses about 1,000–1,800 W, and almost all of that becomes thermal energy. If the box were perfectly insulated and the dryer kept running, the temperature would keep rising until the dryer failed, shut itself off, melted, or possibly started a fire.

For scale: 1 cubic meter of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg. The heat capacity of that air is roughly 1.2 kJ per °C. So a 1,500 W hair dryer could, in an idealized case where only the air heats up, raise the air temperature by about

\[
\frac{1500\ \text{J/s}}{1200\ \text{J/°C}} \approx 1.25^\circ\text{C/s}
\]

That means the air alone could rise tens of degrees in under a minute. In reality, the box walls, the dryer body, and anything else inside would absorb heat too, so the temperature rise would be slower. If the box is not insulated, heat would leak through the walls, and the temperature would eventually settle at a value where heat loss through the box equals the dryer’s power input.

Because the box is sealed and rigid, the pressure would also rise as the air heats. For example, heating the air from 20°C to 100°C would raise the pressure by roughly

\[
\frac{373}{293} \approx 1.27
\]

so the pressure would increase to about 1.27 atmospheres, assuming the box does not expand or leak.

The most likely practical outcome is that the dryer overheats and its thermal cutoff shuts it down. If the safety cutoff fails, the plastic parts, wiring, or surrounding materials could melt, smoke, or catch fire. The sealed box would not explode just because of the fan, but heating the trapped air raises pressure, and fire or failure could create additional hazards.

So the direct answer is: the box gets hotter and more pressurized; the dryer recirculates hot air; eventually the dryer shuts off, fails, or becomes a fire hazard unless heat can escape through the box walls.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects. If it didn’t clog the sink, the rest of the pipes could probably handle it. It might provoke some confusion among the sewage treatment people, but it wouldn’t break anything. But it’d be terrifically boring (and thus unpleasant) to pour cornstarch down a sink all day, so I guess that’s— [Image: image] … Oh. Huh. Well, let’s thicken the cornstarch. When you mix cornstarch and water in a bit under a 2:1 ratio, you get oobleck, a substance with some odd physical properties. This is a great kitchen science experiment everyone should try at least once. At low speeds, oobleck behaves like a liquid. If you gently swish your fingers in a bowl of it, it feels like milk or heavy cream. However, if you make a fist and punch the surface, your hand bounces off with a thud—it’s like hitting a slab of raw meat. If you vibrate oobleck, even stranger things happen (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zoTKXXNQIU). It wouldn’t take much of the mixture to clog a drain. It depends on your plumbing, but you could probably stop up your sink with a small bowl of it. Since your drain is clogged, I guess that’s the answer to your question. [Image: image] Well, ok. I guess some people don’t mind clogged drains. If you keep at it, after a few minutes, your sink will overflow, spilling goop onto your floor. [Image: image] Financially, this will be hard to keep up. If you’re mixing as fast as the water will come out of the sink, this project may cost you in the neighborhood of $5,000 per day if you can’t find a good bulk distributor. [Image: image] At this rate, it should build up on the floor at a rate of an inch or two per day. [Image: image] If your doors are sealed well, it will continue to build up. Once it reaches knee height (a week or two after you started), you may be able to hold the rising tide at bay for a little bit—at least in one room—by getting someone to flush the toilet repeatedly. The pipes there are larger and harder to clog; the limiting factor would probably be how fast the tank filled with water. [Image: image] Eventually, after a month or two, the oobleck would reach the living room window. The pressure would quickly rise, and sooner or later the window would burst. As the deadly Boston Molasses Flood (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Molasses_Disaster) proved, even thick, viscous fluids can flow quickly when in large enough quantities. The oobleck would pour rapidly out onto the lawn, carrying you with it. At this point, the local officials would probably notice and, at the very least, shut off your water. [Image: image] But I guess if you really like cornstarch that much, nothing unpleasant has happened.

items.model_answer:
Practically: don’t pour cornstarch down a drain at all, except for tiny residue amounts rinsed off dishes with plenty of cold water.

There is no safe universal threshold, because it depends on pipe size, trap shape, water flow, and whether the starch meets hot water or grease. But as a rough guide: a teaspoon or so accidentally rinsed away is unlikely to matter if flushed with lots of cold water. A few tablespoons can start accumulating in a P-trap. A cup or more is very likely to cause trouble, especially if it gets wet and settles. With hot water, cornstarch can gelatinize into a thick paste, making clogs worse.

Cornstarch does not dissolve like sugar or salt. It suspends in water, settles in low-flow areas, and can form a sticky, dense mass. In a drain trap it can combine with grease, food particles, soap scum, and hair, eventually making a blockage.

items.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway. It would be pretty hard to hear. The basic idea is pretty straightforward. The stereo is going faster than its own sound, so it will reach you first, followed by the sound it emitted one second ago, followed by the sound it emitted two seconds ago, and so forth. [Image: image] The problem is that the stereo is moving at Mach 2, which means that two seconds ago, it was over a kilometer away. It’s hard to hear music from that distance, particularly when your ears were just hit by (a) a sonic boom, and (b) pieces of a rapidly disintegrating stereo. Wind speeds of Mach 2 would messily disassemble most consumer electronics. The force of the wind on the body of the stereo is roughly comparable to that of a dozen people standing on it: [Image: image] An ordinary stereo wouldn’t make it, but one with some kind of ruggedized high-strength casing might be able to survive. If we put together a durable, heavy-duty stereo and launch it on a ballistic trajectory, it will only be traveling at supersonic speeds for the first 150 meters or so. This means that the target will hear a maximum of about a third of a second of reversed music. This phenomenon is actually confirmed in the 2008 paper Reproduction of Virtual Sound Sources Moving at Supersonic Speeds in Wave Field Synthesis (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/230702229_Reproduction_of_Virtual_Sound_Sources_Moving_at_Supersonic_Speeds_in_Wave_Field_Synthesis), which says that the sound wave field “contains a component carrying a time-reversed version of the source’s input signal”. The sonic boom would be the first thing the target would hear. It would be followed by several sounds played over one another, including both reversed music (rising slightly in pitch as it fades out) and forward-playing music (which would play at half speed and an octave too low), followed by the crash of a stereo demolishing your neighbor’s shed. Which means that if you’re playing one of those albums containing secret demonic messages, the result will be the strangest listening experience of your life: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Assuming an ideal stereo that survives and keeps playing, you would not hear it coming. At Mach 2 it is moving faster than the sound it emits, so its sound cannot spread out ahead of it. The sound is swept into a trailing Mach cone with half-angle

\[
\sin\theta=\frac{c}{v}=\frac{1}{2},
\]

so \(\theta=30^\circ\).

If it flew past you at some distance, you would first see it pass silently. A short time later, when the Mach cone reached you, you would hear a sharp sonic boom. For a closest-approach distance \(d\), that boom would arrive about

\[
\frac{\sqrt{3}\,d}{2c}
\]

after the stereo passed its closest point, where \(c\) is the speed of sound.

After the boom, you would hear the music in a very strange way. The sound emitted near the moment whose wavefront formed the Mach cone would arrive all bunched together, so it would be loud and highly compressed. Then later sounds would arrive normally but Doppler-shifted, while some earlier sounds from before the boom would arrive in reverse order. In other words, it would not sound like an ordinary stereo going by with a pitch shift; it would be mostly silence, then a sonic boom, then a distorted overlapping mixture of forward-playing and backward-arriving music.

In the real world, a stereo flying through air at Mach 2 would likely be torn apart or drowned out by aerodynamic shock noise, so the “music” would be much less noticeable than the sonic boom.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it. Strangely, as of the day I’m writing this, Voyager is actually getting closer (http://voyager.jpl.nasa.gov/where/) to us, because Earth is in a part of its orbit where it’s approaching Voyager faster than Voyager is fleeing. But in a few months, we’ll swing around the Sun and Voyager will again be getting farther away. [Image: image] It has a 35-year head start, so it would be hard to catch. But catching up isn’t the problem. New Horizons, the spacecraft currently headed out of the Solar System by way of Pluto, is never going to catch up to Voyager—it’s not moving fast enough and it’s headed in the wrong direction. But it could have. The reason Voyager is moving so fast is that it got gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn, while New Horizons only got one from Jupiter. [Image: image] Gravity assists aren’t paradoxical magic. It’s just like bouncing a tennis ball off a passing truck. Gyroscopes, on the other hand, ARE magic. If New Horizons had ditched the Pluto objective and waited for the right planetary alignment (the 2030s look promising), it could have swung by Jupiter and Saturn, then caught up to Voyager in as little as a century or two! (Assuming we could manage to hit Voyager from that far away. But I bet we could; our rocket scientists are pretty good at rocket science.) Of course, getting there’s the easy part. The hard part is getting back. Voyager weighs a little less than a ton and is moving away at 17 kilometers per second (if it were in the atmosphere, that would be Mach 50). And since it’s out in interstellar space, there are no speeding Jupiters to grab on to. Stopping Voyager is going to take a lot of fuel. It’s what engineers call the tyranny of the rocket equation (http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition30/tryanny.html): As the amount that you want to change your speed (“delta-v”) goes up, the fuel required increases exponentially. The equation tells us that to turn the 720-kilogram Voyager around, we’re going to need at least 30 tons of fuel. But to get that fuel out there, we need even more fuel. And to get that fuel, we need even more fuel. (This is where the tyrannical rocket equation gets its exponential term.) In fact, to rescue Voyager, we’d have to launch a fleet of—at minimum—60 New Horizons-sized spacecraft loaded with nothing but fuel. Could we do it? Sure. There are a couple plausible ways. Instead of building five to ten dozen fuel-laden Titan IIIEs, we could just build a fleet of ten or fifteen Saturn Vs, and do the whole thing with fewer launches. But however we did it, it would be a massive and expensive operation similar in scale to the Apollo program. The difference between the launch vehicle we’d used to get Voyager out of the Solar System and the fleet we’d need for a round trip is striking: [Image: image] Fortunately, there’s one way around the tyranny of the rocket equation: Ditch the rockets. Ion engines—which use electric fields to accelerate exhaust gas to high speeds—are far more efficient than chemical rockets, and they make accelerating to high speeds much more plausible. The reason we’re not using them for everything is that they produce very little thrust, so it takes a long time to get up to speed. It’s like if you had a car that gets amazing mileage but has a one-horsepower engine. (Actually, are you sure that’s not just a horse?) Ion engines are great; the current ones just take forever to get you moving. But since catching Voyager is going to take a long time anyway, ion engines are fine. We could launch a probe (like this one (https://web.archive.org/web/20150910020454/http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/13644/1/00-0010.pdf)), send it out to Voyager, latch on, turn everything around, and let it spend a few decades slowing Voyager down. Once Voyager had lost nearly all its speed, the Sun’s gravity would take over, and the probe would begin a long slow slide toward the inner Solar System. This would take about 200 years, and with some extremely careful nudges, we could make sure it falls in an Earth-crossing orbit. Two centuries later, Voyager would reach Earth and, with no way to slow down, burn up in our atmosphere, because we didn’t think to send out an aerobraking shell with the rescue craft. So that was a waste of a few centuries of work and billions upon billions of dollars. [Image: image] Maybe a better idea would be to borrow a salvage vessel and set sail for the coast of New South Wales, Australia. There, in the waters off Jervis Bay, the Australian Royal Navy ship Voyager sank in 1964 after an accidental collision. That one’s probably easier to retrieve. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If we launched a one-way spacecraft mission to Voyager 1 today, the main problem would not be “getting to space”; it would be catching something that already has a huge head start and is still moving away from the Sun at about 17 km/s.

Voyager 1 is now roughly 25 billion km from Earth, about 165–170 AU, with a one-way radio light time of about 23 hours. It is in interstellar space and moving outward by about 3.6 AU per year.

A chasing spacecraft would have to exceed Voyager 1’s outward speed. The catch-up time depends almost entirely on its final solar-system escape speed:

At 20 km/s outward, only slightly faster than Voyager, it would take roughly 250–300 years to catch up. At 30 km/s, it would take about 60 years. At 50 km/s, about 25 years. At 100 km/s, about 10 years. At 200 km/s, only a few years, but achieving that as an outbound interstellar trajectory is far beyond ordinary chemical launch capability.

With current or near-current technology, a realistic uncrewed fast probe using a heavy rocket plus gravity assists, perhaps a solar Oberth maneuver, might reach Voyager 1’s distance in several decades, but not soon. It would probably intercept Voyager somewhere around 250–400 AU from the Sun, depending on speed.

There is also a major distinction between a flyby and a rendezvous. A flyby is much easier: the probe just crosses Voyager’s path and photographs or scans it at high relative speed. A rendezvous is far harder because the probe would need to slow down and match Voyager 1’s velocity after catching it. That could require tens of km/s of braking delta-v, which is extremely difficult without a large propulsion system and fuel supply.

By the time such a mission arrived, Voyager 1 itself would almost certainly be dead. Its plutonium power source is declining, and NASA expects its instruments and transmitter to become unusable around the late 2020s or 2030s. Decades later, a chasing probe would likely find a silent, frozen spacecraft coasting through interstellar space.

So the direct answer is: yes, an uncrewed one-way mission to Voyager 1 is physically possible, but with present technology it would probably be a decades-long high-speed flyby, not a rendezvous. A human one-way mission is not realistically feasible. The most practical version would be a specialized interstellar precursor probe launched on a very high-energy trajectory to overtake Voyager 1 far beyond the heliosphere.

edus.text: If we launched a one-way spacecraft mission to Voyager 1 today,
the main problem would not be “getting to space”;
it would be catching something that already has a huge head start and is still moving away from the Sun at about 17 km/s.
Voyager 1 is now roughly 25 billion km from Earth, about 165–170 AU, with a one-way radio light time of about 23 hours.
It is in interstellar space and moving outward by about 3.6 AU per year.
A chasing spacecraft would have to exceed Voyager 1’s outward speed.
The catch-up time depends almost entirely on its final solar-system escape speed:
At 20 km/s outward, only slightly faster than Voyager, it would take roughly 250–300 years to catch up.
At 30 km/s, it would take about 60 years.
At 50 km/s, about 25 years.
At 100 km/s, about 10 years.
At 200 km/s, only a few years,
but achieving that as an outbound interstellar trajectory is far beyond ordinary chemical launch capability.

With current or near-current technology, a realistic uncrewed fast probe using a heavy rocket plus gravity assists, perhaps a solar Oberth maneuver, might reach Voyager 1’s distance in several decades,
but not soon.
It would probably intercept Voyager somewhere around 250–400 AU from the Sun, depending on speed.
There is also a major distinction between a flyby and a rendezvous.
A flyby is much easier:
the probe just crosses Voyager’s path and photographs or scans it at high relative speed.
A rendezvous is far harder
because the probe would need to slow down and match Voyager 1’s velocity after catching it.
That could require tens of km/s of braking delta-v,
which is extremely difficult without a large propulsion system and fuel supply.
By the time such a mission arrived, Voyager 1 itself would almost certainly be dead.
Its plutonium power source is declining,
and NASA expects its instruments and transmitter to become unusable around the late 2020s or 2030s.
Decades later, a chasing probe would likely find a silent, frozen spacecraft coasting through interstellar space.
So the direct answer is: yes, an uncrewed one-way mission to Voyager 1 is physically possible,
but with present technology it would probably be a decades-long high-speed flyby, not a rendezvous.
A human one-way mission is not realistically feasible.
The most practical version would be a specialized interstellar precursor probe launched on a very high-energy trajectory to overtake Voyager 1 far beyond the heliosphere.

items.question: What If Everyone in America Drove West?
human_answers: [Image: image] Thanks to plate tectonics, the United States is drifting west at about (http://hypertextbook.com/facts/ZhenHuang.shtml) a centimeter per year. (The people who live there, on the other hand, are on average drifting west at about a centimeter per minute (http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/facts_for_features_special_editions/cb11ff10.html).) There are 212,309,000 (http://nhts.ornl.gov/tables09/FatCat.aspx) licensed drivers in the US, and since we have more cars than drivers, we can in theory get them all behind the wheel at once. The average car on the road weighs a hair over 4,000 lbs (http://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/05/business/05weight.html), so we have 850 billion pounds of car (plus around 30 billion pounds of driver) to throw around. The North American plate, by comparison, is about 25 million square kilometers in area and probably averages around 35 kilometers thick. Given a density of about 2.7 kg/Liter, its mass is probably in the neighborhood of \(2.3 \times 10^{21}\)kg, so it outweighs our fleet by a factor of about six trillion. [Image: image] But let's say we give it a shot anyway, and all 212 million of us point our vehicles due west and then floor it. For the dozen or so seconds we’d spend accelerating to freeway speed, our cars would exert very close to a trillion newtons of eastward force on the ground. In the absence of other forces, conservation of momentum tells us it would accelerate the plate up to a blistering 18 cm/year, more than enough to reverse the current motion. \[\frac{210,000,000 \text{ cars} \times 4100 \frac{\text{lbs}}{\text{car}} \times 75\text{mph}}{2.3 \times 10^{21}\text{kg}} \approx 18 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}} \gg 0.69 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}}\] But wait. The plates are moving so slowly that their motion isn’t dominated by momentum. They’re held where they are by a balance of forces—the complicated and boring ones from the beginning—and if we’re going to stop them, we probably have to try to figure out what they are. If the plates were drifting along as if they were sliding on ice, then we could push them easily. But it’s possible they’re locked on a slow-but-steady magma conveyer belt, and we can’t move them back without also shifting the flow beneath them. It was only recently—in the mid-20th century—that we discovered that continents move at all, and we’re still getting a handle on the complex forces between the plates and currents in the mantle that control continental motion. But they sound pretty complicated so let’s try to ignore them. We don’t care how it works—we just want to know if we can break it. These forces are hard to measure, so we’re not sure how they all work. There’s some evidence (http://www.umich.edu/~gs265/tecpaper.htm) that the flow of the mantle along the bottom of the plates isn’t as important as the weight of the edges of the crust as it sinks into the mantle, and the forces in the mantle pushing back against it. The geology literature gives us some loose estimates to work with. The drag from the mantle, resisting forward motion, is typically in the neighborhood of \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) newtons per square meter, meaning the existing eastward drag force on the North American plate is on the order of \(10^{19}\) newtons. That’s millions of times more than our fleet. The other forces are greater still. The fact that plates move steadily along in the face of drag that powerful suggests to me that the equilibrium of forces guiding them is probably fairly stable and unlikely to be responsive by our little shove. But conservation of momentum still works—so something has to move, and that something is the entire Earth, whose rotation would be sped up slightly. If our fleet were centered at around 39º N, the day would be shortened by only about 200 attoseconds—about a trillionth of a percent of the time it took you to read the word “attosecond.” If we drove east instead, the day would be lengthened by a similar amount. But considering the gasoline required, those 200 attoseconds would cost at least $50 billion. At 100 octillion times minimum wage, that’s a pretty bad hourly rate. All things considered, it would be a lot easier to just forget to change our clocks next spring and get a whole hour for nothing. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If everyone in the United States tried to drive west at the same time, the main result would be a nationwide traffic disaster, not a dramatic physical effect on Earth.

Roads would jam almost immediately, especially around cities, bridges, tunnels, mountain passes, and the limited east–west highways. Gas stations would be overwhelmed, emergency services would be blocked, and many people would never get far. People already near the West Coast would quickly run out of land unless they turned, stopped, or drove into the Pacific.

If the question is about whether this would affect Earth’s rotation, the answer is: technically yes, but by an absurdly tiny amount. Suppose about 330 million people each drove west in a car at highway speed. The cars would gain westward angular momentum, so Earth would gain a tiny compensating eastward angular momentum and spin very slightly faster. The length of the day would shrink by roughly a nanosecond, about one-billionth of a second, and when the cars stopped, that effect would mostly disappear.

If everyone permanently relocated westward, even that would barely matter geophysically. The shift in Earth’s center of mass would be microscopic, far too small to affect tides, earthquakes, climate, or the planet’s orbit.

So the realistic answer is: America would experience catastrophic gridlock and fuel shortages; Earth itself would barely notice.

items.question: What If a High-Speed Train Had to Go through a Vertical Loop?
human_answers: No. Since this is kind of a disappointing answer, I tried relaxing the requirements a little. Could a high-speed train run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Still no. Could a modified and reinforced high-speed train with a jet engine on top run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Maybe. The Norwegian aluminium and energy company Norsk Hydro ran a pro-education ad (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlczxXqez-Y) in which a bunch of kids build a giant roller-coaster loop on a train track as a prank. This is, of course, unrealistic, but not just for the obvious reasons. There are some problems with the whole idea of sending high-speed trains through loops. The first issue is geometry. The biggest vertical loop which a train could conceivably go around has a radius of about 200 meters. If it’s any bigger than that, even the fastest trains will fail to complete the loop. Unfortunately, a 200 meter loop is much too tight. Most high-speed trains are limited (http://khsrcl.com/downloads/Chapter%204.pdf) to vertical curves with radii no shorter than 20 kilometers. [Image: image] The reason for those limits isn't that trains aren't bendy enough. It's how fast they're going. The spec sheet for the Bombardier ZEFIRO (http://www.superscooper.com/en/1_0/pdf/Bombardier_Zefiro_Technical_Description_en.pdf), for example, says it can handle a pretty tight vertical curve radius—just 900 meters. At the train’s top speed, that curve would create about two gees of acceleration. This might be survivable (for the passengers, at least, if not the train), but it would certainly not be comfortable. Yet a 900 meter radius loop is still too big. Even with the engine at full power, the train wouldn’t even be able to get a quarter of the way around the loop before sliding back down. [Image: image] The CGI train in the Norwegian video is an Di 4 (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSB_Di_4), which is shown moving about twice as fast as it can actually go. Based on its speed and number of cars, the loop appears to have a radius of about 70 meters, which is part of why it’s shown going so fast—the actual Di 4 would be just a little too slow, and would fall off the track at the top. The digital one, however, makes it around the loop in about five seconds, no problem. But the tight loop means the passengers and train are experiencing between 9 and 15 gees. This is at the limit of what fighter pilots can handle in pressure suits. In addition to killing everyone on board, it would certainly destroy the train, to say nothing of the track. 70 meters is much too tight. Clearly, we need a larger loop. 900 meters would be great, but our trains aren’t fast enough for that.\ But maybe we could make the train go faster ... Hmm. [Image: image] Believe it or not, this has been tried before—a number of countries have built jet-engine-powered trains (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbojet_train). Sadly, they never took off. Fortunately, they never took off. A 747 engine mounted atop a bullet train would probably add about 35% to its speed. Is that enough to do a 900-meter loop? [Image: image] Nope. Ok, putting the jet engine on top didn’t work. Maybe we should try something different. [Image: image] ... why did we think that would work? Forget that idea. Clearly, we need some combination of a fast train and a medium-sized loop. The sweet spot for loop size and shape is probably something like this: [Image: image] Of course, given the height, we’d probably have to build it into a small mountain: [Image: image] The shape of the loop, which is common in roller coasters, would spread out the g-forces more evenly, resulting in a max of only a few gees—totally survivable! Of course, the construction costs would be astronomical, and it goes without saying that no group of kids could pull it off alone without the resources of a major government. To any Norwegian kids reading this who were hoping to build a train loop, don't despair—there may still be a way to make this happen. The US Vice President, Joe Biden, served in the US Senate for 36 years. In all that time, he never moved to Washington, DC. Instead, every night, he took the train home to Delaware to see his family. This is very touching, but after the first few years, I'm sure the commute got a little dull. So, if you’re looking for a high-level backer to help you make someone’s train ride a little more exciting, you might just try talking to Joe. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Loop Kinematics and Geometry Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about the speed, radius, and acceleration requirements for a high-speed train to complete a vertical loop, including why ordinary rail curve radii and roller-coaster-style loops differ.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or badly misstates the basic physics; treats the loop as feasible or impossible without speed-radius reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions gravity or centripetal force but gives vague or incorrect relationships between speed, loop size, and completion.
criteria.5-6: Correctly identifies that tight loops cause huge g-forces and large loops require impractically high speeds, but with limited quantitative grounding.
criteria.7-8: Uses sound kinematic reasoning, approximate radii/speeds, and explains why normal high-speed trains cannot complete a survivable loop.
criteria.9-10: Precisely connects loop radius, minimum top speed, vertical curvature limits, and g-loads, including why a feasible radius conflicts with train speed and comfort constraints.

criteria.name: Passenger, Train, and Track Load Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of downstream mechanical and biological effects: passenger comfort/survival, train structural integrity, wheel-rail contact, and track forces during the loop.
criteria.1-2: Omits consequences for passengers, train, or track, or claims they would be unaffected.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger or discomfort generally but does not distinguish human g-tolerance from train/track structural limits.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that passengers and equipment would face severe accelerations, but only partially analyzes failure modes.

items.model_answer:
A conventional high-speed train could not safely do it. A purpose-built vehicle could, but it would have to be more like a giant roller coaster or maglev system than a normal train.

At high speed, the limiting issue is centripetal acceleration. For a train moving through a vertical loop of radius \(R\) at speed \(v\), the required inward acceleration is

\[
a = \frac{v^2}{R}.
\]

At the bottom of the loop, passengers feel heavier:

\[
\text{load} = 1 + \frac{v^2}{Rg}.
\]

At the top, gravity helps provide the inward acceleration. To avoid falling away from the track without restraints, the train needs roughly

\[
\frac{v^2}{R} \ge g.
\]

Take a typical high-speed train speed of about 300 km/h, or 83 m/s. If it went through a circular loop at that speed, then to keep the bottom force to about 2 g, the loop radius would need to be around

\[
R \approx \frac{v^2}{g} \approx 700 \text{ m}.
\]

That means a loop diameter of roughly 1.4 km. A “comfortable” high-speed train loop would be enormous, taller than many mountains or skyscrapers.

If the loop were smaller, the g-forces would become severe. For example, if the train entered a simple unpowered circular loop just fast enough to stay on the track at the top, the bottom of the loop would impose about 6 g. That is dangerous for passengers and likely beyond what a normal train structure, bogies, couplers, and track could tolerate.

There is also an energy problem. A train entering at 300 km/h has enough kinetic energy to climb only about 350 m vertically if unpowered, ignoring losses. A gentle loop suitable for that speed might need to be far taller than that, so the train would need powerful propulsion throughout the climb.

The track would also need to be completely different. Ordinary steel rails rely on gravity keeping the wheels on the track. In a vertical loop, the train would need captive wheels, clamps, guide rails, or magnetic guidance to prevent derailment, especially near the top. Passengers would need restraints, luggage would have to be secured, fluids and equipment would need special design, and the train cars would need to handle huge bending and coupling forces.

So the short answer is: a high-speed train could go through a vertical loop only if the loop were gigantic and the train were specially built for it. A normal high-speed train on normal rails would derail, overstress its structure, and subject passengers to dangerous forces.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball. He concluded that the Earth was smoother but less round (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/09/08/ten-things-you-dont-know-about-the-earth/#.UZrBpmRAC9a), based on published billiard ball roundness tolerances. However, he couldn’t find any information on the size and shape of a billiard ball’s pits and bumps. Fortunately for us, there are people who digitally scan bowling ball surfaces (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5V3rFdAIMY). [Image: image] These scans (along with various measurements of ball roughness[1] (http://classic.bowl.com/news/specsandcerts/index.jsp) tell us that a high-end bowling ball is quite smooth. If blown up to the scale of the Earth, the ridges and bumps[2] (http://www.itbca.bowlingknowledge.info/index.php/winter-2013/85-bowling-ball-shell-chemistry-101) would be between 10 and 200 meters high, and the peaks would be between one and three kilometers apart: [Image: image] By Earth standards, this is quite smooth; our highest mountains are 40 times higher. What would this bowling ball world (we’ll call it “Lebowski”) be like? For starters, bowling balls are a lot less dense than rock, so Lebowski’s surface gravity would be a quarter the strength of Earth’s: [Image: image] It would also (at first) have no atmosphere. [Image: image] The finger holes would be about a thousand kilometers across and a few thousand kilometers deep. [Image: image] On Earth, holes this big would expose the molten interior. But Lebowski doesn’t have a molten interior. The Earth’s core is hot for two reasons: It’s still glowing from the heat of all the dust collapsing together when it formed, and it’s full of radioactive metals. Lebowski wouldn’t have either of these, so its core would start out cold. The holes would be far too big to hold themselves open against gravity; On that scale, the polymers in the bowling ball would behave more like a liquid. In the space of about half an hour, the holes would undergo a slow-motion collapse. [Image: image] As they collapsed, the material around the holes would heat to a glow. At the center of the hole, a white-hot jet of charred hydrocarbons would fountain outward into space. When it was over, Lebowski would be left with massive scars, each marking the location where an abyss collapsed to form a molten sea. [Image: image] And now, thanks to this question, whenever I look at the Moon, I’ll notice the Sea of Tranquility, the Sea of Serenity, and the Sea of Crisis (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FFile%3AMoon_names.svg&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHIe4YcJnAZYmMY278G3Ko63hJnKQ), and I’ll think: Finger holes. But that’s just, like, my opinion, man.

items.model_answer:
If a normal bowling ball were scaled up so its diameter matched Earth’s, it would not remain a recognizable giant bowling ball for long.

Assuming it keeps roughly the same material density, about 1.3–1.5 g/cm³, an Earth-sized bowling ball would have about one quarter of Earth’s mass. Its surface gravity would be only about 2.5 m/s², roughly one quarter of Earth gravity, and its escape velocity would be around 5–6 km/s.

The finger holes would become enormous: a 2.5 cm finger hole would scale to roughly 1,500 km wide, and a several-centimeter-deep hole could become thousands of kilometers deep. But those holes could not survive. At Earth size, the ball’s own gravity would create internal pressures of several to around ten gigapascals, far beyond what bowling-ball resin or filler materials can support. The holes and any large surface features would collapse, flow, fracture, and slump inward. The object would settle into a roughly spherical low-density planet or dwarf-planet-like body.

It would also likely heat dramatically. If the enlargement involved assembling that much material under gravity, the released gravitational energy would be enough to melt or severely alter much of the material. Instead of a polished plastic bowling ball, you would get a hot, crushed, chemically altered planet made of bowling-ball-like material.

If, on the other hand, you somehow enlarged the ball’s size without adding mass, then it would have an absurdly tiny density, far below even a good laboratory vacuum, and it could not behave like a solid object at all.

So the short answer is: an Earth-sized bowling ball with scaled-up mass would be a low-gravity planet at first, but gravity would crush the holes and destroy its bowling-ball shape.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?
human_answers: Answer: [Image: image] Let’s try a more complete answer. We’ll start with ... Radio transmissions Contact popularized the idea of aliens listening in on our transmissions. Sadly, the odds are against it. Here’s the problem: Space is big. Really big.[1] (http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11.The_Hitchhiker_s_Guide_to_the_Galaxy) You can work through the physics of interstellar radio attenuation, but the problem is captured pretty well by considering the economics of the situation: If your TV signals are getting to another star, you’re losing money. Powering a transmitter is expensive, and creatures on other stars aren’t buying the products in the TV commercials that pay your electricity bill. The full picture is more complicated, but the bottom line is that as our technology has advanced, less of our radio traffic has been leaking out into space. We’re closing down the giant transmitting antennas and switching to cable and fiber and tightly-focused cell-tower networks.[2] (http://arxiv.org/PS_cache/arxiv/pdf/1007/1007.0850v1.pdf) While our TV signals may have been detectable—with great effort—for a while,[3] (http://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0610377v2.pdf) that window is closing. In the late 20th century, when we were using TV and radio to scream into the void at the top of our lungs, the signal probably faded to undetectability after a few light-years.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) The potentially habitable exoplanets we’ve spotted so far are dozens of light-years away, so the odds are they aren’t currently repeating our catchphrases (http://xkcd.com/1212/). But TV and radio transmissions still weren’t Earth’s most powerful radio signal. They were outshone by the beams from early-warning radar.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) Early-warning radar, a product of the Cold War, consisted of a bunch of ground and airborne stations scattered around the Arctic. These stations swept the atmosphere with powerful radar beams 24/7, often bouncing them off the ionosphere, and people obsessively monitored the echos for any hints of enemy movement. (I wasn’t alive during most of this period, but from what I hear, the mood was a little tense.) These radar transmissions leaked into space, and could probably be picked up by nearby exoplanets[5] (http://www.astrobio.net/exclusive/4847/seti-on-the-ska) if they happened to be listening when the beam swept over their part of the sky. But the same march of technological progress that made the TV broadcast towers obsolete has had the same effect on early-warning radar. Today’s systems—where they exist at all—are much quieter, and may eventually be replaced completely by new technology. [Image: image] Earth’s most powerful radio signal is the beam from the Arecibo telescope. This massive dish in Puerto Rico can function as a radar transmitter, bouncing a signal off nearby targets like Mercury and the asteroid belt. It’s essentially a flashlight which we shine on planets to see them better. (This is just as crazy as it sounds.) But it transmits only occasionally, and in a narrow beam. If an exoplanet happened to be caught in the beam, and they were lucky enough to be pointing a receiving antenna at our corner of the sky at the time, all they would pick up would be a brief pulse of radio energy, then silence (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wow!_signal). So hypothetical aliens looking at Earth probably wouldn’t pick us up with radio antennas. But there’s also ... Visible light This is more promising. The Sun is really bright [citation needed (http://www.google.com/search?q=site:craigslist.org+chevrolet+citation)] and its light illuminates the Earth.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_(horse))] Some of that light is reflected back into space as “Earthshine”. Some of it skims close to our planet and passes through our atmosphere before continuing on to the stars. Both of these effects could potentially be detected from an exoplanet.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/6432)[6] (http://planetimager.org/) They wouldn’t tell you anything about humans directly, but if you watched the Earth for long enough, you could figure out a lot about our atmosphere from the reflectivity. You could probably figure out what our water cycle looked like, and our oxygen-rich atmosphere would give you a hint that something weird was going on (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxygenation_Event). So in the end, the clearest signal from Earth might not be from us at all. It might be from the algae that have been terraforming the planet—and altering the signals we send into space—for billions of years. [Image: image] Of course, if we wanted to send a clearer signal, we could. A radio transmission has the problem that they have to be paying attention when it arrives. Instead, we could make them pay attention. With ion drives, nuclear pulse propulsion, or just clever use of gravitational slingshots, we could probably send a probe out of the Solar System fast enough to reach a given nearby star in a few dozen millennia. If we can figure out how to make a guidance system that survives the trip (which would be tough) we could use it to steer toward any inhabited planet. To land safely, we’d have to slow down. But slowing down takes even more fuel. And, hey, the whole point of this was for them to notice us, right? So maybe if those aliens looked toward our Solar System, this is what they’d see: [Image: image]

Assuming the nearest habitable exoplanet means Proxima Centauri b, about 4.24 light-years away, an alien civilization there would see Earth as it was 4.24 years ago, not as it is now. In May 2026, they would be receiving light and radio signals that left Earth around early 2022.

To their unaided eyes, they would not see Earth at all. They would see the Sun as a bright, ordinary-looking star in their sky, roughly magnitude 0.4, comparable to some of the brighter stars seen from Earth. Earth would be far too small and faint, and it would appear extremely close to the Sun from their point of view.

With advanced telescopes, they could in principle detect Earth as a very faint “pale blue dot” near the Sun. Its maximum apparent separation from the Sun would be only about 0.8 arcseconds, and it would be around ten billion times fainter than the Sun in visible light. They would need powerful optics or interferometry to separate Earth’s light from the Sun’s glare.

If they could analyze Earth’s light, they might infer a lot. They could detect that Earth has an atmosphere, oceans, clouds, and possibly continents. Spectroscopy could reveal water vapor, oxygen, ozone, carbon dioxide, and methane—strong hints of biology. With sufficiently precise observations, they might notice a 24-hour rotation, seasonal changes, weather patterns, and possibly even a vegetation “red edge.”

They probably would not see Earth transit the Sun, because Proxima Centauri is not aligned with Earth’s orbital plane in the right way. So Earth would not conveniently pass across the face of the Sun from their viewpoint.

If they had very sensitive radio instruments, they could also detect some human-made radio emissions that left Earth about 4.24 years earlier. Ordinary TV and radio leakage would be weak and hard to distinguish at that distance, but powerful radar transmissions or directed signals would be easier to notice.

So the direct answer is: from the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, aliens would see the Sun as a bright star and, with sufficiently advanced technology, Earth as a tiny, faint, blue-white planet showing signs of oceans, atmosphere, and life—specifically Earth as it was a little over four years in the past.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already. A Google search for what if the Sun went out (http://www.google.com/search?q=what+if+the+Sun+went+out) turns up a lot of excellent articles thoroughly analyzing the situation. However, since my recent articles on sunsets, the rate of submission of this question has risen even further, so I’ve decided to do my best to answer it. If the Sun went out ... [Image: image] We won’t worry about exactly how it happens. We'll just assume we figured out a way to fast-forward the Sun through its evolution so that it becomes a cold, inert sphere. What would the consequences be for us here on Earth? Let's look at a few: Reduced risk of solar flares: In 1859, a massive solar flare and geomagnetic storm hit the Earth.[1] (http://www.leif.org/research/1859%20Storm%20-%20Extreme%20Space%20Weather.pdf) Magnetic storms induce electric currents in wires. Unfortunately for us, by 1859 we had wrapped the Earth in telegraph wires. The storm caused powerful currents in those wires, knocking out communications and in some cases causing telegraph equipment to catch fire.[2] (http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/8787/1/02-1310.pdf) Since 1859, we've wrapped the Earth in a lot more wires. If the 1859 storm hit us today, the Department of Homeland Security estimates the economic damage to the US alone would be several trillion dollars[3] (http://www.oecd.org/governance/risk/46891645.pdf)—more than every hurricane which has ever hit the US combined.[4] (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fsciencepolicy.colorado.edu%2Fadmin%2Fpublication_files%2Fresource-2476-2008.02.pdf&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNFnOWO7P0PV6qJSPhUUf56glVwZKQ) If the Sun went out, this threat would be eliminated. Improved satellite service: When a communications satellite passes in front of the Sun, the Sun can drown out the satellite's radio signal, causing an interruption in service.[5] (http://www3.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol49-1970/articles/bstj49-8-1943.pdf) Deactivating the Sun would solve this problem. Better astronomy: Without the Sun, ground-based observatories would be able to operate around the clock. The cooler air would create less atmospheric noise, which would reduce the load on adaptive optics systems and allow for sharper images. Stable dust: Without sunlight, there would be no Poynting–Robertson drag (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting%E2%80%93Robertson_effect), which means we would finally be able to place dust into a stable orbit around the Sun without the orbits decaying. I’m not sure whether anyone wants to do that, but you never know. Reduced infrastructure costs: The Department of Transportation estimates that it would cost $20 billion per year over the next 20 years to repair and maintain all US bridges.[6] (http://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policy/2010cpr/chap7.htm#9) Most US bridges are over water; without the Sun, we could save money by simply driving on a strip of asphalt laid across the ice. [Image: image] Cheaper trade: Time zones make trade more expensive; it's harder to do business with someone if their office hours don't overlap with yours.[7] (http://eeecon.uibk.ac.at/wopec2/repec/inn/wpaper/2012-14.pdf) If the Sun went out, it would eliminate the need for time zones, allowing us to switch to UTC and give a boost to the global economy. Safer Children: According to the North Dakota Department of Health, babies younger than six months should be kept out of direct sunlight.[8] (http://www.ndhealth.gov/familyhealth/mch/babyfacts/Sunburn.pdf) Without sunlight, our children would be safer. Safer combat pilots: Many people sneeze when exposed to bright sunlight. The reasons for this reflex are unknown, and it may pose a danger to fighter pilots during flight.[9] (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8108024) If the Sun went dark, it would mitigate this danger to our pilots. Safer parsnip: Wild parsnip is a surprisingly nasty plant. Its leaves contain chemicals called furocoumarins, which can be absorbed by human skin without causing symptoms ... at first. However, when the skin is then exposed to sunlight (even days or weeks later), the furocoumarins cause a nasty chemical burn. This is called phytophotodermatitis.[10] (http://dnr.wi.gov/wnrmag/html/stories/1999/jun99/parsnip.htm) A darkened Sun would liberate us from the parsnip threat. [Image: image] In conclusion, if the Sun went out, we would see a variety of benefits across many areas of our lives. Are there any downsides to this scenario? We would all freeze and die. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly “went out” meaning it stopped producing light and heat but still kept its mass, Earth would not notice instantly. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth, so for that long everything would look normal. Then the sky would go dark in daytime, the Moon would go dark, and most planets would become very hard or impossible to see except by their own faint heat or reflected artificial light.

Earth would keep orbiting normally, because the Sun’s gravity would still be there. There would be no immediate change in tides or orbit if only the Sun’s radiation stopped.

The biggest effect would be loss of heat. Temperatures would not instantly plunge, because the oceans, land, and atmosphere store a lot of warmth, but the cooling would be severe. Within days to weeks, average surface temperatures would fall below freezing. After a few months, much of the surface would be far below zero. After about a year, average temperatures could be around −70°C or lower. The oceans would begin freezing from the top down; however, thick ice would insulate the deeper water, so parts of the deep ocean could remain liquid for a very long time, helped by geothermal heat from Earth’s interior.

Photosynthesis would stop almost immediately. Plants would begin dying, then herbivores, then predators. Most surface ecosystems would collapse. Some life could survive around deep-sea hydrothermal vents or underground, where energy comes from Earth’s internal heat and chemistry rather than sunlight.

Human survival would become extremely difficult but not instantly impossible. People could survive in sealed, insulated habitats using stored food, nuclear power, geothermal energy, or other artificial energy sources. Long-term survival would require living underground or under ice, with artificial lighting and controlled agriculture.

Over much longer timescales, the atmosphere itself would begin to freeze out. Water vapor and carbon dioxide would condense first; eventually, if Earth cooled enough, even oxygen and nitrogen could liquefy or freeze. Earth would become a dark, frozen world drifting around a dark Sun.

If instead the Sun literally vanished, not just went dark, then after about 8 minutes Earth would also stop feeling its gravity and would fly off in a straight line tangent to its former orbit. But if the Sun merely “went out,” Earth stays in orbit and slowly freezes.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature. Rowing a boat on a sea of mercury just might be possible. Mercury is so dense that steel ball bearings float on the surface (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EGv_YVQHu7U). Your boat would be so buoyant that you'd barely make a dent in the mercury, and you'd have to lean your weight into the paddle to get the end of it below the surface. [Image: image] In the end, it certainly wouldn't be easy, and you wouldn't be able to move fast. But you could probably row a little bit. You should probably avoid splash fights. Bromine is about as dense as water, so a standard rowboat could in theory float on it. However, Bromine is awful. For one thing, it smells terrible; the name "bromine" comes from the ancient Greek "brōmos", meaning "stench". If that weren't enough, it violently reacts (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uCwHzTsx5yY) with a lot of materials. Hopefully, you're not in an aluminium rowboat. [Image: image] If that's not incentive enough to avoid it, the Materials Safety Data Sheet on bromine (http://avogadro.chem.iastate.edu/MSDS/Br2.htm) includes the following phrases: "severe burns and ulceration" "perforation of the digestive tract" "permanent corneal opacification" "vertigo, anxiety, depression, muscle incoordination, and emotional instability" "diarrhea, possibly with blood" You should not get in a splash fight on a bromine lake. Liquid gallium is weird stuff. Gallium melts just above room temperature, like butter, so you can't hold it in your hand for too long. It's fairly dense, though not anywhere near as dense as mercury, and would be easier to row a boat on. However, once again, you'd better hope the boat isn't made of aluminium, because aluminium (like many metals) absorbs gallium like a sponge absorbs water. The gallium spreads throughout the aluminium, dramatically changing its chemical properties. The modified aluminium is so weak it can be pulled apart like wet paper (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FaMWxLCGY0U). This is something gallium has in common with mercury—both will destroy aluminium (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z7Ilxsu-JlY). Like my grandma used to say, don't sail an aluminium boat on a gallium lake. (My grandma was a little strange.) Liquid tungsten is really hard to work with. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element. This means there's a lot we don't know about its properties. The reason for this—and this may sound a little stupid—is that it's hard to study, because we can't find a container to hold it in. For almost any container, the material in the container will melt before the tungsten does. There are a few compounds, like tantalum hafnium carbide, with slightly higher melting points, but no one has been able to make a liquid tungsten container with them. To give you an idea of how hot liquid tungsten is, I could tell you the exact temperature that it melts at (3422°C). But a better point might be this: Liquid tungsten is so hot, if you dropped it into a lava flow, the lava would freeze the tungsten. Needless to say, if you set a boat on a sea of liquid tungsten, both you and the boat would rapidly combust and be incinerated. Liquid nitrogen is very cold. Liquid helium is colder, but they're both closer to absolute zero than to the coldest temperatures in Antarctica, so to someone floating on them in a boat, the temperature difference is not that significant. A Dartmouth engineering page on liquid nitrogen safety (http://engineering.dartmouth.edu/microeng/ln2.html) includes the following phrases: "violent reactions with organic materials" "it will explode" "displace oxygen in the room" "severe clothing fire" "suffocation without warning" Liquid nitrogen has a density similar to that of water, so a rowboat would float on it, but if you were in it, you wouldn't survive for long. If the air above the nitrogen was room temperature when you started, it would cool rapidly, and you and the boat would be smothered in a thick fog as the water condensed out of the air. (This is the same effect that causes steam when you pour out liquid nitrogen.) The condensation would freeze, quickly covering your boat in a layer of frost. The warm air would cause the nitrogen on the surface to evaporate. This would displace the oxygen over the lake, causing you to asphyxiate. If the air (or the nitrogen) were both cold enough to avoid evaporation, you would instead develop hypothermia and die of exposure. Liquid helium would be worse. For one thing, it's only about one-eighth as dense as water, so your boat would have to be eight times larger to support a given weight. [Image: image] But helium has a trick. When cooled below about two degrees kelvin, it becomes a superfluid, which has the odd property that it crawls up and over the walls of containers by capillary forces. It crawls along at about 20 centimeters per second, so it would take the liquid helium less than 30 seconds to start collecting in the bottom of your boat. This would, as in the liquid nitrogen scenario, cause rapid death from hypothermia. If it's any consolation, as you lay dying, you would be able to observe an odd phenomenon. Superfluid helium films, like the one rapidly covering you, carry the same types of ordinary sound waves that most materials do. But they also exhibit an additional type of wave, a slow-moving ripple that propogates along thin films of helium. It's only observed in superfluids, and has the mysterious and poetic name "third sound (http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/packard/current_research/schechter's%20web/page2.html)." Your eardrums may no longer function, and wouldn't be able to detect this type of vibration anyway, but as you froze to death in the floor of a giant boat, your ears would be filled—literally—with a sound no human can ever hear: The third sound. And that, at least, is pretty cool. [Image: image]
