items.model_answer:
Assuming each “lake” is a stable open body of the liquid and you somehow have a compatible boat and protective gear, the experience would range from mechanically rowable to instantly fatal.

Mercury would be one of the most rowable mechanically, but very dangerous chemically. Mercury is about 13.5 times denser than water and only modestly more viscous, so a boat would float extremely high, almost as if sitting on a hard metallic surface. Oar blades would get a strong bite because the fluid is so dense, but they would also feel heavy and resist sudden motion. The lake would look like a bright silver mirror with sluggish, heavy-looking ripples. The main problem is toxicity: mercury vapor is hazardous, and splashing or contamination would be a serious long-term poison risk.

Bromine would be rowable in principle but nightmarish in practice. Liquid bromine is dense, red-brown, volatile, corrosive, and gives off choking toxic fumes. A boat would float well because bromine is about three times denser than water, and the liquid is not so viscous that rowing would be impossible. But the air above the lake would be full of bromine vapor; exposed skin, lungs, eyes, metals, and many plastics would be attacked. It would look like rowing across a dark red, fuming chemical spill. Without full chemical protection, you would not survive long.

Gallium would be surprisingly plausible if it were kept just above its melting point, about 30 °C. It is dense, silvery, and fairly low-viscosity, so a boat would float high and rowing would feel somewhat like rowing on a dense metallic liquid. It is much less volatile and less acutely poisonous than mercury or bromine. The big practical issue is materials: gallium attacks and embrittles aluminum and can wet or infiltrate some metals. A normal aluminum boat could be ruined. Also, if the lake cooled slightly, it would begin freezing into soft metal.

Tungsten would be impossible in any ordinary sense. Tungsten melts only around 3422 °C. A lake of liquid tungsten would be an incandescent white-hot metal lake. The radiant heat alone would ignite, melt, or vaporize ordinary boats, oars, clothing, and people from a distance. Even refractory materials would be under extreme stress. Mechanically, a boat could float very high because liquid tungsten is extremely dense, but you would never get the chance to row it. It would be more like approaching lava far hotter than most natural lava, except metallic and vastly denser.

Liquid nitrogen would be mechanically difficult and physically deadly. It is less dense than water, about 0.8 times water’s density, so a boat would float lower than on water and carry less load. It is also very cold, −196 °C, and would boil violently around anything warm. The lake surface would be covered in fog and bubbling nitrogen gas. Oars and hull materials would become brittle; water vapor and oxygen from the air could condense or freeze nearby; exposed flesh would freeze rapidly. Rowing might be possible briefly with a specially designed cryogenic craft, but the boiling around the boat would make the interaction with the liquid erratic, and the nitrogen gas could displace oxygen and suffocate you.

Liquid helium would be the least rowable of the cryogenic lakes. It is extremely cold, around 4 K at atmospheric pressure, and very low density, only about one-eighth that of water. A normal boat would have very little buoyant support unless it were extremely light and broad. Liquid helium has extraordinarily low viscosity and low surface tension, so oars would get little “grip” compared with water. Any heat leaking from the boat, oars, or environment would boil it rapidly, surrounding you with helium gas and intense cold. If the helium were below the lambda point and became superfluid helium, ordinary rowing would become even stranger: a frictionless component would not respond to oars in the usual way. In practice, you would freeze equipment, boil away the lake locally, and asphyxiate long before having a normal rowing experience.

So the rough ranking is: gallium and mercury are mechanically the most rowable, though mercury is highly toxic; bromine is rowable but chemically horrific; liquid nitrogen is barely conceivable only with specialized cryogenic engineering; liquid helium is almost unrowable and extremely dangerous; and liquid tungsten is effectively impossible because of its extreme temperature.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball. Therefore, to determine the result of an impact, we can make use of what Einstein called a gedankenexperiment, or "thought experiment": [Image: image] In science, it's important that results be repeatable, so let's try that again: [Image: image] The tricky thing about this scenario is that 3,000 one-inch bouncy balls is not as many as you probably think—it'd be enough to fill a large bucket. This bucket would weigh about as much as a small child, which leads us to another gedankenexperiment: [Image: image] Of course, in reality, the average person can't throw a small child as fast as they can throw a bouncy ball.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacean)] Furthermore, they won't all fall in one clump. If you poured the balls from a container, they would bounce around and spread out as they fell, and most of them would probably miss the target. This effect was demonstrated in an experiment by Utah State University students, who poured 20,000 bouncy balls from a helicopter (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fd7D1LWzWmo) as part of their Geek Week. The balls fell as a cloud, rather than a single mass. If you wanted to be sure of killing someone, you'd need a lot more balls. 3,000,000 of them—enough to fill a large room—would be be enough to guarantee that the target would either be crushed to death by the impact or buried too deep to dig themselves out. To your last question, if someone just happened to walk underneath when you dropped the bouncy balls, and they were killed by the impact, you'd most likely be guilty of some form of manslaughter. However, by asking this question, you've shown your intent to cause harm to the victim, demonstrating clear malice aforethought. By writing in to this blog, you've probably upgraded your charge to murder. All in all, you should probably stick to gedankenexperiments. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
From a seven-story parking garage, the Super Balls would hit at roughly 20 m/s, about 45 mph, assuming a height around 20–25 meters. A typical small Super Ball has only a few joules of kinetic energy at that speed, so one ball would be painful but usually not catastrophic, more like being hit by a very hard-thrown rubber ball or large hailstone.

But 3,000 of them changes the situation. Depending on size, that could be something like 30–60 kg or more of rubber falling from the garage, with total energy on the order of 10,000 joules. If they were loose and spread out, the pedestrian would likely be battered, bruised, possibly knocked down, and at serious risk of eye, face, scalp, or fall injuries. It would be very dangerous, but not automatically fatal because the energy is divided among many small impacts and many balls would bounce or miss.

If, however, the balls arrived in a dense cluster or inside a bag/container so that the mass hit as one compact falling object, it could easily cause severe trauma or death. The biggest realistic dangers from loose balls would be head and eye injury, being knocked off balance, and then slipping or falling on the bouncing balls afterward.

So: loose 3,000 Super Balls would be a serious, potentially injurious assault; compacted or contained, it could be lethal.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. criteria.name: Drain physics, flow rate, and timescale under the 10-meter Challenger Deep premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from a 10-meter hole at Challenger Deep, including pressure-driven flow, the immense ocean volume, absence of a dramatic surface whirlpool, and the very long drainage timescale unless additional drains are introduced.
criteria.1-2: Treats the oceans as draining quickly, like a bathtub, or ignores pressure, volume, and hole size entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions high pressure or large ocean volume but gives implausible rates or predicts rapid global emptying without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that drainage is slow relative to intuition and pressure-driven, but lacks quantitative scale or misses key details like weak surface effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains that even a 10-meter hole at great depth drains only a tiny fraction per day and would take hundreds of thousands of years, with little surface whirlpool.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates pressure, orifice scale, ocean volume, depth, and surface-vortex behavior, with sensible order-of-magnitude reasoning and caveats.

criteria.name: Treatment of the outlet destination and conservation consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer handles where the drained water goes and the resulting consequences, distinguishing local recirculation on Earth from removal to a distant location such as Mars or space.
criteria.1-2: Ignores where the water exits or assumes it simply vanishes with no physical implications.
criteria.3-4: Mentions an outlet but gives contradictory or physically impossible consequences, such as Earth losing water while the outlet dumps nearby.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that the destination matters, but only partially explains recirculation, heating, or atmospheric effects.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states that a nearby outlet would return water as rain/steam and disrupt climate, while a distant outlet allows net ocean loss.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual by specifying a distant sink, explains gravitational/thermal recirculation if nearby, and avoids conservation errors.

criteria.name: Bathymetric and geographic evolution as sea level falls
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the major geographic stages caused by falling sea level, including exposed continental shelves, land bridges, isolated basins, mid-ocean ridges, and residual inland seas/trenches.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful geographic progression or claims all seafloor is uniformly exposed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions generic new land or shrinking oceans but misses most bathymetric structure and basin disconnection.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some exposed shelves or land bridges but gives an incomplete or oversimplified global map evolution.
criteria.7-8: Covers major features such as exposed shelves, island-mainland connections, isolated seas, mid-ocean ridges, and remaining deep basins.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent staged account tied to real bathymetry, including examples like Indonesia, Britain/Sri Lanka/New Guinea, Arctic or Black Sea cutoff, ridges, trenches, and residual seas.

criteria.name: Long-range environmental, ecological, and human consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly traces downstream impacts on climate, salinity, ecosystems, weather, coastlines, habitability, and civilization over the long drainage period.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on the spectacle of draining and omits environmental or human consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists disasters vaguely without linking them to sea-level loss, climate change, or ecosystem collapse.
criteria.5-6: Mentions some consequences such as mass extinction, coastal change, or climate disruption, but with shallow causal support.

criteria.9-10: Develops a nuanced long-range chain showing gradual but massive ecological, climatic, hydrologic, geopolitical, and survival implications while respecting the slow timescale.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control

criteria.3-4: Has a basic narrative but repeatedly mixes incompatible assumptions, timescales, or endpoints.

items.model_answer:
Assuming the “10-meter hole” is a circular 10 m diameter drain at Challenger Deep that leads to a magical empty reservoir and never clogs, the oceans would not vanish quickly. They would drain on a million-year timescale.

At Challenger Deep the water pressure is about 110 MPa, roughly 1,100 atmospheres. That pressure could drive water through the hole at an ideal speed of about

\[
v \approx \sqrt{2gh} \approx \sqrt{2(9.8)(10900)} \approx 460\ \text{m/s}.
\]

A 10 m diameter hole has an area of about 78.5 m², so the initial ideal flow rate would be about

\[
Q \approx 3.6\times10^4\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}.
\]

With real losses, turbulence, and contraction at the opening, something like 20,000–30,000 m³/s is more plausible. That is a huge flow, but still only around a tenth of the Amazon River’s discharge.

Spread over the whole ocean surface, the initial sea-level fall would be only a few millimeters per year, roughly comparable to modern sea-level rise but in the opposite direction. Since the oceans contain about \(1.3\times10^{18}\) m³ of water, the absolute lower-bound drain time is about 1 million years. Because the pressure head decreases as sea level falls, the actual idealized time would be more like a few million years.

The effects would be dramatic but slow. Continental shelves would gradually become land. Shallow seas would disappear. Land bridges would form. Climate and ocean circulation would change profoundly. But there would be no sudden global whirlpool or bathtub-style vortex. Far from the hole, ocean currents caused by the drain would be tiny.

In the real world, it would not work as a clean drain. A 10 m hole into Earth’s crust would likely collapse, clog with debris, or become a violent hydrothermal/volcanic system. Water entering hot rock would flash into steam or supercritical fluid, fracture rock, deposit minerals, and probably seal the passage. Also, once sea level fell far enough, many ocean basins would become isolated by ridges and sills, so a single hole at Challenger Deep would not literally empty every basin unless channels were somehow maintained.

So the direct answer is: with a magical uncloggable drain, the oceans would lower by millimeters per year and take on the order of millions of years to drain; with real geology, the hole would almost certainly fail or seal long before the oceans disappeared.

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to. I picked Mars; the Curiosity rover is working so hard to find evidence of water, so I figured we could make things easier for it. [Image: image] Curiosity is sitting in Gale Crater, a round depression in the Martian surface with a peak, nicknamed Mt. Sharp, in the center. There's a lot of water on Mars.[1]Donald Rapp, Accessible Water on Mars (http://spaceclimate.net/Mars.Water.7.06R.pdf), JPL D-31343-Rev.7 The problem is, it's frozen. Liquid water doesn't last long there, because it's too cold and there's too little air. If you set out a cup of warm water on Mars, it'll try to boil, freeze, and sublimate, practically all at once.[2]D. L. Santiago et. al., Mars climate and outflow events (http://spacescience.arc.nasa.gov/mars-climate-workshop-2012/documents/extendedabstracts/Santiago_DL_ExAbst.pdf) Water on Mars seems to want to be in any state except liquid. However, we're dumping a lot of water very fast (all of it at a few degrees above 0°C), and it won't have much time to freeze, boil, or sublimate. If our portal is big enough, the water will start to turn Gale Crater into a lake, just like it would on Earth. We can use the excellent USGS Mars Topographic Map (http://pubs.usgs.gov/imap/i2782/) to chart the water's progress. Here's Gale Crater at the start of our experiment: [Image: image] As the flow continues, the lake fills in, burying Curiosity under hundreds of meters of water: [Image: image] Eventually, Mt. Sharp becomes an island. However, before the peak can disappear completely, the water spills over the north rim of the crater and starts flowing out across the sand. [Image: image] When this kind of thing happens on Mars in real life, the trickle of water quickly dries up before it can get very far.[3]D. L. Santiago et. al., Cloud formation and water transport on mars after major outflow events (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2012/pdf/2438.pdf), 43rd Planetary Science Conference (2012) However, we've got a lot of ocean at our disposal. [Image: image] The water pools in the North Polar Basin: [Image: image] Gradually, it will fill the basin: [Image: image] However, if we look at a map of the more equatorial regions of Mars, where the volcanoes are, we'll see that there's still a lot of land far from the water: [Image: image] Frankly, I think this map is kind of boring; there's not a lot going on. It's just a big empty swath of land with some ocean at the top. [Image: image] We haven't come close to running out of ocean yet. Although there was a lot of blue on the map of the Earth at the end of our last article, the seas that remained were shallow; most of the volume of the oceans was gone. And Mars is much smaller than Earth, so the same volume of water will make a deeper sea. At this point, the water fills in the Valles Marineris (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valles_Marineris), creating some unusual coastlines. The map is less boring, but the terrain around the great canyons makes for some odd shapes. [Image: image] The water now reaches and swallows up Spirit and Opportunity. Eventually, it breaks into the Hellas Impact Crater, the basin containing the lowest point on Mars. In my opinion, the rest of the map is starting to look pretty good. [Image: image] As the water spreads across the surface in earnest, the map splits into several large islands (and innumerable smaller ones). [Image: image] The water quickly finishes covering most of the high plateaus, leaving only a few islands left. [Image: image] And then, at last, the flow stops; the oceans back on Earth are drained. Let's take a closer look at the main islands: [Image: image] Olympus Mons, and a few other volcanoes, remain above water. Surprisingly, they aren't even close to being covered. Olympus Mons still rises well over 10 kilometers above the new sea level. Mars has some huge mountains. Those crazy islands are the result of water filling in 'Noctis Labyrinthus' ('the Labyrinth of the Night'), a bizarre set of canyons whose origin is still a mystery. The oceans on Mars wouldn't last. There might be some transient greenhouse warming, but in the end, Mars is just too cold. Eventually, the oceans will freeze over, become covered with dust, and gradually migrate to the permafrost at the poles.[4]Maggie Fox, Mars May Not Have Been Warm Or Wet (http://rense.com/general32/marsmaynothave.htm) However, it would take a long time, and until it did, Mars would be a much more interesting place. When you consider that there's a ready-made portal system to allow transit between the two planets, the consequences are inevitable: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Assuming you magically placed Earth’s oceans on present-day Mars rather than letting them hit at interplanetary speed, Mars would briefly become a flooded planet, then mostly an ice-covered one—not a second Earth.

Earth’s oceans contain about \(1.3 \times 10^9\) cubic kilometers of water. Mars has a surface area of about \(1.45 \times 10^8\) square kilometers, so if that water were spread evenly it would make a global layer about 9 kilometers deep. Because Mars has huge elevation differences, the water would first fill the northern lowlands and giant basins, producing deep oceans, while the highest southern highlands and volcanic regions—especially Olympus Mons and parts of Tharsis—would remain as islands or continents.

At first the result would be violent: global floods, enormous erosion, landslides, steam, fog, snow, and intense weather. Some water would boil because Mars’ current atmospheric pressure is near the triple point of water, but the boiling would not remove the ocean. Evaporation would cool the water and create a water-vapor atmosphere, much of which would then condense or freeze.

The key point is that Mars is cold and lacks a thick greenhouse atmosphere. Mars receives only about 43% as much sunlight as Earth, and its thin CO₂ atmosphere cannot keep a planet-wide ocean warm. The surface would freeze over. You would likely end up with a thick global ice shell, perhaps kilometers thick, with liquid water surviving underneath in many places because ice is an insulator and Mars has some geothermal heat.

The added water would not make Mars breathable. Water vapor is not oxygen, and although sunlight can split some water into hydrogen and oxygen, the hydrogen would escape to space and the oxygen would react with the Martian surface or be lost over time. Mars’ weak gravity and lack of a global magnetic field would make long-term atmospheric retention difficult compared with Earth.

So the final state would be something like a frozen ocean world: Mars covered by immense seas that quickly become ice-covered, with possible subsurface oceans beneath. It would be wetter, heavier, and geologically transformed, but it would not become Earthlike without also adding a thick, stable atmosphere and a strong long-term warming mechanism.

items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust. I have no real sense for what that number means, so let's put it in different terms: [Image: image] A 747 with all engines at full could roughly balance the weight of a dangling blue whale. With all that weight, how thick would the cable need to be? Surprisingly, not all that thick! A cable a little over an inch in diameter would do it.[1]Bethlehem Wire Rope General Purpose Catalog (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) Let's suppose you don't have a cable lying around. What else could you use? If you're into fishing, you might have some fishing line. A typical line for saltwater fishing might have a 50-100 lb strength,[2]West Marine: Selecting Fishing Line (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) so it would take a brigade of several thousand people armed with fishing rods to restrain the plane. [Image: image] If you don't have fishing line, there's one thing you probably do have: Hair. While hair isn't as strong as steel, it's just about the strongest material in your body,[3]Examples of the Tensile Strength of Materials (http://web2.clarkson.edu/class/me380/materials_tenstrength.pdf) with a tensile strength rivaling or exceeding that of bone.[4]Properties of Textile Fibers (http://www.academia.edu/2179355/Properties_of_Textile_Fibers) This tensile strength is why performers are able to hang by their hair at the circus. In fact, from a materials standpoint, it's actually more impressive that performers are able to hang by their arms. Based on these hair strength figures, a piece of hair three inches in diameter would be strong enough to restrain a 747.[5]If you wanted to measure the strength of a strand of hair, you could use the device described by US Patent #4628742A (http://www.google.com/patents/US4628742), "Tensile strength tester for hair" Hairs that big around are hard to come by.[6]... I hope. Since most of us have many small hairs, instead of one big hair ... [Image: image] ... we'd need to get a lot of hairs and bundle them together. Given that individual hairs can support about 50 grams of weight, we'd need roughly 20 heads of hair to restrain the aircraft. [Image: image] Conclusion: Restraining a plane with a cable would be pretty easy. criteria.name: 747 thrust-to-rope load quantification
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer grounds the counterfactual in the relevant forces: a large jet's takeoff thrust, how that translates into rope tension, and the approximate scale of the load being resisted.
criteria.1-2: Gives only vague claims such as 'the plane would pull hard' with no meaningful force scale or confuses thrust with aircraft weight/lift.
criteria.3-4: Mentions large engine thrust or rope tension but uses implausible magnitudes, omits units, or treats the rope as resisting the entire aircraft weight without explanation.
criteria.5-6: Provides a roughly plausible force estimate for a 747-class aircraft and recognizes the rope mainly resists engine thrust during takeoff, though with limited precision or caveats.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates total thrust on the order of 1 MN, relates it to an intuitive equivalent load, and distinguishes thrust, weight, lift, and tension reasonably well.
criteria.9-10: Accurately and clearly quantifies the thrust/load scale, explains why the rope tension is set primarily by engine thrust and dynamics, and uses comparisons without introducing misleading physics.

criteria.name: Material strength and required rope size reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly reasons from tensile strength or rated breaking strength to the required rope/cable size, including safety and failure considerations.
criteria.1-2: Does not address rope strength, or asserts that any ordinary rope/cable would or would not work with no basis.
criteria.3-4: Mentions strong rope or steel cable but gives unsupported or physically inconsistent size requirements.
criteria.5-6: Uses breaking strength or tensile strength in a plausible way and concludes that a robust steel cable of inch-scale diameter could restrain the thrust, though details may be rough.
criteria.7-8: Connects material strength, cross-sectional area, and total thrust; notes that cable ratings, knots, attachments, and safety factors can dominate real-world failure.
criteria.9-10: Gives a well-calibrated estimate for cable diameter/strength, distinguishes ideal tensile capacity from real rigging limits, and explains likely failure points such as anchors, knots, or connectors.

criteria.name: Takeoff dynamics, anchoring, and causal outcome
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the causal chain of what actually happens when the airplane attempts to take off while tied down: acceleration, tension buildup, possible breakage, anchor failure, aircraft damage, or successful restraint.
criteria.1-2: Offers a cartoon outcome with no causal mechanism, such as the plane simply stops or instantly crashes.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one possible outcome, like the rope snaps, but does not explain how tension develops or what determines the result.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the result depends on rope/anchor strength versus thrust and that a sufficiently strong setup can hold the aircraft while a weak one fails.
criteria.7-8: Traces the sequence from engine spool-up to increasing tension, limited acceleration, load transfer to anchor, and likely failure modes if any component is undersized.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent dynamic scenario including transient loads, runway friction/braking or chocks if relevant, anchor-ground interaction, aircraft structural attachment limits, and the difference between static restraint and a moving snag.

criteria.name: Coverage of alternative restraining materials and scale comparisons
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explores the counterfactual's downstream implications using plausible comparisons such as steel cable, fishing line, hair bundles, or biological analogies, without losing physical consistency.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful scale comparisons or uses fanciful comparisons that contradict the force estimates.
criteria.3-4: Includes one comparison, but it is numerically unsupported or wildly inconsistent with material strengths.
criteria.5-6: Includes at least one plausible alternative-material comparison, such as many fishing lines or many hairs, with order-of-magnitude reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Covers several alternatives and explains how many strands/people/hairs would be needed based on breaking strength, while keeping estimates within plausible ranges.
criteria.9-10: Uses comparisons to deepen understanding of the force scale, accurately translating thrust into quantities of cable, fishing line, hair, or equivalent weight, and avoids overclaiming precision.

criteria.name: Long-range coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a consistent causal model across the entire explanation, flags assumptions, and avoids contradictions about engines, lift, rope behavior, and material limits.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or impossible claims, such as the rope preventing lift by canceling gravity or the aircraft pulling with unlimited force.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions, ignores uncertainty, or changes the scenario mid-answer without notice.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with stated or implied assumptions, though some estimates or causal links are underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent premise and causal chain, acknowledges uncertainty in aircraft model, rope material, attachment, and loading, and separates rough estimates from firm conclusions.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly controlled long-range explanation with explicit assumptions, calibrated uncertainty, no internal contradictions, and conclusions that follow directly from the physics and material limits.

items.model_answer:
If you tied an airplane to a solid anchor with a rope and then advanced the throttles, the airplane would not take off in calm air as long as the rope, anchor, and attachment point could withstand the force.

The key point is that an airplane needs airspeed over its wings to make enough lift. Engines provide thrust, which normally accelerates the airplane down the runway; the wing lift comes from that motion through the air. If a rope prevents the airplane from moving, the wings do not get takeoff airspeed, so they do not produce enough lift to fly.

What happens instead is simple but violent: the engines pull against the rope. The rope tension rises roughly to the airplane’s available thrust, minus small effects like wheel friction and aerodynamic drag. For a small propeller plane, this might be a few thousand newtons, so a strong rope and good anchor could hold it. For a jet airliner, the thrust can be hundreds of thousands of newtons. A normal rope, vehicle, tree, or weak ground anchor would likely fail catastrophically. The rope could snap, the anchor could rip out, or the part of the airplane you tied to could be damaged.

If everything were absurdly strong, the airplane would just sit there with its engines blasting. The brakes and tiedowns on aircraft already do a version of this during engine run-ups, though within safe limits.

There are exceptions. If there were a strong headwind equal to or greater than takeoff speed, the airplane could generate lift while stationary relative to the ground. Then it might rise like a tethered kite, limited by the rope, or it might overload the rope or airframe. But in normal calm runway conditions, tying an airplane to the ground does not make it “fight upward”; it mostly makes it pull horizontally until something gives.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in. [Image: image] The impact could trigger an earthquake. Denali (also known as Mount McKinley) is a mountain in Alaska that sits just to the south of a major fault line.[1]Roger A. Hansen, Earthquake and Seismic Monitoring in Denali National Park (http://www.nps.gov/akso/nature/science/ak_park_science/PDF/2006Vol5-1/Earthquake-Monitoring.pdf), National Park Service This fault is active,[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) and we know that drilling can trigger earthquakes.[3]Van der elst NJ, Savage HM, Keranen KM, Abers GA. Enhanced remote earthquake triggering at fluid-injection sites in the midwestern United States (http://www.sciencemag.org/content/341/6142/164.abstract). Science. 2013;341(6142):164-7. Earthquakes can happen at any time, so there's always a chance that dropping a mountain any distance could trigger one. So could kicking a tree. The only way to find out for sure would be to try it.[4]This article has an awful lot of citations. Assuming it didn't trigger an earthquake, the impact wouldn't be all that dramatic. If you were standing on the mountain when it happened, you'd definitely feel a jolt, but it probably wouldn't even be enough to knock you down. [Image: image] When the mountain hit the ground, the rock under it would be damaged, but only a little. The granite base is strong enough to hold up under the tremendous resting weight of a mountain;[5]Citation: The rock was holding up a mountain when you got there. the shockwave from dropping it an inch doesn't add too much pressure on top of that, and the rock would survive with a little minor cracking. People nearby would definitely feel the impact, and probably hear it; the sound would likely resemble the crack of a lightning strike (if you were standing near the mountain) fading into a long, deep rumble.[6]Citation: A dream I had once. The vibration would be equivalent to that of a 3.5-magnitude earthquake[7]For more on the specific seismic details, see Stein, Seth, and Michael Wysession. "Earthquakes." An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure. Malden, MA: Blackwell Pub., 2003. 241 (http://books.google.com/books?id=-z80yrwFsqoC&lpg=PA241&ots=nrVTZ77_mJ&pg=PA241#v=onepage&q&f=false). Print.; at worst, it would knock a few pictures off the wall if you happened to be living next to the mountain. Frankly, I'd be more worried about debris flying out of the gap.[8]If your magical mountain-cutter put air in the space where the rock used to be, you should avoid standing near the crack when it falls. The air will come jetting out from the closing crack, spraying rocks and dust at speeds approaching, or even—thanks to some fun heat-related effects—exceeding, Mach 1. [Image: image] Oh. You again. Ok. Dropping from a height of one foot wouldn't be all that different. [Image: image] The mountain would hit the ground at 2.5 m/s, or roughly walking speed. The shockwave from that impact would be in the range of 50 megapascals of pressure,[9]You can calculate the peak pressure of the compressive strain wave in the rock using the Joukowsky equation, which says that the peak pressure of the compressive wave in a material is (material's density)x(speed at impact)x(the speed of sound in the material). This equation is is normally used in fluid mechanics, but it works fine here, too! (http://www.win.tue.nl/analysis/reports/rana06-08.pdf) which granite can handle without too much trouble.[10]Bhat HS, Sammis CG, Rosakis AJ. The Micromechanics of Westerley Granite at Large Compressive Loads (http://www.rosakis.caltech.edu/downloads/pubs/2011/181%20The%20Micromechanics%20of%20Westerley.pdf). Pure Appl. Geophys. 2011;168(12):2181-2198. [11]"... for a plane shock wave ... granite will stand a compressive stress of 3000-4000 MPa elastically before failing." Persson, Per-Anders, Roger Holmberg, and Jaimin Lee. Rock Blasting and Explosives Engineering (http://books.google.com/books?id=sdLO5HESJwgC&lpg=PA5&ots=-SJy8Yx-ea&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q&f=false). Boca Raton, FL: CRC, 1994. 5-6. Print. [Image: image] Ok. Let's jump straight to the end of John-Clark's question: [Image: image] After falling from summit height to base height—about 5 kilometers—the mountain would be moving at roughly the speed of sound. The last two impacts were pretty minor. This one wouldn't be. The jolt to the ground would be as violent as in a magnitude 7 earthquake.[12]In addition, there's a good chance that a shock this large will release some existing seismic energy; see: U.S. Congress, Office of Technology Assessment, Seismic Verification of Nuclear Testing Treaties (http://www.princeton.edu/~ota/disk2/1988/8838/883809.PDF), P. 715, OTA-ISC-361 (Washington, DC: U.S. Government Printing Office, May 1988). There wouldn't exactly be a crater, but the mountain would definitely not be shaped like it used to be. The pressure from the impact would be high enough to produce some unusual geologic strutures. If you put a lump of coal under the meteor, the impact would be enough to convert it to diamond (and, unfortunately, smash it to bits).[13]French B. M. (1998) Traces of Catastrophe: A Handbook of Shock-Metamorphic Effects in Terrestrial Meteorite Impact Structures., Chapter 4 (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/publications/books/CB-954/chapter4.pdf), LPI Contribution No. 954,Lunar and Planetary Institute, Houston. 120 pp The good news is that, the last time a magnitude 7+ earthquake hit Denali, no one was killed.[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) Let's just hope nobody is on the mountain itself when we do this. [Image: image] Ok. Last one. We'd need to lift the mountain out of the atmosphere, out past the orbit of the GPS satellites, to the very outer limits of the Earth's gravity well. Then we let go. [Image: image] It would hit Alaska at 10 kilometers per second. The Last Frontier would not fare well. A 50-mile-wide crater would have obliterated Denali National Park. Anchorage would be buried under three meters of gravel.[14]Purdue University ImpactEarth asteroid impact simulator (http://www.purdue.edu/impactearth/) The shaking, combined with the debris falling into the ocean, would cause tsunamis across the Pacific. Across North America, the ground would tremble. A wind would sweep in from the northwest. The sky would darken. In 1815, Mount Tambora erupted in the largest volcanic event in recorded history. The resulting global veil of aerosols made 1816 the "year without a summer". Snow fell in Massachusetts in June, ice formed on rivers in Pennsylvania in August, and frost killed most of the spring crops. The cooling effects lingered for several years. The Alaska impact would be far worse. Over the next few months, the skies around the globe fill with dust. Summer is canceled and winter arrives. But, c'mon, it's a 'global firestorm'. Can you really imagine that every species made it through unscathed? However, our mountain would carry only about 10% of the energy of the Chicxulub impactor, which means that it wouldn't be capable of igniting global firestorms.[17]Osinski, G. R., and E. Pierazzo. "Environmental Effects of Impact Events." In Impact Cratering Processes and Products. (http://books.google.com/books?id=3Vzky11ZR3UC&lpg=PA149&ots=8kqLGZFB1g&pg=PA151#v=onepage&q&f=false). Chicester: Wiley, 2012. 151. The firestorms would, in fact, only cover some of North America. So that's a relief. The northern hemisphere would be covered in ice, but our species would probably manage to limp through. Civilization, on the other hand, might well collapse. A total collapse of modern civilization would be a serious blow to the already sluggish economy, and the economic damage could amount to $80 trillion per year (the total value of all human goods and services). All in all, it would have serious implications for the upcoming elections. And that's that. We've dropped the mountain from as high as it can be dropped, and I hope John-Clark is proud of the resulting devastation. Thanks for reading, and— [Image: image] No, that doesn't actually make sense. rubrics.question_focus: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Immediate Kinematics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as a massive mountain suddenly losing its bottom inch, leaving a one-inch unsupported gap that closes under gravity, and computes or qualitatively estimates the short fall accurately.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats the mountain as disappearing, exploding, floating, or collapsing from summit height without justification.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes a small vertical drop but gives highly implausible timing, speed, or motion, or ignores gravity-driven closure.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that the mountain drops only about one inch and the motion is brief, but with little quantitative grounding.
criteria.7-8: Gives plausible estimates for closure time and impact speed, e.g. tens of milliseconds and under 1 m/s, with mostly sound reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Accurately derives or explains the one-inch free fall, about 70 ms closure time, and modest impact speed while avoiding overstatement.

criteria.name: Impact, Stress, and Seismic Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the mechanical impact of the mountain landing after a one-inch fall, including stress waves, rock strength, seismic shaking, and earthquake-triggering uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Claims inevitable continent-scale destruction, no effect at all, or other outcomes incompatible with the small drop and huge mass.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impact or earthquake effects but with vague, exaggerated, or physically inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the impact would create noticeable shaking and stress but likely not catastrophic damage by itself.
criteria.7-8: Explains that rock can generally withstand the added stress, with local cracking and shaking comparable to a small earthquake, while noting possible triggered seismicity.
criteria.9-10: Balances the modest direct impact with the nonzero chance of triggering an existing fault, distinguishing induced seismic release from impact energy itself.

criteria.name: Local Hazards and Material Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-field effects specific to a one-inch mountain-wide gap, including air expulsion, dust and rock jets, cracking, sound, vibration, and danger to people at or near the base.
criteria.1-2: Ignores local hazards or invents unrelated effects such as lava, nuclear fireballs, or universal liquefaction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger nearby but gives little mechanism or focuses only on generic earthquake damage.
criteria.5-6: Covers some local effects such as a jolt, noise, dust, or rock fracture, but misses key gap-closure hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains that compressed/expelled air, debris, dust, and cracking near the gap may be more dangerous locally than the fall itself.
criteria.9-10: Provides a vivid but physically grounded account of local hazards, including high-speed air/debris expulsion, lightning-like crack/rumble sounds, minor cracking, and risk to nearby observers.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer traces downstream consequences from the initial vanishing inch through immediate impact, local damage, possible seismic triggering, and broader human/geological effects without skipping causal links.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected conclusions with no causal chain or jumps directly to apocalyptic/global outcomes from the one-inch event.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but relies on unsupported leaps, such as assuming total mountain collapse or global climate effects.
criteria.5-6: Gives a reasonable immediate-to-local sequence but treats longer-range effects shallowly or inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a coherent sequence from gap creation to fall, impact, vibrations, local hazards, and conditional earthquake effects.
criteria.9-10: Builds a clear, conditional, multi-stage causal narrative that separates likely local outcomes from rarer long-range seismic consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids internal contradictions; and remains faithful to the counterfactual premise without mixing in unrelated drop heights unless clearly labeled.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself repeatedly, treats speculation as certainty, or changes the scenario without notice.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but makes confident unsupported claims or conflates one-inch, one-foot, summit-height, and space-drop scenarios.

items.model_answer:
A real mountain does not have a clean “bottom inch” like a block sitting on a table; it is continuous with the crust beneath it. But if, by magic, a one-inch-thick horizontal layer under the whole mountain suddenly vanished, the overlying rock would lose support and begin to collapse into the gap.

It would not fall far: only about 2.5 cm. In free fall over that distance, the rock would hit the lower surface at only about 0.7 m/s, roughly walking speed. But because the mass involved is enormous, the energy release would be huge. For a large mountain with a mass around \(10^{15}\) kg, dropping one inch releases roughly

\[
E \approx Mgh \approx 10^{15} \times 9.8 \times 0.025 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{14}\text{ J},
\]

which is comparable to tens of kilotons of TNT. For an even larger massif, it could be hundreds of kilotons equivalent.

The result would be a violent local geologic event: intense cracking, crushing of the bottom rock, seismic waves, rockfalls, landslides, and possibly a quake-like shock felt far away. The mountain would not leap into the air or disappear; it would mostly settle downward by about an inch, but unevenly and destructively. The impact and stress redistribution would pulverize rock in places and could destabilize slopes over a wide region.

It would not destroy the planet or launch the mountain upward. It would be more like a sudden, shallow, mountain-sized collapse producing a significant earthquake and catastrophic landslides near the mountain.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard to get to orbit because you have to go so fast. Space isn't like this: [Image: image] Space is like this: [Image: image] Space is about 100 kilometers away. That's far away—I wouldn't want to climb a ladder to get there—but it isn't that far away. If you're in Sacramento, Seattle, Canberra, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Phnom Penh, Cairo, Beijing, central Japan, central Sri Lanka, or Portland, space is closer than the sea. Getting to space[1]Specifically, low Earth orbit, which is where the International Space Station is and where the shuttles could go. is easy. It's not, like, something you could do in your car, but it's not a huge challenge. You could get a person to space with a small sounding rocket the size of a telephone pole. The X-15 aircraft reached space[2]The X-15 reached 100 km on two occasions, both when flown by Joe Walker. just by going fast and then steering up.[3]Make sure to remember to steer up and not down, or you will have a bad time. [Image: image] But getting to space is easy. The problem is staying there. Gravity in low Earth orbit is almost as strong as gravity on the surface. The Space Station hasn't escaped Earth's gravity at all; it's experiencing about 90% the pull that we feel on the surface. To avoid falling back into the atmosphere, you have to go sideways really, really fast. The speed you need to stay in orbit is about 8 kilometers per second.[4]It's a little less if you're in the higher region of low Earth orbit. Only a fraction of a rocket's energy is used to lift up out of the atmosphere; the vast majority of it is used to gain orbital (sideways) speed. This leads us to the central problem of getting into orbit: Reaching orbital speed takes much more fuel than reaching orbital height. Getting a ship up to 8 km/s takes a lot of booster rockets. Reaching orbital speed is hard enough; reaching to orbital speed while carrying enough fuel to slow back down would be completely impractical.[5]This exponential increase is the central problem of rocketry: The fuel required to increase your speed by one km/s multiplies your weight by about 1.4. To get into orbit, you need to increase your speed to 8 km/s, which means you'll need a lot of fuel: $ 1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\approx 15$ times the original weight of your ship. Using a rocket to slow down carries the same problem: Every 1 km/s decrease in speed multiplies your starting mass by that same factor of 1.4. If you want to slow all the way down to zero—and drop gently into the atmosphere—the fuel requirements multiply your weight by 15 again. These outrageous fuel requirements are why every spacecraft entering an atmosphere has braked using a heat shield instead of rockets—slamming into the air is the most practical way to slow down. (And to answer Brian's question, the Curiosity rover was no exception to this; although it used small rockets to hover when it was near the surface, it first used air-braking to shed the majority of its speed.) How fast is 8 km/s, anyway? I think the reason for a lot of confusion about these issues is that when astronauts are in orbit, it doesn't seem like they're moving that fast; they look like they're drifting slowly over a blue marble. But 8 km/s is blisteringly fast. When you look at the sky near sunset, you can sometimes see the ISS go past ... and then, 90 minutes later, see it go past again.[6]There are some good apps and online tools to help you spot the station, along with other neat satellites. My favorite is ISS Detector (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.runar.issdetector), but if you Google you can find lots of others. In those 90 minutes, it's circled the entire world. The ISS moves so quickly that if you fired a rifle bullet from one end of a football field,[7]Either kind. the International Space Station could cross the length of the field before the bullet traveled 10 yards.[8]This type of play is legal in Australian rules football. Let's imagine what it would look like if you were speed-walking across the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. To get a better sense of the pace at which you're traveling, let's use the beat of a song to mark the passage of time.[9]Using song beats to help measure the passage of time is a technique also used in CPR training, where the song "Stayin' Alive" is used to . suppose you started playing the 1988 song by The Proclaimers, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles). That song is about 131.9 beats per minute, so imagine that with every beat of the song, you move forward more than two miles. In the time it took to sing the first line of the chorus, you could walk from the Statue of Liberty all the way to the Bronx: [Image: image] It would take you about two lines of the chorus (16 beats of the song) to cross the English Channel between London and France. The song's length leads to an odd coincidence. The interval between the start and the end of I'm Gonna Be is 3 minutes and 30 seconds,[10]Based on timing from the official Youtube video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbNlMtqrYS0) and the ISS is moving at 7.66 km/s. This means that if an astronaut on the ISS listens to I'm Gonna Be, in the time between the first beat of the song and the final lines ... [Image: image] ... they will have traveled just about exactly 1,000 miles.

items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle a spacecraft could use rockets to slow to only a few miles per hour during reentry, but for an orbital spacecraft it would be extremely inefficient and would require a huge amount of propellant.

A spacecraft in low Earth orbit is moving about 17,500 mph, or 7.8 km/s. To slow almost to a stop using rockets, it would need to cancel nearly all of that orbital velocity. That is roughly comparable to the velocity change needed to reach orbit in the first place. Because rockets must carry their own propellant, the mass penalty is enormous: the spacecraft would need to launch with many times its dry mass in fuel just to brake itself back down.

Also, slowing to a few miles per hour high in the atmosphere would not solve the whole problem. If the spacecraft is still tens of kilometers above the ground and moving only a few mph, it will simply begin falling again under gravity. It would then need to keep firing rockets all the way down, essentially hovering or performing a powered descent, which costs still more propellant.

If the spacecraft waits until lower altitude to use rockets, it still has to survive the earlier high-speed atmospheric entry. Aerodynamic drag would produce intense heating unless the vehicle had already slowed significantly before encountering dense air. That is why most returning spacecraft use the atmosphere itself as a “free brake”: the heat shield absorbs and dissipates the orbital kinetic energy, then parachutes, wings, or small landing rockets handle the final descent.

So the answer is: it is physically possible, and vehicles can use rockets for part of reentry or landing, but using rockets to slow an orbital spacecraft to a few miles per hour during reentry would be impractical for most missions because the propellant requirement would be enormous. It is far more efficient to use atmospheric drag for most of the braking and reserve rockets, parachutes, or wings for the final landing phase.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.

criteria.9-10: Shows strong long-range reasoning, explicitly separates assumptions from conclusions, avoids double-counting, and keeps all downstream effects mutually consistent.

items.model_answer:
If you mean “print a current snapshot of the English Wikipedia, and keep the paper copy current as edits happen,” the result is a huge but not physically impossible printing job; the absurd part is maintaining it.

The English Wikipedia is on the order of several billion words. Printed as ordinary text, with references and formatting, it would be roughly 10–20 million printed pages. On double-sided paper, that is millions of sheets: tens of tonnes of paper and a stack well over a kilometer high if piled up. A normal office laser printer printing 30–60 pages per minute would take months to print one full copy.

But Wikipedia would not sit still while you printed it. The English Wikipedia receives roughly one to two edits per second, or around 100,000+ edits per day. If every edit forced you to print a replacement page, you would need several office printers running continuously just to keep up with the changes, plus an enormous system for collating, replacing, recycling, and rebinding pages. If you reprinted entire edited articles rather than just changed pages, the demand would grow to many more printers.

If you interpreted the task even more literally—reprint the entire encyclopedia every time it changes—it becomes hopeless. With edits arriving every second or so and each full copy requiring millions of pages, you would need millions of pages per second of printing capacity.

So the direct answer is: printing a static English Wikipedia is merely gigantic; printing it “in real time” as a perfectly current physical encyclopedia is effectively impractical. You could keep up with the raw edit stream using a modest bank of printers, but producing a usable, always-current printed Wikipedia would be a logistical nightmare of paper, ink, sorting, and constant obsolescence.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium one from a party obviously won't do the trick. [Image: image] If the balloon is large enough, you don't even need the helium. A balloon will act as a parachute, slowing your fall to non-fatal speeds. Avoiding a high-speed landing is, unsurprisingly, the key to survival. As one medical paper[1]De Haven H. Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet (http://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/6/1/62.3.long). Injury Prevention. 6(1):62-b-68. put it, It is, of course, obvious that speed, or height of fall, is not in itself injurious ... but a high rate of change of velocity, such as occurs after a 10 story fall onto concrete, is another matter. ... which is just a wordy version of the old saying, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." To act as a parachute, a balloon filled with air, rather than helium, would have to be 10 to 20 meters across—far too big to be inflated with portable tanks. A powerful fan could be used to fill it with ambient air, but at that point, you may as well just use a parachute. Helium The helium makes things easier. It doesn't take too many helium balloons to lift a person. In 1982, Larry Walters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters) flew across Los Angeles in a lawn chair lifted by weather balloons, eventually reaching several miles in altitude. After passing through LAX airspace, he descended by shooting some of the balloons with a pellet gun. On landing, Walters was arrested, although the authorities had some trouble figuring out what to charge him with. At the time, an FAA safety inspector told the New York Times, "We know he broke some part of the Federal Aviation Act, and as soon as we decide which part it is, some type of charge will be filed."[2]ARMCHAIR AIRMAN SAYS FLIGHT FULFILLED HIS LIFELONG DREAM (http://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/04/us/armchair-airman-says-flight-fulfilled-his-lifelong-dream.html?pagewanted=all), New York Times, July 4, 1982 A relatively small helium balloon—certainly smaller than a parachute—will suffice slow your fall, but it still has to be huge by party balloon standards. The biggest consumer rental helium tanks are about 250 cubic feet, and you'd need to empty at least 10 of them to put enough air in the balloon to support your weight. You'd have to do it quickly. The compressed helium cylinders are smooth and often quite heavy, which means they have a high terminal velocity. You'll only have a few minutes to use up all the cylinders. (As soon as you emptied one, you could drop it.) You can't get around this problem by moving your starting point higher. Since the upper atmosphere is pretty thin, anything dropped from the stratosphere up will accelerate to very high speeds until it hits the lower atmosphere, then fall slowly the rest of the way. This is true of everything from small meteors[3]By the time meteors hit the Earth, they have slowed down (http://www.geology.wisc.edu/~museum/meteorite.html) to a few hundred miles per hour. to Felix Baumgartner.[4]Jason Martinez, Falling Faster than the Speed of Sound (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/), Wolfram Blog, October 24, 2012 [Image: image] But if you inflated the balloons quickly, possibly by connecting many canisters to it at once, you'd be able to slow your fall. Just don't use too much helium, or you'll end up floating at 16,000 feet like Larry Walters.http://xkcd.com/1110 [Image: image] While researching this article,[5]Additionally, while researching impact speeds for this article, I came across a discussion (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=361878) on the Straight Dope Message Boards about survivable fall heights. One poster compared a fall from height to being hit by a bus. Another user, a medical examiner, replied (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showpost.php?p=7180162&postcount=40) that this was a bad comparison: "When hit by a car, the vast majority of people are not run over; they are run under. The lower legs break, sending them into the air. They usually strike the hood of the car, often with the back of the head impacting the windshield, "starring" the windshield, possibly leaving a few hairs in the glass. They then go over the top of the car. They are still alive, although with broken legs, and maybe with head pain from the nonfatal windshield impact. They die when they hit the ground. They die from head injury." The lesson: Don't mess with medical examiners. They're apparently pretty hardcore. I managed to lock up my copy of Mathematica several times on balloon-related differential equations, and subsequently got my IP address banned from Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=how+many+days+have+i+been+alive) for making too many requests. The ban-appeal form asked me to explain what task I was performing that necessitated so many queries, so this is what I put: [Image: image] I hope they understand.

criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent quantitative or semi-quantitative account of needed balloon volume, helium lift, drag area, and why an air-filled balloon could slow descent even without helium.

criteria.3-4: Mentions falling or inflation but omits major timing or sequencing problems during free fall.

criteria.9-10: Tracks the full long-range scenario with strong causal continuity, including acceleration before deployment, limited time to empty tanks, changing descent rate, possible excessive lift, and final impact dynamics.

criteria.name: Treatment of altitude, atmosphere, and terminal velocity

criteria.3-4: Mentions altitude but misses how thin air, acceleration, or terminal velocity change during descent.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that altitude affects fall speed and available time, but gives incomplete treatment of atmospheric density.
criteria.7-8: Explains that very high starts can cause high speeds in thin air before slowing in denser air, limiting the benefit of extra altitude.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, air density, terminal velocity, balloon expansion/drag, and descent timing, avoiding simplistic 'start higher' reasoning.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately qualifies uncertain details, avoids internal contradictions, and keeps speculative extensions consistent with the physics of the scenario.
criteria.1-2: Presents confident but inconsistent claims, such as saying the balloon both cannot help and can safely land the person without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but also contains contradictions or unjustified certainty about survival, tank counts, or balloon dimensions.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids contradictions and acknowledges some uncertainty, though estimates or assumptions may be underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable caveats about equipment, human control, inflation rate, and landing conditions while maintaining a consistent conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates known physics from rough estimates, states assumptions, flags practical unknowns, and keeps all claims mutually consistent throughout the counterfactual analysis.

items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane carrying helium tanks and a giant balloon, it would almost certainly not save you. You would likely fall, fail to inflate the balloon safely, and hit the ground at a lethal speed.

A helium balloon can lift you only by displacing air. At sea level, supporting a person plus gear of about 100 kg would require roughly 100 cubic meters of helium, corresponding to a spherical balloon about 6 meters across. At typical aircraft altitude, where the air is thinner, you would need an even larger balloon—perhaps 8–10 meters across or more—to get the same lift.

The helium tanks are a major problem. To lift 100 kg, you need on the order of 15–20 kg of helium, plus the weight of the balloon, harness, valves, and tanks. High-pressure helium cylinders capable of carrying that much gas would be very heavy, possibly heavier than the lift they help create. So carrying enough helium in tanks while jumping is not practical.

Inflating the balloon during the fall would also be extremely difficult. You would be falling at perhaps 50–60 m/s before slowing, with violent airflow whipping the balloon around. A giant lightweight balloon would tangle, tear, or fail to deploy cleanly. If it inflated suddenly, the deceleration could injure or kill you, much like opening an enormous parachute incorrectly.

Even if the balloon did inflate, it would not behave like a parachute. A parachute is designed to open in high-speed airflow and create stable drag. A helium balloon is designed for buoyancy, not violent deployment. It could rupture, spin, collapse, or drag you unpredictably.

If, by magic, you already had a large enough fully inflated helium balloon attached before leaving the plane, then you might descend slowly or even float upward depending on the lift. But that would be more like stepping out with a small airship or balloon system, not jumping with tanks and inflating it midair.

So the direct answer is: with real equipment, you would probably die. The tanks are too heavy, the balloon would be too large, and deployment during free fall would be uncontrollable. A parachute is vastly simpler, lighter, and safer because it is designed for exactly this job.
