items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. rubrics.question_focus: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of punch-card storage scale
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer estimates the physical magnitude of storing modern digital data on punch cards using defensible orders of magnitude, especially bytes per card, number of cards, volume/mass/area, and comparison to real-world geographic or industrial scales.
criteria.1-2: Gives no meaningful quantitative estimate or uses wildly impossible units without recognizing scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions that the card volume would be enormous but provides little or incorrect arithmetic.
criteria.5-6: Uses plausible card capacity and data-size assumptions but has limited or rough physical-scale calculations.
criteria.7-8: Computes credible orders of magnitude for cards, boxes, volume, mass, land area, or depth with clear assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Provides robust, internally checked scale estimates and vivid comparisons while noting sensitivity to data-size assumptions.

criteria.name: Fidelity to the counterfactual premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the premise that all digital data must be stored on punch cards, rather than slipping back into magnetic, optical, semiconductor, or cloud storage for primary storage.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or continues to rely on ordinary digital storage as if unchanged.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges punch cards but repeatedly contradicts the premise with modern storage assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise, with some ambiguous or minor lapses about backups, caches, or transmission.
criteria.7-8: Maintains the punch-card constraint across storage, backup, indexing, and retrieval scenarios.
criteria.9-10: Applies the premise rigorously, including edge cases such as metadata, redundancy, logs, encryption keys, and temporary data.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for storage, retrieval, and computation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the concrete mechanisms by which punch-card-only data storage would affect writing, reading, sorting, searching, updating, backing up, and computing over data.
criteria.1-2: Only says the system would be slow or impossible, with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as storage space or read speed, superficially.
criteria.5-6: Explains several mechanisms, including read/write throughput, mechanical handling, and indexing.
criteria.7-8: Connects storage density, card readers, sorting systems, error rates, duplication, and update costs into a coherent operating model.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes the full data lifecycle, including random access, distributed processing, versioning, checksums, failures, and archival workflows.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible cascading effects on data centers, internet services, science, commerce, surveillance, personal devices, energy use, labor, logistics, and the environment.
criteria.1-2: Provides only an immediate observation, such as 'there would be lots of cards.'
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences but does not connect them causally.
criteria.5-6: Covers several downstream effects with basic causal links, such as slower internet and larger warehouses.
criteria.7-8: Develops coherent chains from physical storage limits to altered computing, economics, infrastructure, and society.
criteria.9-10: Explores broad, long-range systemic changes while distinguishing likely effects from speculative ones.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertain quantities, avoids overclaiming, and keeps assumptions consistent when estimating total global or organizational data stored on punch cards.
criteria.1-2: States precise claims with no basis and contains major internal contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but mixes incompatible assumptions or unjustified exact numbers.
criteria.5-6: Uses rough ranges and acknowledges uncertainty, though some assumptions remain underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates known values, estimates, and speculation; avoids most contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, tests assumptions with ranges, and maintains consistency across all calculations and causal claims.

items.model_answer:
If all digital data were stored on punch cards, modern computing would become physically and logistically impossible.

Take a standard IBM-style punch card: about 80 characters of data, roughly 80 bytes in ordinary use. A single 1 MB file would need about 12,500 cards. A 1 GB movie would need about 12.5 million cards. A 1 TB drive would require about 12.5 billion cards.

For the world’s digital data, the numbers become absurd. Humanity has on the order of 100–200 zettabytes of digital data, depending on what is counted. Using 150 zettabytes as a rough estimate:

150 ZB = 150,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes.

At 80 bytes per card, that would require about 1.9 sextillion punch cards:

1,900,000,000,000,000,000,000 cards.

Physically, that is catastrophic. A punch card is thin, but not that thin. Stacked together, those cards would form a pile tens of light-years long. As a dense block, ignoring shelving and access space, they would occupy a cube roughly 170 kilometers on each side. Their mass would be on the order of several quintillion kilograms of cardstock, far beyond any realistic paper industry and vastly beyond Earth’s available forests if made from wood pulp.

Access speed would be even worse. A fast punch-card reader might read around 1,000–2,000 cards per minute, which is only a few kilobytes per second. Reading a modern hard drive’s worth of data would take years. Searching, copying, backing up, or streaming data would require immense mechanical warehouses full of readers, sorters, conveyors, and workers or robots. A single video stream, database query, or software update could involve moving mountains of cards.

Reliability would also be poor. Punch cards can last a long time in controlled archival conditions, but they are vulnerable to fire, water, mold, tearing, misordering, and physical wear. Digital error correction and redundancy would require even more cards, multiplying the already impossible storage burden.

So the practical result would be that most modern digital life would disappear. No large-scale internet, no cloud computing, no streaming media, no real-time search engines, no modern AI training, no global software distribution, and no dense personal storage. Society would have to store only tiny amounts of essential data, and computing would resemble mid-20th-century batch processing: slow, expensive, physical, and heavily rationed.

In short: storing all digital data on punch cards is not merely inefficient; it would turn the information age into a planet-scale paper-handling problem, and the system would collapse under its own size.

Take a standard IBM-style punch card:
about 80 characters of data, roughly 80 bytes in ordinary use.
A single 1 MB file would need about 12,500 cards.
A 1 GB movie would need about 12.5 million cards.
A 1 TB drive would require about 12.5 billion cards.
For the world’s digital data, the numbers become absurd.

Physically, that is catastrophic.
A punch card is thin,
but not that thin.
Stacked together, those cards would form a pile tens of light-years long.
As a dense block, ignoring shelving and access space, they would occupy a cube roughly 170 kilometers on each side.
Their mass would be on the order of several quintillion kilograms of cardstock, far beyond any realistic paper industry and vastly beyond Earth’s available forests if made from wood pulp.
Access speed would be even worse.
A fast punch-card reader might read around 1,000–2,000 cards per minute,
which is only a few kilobytes per second.

Searching, copying, backing up, or streaming data would require immense mechanical warehouses full of readers, sorters, conveyors, and workers or robots.
A single video stream, database query, or software update could involve moving mountains of cards.

Punch cards can last a long time in controlled archival conditions,
but they are vulnerable to fire, water, mold, tearing, misordering, and physical wear.
Digital error correction and redundancy would require even more cards,
multiplying the already impossible storage burden.
So the practical result would be that most modern digital life would disappear.
No large-scale internet, no cloud computing, no streaming media, no real-time search engines, no modern AI training, no global software distribution, and no dense personal storage.
Society would have to store only tiny amounts of essential data,
and computing would resemble mid-20th-century batch processing: slow, expensive, physical, and heavily rationed.

it would turn the information age into a planet-scale paper-handling problem,
and the system would collapse under its own size.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you only had an initial upward speed of one foot per second, normal gravity would stop you almost immediately: you would rise only about half a centimeter before falling back down. So the interesting version is: some mysterious force keeps you rising at a constant 1 ft/s, about 0.3 m/s.

At that speed you would climb about 3,600 feet per hour, or 26 km per day. For the first few minutes it would just be dangerous and awkward: after 30 seconds you are 30 feet up, already high enough that falling could injure or kill you. After an hour you are around 1.1 km up; after 5 hours, around 5.5 km, where the air is thin enough that an unacclimatized person would be badly impaired. You would also be getting very cold.

Without rescue, oxygen, and warm gear, you would probably become confused and incapacitated after several hours. By about 8–10 hours, you would be near Everest/commercial-airliner altitudes, where the air pressure is far too low for normal survival and temperatures may be around −40 to −60 °C. You would likely be unconscious and soon dead from hypoxia and exposure.

If you had supplemental oxygen and heavy insulation, you could last longer, but pressure would become the next problem. Around 18–19 km up, reached after roughly 17 hours, you approach the Armstrong limit, where body fluids can boil at body temperature unless you are in a pressure suit. Above that, an oxygen mask is not enough; you need a pressurized suit or cabin.

With a full pressure suit and life support, you would reach the edge of space, about 100 km up, after about 91 hours, or just under 4 days. But you would not be “in orbit”; one foot per second is far, far too slow for that. If the upward force stopped, you would fall back to Earth. If it kept going, you would simply drift slowly outward, taking about 15 days to reach the altitude of the ISS and about 40 years to reach the Moon’s distance.

So, in ordinary clothes, the answer is: you could be saved early, but if not, you would die within the first day, probably within the first 8–12 hours, from cold and lack of oxygen.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies. Getting shot doesn't really make someone fly backward. The vacuum of space doesn't make your skin explode. But high wind can definitely pick up a person. In fact, if you were standing in the parking lot, the wind wouldn't just pick you up—it would also peel the pavement from the ground! [Image: image] It wouldn't be strong enough to peel your skin off. Humans can survive blasts of 500 mph wind, which is important because pilots sometimes need to eject from airplanes at those speeds. In the 1940s, the US government put pilots in wind tunnels to learn how they reacted to high winds. Have you ever been curious what happens to a person's face in 457 mph winds? Well, you can watch a video of one of those wind tunnel tests here (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IU4SDDNXuUA). (That test was conducted at NASA Langley Research Center, where I worked before I started drawing internet comics for a living.) It doesn't look very comfortable—I didn't know cheeks could flap like that—but the pilot appears to stay alive. Luckily, he's strapped into that chair. He wouldn't be able to stand up in those winds! If he tried, he would go flying backward down the tunnel. High wind is really powerful. In a paper in the journal Weather, J. F. R. McIlveen showed how to calculate the force of wind on the human body.[1]McIlveen, J. F. R.. "The Everyday Effects Of Wind Drag On People. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1256/wea.29.02/pdf)" Weather 57, no. 11 (2002): 410-413. The calculations on page 2 show how far you'd have to lean to stay upright in wind of various speeds. [Image: image] When wind speed rises above about 120 mph, it's no longer possible to stay upright no matter how far you lean; you'll start to slide backward across the ground,[2]When Hurricane Isabel hit Virginia in 2003, I had the bright idea of standing on a skateboard with a poncho held up like a sail, so the wind would blow me down the street. But the moment I got the sail up, the wind fell quiet. Later, I learned that people die from doing that (http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-1327705/Kite-surfer-28-dies-gale-drags-100mph-beach-drops-50ft.html). Oops. then quickly go head over heels and start to tumble. You wouldn't necessarily be thrown very high. If the wind were perfectly level, you'd tumble along the surface, bouncing against the ground. However, if there were any updrafts, you could easily be lifted up and carried away. The good news is that 500 mph winds are rare. The strongest hurricanes have wind speeds around 200 mph with gusts up to 250.[3]Courtney, J.; Buchan, S.; Cerveny, R.S.; Bessemoulin, P.; Peterson, T.C.; Rubiera Torres, J.M.; Beven, J.; King, J.; Trerwin, B.; Rancourt, K.. 2012 "Documentation and verification of the world extreme wind gust record: 113.3 m s–1 on Barrow Island, Australia, during passage of tropical cyclone Olivia. (http://www.bom.gov.au/amoj/docs/2012/courtney_hres.pdf)" Australian Meterological and Oceanographic Journal, 62 (1). 1-9. Tornadoes can reach 300 mph.[4]It's difficult to get accurate measurements of surface winds since those tornadoes destroy most measuring equipment (http://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/#History)! 300 is a far cry from 500; the force from a 500 mph wind is several times stronger than the force from a 300 mph wind. There are a few ways you could experience wind speeds faster than 500 mph. One is to stand on top of a volcano when it erupts. When Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980, the column of ash was blasted outward at 700 mph, which is close to the speed of sound.[5]Kieffer, S. W., 1981, Fluid dynamics of the May 18 blast at Mount St. Helens, in Lipman, P.W., and Mullineux, D.R., eds., The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens, Washington: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1250, p. 379-400. Another way to experience 500 mph winds is to trigger a hypercane.[6]Limits on Hurricane Intensity (http://wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/holem/holem.html) A hypercane is an exotic type of hurricane with 500 mph winds spinning in a very tight vortex just a few miles across. Hypercanes can't exist on Earth right now. To form, they require ocean temperatures of about 50°C. No matter how much we warm the planet, we're not going to get the temperature that high any time soon. However, there's one way these storms might happen. When an asteroid or comet—coincidentally, one about the size of the recently-named 4942 Munroe (http://blog.xkcd.com/2013/09/30/asteroid-4942-munroe/)—hit Mexico 65 million years ago, it punched a hole in the crust and left behind a sea of lava.[7]Christeson, Gail L., Gareth S. Collins, Joanna V. Morgan, Sean P.S. Gulick, Penny J. Barton, and Michael R. Warner. "Mantle Deformation Beneath The Chicxulub Impact Crater (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/4214/1/icpub.pdf)." Earth and Planetary Science Letters 284, no. 1-2 (2009): 249-257. When water flowed back in to fill the hole, it would have been heated by contact with the molten rock. This might have created the conditions for hypercanes to form, and one paper suggests that these storms could have lifted a large amount of dust and debris into the upper atmosphere—thus contributing to a global winter and extinction of the dinosaurs.[8]Emanuel, Kerry A., Kevin Speer, Richard Rotunno, Ramesh Srivastava, and Mario Molina. "Hypercanes: A Possible Link In Global Extinction Scenarios (ftp://texmex.mit.edu/pub/emanuel/PAPERS/hypercane95.pdf)." Journal of Geophysical Research 100, no. D7 (1995): 13755-13765. [Image: image] In short, the answer to Grey's question is yes—500 mph winds would send you flying through the air. But don't worry about that. Instead, worry about is the thing that created the 500 mph winds. Odds are, that's what's going to kill you. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
A 500-mile-per-hour wind at ground level would be catastrophically destructive. It would be stronger than the winds in the most violent tornadoes and far beyond any normal hurricane.

At 500 mph, the air is moving about 223 meters per second, roughly two-thirds the speed of sound. The wind pressure would be enormous: about 30,000 pascals, or around 0.3 atmospheres of dynamic pressure. That is enough to tear apart houses, rip steel roofing and siding from buildings, snap or uproot trees, overturn vehicles, destroy power lines, and turn debris into high-speed projectiles. A person exposed in the open would not be able to stand or breathe normally and would likely be lifted, tumbled, or struck by debris almost immediately.

Most ordinary buildings would fail. Wood-frame houses would be shredded. Windows would explode inward or outward depending on pressure differences. Roofs would be peeled off, walls could collapse, and even many reinforced structures would suffer severe damage if they were not specifically designed for extreme wind loads. Skyscrapers might not simply “blow over,” because they are engineered for wind, but windows, cladding, antennas, and exterior equipment would be heavily damaged or stripped away.

If this wind occurred over the ocean, it would generate extreme waves, dense sea spray, and potentially devastating storm surge near coasts. Ships would be in grave danger. If it swept over land for an extended time, it would scour soil, flatten forests, destroy crops, and fill the air with dust, sand, vegetation, glass, metal, and wreckage.

It would not be like a nuclear blast, and it would not by itself strip away Earth’s atmosphere or level mountains. But at the surface, a sustained 500 mph wind would make most exposed areas unsurvivable and would leave damage comparable to or worse than the core of the most violent tornadoes, especially because the destruction would be spread over whatever area the wind covered.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one. [Image: image] The Little Prince, by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, is a story about a traveler from a distant asteroid. It's simple and sad and poignant and memorable.[1]For another take on the Petit Prince, scroll down to the last section of this wonderful piece (http://the-toast.net/2013/08/02/texts-from-peter-pan-et-al/) by Mallory Ortberg. It's ostensibly a children's book, but it's hard to pin down who the intended audience is. In any case, it certainly has found an audience; it's among the best-selling books in history. [Image: image] It was written in 1942. That's an interesting time to write about asteroids, because in 1942 we didn't actually know what asteroids looked like. Even in our best telescopes, the largest asteroids were only visible as points of light. In fact, that's where their name comes from—the word asteroid means "star-like." We got our first confirmation of what asteroids looked like in 1971, when Mariner 9 visited Mars and snapped pictures of Phobos and Deimos.[2]Here's (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/m09_mtvs4109_09.html) a picture of Phobos looking like the archetypical asteroid. The archived images from the mission are at the NASA Space Science Data Center (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?ds=PSPG-00235), but strangely, the NSSDC refers readers to someone's personal Tripod page (http://petermasek.tripod.com/mariner9.html) to browse the actual images. These moons, believed to be captured asteroids,[3]Ironically, while Phobos and Deimos look like asteroids, new research suggests they're not. See Craddock, Robert A.. "Are Phobos And Deimos The Result Of A Giant Impact? (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0019103510004100)". Icarus (2010) solidified the modern image of asteroids as cratered potatoes. [Image: image] Before the 1970s, it was common for science fiction to assume small asteroids would be round, like planets.[4]Not always; plenty of people had a good idea of what they would look like. And there were stranger ideas (http://pencilink.blogspot.com/2010/08/uncle-scrooge-29-carl-barks-art-cover.html) ... The Little Prince took this a step further, imagining an asteroid as a tiny planet with gravity, air, and a rose. There's no point in trying to critique the science here, because (1) it's not a story about asteroids, and (2) it opens with a parable about how foolish adults are for looking at everything too literally. So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, the main problem would be gravity. A small radius plus a huge mass gives enormous surface gravity:

\(g = GM/R^2\)

So if the asteroid were only a few hundred meters wide but had the mass of a planet, you would not “walk around” on it. You would be crushed almost instantly, and the difference in gravity between your feet and your head could be large enough to stretch or tear you apart. That tidal force scales roughly as \(2gh/R\), so on a very small massive body it becomes severe.

It also would not behave like a normal asteroid. Ordinary rock could not remain a lumpy asteroid under that much self-gravity. It would collapse into a sphere and, if dense enough, into exotic matter. If its mass were packed inside its Schwarzschild radius,

\(R_s = 2GM/c^2\),

it would be a black hole, meaning there would be no solid surface to live on at all.

If the mass were carefully chosen so that surface gravity was about Earth-like, the world would still be bizarre. For example, a 100-meter-radius object with 1 g gravity would have a circumference of only about 628 meters. The horizon would be very close, gravity would noticeably weaken as you climbed even a few dozen meters, and orbital speed near the surface would be only tens of meters per second. But such a tiny world could not naturally hold a breathable atmosphere for long unless it were sealed or artificially maintained.

So the direct answer is: if it were merely “tiny but dense” and tuned to Earth-like gravity, you could survive only in an engineered habitat and the environment would feel very strange. If it were truly ultra-massive, you could not live there—the gravity, tides, pressure, and possible collapse into a black hole would make it instantly fatal.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.

items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle you can boil water by stirring it, because stirring does mechanical work on the water, and that work is eventually dissipated as heat through viscosity and turbulence.

For example, to heat 1 liter of water from 20°C to 100°C requires about

\[
Q = mc\Delta T \approx (1\,\text{kg})(4180\,\text{J/kg·°C})(80°C) \approx 334{,}000\,\text{J}.
\]

So if you could put 100 watts of mechanical power directly into the water as stirring and keep it well insulated, it would take roughly

\[
334{,}000/100 \approx 3300\,\text{s} \approx 55\,\text{minutes}
\]

just to reach the boiling point. To actually boil away a significant amount of water requires much more energy, because vaporization takes about 2.26 million joules per kilogram.

In practice, boiling water by hand-stirring is essentially impossible: a person cannot sustain enough power into the water, and heat losses to the container and air would usually exceed the heating from stirring. But with a powerful mechanical stirrer, blender, or paddle in a well-insulated vessel, yes, the water could eventually be heated to boiling purely by stirring.

So the careful answer is: yes physically, but not realistically by ordinary hand stirring.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it. If you're not a physics person, it might not sound odd to you, so here's a little context for why it's such a surprising idea: Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with the world at all. Look at your hand—there are about a trillion neutrinos from the Sun passing through it every second. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the neutrino flood is that neutrinos hardly interact with ordinary matter at all. On average, out of that massive flood, only one neutrino will "hit" an atom in your body every few years.[1]Less often if you're a child, since you have fewer atoms to be hit. Statistically, my first neutrino interaction probably happened somewhere around age 10. In fact, neutrinos are so shadowy that the entire Earth is transparent to them; nearly all of the Sun's neutrino flood goes straight through it unaffected. To detect neutrinos, people build giant tanks filled with hundreds of tons of material in the hopes that they'll register the impact of a single solar neutrino. This means that when a particle accelerator (which produces neutrinos) wants to send a neutrino beam to a detector somewhere else in the world, all it has to do is point the beam at the detector—even if it's on the other side of the Earth! [Image: image] That's why the phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" sounds weird—it mixes scales in an incongruous way. It's like the idiom "knock me over with a feather" or the phrase "football stadium filled to the brim with ants".[2]Which would still be less than 1% of the ants in the world. If you have a math background, it's sort of like seeing the expression "ln(x)e"—it's not that, taken literally, it doesn't make sense, but it's hard to imagine a situation where it would apply.[3]If you want to be mean to first-year calculus students, you can ask them to take the derivative of ln(x)e dx. It looks like it should be "1" or something, but it's not. Similarly, it's so hard to get enough neutrinos to compel even a single one of them to interact with matter, making it hard to picture a scenario in which there'd be enough of them to affect you. Supernovae[4]"Supernovas" is also fine. "Supernovii" is discouraged. provide that scenario. The physicist who mentioned this problem to me told me his rule of thumb for estimating supernova-related numbers: However big you think supernovae are, they're bigger than that. Here's a question to give you a sense of scale: Which of the following would be brighter, in terms of the amount of energy delivered to your retina: A supernova, seen from as far away as the Sun is from the Earth, or The detonation of a hydrogen bomb pressed against your eyeball? [Image: image] Applying the physicist rule of thumb suggests that the supernova is brighter. And indeed, it is ... by nine orders of magnitude. That's why this is a neat question; supernovae are unimaginably huge and neutrinos are unimaginably insubstantial. At what point do these two unimaginable things cancel out to produce an effect on a human scale? A paper by radiation expert Andrew Karam provides an answer.[5]Karam, P. Andrew. "Gamma And Neutrino Radiation Dose From Gamma Ray Bursts And Nearby Supernovae. (http://wayback.archive.org/web/20120313045458/http://www.andrewkaram.com/andy/pdf/HPJ.pdf)" Health Physics 82, no. 4 (2002): 491-499. It explains that during certain supernovae, the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star, 1057 neutrinos can be released (one for every proton in the star that collapses to become a neutron). Karam calculates that the neutrino radiation dose at a distance of one parsec[6]3.262 light-years, or a little less than the distance from here to Alpha Centauri. would be around half a nanosievert, or 1/500th the dose from eating a banana.[7]xkcd.com/radiation (http://xkcd.com/radiation/) A fatal radiation dose is about 4 sieverts. Using the inverse-square law, we can calculate the radiation dose: \[ 0.5\text{ nanosieverts} \times\left ( \frac{1\text{ parsec}}{x}\right )^2 = 5\text{ sieverts} \] \[ x=0.00001118\text{ parsecs}=2.3\text{ AU} \] 2.3 AU is a little more than the distance between the Sun and Mars. Core collapse supernovae happen to giant stars, so if you observed a supernova from that distance, you'd probably be inside the outer layers of the star that created it. [Image: image] The idea of neutrino radiation damage reinforces just how big supernovae are. If you observed a supernova from 1 AU away—and you somehow avoided being being incinerated, vaporized, and converted to some type of exotic plasma—even the flood of ghostly neutrinos would be dense enough to kill you. If it's going fast enough, a feather can absolutely knock you over. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Physical Scale Handling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the unusual premise: neutrinos are normally weakly interacting, but a core-collapse supernova can produce an enormous enough flux that lethal dose becomes meaningful only at extremely close astronomical distances.
criteria.1-2: Treats neutrinos like ordinary radiation or ignores why the premise is unusual; gives no credible scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions neutrinos are weakly interacting or supernovae are energetic, but does not connect the two quantitatively or causally.
criteria.5-6: Explains the weak interaction of neutrinos and the huge supernova output, with rough but incomplete scale reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains the tension between ghostly neutrinos and supernova scale, including inverse-square dilution or comparable scaling.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual with correct physical intuition, emphasizing that only an extreme nearby core-collapse event makes lethal neutrino radiation plausible.

criteria.name: Endpoint Accuracy: Lethal Neutrino Dose Distance
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer reaches or respects the key quantitative endpoint: a lethal neutrino dose requires being roughly a few AU from the supernova, about 2.3 AU using the cited assumptions, not light-years away.
criteria.1-2: Claims lethal neutrino effects at ordinary stellar distances or gives wildly incorrect distances without caveat.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes lethal neutrino exposure needs closeness but places it at an implausible scale, such as many light-years or inside Earth-like ranges without reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Gives a roughly close-in astronomical distance but lacks calculation, units, or connection to dose.
criteria.7-8: Uses a plausible dose comparison and inverse-square scaling to locate lethality at a few AU.
criteria.9-10: Correctly identifies the approximate lethal radius near 2.3 AU, explains assumptions such as dose threshold and parsec-to-AU scaling, and avoids overstating precision.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage: Neutrino Interaction and Biological Dose
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses depth and correctness of the causal mechanism by which neutrinos, despite rarely interacting, could deposit a harmful radiation dose in tissue under an extreme supernova flux.
criteria.1-2: Provides no mechanism or invents nonphysical effects such as neutrinos heating matter efficiently at normal fluxes.
criteria.3-4: Says neutrinos can damage cells but gives little explanation of interaction rarity or radiation dose.
criteria.5-6: Connects rare neutrino interactions to ionizing radiation dose, but with limited biological or particle-physics detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that enormous flux compensates for tiny cross sections, producing enough interactions in body tissue to create a lethal sievert-scale dose.
criteria.9-10: Accurately links neutrino production, weak interaction probability, energy deposition, ionization, and fatal whole-body dose while distinguishing this from ordinary solar neutrino exposure.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Chain and Competing Hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer coherently follows downstream effects of being close enough for lethal neutrino radiation, including the fact that other supernova-related hazards and stellar structure would likely dominate.
criteria.1-2: Considers only neutrinos and ignores the broader consequences of being within a few AU of a supernova.
criteria.3-4: Mentions other dangers vaguely, such as heat or blast, without integrating them into the scenario.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that light, gamma rays, ejecta, or stellar material would also be catastrophic, but the causal ordering is incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Coherently explains that at a few AU Earth would likely be incinerated, engulfed, stripped, or otherwise destroyed apart from the neutrino dose.
criteria.9-10: Integrates neutrino lethality with the full counterfactual chain: progenitor size, radiation flash, plasma/ejecta, orbital context, and why neutrino death is a theoretical threshold rather than the practical main danger.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids internal contradictions and calibrates uncertainty around supernova type, neutrino energies, dose models, biological thresholds, and geometric assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident false claims or contradicts itself about neutrino harmlessness versus lethality.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but mixes incompatible assumptions or overgeneralizes across all supernovae.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with basic caveats about supernova type or dose thresholds, but some imprecision remains.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a consistent model and notes key dependencies such as core-collapse neutrino yield, distance, shielding irrelevance, and fatal-dose approximation.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes robust conclusions from model-dependent numbers, avoids contradictions, and clearly states that the result is an order-of-magnitude counterfactual estimate.

items.model_answer:
A supernova can only give Earth a lethal neutrino dose if it is absurdly close: roughly within a few astronomical units of the collapsing core, comparable to the scale of the inner Solar System, not “nearby” in the usual astronomical sense of tens or hundreds of light-years.

In that scenario, the neutrino burst would arrive first. A core-collapse supernova releases about \(10^{58}\) neutrinos in roughly 10 seconds. Almost all of them would pass straight through Earth, but at a distance of only a few AU the flux would be so enormous that enough would interact inside living tissue to deliver a fatal whole-body radiation dose. Shielding would not help: the neutrinos would pass through the atmosphere, oceans, mountains, bunkers, and the entire planet. People on the night side of Earth would be irradiated almost as much as people facing the supernova.

The immediate biological effect would be acute radiation exposure throughout the body. At a merely “lethal” dose, humans and many animals would not necessarily die instantly, but would suffer severe radiation sickness and die over hours to weeks. At closer distances, the dose could be high enough to cause rapid neurological failure and near-immediate death. Microbes and some radiation-resistant life might survive the neutrino burst itself, depending on the dose.

But the neutrinos would not be the main long-term problem. If a supernova were close enough for its neutrinos to be lethal, the rest of the explosion would be catastrophically worse. The optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray output would bake and ionize the atmosphere and surface. Later, the expanding supernova ejecta would arrive and could strip atmosphere, vaporize oceans, and sterilize or physically devastate the planet. At a few AU, Earth would be inside the supernova’s immediate blast environment.

So the direct answer is: Earth would receive a planet-wide, unshieldable burst of radiation lasting seconds, likely killing most complex life everywhere at once or soon after. But a supernova close enough to do that with neutrinos would also destroy Earth’s habitability by ordinary radiation and blast effects shortly afterward. For any realistic supernova at stellar-neighborhood distances, such as tens or hundreds of light-years away, neutrino radiation would be harmless; the danger would come from photons, cosmic rays, and atmospheric damage, not neutrinos.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels. or a quarter of the diameter of the Death Star thermal exhaust port. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. [Image: image] A few months later, the kid would surpass Robert Wadlow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wadlow) to become the tallest human in history. At age 5, the child would be π meters tall (10'4"): [Image: image] At age 7, the child would be 4.2 meters tall, able to stare down a T-rex: [Image: image] By age 10, the child would be 5.8 meters tall (19 feet). If we assume these giants are proportioned like adult humans, this kid would weigh over a metric ton. [Image: image] Actual humans wouldn't be able to grow to such heights. Thanks to the square-cube law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-cube_law), our bones would be too thin to support our weight and our hearts would be unable to pump blood around our bodies. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image] In addition to the insurmountable health problems, someone with this rapid growth rate would face another hardship. To ride roller coasters, you have to be above a certain minimum height. However, they generally also have a maximum height. [Image: image] Bizarro, a coaster at Six Flags New England, has a minimum height of 137 cm (4'6") and a maximum height of 193 cm (6'4"). Our child would be tall enough to ride Bizarro at age 2 ... and too tall by age 3. Their coaster-riding window would last only 387 days. It's a sad truth: Roller coasters just aren't for everyone. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If humans kept growing at the absolute growth rate of a typical one-month-old baby, they would become giants but not survive in anything like a normal human form.

A one-month-old baby gains roughly 0.7–1 kg per month and grows about 3–4 cm in length per month. If that continued linearly until age 18, a person could be around 7–9 meters tall and weigh perhaps 170–220 kg based only on the baby’s monthly weight gain.

But that body would not work. A human scaled up to 7–9 meters tall with normal proportions would weigh several tons, not a couple hundred kilograms, because volume and mass scale roughly with the cube of height. The skeleton, heart, lungs, joints, and blood vessels would fail under square-cube-law effects: bones and muscles would not become strong enough fast enough to support the mass, circulation would be extremely difficult, and heat regulation would be a major problem.

If “rate” meant percentage growth rather than absolute growth, the result would be far more absurd. Babies grow by a large fraction of their body size each month; maintaining that exponential rate for years would produce bodies of impossible size, eventually asteroid-scale in mass.

So the careful answer is: if growth continued at a one-month-old’s absolute rate, adults would be several meters tall and biologically nonviable; if it continued at the same percentage rate, the growth would become catastrophically exponential and physically impossible very quickly.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] The 33,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide sell something like 15 billion hamburger patties per year,[5]They stopped reporting the "x billions served" number on their signs, but this website (http://overhowmanybillionserved.blogspot.com/) has some extrapolations. for an average of 1,245 burgers per restaurant per day. 1,245 burgers is about 600,000 calories, which means that each T-rex only needs about 80 hamburgers per day to survive, and one McDonald's could support over a dozen tyrannosaurs on hamburgers alone. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. And then if the T-rex goes for your friend anyway, hey, you have 80 burgers. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in New York City, the result would be dangerous and chaotic at first, but it would probably not become a long-term city-destroying catastrophe.

A T. rex was an enormous predatory animal, roughly 12–13 meters long and weighing several tons. In a dense urban area, it could kill people, crush cars, break storefronts, and cause mass panic. Its bite would be devastating, and ordinary barriers like glass doors, light fencing, or parked vehicles would not reliably stop it. The greatest immediate danger might come from crowds fleeing, traffic accidents, subway and street evacuations, and confusion rather than from the animal killing large numbers of people directly.

However, a T. rex would also face serious limits in New York City. It was not a movie monster with unlimited stamina or intelligence. It would be confused by noise, lights, vehicles, buildings, slick pavement, and dense obstacles. Manhattan streets are narrow relative to its body size, full of hard surfaces, and surrounded by barriers, tunnels, bridges, and water. It would have difficulty maneuvering in many areas, could injure itself on pavement or debris, and would likely avoid some loud or unfamiliar stimuli.

Police and emergency services would likely establish a perimeter, evacuate nearby streets and buildings, shut down traffic and transit in the area, and track it with helicopters, drones, and cameras. The goal would probably be containment first, then tranquilization or, if necessary, lethal force. Sedating an animal that large would be difficult: the dose would need to be accurate, and tranquilizers do not work instantly. A wounded or partially sedated T. rex could remain dangerous for several minutes. If it posed an immediate threat to many people, authorities might use heavy firearms or military support.

Could it survive? Not for long on its own. It would need enormous amounts of food, water, and space. New York has plenty of potential prey in the form of humans, dogs, horses, zoo animals, and refuse, but the city is not an appropriate habitat for a giant theropod. It would be isolated, highly visible, and quickly surrounded. Disease exposure, stress, injury, and lack of suitable territory would all work against it.

So the likely outcome is: several hours of extreme disruption, possible deaths and injuries, major property damage, a massive emergency response, and then capture or killing of the animal. It would be terrifying, but modern surveillance, vehicles, barriers, weapons, and coordinated emergency services would make it very unlikely that a single T. rex could roam New York City for more than a short time.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.

items.model_answer:
Assuming “all the world’s tea” means about one year of global dry tea production, roughly 6–7 million metric tons, the Great Lakes would not become a giant drinkable pot of tea.

The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or about 2.27 × 10¹⁶ liters. Spreading 7 million tons of dry tea through that volume gives only about 0.3 milligrams of tea leaves per liter of lake water. A normal cup of tea is brewed with something like 8 grams of leaves per liter, so the Great Lakes mixture would be around 25,000–30,000 times weaker than ordinary tea, even before accounting for the fact that cold lake water would extract tea compounds poorly.

If all that tea were brewed first and then poured in, it would still be tiny compared with the lakes. One year’s tea would make under 1 cubic kilometer of beverage, diluted into 22,700 cubic kilometers of lake water. If it were boiling hot, it would warm the Great Lakes by only a few thousandths of a degree Celsius. The lake level would rise by only a few millimeters.

Chemically, the caffeine would be measurable but not stimulating. If the tea were about 3% caffeine by dry mass and all of it dissolved, the lakes would end up around 5–10 micrograms of caffeine per liter. You would need thousands of liters of lake water to get the caffeine in a single cup of tea.

The main effects would be local pollution, not lake-wide tea. If dumped in one place, the tea leaves would form huge floating and sinking mats, clog shorelines and water intakes, stain the water brown nearby, and decompose. That decomposition could consume oxygen and cause localized fish stress, bad smells, bacterial growth, and nutrient pulses, especially in shallower areas like Lake Erie. Cleanup would be annoying and expensive.

But on the scale of the whole Great Lakes system, all the world’s annual tea production is surprisingly small. It would make a mess where you dumped it, but it would not turn the Great Lakes into tea, noticeably heat them, or make them caffeinated in any meaningful human sense.
