items.question: What If You Made a Lava Lamp with Real Lava?
human_answers: This is a surprisingly reasonable idea, by What If standards. I mean, it's not that reasonable. At the very least, I'm guessing you would lose your teaching license, and possibly some of the students in the front row. But you could do it. [Image: image] Just a warning: I'm going to be linking to a lot of videos (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2x7FGzjbqQ) of lava flowing and people poking it with sticks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SbcM7lh6DSQ), so you may have a hard time getting to the end of the article without getting sidetracked into watching a bunch of them (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6M-YX-r0Ll4) like I did while writing it. You have a few choices for transparent materials that could hold the lava without rupturing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a6pXf05Ph9Q) and splattering half the classroom with red-hot droplets. Fused quartz glass would be a great choice. It's the same stuff they use in high-intensity lamp bulbs, the surface of which can easily get up to mid-range lava (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kHO389dvj6Y) temperatures.[1]This bulb (http://www.amazon.ca/Philips-400w-GY9-5-Short-Light/dp/B0062ATTRW), for example, can supposedly handle bulb temperatures of up to 1000°C, which is hotter than many types of lava. Another possibility is sapphire, which stays solid up to 2,000°C, and is commonly used as a window (http://www.newport.com/Sapphire-Optical-Windows/378626/1033/info.aspx) into high-temperature chambers.[2]That link wasn't a lava video, but this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v_VyKplXtOM) is. [Image: image] The question of what to use for the clear medium (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=scGvM_VoPwk#t=31) is trickier. Let's say we find a transparent glass that melts[3]Some people say glass is a liquid that flows very slowly. Other people smugly point out that this is actually wrong. Then another group of people dissects how we know it's wrong, and where this incorrect idea got started. And then at the end of the chain, a Metafilter user steps back and asks some supremely insightful questions about what's really going on here (http://www.metafilter.com/141772/MetaFolkloreFilter#5676767) as we variously repeat and debunk these kinds of factoids. at low temperatures. Even if we ignore the impurities from the hot lava that would probably cloud the glass, we're going to have a problem.[4]And later, when the school board finds out, we'll have another. Molten glass is transparent (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1WmJOhbpyKY). So why doesn't it look transparent?[5]Which sounds sorta contradictory. "This music is loud, but it doesn't sound loud." The answer is simple: It glows. Hot objects give off blackbody radiation (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QhU8eMR4IQ); molten glass glows just like molten lava does, and for the same reason. So the problem (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bWswq8PmRII) with a lava lamp is that both halves of it will be equally bright (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xsJn8izcKtg), and it will be hard to see the lava. We could try having nothing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xiYzYaLM-hQ) in the top half of the lamp—after all, when it's hot enough, lava bubbles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EFVQhcuT2U0) pretty well on its own. Unfortunately, the lamp itself would also be in contact with the lava. Sapphire might not melt (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2dww24LeoEk) easily, but it will glow, making it hard to see whatever the lava was doing inside. [Image: image] Unless you hooked it up to a really bright bulb, this lava lamp would cool down quickly. Just like individual blobs of lava, the lamp would solidify and stop glowing within the first minute, and by the end of the class period (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zf4wKY8PJtg) you'd probably be able to touch it without being burned. A solidified lava lamp is just about the most boring thing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TszHiC6fjDg) in the world. But the scenario made me wonder: If making a lamp out of molten lava wouldn't be very exciting, then what about a volcano made of lamps (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7V2_aMG3YsI)? [Image: image] This is probably the most useless calculation I've ever done,[6]Ok, there's no way that's true. but ... what if Mount Saint Helens (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jxvisqt-U-8) erupted again today, but instead of tephra,[7]The technical term for "whatever crap comes out of a volcano." it spewed compact fluorescent bulbs? Well, if it did, the mercury (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cFvijBpzD_Y) released into the atmosphere would be several orders of magnitude larger than all manmade emissions combined.[8]45% of which (http://www.chem.unep.ch/mercury/Atmospheric_Emissions/UNEP%20SUMMARY%20REPORT%20-%20CORRECTED%20May09%20%20final%20for%20WEB%202008.pdf) come from gold mining. [Image: image] All in all, I think making a lava lamp out of lava would be kind of anticlimactic, and would much rather go find some actual lava and poke it with a stick. I also think that it's probably good that Mount Saint Helens didn't erupt compact fluorescent bulbs. And I think that if I were in Ms. Johnstone's class, I'd try to sit toward the back of the room. Lastly, for old time's sake, I'd like to share one final link with you: The music video for Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q8NXO6YxBmU#t=3)

criteria.name: Thermal and Materials Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically handles lava temperatures, containment materials, melting/softening limits, thermal shock, and heat transfer in a real-lava lamp scenario.
criteria.1-2: Ignores lava temperatures or assumes ordinary glass/plastic can safely contain lava.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heat danger but gives vague or incorrect material claims.
criteria.5-6: Identifies need for high-temperature transparent materials but misses key limits such as thermal stress or heat loss.
criteria.7-8: Accurately discusses plausible materials such as fused quartz or sapphire, lava temperature ranges, and containment risks.
criteria.9-10: Gives a physically coherent treatment of material survival, rupture risk, thermal gradients, cooling rate, and practical engineering constraints.

criteria.name: Lava-Lamp Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly adapts the ordinary lava lamp mechanism to real lava, including density, convection, phase behavior, visibility, and the role of a surrounding medium.
criteria.1-2: Treats real lava as if it would behave like wax in a normal lamp with no physical explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions bubbling or movement but misunderstands why lava lamps work.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes convection and molten material movement but gives incomplete treatment of medium, density, or phase changes.
criteria.7-8: Explains that a transparent compatible medium is difficult, lava may bubble or convect, and both components may glow or solidify.
criteria.9-10: Clearly compares real lava to wax-lamp dynamics and explains why density contrast, viscosity, heating, gas bubbles, cooling, and medium compatibility make the effect limited or unlike a normal lamp.

items.model_answer:
A lava lamp made with real lava would not behave like a normal lava lamp; it would be a small furnace and an extreme explosion/fire hazard.

A normal lava lamp works because two carefully chosen liquids have similar densities and do not mix. Heat makes the wax slightly less dense, so it rises; cooling makes it sink. Real lava is molten rock at roughly 700–1,200°C, far hotter, denser, more corrosive, and much more dangerous than lamp wax.

If you put real lava into a regular lava lamp, several things would happen almost immediately: the glass would crack or soften from thermal shock, the liquid inside would violently boil, and any oil or wax would ignite or decompose. If water were present, it could flash into steam so fast that the lamp could burst or explode. The expanding gases in a sealed container would make it even more dangerous.

Even if you built a special high-temperature transparent container, it still would not look like a classic lava lamp. The lava would be much denser than most liquids, so it would sink rather than form floating blobs. Most surrounding liquids would either boil, burn, or chemically break down. The lava would also begin to cool and solidify unless continuously heated by a powerful furnace.

So the practical answer is: a “real lava lamp” would be less like a decorative lamp and more like a hazardous molten-rock experiment. It would glow, radiate intense heat, probably destroy its container if not specially engineered, and could explode if any volatile liquid or trapped gas were involved.

items.question: What If Every Child's First Laugh Created an Immortal Fairy?
human_answers: "There are always a lot of young ones," explained Wendy, who was now quite an authority, "because you see when a new baby laughs for the first time a new fairy is born, and as there are always new babies there are always new fairies. They live in nests on the tops of trees; and the mauve ones are boys and the white ones are girls, and the blue ones are just little sillies who are not sure what they are." —Peter Pan Interestingly, fairies in the Peter Pan mythology definitely don't live forever. At the end of the book, Peter comes to visit Wendy a year after their adventures. Wendy asks about Tinker Bell, and Peter says he can't remember her and assumes she's died, and Wendy observes that fairies don't live very long.[1]When she expressed a doubtful hope that Tinker Bell would be glad to see her he said, "Who is Tinker Bell?" "O Peter," she said, shocked; but even when she explained he could not remember. "There are such a lot of them," he said. "I expect she is no more." I expect he was right, for fairies don't live long, but they are so little that a short time seems a good while to them. This suggests that at any given time, there are probably be far fewer fairies than humans in the Peter Pan universe, since they have the same birth rate and shorter lifespans. [Image: image] But Mira's scenario assumes immortal fairies, so let's talk about immortal fairy demographics. A fairy is created by every[2]Approximately, anyway, but we'll round up by assuming that all babies laugh. newborn baby. The total number of humans who have ever lived is somewhere around 100-120 billion,[3]There are various groups who have estimated this, and they all tend to come up with a number around in this range. If you take a set of estimates for ancient human population (Wikipedia has a table of them (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population_estimates)) and assume a birth rate near the biological maximum before the 20th century (35 to 45 births per 1,000, according to this paper (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/231918377_The_Use_of_Historical_Demography_in_Ancient_History)), you can derive a similar number yourself. meaning 100-120 billion fairies have been created. How much do all those fairies weigh? Tinker Bell, the main fairy from the Peter Pan universe, seems to be a little under six inches tall. In a scene in Hook, Tinker Bell (played by the 5 foot 9 inch Julia Roberts) fits comfortably in a 1/12 scale dollhouse, suggesting a height of 5.75 inches. As another data point, the statue of Tinker Bell (http://www.madametussauds.com/london/newsandevents/tinkerbell/) at Madam Tussaud's wax museum is 5.5 inches. This suggests that fairies in Peter Pan are pretty close to 1/12th scale. If fairies are 1/12th the size of humans, then they weigh \( \left( \tfrac{1}{12\text{th}}\right) ^3=\tfrac{1}{1728\text{th}} \) as much as us, which means Julia Roberts's Tinker Bell is probably around 35 grams.[4](two mice) As of 2015, total fairy biomass would be about 4 million tons. That's less than humans or horses (http://xkcd.com/1338/), and probably comparable to the total mass of all humpback whales (http://iwc.int/estimate).[5]Fairies also probably outweigh wild birds. At these numbers, fairies would be a minor piece of the ecosystem, although possibly a pretty annoying one. [Image: image] But it wasn't always the case. In the early days of our species, our high birth rates (and death rates) plus our low population mean that we would have accumulated fairies quickly. The exact numbers depend on when the modern human (fairy-generating) species developed, but by the time the last ice age was over, the accumulated fairies could have outweighed our tiny living human population 10 to 1. [Image: image] Once our population started growing following the agricultural revolution (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution), we would have quickly outstripped fairies in terms of weight. In 2015, fairy biomass would be down to about 1.2% of human biomass, and by the mid-21st-century, they'd bottom out at less than 1%. But as long as humans keep reproducing, the fairy population would keep growing. If we assume the human population will level off (http://www.un.org/esa/population/publications/longrange2/WorldPop2300final.pdf) at around 9 billion partway through this century, then the share of mass occupied by fairies would continue rising steadily. If our population stays at a stable 9 billion indefinitely, by 2100, they'll be back above 1% of human biomass, and they'll reach 2% by the year 3000. In the year 100,000, if our species is somehow still around, they'll outweigh us. This makes things interesting. Let's assume fairies need to eat. If fairies weigh about as much as us, they'd presumably be consuming a similar share of food and water. So even if the Earth can support 400 million tons of human, it may not be able to support 400 million tons of human and another 400 million tons of fairy. This suggests that, sometime in the next hundred millennia, the growing fairy population would start to crowd out the human population. But if fairies crowd out humans, that would in turn reduce the growth rate of the fairies, slowing down the replacement process. The end result (in this idealized model) would be that the fairy population growth would taper off as the human population declined. The situation would never quite reach a stable equilibrium, because every 1,728 human births would create one human's weight in fairies, reducing the Earth's total human carrying capacity by 1. But since the rate of fairy creation would slow down as the human population shrank, the process would stretch out for a very long time. This odd situation would only exist because fairies—in Mira's scenario—are immortal. The scenario would change dramatically if we introduced a fairy death rate. Perhaps fairies don't age or experience natural deaths, but can still die from other causes. What would kill the fairies? Who knows.[6]J. M. Barrie introduces a fairy-killing mechanism in Peter Pan; any time anyone says "I don't believe in fairies", a random fairy dies. In a world of immortal fairies, this could serve as an effective feedback. If no one has heard of fairies, no one will say they don't believe in them, and their population will grow. As fairies start to be common enough to be noticed, people will have a reason to say they don't believe in them, and their population will drop. Eventually, civilization would start documenting (http://xkcd.com/1235/) the existence of fairies, and then no one would have any reason to disbelieve their existence, and the feedback loop would break down. But ecosystems aren't static. If you mess with one part, the other parts change in response. Fairies could become the dominant species, but the system they learned to dominate wouldn't be there forever. If fairies represent most of the biomass in the ecosystem, eventually, given enough time ... [Image: image] ... something will learn to eat them.

criteria.3-4: Mentions fairy creation from first laughs but gives little or no cumulative demographic reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that fairy population tracks total historical births and accumulates because fairies are immortal, with rough qualitative estimates.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible human birth/history figures to estimate tens or hundreds of billions of immortal fairies and compares them to living humans.
criteria.9-10: Clearly models cumulative fairy creation from all past first laughs, handles assumptions such as not every infant surviving/laughing, and gives well-calibrated population ranges.

criteria.name: Physical scaling, biomass, and resource implications
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses STEM-style physical reasoning to estimate fairy size, mass, biomass, metabolism, and resource demand under the immortal-fairy premise.

criteria.3-4: Mentions that many fairies would need space or food but without scale, mass, or conservation reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Makes a plausible size/mass assumption and derives broad implications for biomass or resource consumption.
criteria.7-8: Applies scaling logic, such as cube-law mass scaling from small human-like bodies, and compares total fairy biomass to humans or animals.
criteria.9-10: Quantifies size, mass, total biomass, metabolism, food/water needs, and carrying-capacity effects while noting sensitivity to fairy physiology assumptions.

criteria.name: Long-range causal dynamics and feedback loops
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the counterfactual over long timescales, including accumulation, growth-rate changes, carrying capacity, and possible feedback mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Only describes immediate effects after babies laugh, with no long-range consequences.
criteria.3-4: States that fairies would accumulate over time but does not analyze how this changes future human or fairy populations.
criteria.5-6: Explains that immortal fairies would eventually become a growing burden or ecological presence as births continue.
criteria.7-8: Tracks dynamics across prehistory, modernity, and future scenarios, including how fairy accumulation could reduce human carrying capacity and slow future fairy creation.
criteria.9-10: Presents coherent long-run feedbacks, such as resource competition reducing human births, possible fairy mortality mechanisms, ecological adaptation, and non-equilibrium outcomes over millennia.

criteria.name: Coverage of downstream ecological and societal mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores major consequences beyond raw population counts, including ecosystems, human institutions, culture, conflict, and adaptation.
criteria.1-2: Lists superficial consequences or fantasy tropes with little causal connection to the premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few impacts, such as annoyance or overcrowding, but leaves most mechanisms undeveloped.
criteria.5-6: Covers several plausible effects on ecosystems, food systems, housing, law, religion, or family life.
criteria.7-8: Connects fairy demographics to ecological niches, predation, agriculture, public policy, social norms, and human-fairy conflict or cooperation.
criteria.9-10: Broadly and causally explores biological, environmental, economic, legal, cultural, and evolutionary consequences, including how societies and ecosystems adapt over very long periods.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes assumptions from conclusions, avoids internal contradictions, and remains consistent with the stated counterfactual rather than importing incompatible fairy lore.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, unsupported certainty, or incompatible claims such as fairies both immortal and naturally short-lived.
criteria.3-4: Has some consistent reasoning but mixes assumptions, lore, and conclusions unclearly.
criteria.5-6: States key assumptions about fairy mortality, biology, visibility, or magic and avoids the most obvious contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Separates premise-implied results from speculative branches, gives uncertainty ranges, and flags where outcomes depend on fairy physiology or magic rules.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous consistency throughout, explicitly manages uncertain parameters, compares alternate assumptions, and prevents speculative mechanisms from undermining the core immortal-fairy premise.

items.model_answer:
If every child’s first laugh created an immortal fairy, the biggest consequence would be that humanity would generate a permanently accumulating second population.

A child’s first real laugh usually happens around 3–4 months of age. With roughly 130–140 million births per year today, the world would create about 130–140 million new fairies every year. If this had been true for all of human history, there would likely be on the order of 100 billion fairies already, roughly comparable to the total number of humans who have ever lived.

The physical impact depends on what “fairy” means. If fairies are nonmaterial magical beings that do not eat, breathe, occupy space, or consume energy, then the main effects would be cultural, religious, legal, and psychological. Every baby’s first laugh would become an event of enormous importance. Families might celebrate it like a birth, governments might register fairies, and societies would form entire institutions around fairy rights, fairy duties, and fairy-human relationships.

If fairies are physical beings, the consequences become much more serious. Immortality means their population never decreases, so even a small annual addition eventually becomes enormous. If each fairy had mass, needed food, used energy, or occupied living space, Earth would face a steadily worsening resource burden. A population of 100 billion tiny beings might be manageable if they were insect-sized and low-energy, but disastrous if they were human-sized or metabolically active. Even at modest energy use, billions of immortal beings could consume a significant fraction of global resources.

Scientifically, the creation event would violate ordinary conservation laws unless the fairy’s matter and energy came from somewhere. If each laugh literally produced mass from nothing, physics would need a new mechanism allowing sound, emotion, or neurological development to trigger matter creation. If the fairy’s body were assembled from surrounding air, dust, or some hidden energy field, then researchers would intensely study first laughter as a reproducible matter-generation event.

Socially, birth rates would take on a new meaning. Having children would not only create humans but also immortal fairies, so population ethics would change. Pronatalist societies might value fairy creation; others might worry about immortal overpopulation. There could be debates over whether delaying or suppressing a baby’s first laugh was ethical. Children who never laughed because of illness, neglect, or developmental differences might be treated with tragic or mystical significance, which could create harmful stigma unless societies were careful.

Over long timescales, immortality is the central problem. Human populations rise and fall, but fairy populations would only rise. After thousands or millions of years, unless fairies could leave Earth, enter dormancy, shrink their footprint, or exist outside normal ecology, their accumulation would dominate the biosphere. The world would eventually become less a human planet than a fairy-human civilization shaped by every baby’s first joy.

So the direct answer is: every child’s first laugh creating an immortal fairy would turn laughter into a biological-cosmic reproduction mechanism. In the short term it would make infancy sacred and socially transformative; in the long term it would create an ever-growing immortal population whose impact would range from harmlessly mystical to ecologically catastrophic depending on whether fairies need matter, space, and energy.

items.question: What If There Were a Lake on the Moon?
human_answers: This would be so cool. In fact, I honestly think it's cool enough that it gives us a pretty good reason to go to the Moon in the first place. At the very least, it's better than the one Kennedy gave. [Image: image] Floating would feel about the same on the Moon as on Earth, since how high in the water you float depends only on your body's density compared to the water's, not the strength of gravity. Swimming underwater would also feel pretty similar. The inertia of the water is the main source of drag when swimming, and inertia is a property of matter[1]♬ BILL NYE THE SCIENCE GUY ♬ independent of gravity. The top speed of a submerged swimmer would be about the same on the Moon as here—about 2 meters/second. Everything else would be different and way cooler. The waves would be bigger, the splash fights more intense, and swimmers would be able to jump out of the water like dolphins. This[2]Not this one. The other one.​[3]The simplest approach, which gives us an approximate answer, is to treat the swimmer as a simple projectile. The formula for the height of a projectile is: \( \frac{\text{speed}^2}{2\times\text{gravity}} \) ... which tells us that a champion swimmer moving at 2 meters per second (4.5 mph) would only have enough kinetic energy to lift their body about 20 centimeters (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%282+m%2Fs%29%5E2+%2F+%282+*+earth+gravity%29) against gravity. That's not totally accurate, although it's enough to tell us that dolphin jumps on Earth probably aren't in the cards for us. But to get a more accurate answer (and an equation we can apply to the Moon), we need to account for a few other things. When a swimmer first breaks the surface, they don't have to lift their full weight; they're partially supported by buoyancy. As more of their body leaves the water, the force of buoyancy decreases, since their body is displacing less water. Since the force of gravity isn't changing, their net weight increases. You can calculate how much potential energy is required to lift a body vertically through the surface to a certain height, but it's a complicated integral (you integrate the displacement of the submerged portion of their body over the vertical distance they travel) and depends on their body shape. For a human body moving fast enough to jump most of the way out of the water, this effect probably adds about half a torso-length to their final height—and less if they're not able to make it all the way out. The other effect we have to account for is the fact that a swimmer can continue kicking as they start to leave the water. When a swimmer is submerged and moving at top speed, the drag from the water is equal to the thrust they generate by kicking and ... whatever the gerund form of the verb is for the things your arms do while swimming. My first thought was "stroking," but it's definitely not that. Anyway, once the jumping swimmer breaks the surface, the drag almost vanishes, but they can keep kicking for a few moments. To figure out how much energy this adds, you can multiply the thrust from kicking by the distance over which they're kicking after breaking the surface, since energy equals force times distance. The distance is most of a body length, or 1 to 1.5 meters. As for the force from kicking, random Google results for a search for lifeguard qualifications suggest that good swimmers might be able to carry 10 lbs over their heads for a short distance, which means they're generating a little more than 10 pounds-force (50+ N) of kicking thrust. We can combine all these together into a big ol' equation: \[ \text{Jump height}=\left(\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\times\text{body mass}\times\left(\text{top speed}\right)^2+\text{kick force}\times\text{torso length}}{\text{Earth gravity}\times\text{body mass}}\right)+\left(\text{buoyancy correction} \right) \] footnote contains some detail on the math behind a dolphin jump. Calculating the height a swimmer can jump out of the water requires taking several different things into account, but the bottom line is that a normal swimmer on the Moon could probably launch themselves a full meter out of the water, and Michael Phelps may well be able to manage 2 or 3. [Image: image] The numbers get even more exciting when we introduce fins. Swimmers wearing fins (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finswimming) can go substantially faster than regular swimmers (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Schwimmer) without them (although the fastest swimmer wearing flippers will still lose to a runner, even if the runner is also wearing flippers and jumping over hurdles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRDnajV1A3w)). Champion finswimmers can go almost 3.2 m/s wearing a monofin, which is fast enough for some pretty impressive jumps—even on Earth (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z09RmuaPyVU). Data on swimfin top speeds (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_finswimming) and thrusts[4]This paper (http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/xmlui/bitstream/handle/123456789/3936/12841609.pdf) provides some sample data. suggest that on the Moon, a champion finswimmer (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanna-Maria_Sepp%C3%A4l%C3%A4) could probably launch themselves as high as 4 or 5 meters into the air. In other words, on the Moon, you could conceivably do a high dive in reverse. [Image: image] But it gets even better. A 2012 paper (http://www.plosone.org/article/fetchObject.action?uri=info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0037300&representation=PDF) in PLoS ONE, titled Humans Running in Place on Water at Simulated Reduced Gravity, concluded that while humans can't run on the surface of water on Earth,[5]They actually provide a citation for this statement, which is delightful. they might just barely be able to do so on the Moon. (I highly recommend reading their paper, if only for the hilarious experimental setup illustration on page 2.) Because of the reduced gravity on the Moon, the water would be launched upward more easily, just like the swimmers. The result would be larger waves and more flying droplets. In technical terms, a pool on the Moon would be more "splashy".[6]The SI unit of splashiness is the splashypant. To avoid splashing all the water out, you'd want to design the deck so water drains quickly back into the pool. You could just make the rim higher, but then you'd spoil one of the key joys of a pool on the Moon—exiting via Slip 'N Slide: [Image: image] I 100% support this idea. If we ever build a Moon base, I think we should absolutely build a big swimming pool there. Sure, sending a swimming pool's worth of water (135 horses (http://xkcd.com/1461/)) to the Moon's surface would be expensive.[7]If you decided to bundle a backyard pool into individual two-liter bottles, and sent them in 3,000 batches of 10 each via the startup Astrobotic (https://www.astrobotic.com/), it would cost you $72 billion (according to their website's calculator (https://www.astrobotic.com/configure-mission)). But on the other hand, this lunar base is going to have people on it, so you need to send some water anyway.[8]Sending a supply of water and a filter system is probably cheaper than sending a replacement astronaut every 3 or 4 days, although I encourage NASA to run the numbers on that to be sure. And it's really not impossible. A large backyard swimming pool weighs about as much as four Apollo lunar landers. A next-generation[9](or, heck, previous-generation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V)) heavy-lift rocket, like Boeing's NASA SLS or Elon Musk's SpaceX Falcon Heavy, would be able to deliver a good-sized pool to the Moon in not too many trips. So maybe the next step, if you really want a swimming pool on the Moon, is to call Elon Musk and ask for a quote. [Image: image]

criteria.9-10: Delivers an internally consistent long-range analysis with explicit assumptions, no major physical contradictions, and well-calibrated uncertainty across competing scenarios.

items.model_answer:
An exposed liquid lake on the Moon would not remain a lake for long.

Because the Moon has essentially no atmosphere, the pressure at the surface is near vacuum. Liquid water is not stable under those conditions. If you somehow placed a lake of liquid water on the lunar surface, the top layer would begin to boil rapidly, even if the water were cold, because there is almost no air pressure holding it in liquid form. That boiling would carry away heat, so the remaining water would quickly cool and start to freeze. The result would be a violent mix of boiling, vapor, frost, and ice.

After the initial chaos, the lake would mostly become ice. Any exposed ice would slowly sublimate: it would turn directly from solid into vapor, especially in sunlight. Some of that water vapor would escape into space, while some molecules might hop across the lunar surface and eventually collect in very cold, permanently shadowed craters near the poles. In direct sunlight, the ice would disappear much faster; in a permanently shadowed crater, it could survive for a very long time as ice, but not as an open liquid lake.

If the lake were inside a sealed dome with Earth-like air pressure and temperature, then it could exist as a normal liquid lake. It would still feel “lunar” in some ways: gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, so waves would move more slowly, splashes would rise higher, and objects would feel lighter. Boats would float similarly in terms of how much of them sits above water, because both weight and buoyancy scale with gravity, but motions on and in the water would be slower and more exaggerated.

So the direct answer is: an open lake on the Moon would boil, freeze, and gradually vanish into space or migrate as ice to cold traps. A lasting liquid lake would require an artificial atmosphere or enclosure.

edus.text: An exposed liquid lake on the Moon would not remain a lake for long.
Because the Moon has essentially no atmosphere,
the pressure at the surface is near vacuum.
Liquid water is not stable under those conditions.
If you somehow placed a lake of liquid water on the lunar surface,
the top layer would begin to boil rapidly,
even if the water were cold,
because there is almost no air pressure holding it in liquid form.
That boiling would carry away heat,
so the remaining water would quickly cool and start to freeze.
The result would be a violent mix of boiling, vapor, frost, and ice.
After the initial chaos,
the lake would mostly become ice.
Any exposed ice would slowly sublimate:
it would turn directly from solid into vapor,
especially in sunlight.
Some of that water vapor would escape into space,
while some molecules might hop across the lunar surface and eventually collect in very cold, permanently shadowed craters near the poles.
In direct sunlight, the ice would disappear much faster;
in a permanently shadowed crater, it could survive for a very long time as ice,
but not as an open liquid lake.
If the lake were inside a sealed dome with Earth-like air pressure and temperature,
then it could exist as a normal liquid lake.
It would still feel “lunar” in some ways:
gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s,
so waves would move more slowly,
splashes would rise higher,
and objects would feel lighter.
Boats would float similarly in terms of how much of them sits above water,
because both weight and buoyancy scale with gravity,
but motions on and in the water would be slower and more exaggerated.
So the direct answer is: an open lake on the Moon would boil, freeze, and gradually vanish into space or migrate as ice to cold traps.
A lasting liquid lake would require an artificial atmosphere or enclosure.

items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true. Bowling balls all have about the same volume, so they all displace the same weight in seawater—12.13 lbs, or about 5.5 kg. But their weights vary substantially, from as little as 6 lbs to a max of 16. Only the balls that weigh more than 12.13 lbs will sink. [Image: image] "Hang on a moment," the serious bowlers reading this are saying, "most bowling balls are at the heavy end of that range. The usual range is more like 14-16 lbs for men and 10-14 lbs for women. Maybe the average women's ball floats, but the overall average ball surely sinks." This is definitely true for serious bowlers, but for casual bowlers, it might be better to define the "average" ball using the distribution on the rack of balls at the local bowling alley. These house balls often list the weight on them, so rather than go to a bowling alley, I just sifted through all the Flickr photos of bowling balls and tallied up all the visible weights. The average was 10½ lbs. [Image: image] So at the very least, for most people, the average bowling ball they've picked up in their lives probably floats. If nothing else, this makes the popular simile "sank like a bowling ball"—which appears in a number of books (https://www.google.com/search?q=%22sank+like+a+bowling+ball%22&btnG=Search+Books&tbm=bks&tbo=1)—seem a little poorly chosen.[1]In defense of the authors of Volume 53 of North Dakota Quarterly, the simile they used is, "sank like a bowling ball in whipped cream," which is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, How To Hook a Man (And a Baby) and The Year's Work in Lebowski Studies are on their own. But Doug's bowling ball is 7 kg (15.5 lbs), making it plenty heavy enough to sink in the ocean. How fast will it fall? Small falling spheres in viscous (goopy) liquids (like hair gel (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1108.3427.pdf)) exhibit weird behaviors and sometimes complex oscillation, but bowling balls falling through water are pretty straightforward. Their falling speed is determined by the drag equation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_equation) and their weight (accounting for buoyancy). For Doug's bowling ball, that terminal velocity will be roughly 1.3 meters per second, which means it will take two hours and 20 minutes to reach the bottom. That's plenty of time to enjoy a two-hour movie (http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0118715/). A 13-pound bowling ball, which is much closer to neutrally buoyant in seawater, would take four and a half hours to reach the bottom. On the other hand, a bowling ball made of solid iron would reach the bottom in half an hour. A bowling ball made of lead would reach the bottom in 23 minutes, and a bowling ball made of solid gold would make it in 17. However, a bowling ball made of solid gold would also weigh more than the average bowler.[2]At least, I think it would, but I can't think of a way to sample the weight of the average bowler without getting punched. A bowling ball made of solid osmium, the heaviest naturally-occurring element, would weigh 120 kilograms, and could sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in just 16 minutes. But what if you got the weight wrong? What if the bowling ball you were using turned out to be 7 pounds, not 7 kilograms? Or maybe it's 10.5 pounds—the "average" bowling ball, at least according to a dubious Flickr sample. In that case, the ball would never reach the bottom. Instead, it would drift sideways with the currents. We can track what course it would take using the Adrift.org.au ocean plastic tracking tool (http://www.adrift.org.au/map?lat=11.3&lng=142.6&center=-180&startmon=Jan). The bowling ball would first drift west, past Luzon in the Philippines, then probably north along the coast of China, turning right at Japan and heading out over the Pacific. Sometime in the summer of 2018, it would approach the coast of California. Most likely, it would follow the coast for a little while, then become swept up in the great Pacific garbage patch (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch). However, it's possible that it would be swept up on shore instead. If, during those three years, Doug took his boat from the Mariana islands to Los Angeles, found a nice, sheltered cove, and set up ten carefully weighted bowling pins just below the surface, then there is a tiny, tiny chance ... [Image: image] ... that he could succeed in bowling the single most improbable strike of all time.

items.model_answer:
A 7‑kilogram bowling ball would sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, but not dramatically fast.

A regulation bowling ball is about 22 cm in diameter. At 7 kg, its average density is greater than seawater, so buoyancy would not hold it up. After hitting the water, drag would quickly slow it to a terminal sinking speed of roughly 1–2 m/s, depending on the exact ball, finger holes, surface roughness, and water density. Since the Challenger Deep is about 11 km deep, the trip to the bottom would take on the order of 2–3 hours.

The pressure at the bottom is enormous: about 110 megapascals, or roughly 1,100 atmospheres. But pressure acts from all directions, so the ball would not be “squashed flat” like in a cartoon. A typical solid bowling ball would compress slightly, perhaps by millimeters to a few percent in volume depending on its material. If it had trapped air pockets or sealed cavities, those could collapse or crack the ball. Open finger holes would simply fill with water.

When it reached the seafloor, it would not hit like a meteor. At terminal speed its kinetic energy would be only a few to perhaps tens of joules, so it would make a small puff in the sediment and settle there.

So the short answer is: it would sink slowly for a few hours, compress slightly under the immense pressure, maybe crack if it contained trapped air, and then come to rest on the trench floor.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If there were both a space elevator and a stairway to space, the space elevator would be the useful transportation system, while the stairway would mostly be a symbolic, emergency, or novelty structure unless it were magically strong.

A space elevator works by extending a cable from Earth’s equator up past geostationary orbit, about 35,786 km above the surface, with a counterweight beyond that. Earth’s rotation keeps the cable under tension. Climbers can crawl up the cable using electrical power, reaching orbit without rockets. It would make access to space vastly cheaper, enable large orbital construction projects, solar-power satellites, easier Moon and Mars missions, and perhaps permanent space industry.

A literal stairway to space is a different matter. If it only reached the Kármán line, about 100 km up, walking up it would get you “to space” in the atmospheric sense, but not into orbit. You would still lack orbital speed, so if you stepped off you would fall back to Earth. You would also need a pressure suit, oxygen, radiation protection, and probably days of climbing. It would be more like climbing an impossibly tall mountain than launching into space.

If the stairway reached geostationary orbit, then it would effectively have to be part of the same kind of structure as the space elevator. At geostationary altitude, a person standing on the stairway would already be moving around Earth at the correct orbital speed because the whole structure rotates with Earth. Stepping off there could place you into geostationary orbit. Below that altitude, stepping off would generally lead to falling back; above it, you would have excess orbital energy.

The main difference is mechanical. A space elevator cable is under tension, which is at least conceptually plausible with extremely strong materials. A free-standing stairway would be under compression and bending loads, battered by winds in the lower atmosphere and stressed by Earth’s rotation. No known material could support such a structure from the ground to space. So in realistic engineering terms, the “stairway” would probably need to be suspended from or built around the space elevator cable, like a ladder or maintenance access path, rather than standing on its own.

In everyday use, nobody would take the stairs except perhaps for ceremonial events, maintenance over short sections, or emergencies. The distances are absurd: climbing even 100 km vertically would be extreme; climbing to geostationary orbit would mean tens of millions of steps and would take months or years on foot. The elevator would carry cargo and people efficiently, while the stairway would be a strange accessory.

The combined result would be transformative but dangerous. Earth would have a fixed gateway to orbit, likely located near the equator and heavily protected. Space travel would become cheaper, orbital cities and factories could grow, and launch rockets would become less central. At the same time, the structure would be a geopolitical prize, a collision hazard, a target, and a vulnerability: if a space elevator failed, parts of the cable could fall across huge regions.

So the direct answer is: the space elevator would make civilization spacefaring; the stairway would not replace it. Unless supported by the elevator or by impossible materials, the stairway could not exist physically. If it did exist, it would let people “walk to space,” but only the elevator-scale structure would let them practically reach orbit.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.

items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, the basic physics would be almost the same: the contest would still be decided mostly by which team can generate more horizontal force against the ground without slipping.

The rod would be in tension, just like the rope. Each team pulls on its end, and the rod pulls back on them. If the teams are evenly matched, the rod stays nearly still. If one team can push harder against the ground and maintain traction, it drags the other team toward it.

The main difference is that an iron rod is much stiffer than a rope. A rope stretches noticeably, storing elastic energy and softening jerks. An iron rod would stretch only a tiny amount. For example, a several-meter iron rod under a few thousand newtons of pull might elongate by less than a millimeter. So the teams would feel each other’s tugs much more abruptly, with very little “give.”

That stiffness would make the contest harsher and more dangerous. Sudden pulls would transmit sharp jerks to hands, arms, shoulders, and backs. If someone slipped or let go, the rod could lurch or swing like a heavy metal bar. It would also be harder to grip, especially if it were smooth, and multiple people could not easily hold it the way they can hold a rope.

If the rod were strong enough, it would not break; it would simply carry the tension. If the force exceeded the rod’s yield strength, it could permanently stretch or bend. If pushed beyond its ultimate strength, it could snap, though ordinary iron or steel rods can withstand very large tensile loads if thick enough.

So, in short: an iron rod would still transmit the tug-of-war force, and the stronger or better-traction team would still win. But compared with a rope, it would barely stretch, be harder to hold, transmit violent jerks, and be much less safe.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If the Moon were replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass, in the same orbit, Earth would not be sucked in and there would be no immediate gravitational catastrophe.

A black hole with the Moon’s mass would have the same gravitational pull as the Moon at Earth’s distance. So the major dynamical effects would remain almost unchanged: ocean tides would be about the same, Earth’s axial stabilization by the lunar companion would remain about the same, and the Earth–black-hole system would orbit its barycenter much as the Earth–Moon system does now.

The black hole itself would be tiny. The Moon’s mass is about \(7.35\times 10^{22}\) kg, giving a Schwarzschild radius of roughly 0.1 millimeters. Its event horizon would be smaller than a grain of sand. It would not look like a giant dark sphere in the sky; it would be essentially invisible except through its gravity.

The most obvious everyday change would be optical: there would be no moonlight, no visible lunar phases, and no normal solar or lunar eclipses. Nights would be much darker. A Moon-mass black hole could gravitationally lens background stars very slightly, but the effect would be tiny and not obvious to the naked eye.

Tides would remain because tides depend mainly on the companion’s mass and distance, not whether it is made of rock or is a black hole. The black hole would also continue to raise tides in Earth’s oceans and crust. Long-term tidal evolution, such as the gradual slowing of Earth’s rotation and outward drift of the companion’s orbit, would be broadly similar, though details involving the Moon’s physical deformation would disappear.

It also would not rapidly consume Earth. At the Moon’s current distance, its gravity is no stronger than the Moon’s. Only objects passing extremely close to the black hole would be in danger. Near the event horizon the tidal forces would be enormous, but from Earth’s distance they are perfectly ordinary lunar gravity.

Accretion would be negligible. The black hole might capture tiny amounts of solar wind, dust, or meteoroids, but not enough to produce a dangerous accretion disk or intense radiation. Its Hawking radiation would also be insignificant; a Moon-mass black hole would be extremely cold and long-lived.

So the short answer is: replacing the Moon with a black hole of the same mass would make the Moon vanish from sight, eliminate moonlight and normal eclipses, and make lunar exploration impossible, but Earth’s tides, orbit, and overall gravitational environment would remain largely the same.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
A high-power microwave mounted on a car would be a poor and dangerous way to melt road ice. In principle, microwaves can heat materials by making polar molecules and ions dissipate energy, and liquid water absorbs microwaves fairly well. But road ice is a bad target: solid ice absorbs common microwave frequencies much less efficiently than liquid water, so a lot of the microwave energy would pass through, reflect, or heat wet/slushy patches unevenly rather than cleanly melting the ice.

The energy requirement is the biggest problem. Melting ice takes about 334 kJ per kilogram just for the phase change, not counting warming it up from below freezing. A 1 mm layer of ice over 1 square meter has a mass of about 1 kg, so it needs at least 334 kJ to melt. If a car moving 10 m/s tried to clear a 2 m wide strip with only 1 mm of ice, it would encounter about 20 kg of ice per second, requiring roughly 6–7 megawatts of heat delivered perfectly into the ice. Real microwave delivery would be far less efficient, so the required transmitter power could be many megawatts. For thicker ice, the power requirement becomes tens of megawatts.

A normal microwave-oven magnetron is around 1 kW. Even a “high-power” unit of several kilowatts would barely affect the road at driving speed. It might warm a small wet patch if the car sat still, but it would not clear a lane in real time.

It would also be hazardous. A microwave beam strong enough to melt ice quickly could injure people and animals, cause burns or eye damage, interfere with vehicle electronics, communications, pacemakers or sensors, and reflect unpredictably off metal objects, road infrastructure, guardrails, vehicles, and wet surfaces. It could also heat water trapped in asphalt or concrete and potentially damage the surface. Operating such a device on public roads would almost certainly violate radio-frequency emission and safety regulations.

So the practical answer is: it would not work well as an ice-clearing system, and making it powerful enough to work would make it unsafe, inefficient, and likely illegal. Plows, salt/brine, heated fluids, abrasive grit, and conventional thermal deicing are far more practical.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]
