items.question: What If There Were a Fireman's Pole from the Moon to Earth?
human_answers: First, let's get a few things out of the way: In real life, we can't put a metal pole between the Earth and the Moon.[1]For one, someone at NASA would probably yell at us. The end of the pole near the Moon would be pulled toward the Moon by the Moon's gravity, and the rest of it would be pulled back down to the Earth by the Earth's gravity. The pole would be torn in half. [Image: image] Another problem with this plan. The Earth's surface spins faster than the Moon goes around, so the end that dangled down to the Earth would break off if you tried to connect it to the ground: [Image: image] There's one more problem:[2]Ok, that's a lie—there are, like, hundreds more problems. The Moon doesn't always stay the same distance from Earth. Its orbit takes it closer and farther away. It's not a big difference,[3]You may occasionally see people get excited about the "supermoon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermoon)," a full Moon that appears slightly larger because it happens at the time of the month when the Moon is closest to Earth. But really, the full Moon always looks surprisingly large and pretty when it's near the horizon, thanks to the Moon illusion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_illusion). In my opinion, it's worth going outside and looking at the Moon (https://twitter.com/moonreminder) whenever it's full, regardless of whether it's super or not. but it's enough that the bottom 50,000 km of your fire station pole would be squished against the Earth once a month. But let's ignore those problems! What if we had a magical pole that dangled from the Moon down to just above the Earth's surface, expanding and contracting so it never quite touched the ground? How long would it take to slide down from the Moon? If you stood next to the end of the pole on the Moon, a problem would become clear right away: You have to slide up the pole, and that's not how sliding works. [Image: image] Instead of sliding, you'll have to climb. People can climb poles pretty fast. World-record pole climbers[4]Of course there's a world record for pole climbing. can climb at over a meter per second in championship competition (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=pole+speed+climbing).[5]Of course there are championship competitions. On the Moon, gravity is much weaker, so it will probably be easier to climb. On the other hand, you'll have to wear a spacesuit, so that will probably slow you down a little. If you climb up the pole far enough, Earth's gravity will take over and start pulling you down. When you're hanging onto the pole, there are three forces pulling on you: The Earth's gravity pulling you toward Earth, the Moon's gravity pulling you away from Earth, and centrifugal force[6]As usual, anyone arguing about "centrifugal" versus "centripetal" force will be put in a centrifuge (https://xkcd.com/123/). from the swinging pole pulling you away from Earth.[7]At the distance of the Moon's orbit and the speed it's traveling, centrifugal force pushing away is exactly balanced by the Earth's gravity—which is why the Moon orbits there. At first, the combination of the Moon's gravity and centrifugal force are stronger, pulling you toward the Moon, but as you get closer to the Earth, Earth's gravity takes over. The Earth is pretty big, so you reach this point—which is known as the L1 Lagrange point—while you're still pretty close to the Moon. [Image: image] Unfortunately for you, space is big, so "pretty close" is still a long way. Even if you climb at better-than-world-record speed, it will still take you several years to get to the L1 crossover point. As you approach the L1 point, you'll start to be able to switch from climbing to pushing-and-gliding: You can push once and then coast a long distance up the pole. You don't have to wait to stop, either—you can grab the pole again and give yourself a push to move even faster, like a skateboarder kicking several times to speed up. [Image: image] Eventually, as you reach the vicinity of the L1 point and are no longer fighting gravity, the only limit on your speed will be how quickly you can grab the pole and "throw" it past you. The best baseball pitchers can move their hands at about 100 mph while flinging objects past them, so you probably can't expect to move much faster than that. Note: While you're flinging yourself along, be careful not to drift out of reach of the pole. Hopefully you brought some kind of safety line so you can recover if that happens. [Image: image] After another few weeks of gliding along the pole, you'll start to feel gravity take over, speeding you up faster than you can go by pushing yourself. When this happens, be careful—soon, you'll need to start worrying about going too fast. As you approach the Earth and the pull of its gravity increases, you'll start to speed up quite a bit. If you don't stop yourself, you'll reach the top of the atmosphere at roughly escape velocity—11 km/s[8]This is why anything that falls into the Earth hits the atmosphere fast enough to burn up. Even if an object is moving slowly when it's drifting through space, when it gets close to the Earth it gets accelerated up to at least escape velocity by that final segment of the trip down into the Earth's gravity well.—and the impact with the air will produce so much heat that you risk burning up. Spacecraft deal with this problem by including heat shields, which are capable of absorbing and dissipating this heat without burning up the spacecraft behind it.[9]People often ask why we don't use rockets to slow down, to avoid the need for a heat shield. You can read this article for an explanation, but the bottom line is that changing your speed by 11 km/s takes either a tank of fuel the size of a building or a tiny heat shield, and the tiny heat shield is a lot easier to carry. Thanks to heat shields, slowing down is much easier than speeding up—which requires the aforementioned giant fuel tank. (For more on this, see this What If question (https://what-if.xkcd.com/58/)). Heat shields only work for slowing down; if there were a way to use the same heat shield mechanism to speed up, space travel would get a lot easier. Sadly, no one's figured out a practical way to build a "reverse heat shield" rocket. However, while the idea seems silly, in a sense it's sort of the principle behind both Project Orion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Orion_(nuclear_propulsion)) and laser ablation propulsion (https://www.osti.gov/biblio/21439582). Since you have this handy metal pole, you can control your descent by clamping onto it and controlling your rate of descent through friction. [Image: image] Make sure to keep your speed low during the whole approach and descent—and, if necessary, pausing to let your hands or brakepads cool down—rather than waiting until the end to try to slow down. If you get up to escape velocity, then at the last minute remember that you need to slow down, you'll be in for an unpleasant surprise as you try to grab on to the pole. At best, you'll be flung away and plummet to your death. At worst, your hands and the surface of the pole will both be converted into exciting new forms of matter, and then you'll be flung away and plummet to your death. [Image: image] Assuming you descend slowly and enter the atmosphere in a controlled manner, you'll soon encounter your next problem: Your pole isn't moving at the same speed as the Earth. Not even close. The land and atmosphere below you are moving very fast relative to you. You're about to drop into some extremely strong winds. [Image: image] The Moon orbits around the Earth at a speed of roughly one kilometer per second, making a wide circle[10]Yes, I know, orbits are conic sections which in the case of the Moon is technically not exactly a circle. It's actually a pentagon. every 29 days or so. That's how fast the top end of our hypothetical fire pole will be traveling. The bottom end of the pole makes a much smaller circle in the same amount of time, moving at an average speed of only about 35 mph relative to the center of the Moon's orbit: [Image: image] 35 miles per hour doesn't sound bad. Unfortunately for you, the Earth is also spinning,[11]I mean, unfortunately in this specific context. In general, the fact that the Earth spins is very fortunate for you, and for the planet's overall habitability. and its surface moves a lot faster than 35 mph; at the Equator, it can reach over 1,000 miles per hour.[12]It's common knowledge that Mt. Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth, measured from sea level. A somewhat more obscure piece of trivia is that the point on the Earth's surface farthest from its center is the summit of Mt. Chimborazo in Ecuador, due to the fact that the planet bulges out at the equator. Even more obscure is the question of which point on the Earth's surface moves the fastest as the Earth spins, which is the same as asking which point is farthest from the Earth's axis. The answer isn't Chimborazo or Everest. The fastest point turns out to be the peak of Mt. Cayambe, a volcano north of Chimborazo. And now you know.​[13]Mt. Cayambe's southern slope also happens to be the highest point on Earth's surface directly on the Equator. I have a lot of mountain facts. [Image: image] Even though the end of the pole is moving slowly relative to the Earth as a whole, it's moving very fast relative to the surface. [Image: image] Asking how fast the pole is moving relative to the surface is effectively the same as asking what the "ground speed" of the Moon is. This is tricky to calculate, because the Moon's ground speed varies over time in a complicated way. Luckily for us, it doesn't vary that much—it's usually somewhere between 390 and 450 m/s, or a little over Mach 1—so figuring out the precise value isn't necessary. [Image: image] Let's buy a little time by trying to figure it out anyway. The Moon's ground speed varies pretty regularly, making a kind of sine wave. It peaks twice every month as it passes over the fast-moving equator, then reaches a minimum when it's over the slower-moving tropics. Its orbital speed also changes depending on whether it's at the close or far point in its orbit. This leads to a roughly sine-wave shaped ground speed: [Image: image] Well, ready to jump? [Image: image] Ok, fine. There's one other cycle we can take into account to really nail down the Moon's ground speed. The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° relative to the Earth-Sun plane, while the Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5°. This means that the Moon's latitude changes the way the Sun's does, moving from the northern tropics to the southern tropics twice a year. However, the Moon's orbit is also tilted, and this tilt rotates on an 18.9-year cycle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metonic_cycle). When the Moon's tilt is in the same direction as the Earth's, it stays 5° closer to the Equator than the Sun, and when it's in the opposite direction, it reaches more extreme latitudes. When the Moon is over a point farther from the equator, it has a lower "ground speed," so the lower end of the sine wave goes lower. Here's the plot of the Moon's "ground speed" over the next few decades: [Image: image] The Moon's top speed stays pretty constant, but the lowest speed rises and falls with an 18.9-year cycle. The lowest speed of the next cycle will be on May 1st, 2025, so if you want to wait until 2025 to slide down, you can hit the atmosphere when the pole is moving at only 390 m/s relative to the Earth's surface. [Image: image] When you do finally enter the atmosphere, you'll be coming down near the edge of the tropics. Try to avoid the tropical jet stream (https://earth.nullschool.net/#current/wind/isobaric/250hPa/orthographic=326.35,-1.08,372), an upper-level air current which blows in the same direction the Earth rotates. If your pole happens to go through it, it could add another 50-100 m/s to the wind speed. Regardless of where you come down, you'll need to contend with supersonic winds, so you should wear lots of protective gear.[15]For aerodynamic reasons, this gear should probably make it look like you're wearing a very fast airplane. Make sure you're tightly attached to the pole, since the wind and various shockwaves will be violently battering and jolting you around. People often say, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." Unfortunately, in this case, it's probably going to be both.[17]If it helps, people have survived supersonic ejections (https://jalopnik.com/5894022/what-happens-when-you-eject-out-of-a-jet-at-800-mph) before—and even a supersonic aircraft disintegration (http://roadrunnersinternationale.com/weaver_sr71_bailout.html)—so there's hope. [Image: image] At some point, to reach the ground, you're going to have to let go of the pole. For obvious reasons, you don't want to jump directly onto the ground while moving at Mach 1. Instead, you should probably wait until you're somewhere near airline cruising altitude, where the air is still thin, so it's not pulling at you too hard—and let go of the pole. items.model_answer:
A real fireman’s pole from the Moon to Earth could not exist in any ordinary sense. The Earth and Moon are not fixed relative to each other: the Moon orbits Earth, Earth rotates underneath it once per day, and the Earth–Moon distance changes by tens of thousands of kilometers over a month. A rigid pole connecting them would have to stretch, compress, bend, and sweep across Earth’s surface at roughly supersonic speed. No known material could survive that, and it would be catastrophically destructive where it touched the atmosphere or ground.

If we ignore those problems and imagine a magical indestructible pole always connecting the near side of the Moon to Earth, you still would not simply “slide down from the Moon.” Near the Moon, lunar gravity pulls you back toward the Moon. For the first several tens of thousands of kilometers, “down” is actually toward the lunar surface, so you would have to climb away from the Moon rather than slide.

Farther along, near the Earth–Moon L1 region, Earth’s gravity becomes dominant. After that point you would begin falling toward Earth. By the time you reached the atmosphere, you would be moving at nearly Earth escape-speed scale, around 10–11 km/s if you did not brake. Sliding on a pole at that speed would vaporize you from friction and atmospheric heating.

So the direct answer is: a Moon-to-Earth fireman’s pole is physically impossible, and even in a magical version it would not be a gentle slide. You would first have to climb away from the Moon, then you would fall toward Earth at spacecraft reentry speeds unless you had a way to brake.

items.question: What If Hailstones Were the Size of Soccer Balls?
human_answers: When you think about it, it's honestly kind of weird that hailstones haven't killed all of us already. I mean, they're chunks of ice that plunge from the sky! [Image: image] Hailstones fall from really high up. There's a popular myth that a penny dropped from the Empire State Building can kill you. The myth isn't true,[1]Mythbusters tried it in Season 1 Episode 7 and found that the penny would really sting and make you go "ow!!" but for anyone who believes it, hailstones should be terrifying—after all, they often fall from the height of ten Empire State Buildings. [Image: image] Luckily, the same thing that saves us from falling pennies also generally protects us from hailstones: Air resistance. As they fall, both pennies and hailstones quickly reach terminal velocity, the speed at which drag balances out gravity and prevents them from speeding up any more. For a small hailstone the size of a pea or a marble, terminal velocity might be only 10 or 20 miles per hour, the speed of an object tossed across a room. Getting hit by them isn't comfortable, but it's not likely to cause serious injury.[2]While dropping a penny on someone from the height of the Empire State Building wouldn't kill them, dropping the Empire State Building on a them from the height of a penny would, as demonstrated by the tragic demise of Jebediah Mythbuster in the pilot episode of the show eventually named in his memory. [Image: image] Large hailstones travel much faster than small ones and can be a lot more dangerous. The terminal velocity of a golf-ball-sized hailstone is about 60 miles per hour,[3]A little slower than an actual golf ball, thanks to the golf ball's greater weight and those weird drag-reducing dimples. which could easily cause serious injury. Large hailstorms often cause extreme damage to cars (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=hail+car+windows), and the largest hailstones can be deadly. A storm in China in 2002 (http://edition.cnn.com/2002/WEATHER/07/22/weather.china.hail/) dropped egg-sized and baseball-sized hailstones that killed several dozen people and hospitalized many others. Luckily, deaths from hail aren't very common, for two main reasons: First, because hailstones big enough to be deadly are rare, and second, because when there's a thunderstorm severe enough to produce such large hail, people generally try to take shelter. [Image: image] A hailstone the size and shape of a regulation soccer ball would be more than twice the weight of the heaviest hailstones on record. It would have a terminal velocity of roughly 140 miles per hour, which is really fast. If one of them hit your car, it wouldn't just dent the body or crack the windshield, it could punch right through the roof. Sheltering indoors might not be enough to protect you, unless you had a particularly sturdy roof or possibly several floors above you. [Image: image] When a hailstorm is nearby, it's good to take shelter even if you're not right below the storm. As a hailstone forms in a thunderstorm updraft, it bounces around like popcorn in a popcorn machine. Usually, it falls out of the bottom of the storm, but sometimes it's ejected out of the top or sides, then carried by wind to fall some distance from the storm. Aircraft flying near thunderstorms have been hit by hail when they have nothing but blue sky above them. [Image: image] Real hailstones, especially large ones, aren't round like a soccer ball. As they tumble around in a thunderstorm, they grow via water freezing onto their sides. If they have a lump on one side, the protrusion can collect more water and grow faster than the areas around it, forming a blobby appendage. Liquid water can also run out to the edges of a rotating hailstone and freeze, forming icicle-like features. [Image: image] The weird shapes of large hailstones are good news for us ground-dwellers with breakable bones, because these protrusions tend to increase their drag and lower their terminal velocity. But the weird shapes of hailstones also raises an interesting possibility. If a hailstone had just the right combination of lobes, it's possible—if unlikely—that it might happen to form a lifting body. This strange category of aircraft—which includes the Space Shuttle, the M2-F1 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_M2-F1), and the Dream Chaser (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream_Chaser)—can be unexpectedly aerodynamic despite their compact shapes, capable of gliding or even swoops. [Image: image] It's unlikely that any gliding hail has ever been observed, but in the 4 billion years that Earth has had water and thunderstorms, there have probably been some pretty strange hailstones. Not only has there likely been one the size of a soccer ball ... [Image: image] ... there might even have been one able to score a goal.

items.model_answer:
If hailstones were the size of soccer balls, they would be extremely dangerous—more like falling blocks of ice than ordinary hail.

A soccer ball is about 22 cm in diameter. If a hailstone that size were mostly solid ice, it would have a mass of roughly 4–5 kg. Falling through the atmosphere, it could reach a terminal velocity around 60–75 m/s, or about 215–270 km/h, depending on shape and air resistance. Its impact energy would be on the order of 10,000 joules, comparable to dropping a heavy bowling ball from a tall building.

The effects would be severe. A direct hit on a person or animal could easily be fatal. Cars would be crushed or punctured, windshields would not merely crack but likely cave in, and ordinary roofs, skylights, solar panels, greenhouses, and aircraft surfaces could be badly damaged or penetrated. Crops would be shredded, trees stripped, and livestock exposed outdoors would be at serious risk.

Meteorologically, producing hail that large would require an exceptionally powerful thunderstorm. Hailstones grow when strong updrafts keep ice suspended in a storm while supercooled water freezes onto them. A soccer-ball-sized hailstone would need an updraft strong enough to support several kilograms of ice—likely tens of meters per second, comparable to the strongest supercell thunderstorms. Such storms would probably also bring destructive winds, intense lightning, flash flooding, and possibly tornadoes.

In reality, hailstones near this size are extraordinarily rare. The largest recorded hailstones have approached soccer-ball diameter, but they are usually irregular, partly porous, and not solid smooth spheres. A truly solid soccer-ball-sized hailstone would be much heavier and more destructive than most record hail.

So, if soccer-ball-sized hail became common, severe thunderstorms would become major life-threatening disasters. Outdoor exposure would be deadly, vehicles would offer limited protection, and robust shelters—substantial buildings, basements, or reinforced structures—would be necessary during such storms.

items.question: What If You Built a Bridge of Cars across the Atlantic?
human_answers: After extensive research, I can conclusively state that this would be a violation of your rental car agreement. Also, you would disrupt ocean circulation in the North Atlantic, potentially seriously altering the climate in the northern hemisphere. That's very bad, although not necessarily a violation of your rental car agreement. [Image: image] If you try to drive from the US to Europe, your car will stop working pretty quickly, since according to Google Maps there's a large hole between them and it's full of water. Once your car gets stuck, you'll have to leave it there and go get another one. [Image: image] Driving your second car onto the roof of the sunken first one could get you a little closer to Europe. If we assume you're starting in Boston and heading toward Lisbon, using a car as a bridge would get you about a millionth of the way there, since Boston and Lisbon are about a million car-lengths apart. If the Atlantic Ocean were two feet deep, you could make a bridge out of a million cars placed end to end. Unfortunately, a quick rewatch of Titanic (1997) suggests that the Atlantic Ocean is more than two feet deep. You'll quickly have to start piling up cars in multiple layers. [Image: image] At first, when the bridge would be just one or two cars high, you could stack them in a single vertical column. But as the water gets deeper, you'll need to create a wider base to keep the wall of cars from tipping over.[1]A glance at piles of cars (https://www.google.com/search?q=junk+car+piles&tbm=isch) in a junkyard suggests that they often end up in stacks with an angle of repose of 30 or 45 degrees, but a stack with a 10°-15° angle of repose at the bottom should be stable once the cars are sufficiently crushed. The North Atlantic current (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Current) would push against the car causeway, but the tipping force from the water motion would be relatively minor compared to the pile's tendency to topple under its own weight.[2]Mike Ashby's Useful Solutions to Standard Problems (https://cushman.host.dartmouth.edu/courses/engs171/UsefulSolutionsForStandardProblems.pdf) is a fantastic resource for these kinds of calculations. In this case, you could use it to figure out how a column of cars will topple, which would require an estimate of the compressibility of a stack of cars at different stages of flattening. I used specs from hydraulic car crushers to come up with my rough estimates here, but these estimates could probably be refined with experiment if you know someone with a lot of cars (https://cars.usnews.com/cars-trucks/features/jay-lenos-car-collection). [Image: image] As you built your bridge out into the deep ocean, the cars on the bottom of the stack would be crushed. The pressure crushing them wouldn't be the water pressure. Once the windows broke and the interior of the car flooded, the pressure would equalize and the cars would hold their shape, relatively unaffected by the weight of the ocean above them. Instead, what would crush the cars would be the weight of the other cars sitting on top of them. Even when they're underwater, cars weigh a lot. About 50% of the weight of modern cars is steel and iron, which is much denser than water,[3]Citation: You don't see a lot of anchors floating around. so submerged cars are still quite heavy—about 60% to 70% of their surface weight, depending on their exact composition. The cars on the bottom of a mile-high stack would be subjected to extreme pressures, even greater than what they experience in hydraulic car crushers. Those crushers[4]Most famous, of course, for imperiling George Frankly in an episode of MathNet, the detective show on PBS's Square One TV. are capable of flattening a car into a pancake a foot or two thick, and the same thing would happen to the cars on the bottom of our stack. [Image: image] The first part of your bridge to Europe would be over the continental shelf, where the water is relatively shallow—just a few hundred crushed cars deep. [Image: image] You'd still need a lot of cars to form this shallow-water portion of the bridge; getting out to the edge of the continental shelf would take about a billion of them, which is probably close to the total number of cars in the world. Parking lots hold about 1 car per 30 square meters, so a billion cars would cover a large portion of eastern Massachusetts.[5]Apparently all the world's cars would take up slightly more space than all the world's people. After the continental shelf, the water gets a lot deeper. The deep-ocean portion of your bridge would require a lot more cars—likely about a trillion of them. This is far more cars than exist in the world; a parking lot big enough to hold them would take up most of the Earth's land area. So you can't rent anywhere close to a billion or a trillion cars—Enterprise, for example, only has about half a million (https://www.enterprise.com/en/about.html) cars in its fleet. But if you tried, you'd run into other problems, too. I got a copy of a recent Enterprise rental car agreement, and I have some bad news: 4. Prohibited Use and Termination of Right to Use. a. Renter agrees to the following limits on use: [...] (4) Vehicle shall not be used for: any illegal purposes; in any illegal or reckless manner; in a race or speed contest; or to tow or push anything. [...] (8) Vehicle shall not be loaded in excess of Vehicle’s Gross Vehicle Weight Rating [...] (9) Vehicle shall not be driven on an unpaved road or off-road. You'd clearly be in violation of 4(a)(9) by driving it off-road. I think you'd also be violating 4(a)(4) and probably 4(a)(8) as well. This would result in you being—at minimum—on the hook for the total cost of the rental car.[6]If you continue to operate the vehicle in such a manner, 4(d) says the company has the right to notify police that it has been stolen. Some credit cards offer coverage for rental car damage, so you might think that—if you're a high-status cardholder—you could try to get the company to foot the bill. Unfortunately, I took a look at the agreement (https://www.americanexpress.com/content/dam/amex/us/credit-cards/features-benefits/policies/NAC-Benefit-Guides/CRLDI_Benefit_Guide_371.397_EDT_02.20REV_10.20.pdf) for the American Express Centurion card, and the "What is Not covered" section clearly addresses this scenario: What is Not Covered? ANY COVERED EVENT BASED UPON OR ARISING OUT OF: [...] 3. Use of the Rental Vehicle in violation of the terms and conditions of the Rental Agreement [...] 8. off-road operation [...] of the Rental Vehicle [...] 11. intentional damage [...] to the Rental Vehicle Interestingly, American Express will also not cover damages incurred by using the rental car in a war: [...] 1. War or acts of war (whether declared or undeclared), service in the armed forces or units auxiliary to it [...] This rule could actually end up being relevant here. Your car bridge across the Atlantic, in addition to potentially disrupting ocean circulation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_meridional_overturning_circulation), would cut off shipping access (https://digital-commons.usnwc.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1429&context=ils) to northern Europe and much of Atlantic Canada... ...which may qualify as a naval blockade. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you tried to build a “bridge of cars” across the Atlantic, it would fail almost immediately unless you changed the cars so much that they were no longer really cars.

A single-file line of cars from North America to Europe would need roughly 1 million cars, since the Atlantic crossing is about 4,000–5,500 km depending on the route and a car is about 4–5 m long. A usable road-width bridge would need several million cars at minimum.

But the main problem is not the number of cars. It is that cars are not bridge elements.

If the cars were simply placed on the ocean, most would eventually flood and sink. Some cars can float briefly because the cabin traps air, but they are unstable, leak through vents and seams, and are quickly overwhelmed by waves. The Atlantic has storms with waves many meters high, sometimes over 20 m. A chain of floating cars would be torn apart.

If you tried to make a floating pontoon bridge out of sealed cars, it still would not work well. Cars are too weak, too flexible, and not shaped for ocean loads. The connections between them would experience enormous forces from waves, wind, currents, and tides. A floating bridge across an ocean would also need anchoring in water several kilometers deep, which is far beyond what a car-based structure could handle.

If instead you tried to support the bridge from the seafloor, the problem becomes even worse. The Atlantic is commonly 3–5 km deep. You would need towers or piles thousands of meters tall. Cars stacked that high would buckle and collapse under their own weight long before reaching the surface. At depth, ocean pressure would crush them; at 4 km down, the pressure is about 400 atmospheres.

Even if you magically arranged the cars into place, corrosion, saltwater, storms, and fatigue would destroy the structure. It would also block shipping lanes and be almost impossible to maintain.

So the direct answer is: a bridge made of cars across the Atlantic would not be a bridge for more than a short time. If floating, it would break apart and sink. If supported from the seafloor, it would collapse or be crushed. The amount of material is large but not the real obstacle; the real obstacle is that cars are nowhere near strong, stable, durable, or seaworthy enough to function as an ocean-spanning bridge.

items.question: What If Every Nation's Airspace Extended Forever into Space?
human_answers: Today's question is adapted from What If 2: Additional Serious Scientific Answers to Absurd Hypothetical Questions (https://xkcd.com/what-if-2/), which contains many more What If answers and is available now (https://xkcd.com/what-if-2/)! Congratulations to Australia, new rulers of the galaxy. The Australian flag has a number of symbols on it, including five stars that represent the stars of the Southern Cross.[1]Epsilon Crucis has five points, while the others have seven, implying that the view of Epsilon is from a telescope with different lens geometry from the others. Minor symbolic/graphic design choice? Or clue to a secret multiversal alliance between parallel universe Australias? No way to know for sure! Based on the answer to this question, maybe their flag designers should think bigger. [Image: image] Countries in the southern hemisphere have an advantage when it comes to star ownership. Earth's axis is tilted relative to the Milky Way; our North Pole points generally away from the galaxy's center. [Image: image] If each country's airspace extended upward forever, the core of the galaxy would stay under the control of countries in the southern hemisphere, changing hands over the course of each day as the Earth rotates. At its peak, Australia would control more stars than any other country. The supermassive black hole at the core of the galaxy would enter Australian airspace every day south of Brisbane, near the small town of Broadwater. [Image: image] After about an hour, almost the entire galactic core—along with a substantial chunk of the disk—would be within Australian jurisdiction. [Image: image] At various times throughout the day, the galactic core would pass through the domain of South Africa, Lesotho, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile. The United States, Europe, and most of Asia would have to be content with outer sections of the galactic disk. The northern hemisphere isn't left with the dregs, though. The outer galactic disk has some cool things in it—like Cygnus X-1, a black hole currently devouring a supergiant star.[2]Cygnus X-1 was the subject of a famous bet between astrophysicists Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne over whether it was a black hole or not. Hawking, who had spent much of his career studying black holes, bet that it wasn't. He figured that if black holes turned out not to exist, at least he would win the bet as a consolation prize. In the end, luckily for his legacy, he lost. Each day, as the core of the galaxy crossed the Pacific, Cygnus X-1 would enter the United States's airspace over North Carolina. [Image: image] While owning a black hole would be cool, the United States would also have millions of planetary systems constantly moving in and out of its territory—which might cause some problems. The star 47 Ursae Majoris has at least three planets and probably more. If any of those planets have life on them, then once a day all that life passes through the United States. That means that there's a period of a few minutes each day where any murders on those planets technically happen in New Jersey. Luckily for the New Jersey court system, altitudes above about 12 miles are generally considered "high seas." According to the American Bar Association's Winter 2012 issue of the Admiralty and Maritime Law Committee Newsletter, this means that deaths above these altitudes—even deaths in space—are arguably covered by the 1920 Death on the High Seas Act, or DOHSA. But if any aliens on 47 Ursae Majoris are considering bringing a lawsuit in a US court under DOHSA, they're going to be disappointed. DOHSA has a statute of limitations of 3 years, but 47 Ursae Majoris is more than 40 light-years away... [Image: image] ...which means it's physically impossible for them to file charges in time.

items.model_answer:
If every nation’s airspace legally extended forever into space, modern space activity would become almost unworkable.

The key change would be that outer space would no longer be a global commons. Under current law, national sovereignty ends somewhere above aviation altitudes, and outer space is governed by the principle of free access and non-appropriation. Satellites can orbit Earth without asking permission from every country they pass over. If airspace extended indefinitely, that would no longer be true: every satellite in low Earth orbit would cross many countries’ sovereign airspace every 90 minutes or so.

That would mean satellite operators would need permission from every country whose “vertical column” of territory the satellite passed through. Weather satellites, GPS, communications satellites, spy satellites, Earth-observation satellites, crewed spacecraft, and even space stations would constantly violate national airspace unless they had broad international clearance. A single hostile or uncooperative state could legally block certain orbits.

Launches would also become far harder. A rocket does not go straight up and stay above the launching country; it follows a curved trajectory and often passes over ocean or other states’ territory. If national airspace extended forever, launch providers would need negotiated corridors through space, much like aircraft overflight rights but vastly more complicated.

Military and intelligence activities would be especially affected. Reconnaissance satellites currently pass over other countries legally because space is not treated as national airspace. In this counterfactual world, such satellites would be equivalent to unauthorized aircraft overflights and could be treated as violations of sovereignty. Countries might claim a right to intercept, disable, or demand removal of satellites passing above them.

Geostationary orbit would become politically contentious too. Countries on the equator could claim that the geostationary belt above their territory is part of their sovereign airspace. That would give equatorial states enormous leverage over communications satellites, broadcasting, and weather monitoring. Something similar was once argued in the real world by some equatorial countries, but it was not accepted internationally.

The idea becomes even stranger if “forever” is taken literally. A nation’s sovereign column would extend not only through low Earth orbit but outward toward the Moon, planets, and stars. Because Earth rotates, those columns would sweep through space. A point in space could move in and out of different countries’ claimed jurisdictions depending on Earth’s rotation and the object’s motion. The Moon, for example, would periodically lie “above” different countries. That would make the concept legally absurd unless special exceptions were created.

In practice, the world would probably be forced to invent treaties restoring something like the current system: a defined upper limit to national airspace, guaranteed orbital transit rights, or international space corridors. Without that, spaceflight, satellite services, planetary exploration, and global communications would be crippled by overlapping sovereignty claims and constant diplomatic disputes.

So the direct answer is: if national airspace extended forever into space, every orbit would become an international overflight problem, satellites would need permission from many states, reconnaissance and communications systems would be legally vulnerable, equatorial and large countries would gain major leverage, and space would likely become so difficult to use that nations would have to renegotiate the rule almost immediately.

items.question: What If You Crashed a Comet into the Ocean to Cool the Earth?
human_answers: No. In fact, it's honestly sort of impressive to find a solution that would actively make the problem worse in so many different ways. [Image: image] Dropping a comet into the ocean to cool the planet, famously suggested by the 2002 Futurama episode None Like It Hot,[1]I'm used to stuff making me feel old, but the fact that this episode aired 20 years ago is distressing in multiple ways. wouldn't work for a few reasons. One is that dropping things from space creates heat. When water—or anything else—falls, it gains kinetic energy. When it stops falling, that energy has to go somewhere. Generally, it turns into heat. Water that goes over Niagara Falls, for example, gains enough kinetic energy during the 50-meter plunge to warm it up by about 0.1°C by the time it reaches the bottom. (This added heat is minor compared to the cooling effects of evaporation on the way down, so the actual temperature at the bottom is likely colder.) Outer space is a lot higher up than Niagara Falls,[citation needed] so the plunge down into the atmosphere at the bottom of Earth's gravity well adds a lot more than 0.1 degrees worth of heat. A chunk of ice from space that falls to Earth gains enough energy to warm the ice up, melt it, boil it into vapor, and then heat the vapor to thousands of degrees. If you built an icy waterfall from space, the water would arrive at the bottom as a river of superheated steam. [Image: image] Small chunks of ice falling from space disintegrate and boil away before they reach the ground, warming the upper atmosphere. Large comets can reach the ground intact and be vaporized on impact as their kinetic energy is converted to heat all at once. This heat energy would be about 100 times greater than the energy needed to bring even a very cold comet up to room temperature, so a comet falling from space would heat the Earth 100 times more than it cooled it. [Image: image] But let's suppose you figure out a way to lower the comet slowly, using some kind of magical crane,[2]Magical storks deliver babies, magical cranes deliver comets. and gently set the comet in the ocean. [Image: image] Comets are more dust than ice, but they're not particularly dense. A tiny piece of a comet would float for a short time until it became waterlogged, melted, and broke apart. A full-size comet wouldn't be strong enough to support its own weight, and would collapse like a drying sand sculpture. [Image: image] If the comet were placed in the ocean,[3]It actually wouldn't have much effect on global sea level, but the influx of cold water on the surface—and the dust released into the air—could definitely mess with the atmosphere. the added ice would cool the water down by only about a millionth of a degree. If you set the comet on land, it would soak up heat from the atmosphere—which contains much less stored heat than the oceans—briefly cooling the air by an average of one or two thousandths of a degree. Okay, so we just need thousands of comets, right? Each one will cool the air a little bit. With a large enough supply of comets, we can keep the Earth nice and cool, as long as we make sure they're lowered slowly. [Image: image] Unfortunately, comets would affect the Earth's temperature in another way. In addition to dust and water, they contain a small amount of CO2, which would be released into the atmosphere as the comet melted. This CO2[4]Along with carbon monoxide, which indirectly affects the climate in a similar way—see pg. 718-719 of the IPCC WG1 AR5 report (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/WG1AR5_Chapter08_FINAL.pdf) for more. would change Earth's radiation balance, trapping heat near the surface and raising the planet's temperature. After a few years, the comet's greenhouse effect would have trapped more heat than the ice absorbed, and over the decades to follow, the extra heat would keep piling up. The CO2 released from the comet would raise the temperature of the Earth for centuries. It wouldn't just cancel out the cooling effect of the ice—over time, the comet's greenhouse effect would deliver as much heat as if you'd just let it slam into the planet and vaporize.[5]Although letting a comet slowly decay on the surface would definitely be preferable to a high-speed impact, as any dinosaur from the end of the Cretaceous can tell you. It's okay. Despite all this, your scenario could fix global warming. Remember that hypothetical crane that lets you lower comets to the surface? items.model_answer:
Crashing a comet into the ocean would not be a practical way to cool Earth. It would be a global disaster, and depending on the comet’s size it would either do almost nothing useful for climate or cause an impact winter with catastrophic side effects.

A comet is mostly ice, so it sounds as if it might “add cold” to the planet. But that intuition fails because the comet would arrive at tens of kilometers per second. Its kinetic energy would vastly exceed any cooling effect from its ice. A 1-kilometer-wide comet hitting at around 50 km/s would release roughly \(10^{20}\)–\(10^{21}\) joules of energy, comparable to tens of thousands of megatons of TNT. The impact would flash-vaporize enormous amounts of seawater, generate mega-tsunamis, blast material into the atmosphere, and heat the local ocean-atmosphere system violently.

Could the debris cool Earth by blocking sunlight? Possibly, but only if the impact were large enough to loft huge quantities of fine particles into the stratosphere. That is similar to the “impact winter” scenario after major asteroid impacts. Sunlight would be reduced, temperatures could drop sharply for months to years, photosynthesis would decline, crops would fail, and ecosystems would be severely damaged. That is not controlled climate cooling; it is a mass-casualty planetary shock.

An ocean impact is also not ideal for producing long-lived reflective dust. A land impact into sulfur- or carbonate-rich rock can inject dust and sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight. An ocean impact mostly injects water vapor, salt, and some impactor material. Much of the water vapor would condense and rain out, while any water vapor that reached the stratosphere could act as a greenhouse gas and alter ozone chemistry. Salt aerosols and nitrogen oxides from the impact plume could damage the ozone layer and produce acid rain.

The size tradeoff is fatal:

If the comet is small, it causes regional destruction, tsunamis, atmospheric chemistry problems, and heating from the impact, but little meaningful global cooling.

If the comet is large enough to cool the planet noticeably, it risks global crop failure, extreme weather disruption, ozone damage, ocean and atmospheric contamination, and potentially mass extinction-scale consequences.

So the careful answer is: crashing a comet into the ocean could, in the extreme case, cool Earth temporarily by creating an impact winter, but it would do so through catastrophic destruction rather than safe climate control. It would be far worse than the warming problem it was meant to solve.

items.model_answer:
If the existence of God were scientifically proven, the consequences would depend heavily on what exactly had been proven.

If science established that some kind of divine creator or intelligent cosmic mind exists, that would be one of the largest discoveries in human history. It would transform physics, cosmology, philosophy, theology, and probably politics and culture. But it would not automatically prove every religious doctrine, scripture, moral rule, miracle claim, or afterlife belief. Proving “God exists” would answer one enormous question, but it would raise many others: What is God like? Does God intervene in the universe? Is God personal or impersonal? Does God care about human behavior? Which, if any, religion has described God accurately?

Scientifically, the discovery would become part of the natural body of knowledge. If God’s existence were demonstrated through repeatable evidence, measurable effects, or a reliable explanatory theory, then scientists would study those effects the same way they study gravity, quantum fields, or consciousness. Science would not necessarily end; it would expand. The “supernatural” would, in some sense, become a subject of investigation, at least wherever it produced detectable consequences.

Religiously, many believers would feel vindicated, but different traditions would interpret the proof differently. Christians, Muslims, Jews, Hindus, deists, and others might all argue that the discovery supports their view. A scientifically proven creator would not automatically settle disputes about the Trinity, prophecy, reincarnation, salvation, divine law, or sacred texts unless the proof specifically included those details. Some religions might adapt easily; others might face major reinterpretation.

For atheism and agnosticism, the result would be decisive only with respect to the specific claim proven. Atheism about that God would become unreasonable in the same way denying a well-established scientific fact is unreasonable. But skepticism about particular religions, priesthoods, miracles, or moral claims could still remain rational.

Philosophically, the discovery would reshape debates about the origin of the universe, consciousness, morality, free will, and meaning. If God were shown to be the creator of the universe, arguments about why there is something rather than nothing would change dramatically. If God were shown to be morally perfect, then moral philosophy would also be affected. But even then, humans would still have to interpret what divine goodness means and how it applies to real ethical problems.

Socially, the effects could be destabilizing. Some people would become more religious, some would panic, some would resist the evidence, and some institutions would try to claim authority over the discovery. Governments might attempt to regulate religious claims more aggressively, or religious movements might gain power. There could be unity, but also conflict, especially if groups disagreed about what the proof implied.

Personally, many people would experience a profound shift in meaning. Death, suffering, purpose, and moral responsibility would feel different if people knew a divine reality existed. But the emotional impact would depend on the nature of the proven God. A loving and just God would inspire hope; a distant creator might inspire awe but not necessarily comfort; a judgmental or incomprehensible God might inspire fear.

The most careful answer is: scientifically proving God’s existence would be revolutionary, but it would not automatically answer all theological, moral, or religious questions. It would establish that reality includes a divine dimension, but humanity would still have to determine what that means, how much can be known about God, and how life should change in response.

items.question: What Would It Take to Run Santa Claus's Global Delivery Operation?
human_answers: Pay for elves Joe estimates that it would take 85,851 elves working 16 hours each day for 364 days to make roughly 2 billion toys. If Santa pays his elves about \$10.00 per hour (in US dollars), that costs $$85,851 \text{ elves}\times\$10.00\text{ per hour}...

Outsourcing delivery The obvious solution is to use external fulfillment services instead of delivering himself, in the vein of dropshipping. In this model, Santa would produce all his toys at the North Pole, and deliver them somewhere else, say by November...
items.original_question: 圣诞老人破产了。让别人成为圣诞老人要花多少钱？好吧，圣诞老人终于做到了。由于一些相当可疑的投资和房地产市场上的一些坏运气（他出租的几块冰盖刚刚融化），他破产了。因此，克里斯·克林格尔必须吸引我们这些凡人，找到一个人——最好是个人——能够为他的运营提供一年的资金，同时他试图确保更好的财务基础。圣诞老人委托我做一项可行性研究——也就是说，看看是否有人愿意帮助他。我必须首先计算出他每年成为圣诞老人要花多少钱（不，他没有告诉我，而且可能不会 - 圣诞老人是秘密的），在一个数量级之内。我已经确定了圣诞老人肯定会在一些关键地方使用金钱。它们包括： 获取制造玩具的原材料。付钱给小精灵制作玩具。产生他运行北极所需的所有能量。与驯鹿打交道。考虑到这些 - 以及我错过的任何事情 - 为圣诞老人的运营提供一年的资金需要多少钱？ 基本假设和说明：圣诞老人需要向他名单上的大约 20 亿儿童每人分发一个玩具。他需要在一晚上之内完成这件事。他有一整年的时间来制作玩具，但他需要精灵在他的工作室里制作它们（而且他们需要得到报酬！）。不分包；必须找到投资者已经够尴尬的了。圣诞老人的工作室位于北极或附近。圣诞老人还保留着去年的驯鹿、作坊等。然而，他今年仍然需要​​购买新的原材料、食物等，以及产生能源。我们不是从头开始。雪橇由驯鹿提供动力；在考虑运输所需的能量时，我们必须考虑喂养驯鹿所需的能量（我使用的模型类似于圣诞老人的驯鹿必须消耗多少卡路里？）。

criteria.1-2: Rejects the premise outright or gives a joke/fantasy answer with little operational reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Accepts the premise superficially but leaves scope vague, such as toys, children, geography, or timing.

criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear, mostly consistent operational model including demand, timing, labor, logistics, and constraints.

criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the major mechanisms required to run the operation: toy demand forecasting, manufacturing, labor, materials, warehousing, packaging, routing, delivery, customs/security, and post-delivery support.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only one mechanism, such as magic sleigh speed, with no system-level coverage.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few obvious elements like elves and delivery but ignores most supply-chain requirements.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several major components, including production and delivery, but leaves important bottlenecks underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains most relevant mechanisms and how they interact across the full year-long operation.
criteria.9-10: Provides integrated, end-to-end coverage of production, fulfillment, logistics, labor, infrastructure, and failure handling.

criteria.name: Quantitative Plausibility and Scaling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses reasonable estimates and scaling logic for the number of children, toys, labor hours, production rates, costs, payloads, travel speeds, warehouses, and delivery throughput.
criteria.1-2: Uses no numbers or wildly impossible figures without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes a few estimates but they are unsupported, inconsistent, or not scaled to billions of deliveries.
criteria.5-6: Uses some plausible order-of-magnitude calculations but misses major quantities or bottlenecks.
criteria.7-8: Applies coherent back-of-the-envelope math to production, labor, cost, and delivery capacity.
criteria.9-10: Builds a well-calibrated quantitative model with transparent assumptions, sensitivity ranges, and credible scale comparisons.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces downstream consequences over the full operational cycle, including how early decisions about production, outsourcing, inventory, or routing affect later delivery feasibility and costs.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected ideas with no causal links or temporal sequence.
criteria.3-4: Shows short causal links but fails to connect year-round preparation to Christmas Eve delivery.
criteria.5-6: Provides a partial chain from manufacturing to delivery but overlooks several downstream dependencies.
criteria.7-8: Presents a coherent long-range chain connecting planning, production, distribution, final-mile delivery, and risk management.
criteria.9-10: Demonstrates robust multi-step causal reasoning across the entire operation, including bottleneck propagation and contingency effects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer acknowledges uncertainty in assumptions while avoiding internal contradictions, impossible logistics under its own model, or unexplained switches between magical and nonmagical mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or assumes mutually incompatible mechanisms without noticing.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty minimally but relies on inconsistent assumptions or unexplained magic when convenient.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, with some uncertainty noted, but has unresolved tensions in costs, capacity, timing, or technology.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertain estimates and maintains consistency between assumptions, calculations, and proposed solutions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertainty, compares alternatives, avoids contradictions, and explains how assumptions affect feasibility conclusions.

items.model_answer:
Under ordinary physics, Santa’s traditional “one sleigh, one night, every home” operation would require technology far beyond anything known: effectively teleportation, extreme automation, or spacetime manipulation. As a real logistics problem, it would have to be massively distributed, not handled by one vehicle.

A reasonable estimate starts with the number of stops. If Santa visits only households that celebrate Christmas, the target might be on the order of 500 million to 800 million homes. Because of time zones, he could exploit roughly 31 hours of nighttime by traveling westward around the Earth. That gives about 110,000 seconds.

For 500 million homes, that is:

\[
\frac{500,000,000}{110,000} \approx 4,500
\]

deliveries per second.

For 800 million homes, it is over 7,000 deliveries per second.

That means a single sleigh could not “stop” in any normal sense. Even if the sleigh spent only one millisecond per house, that would still be too slow unless many deliveries happened simultaneously.

The travel speed would also be extreme. Even with an optimized route, visiting hundreds of millions of scattered homes would require traveling at thousands of kilometers per second. That is a significant fraction of the speed of light. At those speeds, flying through the atmosphere would cause catastrophic heating, shock waves, and energy losses. The sleigh would behave less like an aircraft and more like a meteor or reentry vehicle—except moving much faster and stopping constantly.

The payload is another problem. Suppose each child receives only 1 kilogram of gifts. If there are 500 million recipient children, that is 500 million kilograms of cargo, or 500,000 metric tons. If the average gift load is 2 kilograms, it doubles. No biological reindeer team could accelerate or carry anything remotely close to that.

The energy requirement is enormous. Accelerating even 500 million kilograms to 1,000 km/s would require roughly:

\[
E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2
\]

\[
E \approx \frac{1}{2}(5 \times 10^8)(10^6)^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{20} \text{ joules}
\]

That is comparable to several days of total human civilization’s energy use, and that ignores braking, maneuvering, air drag, heat shielding, takeoff, landing, and inefficiencies. At higher speeds, the energy requirement rises with the square of velocity.

So, for the classic Santa story to work literally, Santa would need several impossible or near-impossible capabilities: near-instant delivery to thousands of homes per second, inertial shielding so the sleigh and occupants are not destroyed by acceleration, some way to avoid atmospheric drag and sonic booms, a payload system far larger than any conventional aircraft, and possibly teleportation or local materialization of gifts.

A more physically realistic Santa operation would look nothing like the myth. It would require a global logistics network with regional warehouses, millions of autonomous drones or human couriers, predictive inventory placement, advanced routing software, and weeks or months of preparation. If each delivery worker or drone handled 100 homes in a night, then 500 million homes would require about 5 million delivery units operating in parallel. That is huge, but it is at least conceptually within the realm of large-scale human logistics. The “magic” would then be coordination, secrecy, automation, and manufacturing—not one sleigh moving at relativistic speed.

So the direct answer is: one Santa with one sleigh cannot run the global delivery operation under known physics. To make it work, Santa would need either supernatural/sci-fi technology such as teleportation and inertial control, or he would need to be the front end of a planet-scale distributed logistics system with millions of parallel delivery agents.

edus.text: Under ordinary physics, Santa’s traditional “one sleigh, one night, every home” operation would require technology far beyond anything known: effectively teleportation, extreme automation, or spacetime manipulation.
As a real logistics problem, it would have to be massively distributed, not handled by one vehicle.
A reasonable estimate starts with the number of stops.
If Santa visits only households that celebrate Christmas, the target might be on the order of 500 million to 800 million homes.
Because of time zones, he could exploit roughly 31 hours of nighttime by traveling westward around the Earth.
That gives about 110,000 seconds.
For 500 million homes, that is \(\frac{500,000,000}{110,000} \approx 4,500\) deliveries per second.
For 800 million homes, it is over 7,000 deliveries per second.
That means a single sleigh could not “stop” in any normal sense.
Even if the sleigh spent only one millisecond per house, that would still be too slow unless many deliveries happened simultaneously.
The travel speed would also be extreme.
Even with an optimized route, visiting hundreds of millions of scattered homes would require traveling at thousands of kilometers per second.
That is a significant fraction of the speed of light.
At those speeds, flying through the atmosphere would cause catastrophic heating, shock waves, and energy losses.
The sleigh would behave less like an aircraft and more like a meteor or reentry vehicle—except moving much faster and stopping constantly.
The payload is another problem.
Suppose each child receives only 1 kilogram of gifts.
If there are 500 million recipient children, that is 500 million kilograms of cargo, or 500,000 metric tons.
If the average gift load is 2 kilograms, it doubles.
No biological reindeer team could accelerate or carry anything remotely close to that.
The energy requirement is enormous.
Accelerating even 500 million kilograms to 1,000 km/s would require roughly \(E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), or \(E \approx \frac{1}{2}(5 \times 10^8)(10^6)^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{20}\) joules.
That is comparable to several days of total human civilization’s energy use.
That ignores braking, maneuvering, air drag, heat shielding, takeoff, landing, and inefficiencies.
At higher speeds, the energy requirement rises with the square of velocity.

So, for the classic Santa story to work literally, Santa would need several impossible or near-impossible capabilities: near-instant delivery to thousands of homes per second, inertial shielding, atmospheric-drag avoidance, a huge payload system, and possibly teleportation or local materialization of gifts.
A more physically realistic Santa operation would look nothing like the myth.

It would require a global logistics network with regional warehouses, millions of autonomous drones or human couriers, predictive inventory placement, advanced routing software, and weeks or months of preparation.
If each delivery worker or drone handled 100 homes in a night, then 500 million homes would require about 5 million delivery units operating in parallel.
That is huge.
But it is at least conceptually within the realm of large-scale human logistics.
The “magic” would then be coordination, secrecy, automation, and manufacturing—not one sleigh moving at relativistic speed.
So the direct answer is: one Santa with one sleigh cannot run the global delivery operation under known physics.
To make it work, Santa would need either supernatural/sci-fi technology such as teleportation and inertial control.
Or he would need to be the front end of a planet-scale distributed logistics system with millions of parallel delivery agents.

items.model_answer:
If the speed of light were 100 times faster, the most immediate change would be that the universe’s “speed limit” would be 100 times higher. Light from the Sun would reach Earth in about 5 seconds instead of 8 minutes 20 seconds. Light from the Moon would arrive in about 0.013 seconds. A light-speed trip to Alpha Centauri would take about 16 days instead of 4.3 years.

But the deeper answer depends on what else changes, because the speed of light is not an isolated setting in physics. It is tied to electromagnetism, relativity, atomic structure, gravity, and the definition of mass-energy. Changing only “c” while keeping everything else the same is not fully physically well-defined.

If we imagine the simplest case — a universe mostly like ours, but with the relativistic speed limit set to \(100c\) — then everyday life would look almost unchanged. Human walking speeds, cars, aircraft, weather, sound, and planetary motion are all already far slower than light, so making light 100 times faster would not noticeably affect ordinary daily motion. Relativistic effects such as time dilation, length contraction, and the increase of energy with speed would become much harder to notice, because they would only become significant at speeds close to the new, much higher light speed.

Astronomy and communication would change a lot. Telescopes would see distant events with 100 times less delay. Spacecraft communication delays would shrink dramatically. Interplanetary control would be easier: Mars would be seconds or tens of seconds away by radio instead of minutes. The observable universe, assuming the same cosmic age and expansion history, would be much larger because light could have traveled 100 times farther since the Big Bang.

Gravity would also behave differently in relativistic situations. The Schwarzschild radius of a black hole,

\[
r_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2},
\]

would become 10,000 times smaller for the same mass. That means black holes would be harder to form: matter would have to be compressed much more tightly before becoming a black hole. Relativistic corrections to planetary orbits, gravitational time dilation, and gravitational-wave effects would generally be weaker for the same masses and distances.

Mass-energy conversion would become far more extreme. Since

\[
E=mc^2,
\]

raising \(c\) by a factor of 100 raises the rest energy of a given mass by a factor of 10,000. If mass stayed the same in kilograms, complete conversion of matter to energy would release 10,000 times more energy than in our universe. Nuclear reactions could therefore be vastly more energetic if the relevant particle masses and binding processes otherwise remained comparable.

Atomic physics is where the answer becomes most delicate. The speed of light appears in the fine-structure constant,

\[
\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c},
\]

which controls the strength of electromagnetic interactions in atoms. If \(c\) became 100 times larger while charge, Planck’s constant, and the electric force stayed the same, then \(\alpha\) would become 100 times smaller. Relativistic effects inside atoms would be much weaker, spectral fine structure would shrink, magnetism would be altered, and chemistry might be similar in broad outline but different in detail. items.model_answer:
Humans could survive on an oxygen-bearing planet only if the atmosphere were close enough to Earth’s in the ways that matter physiologically. The key factor is not the percentage of oxygen, but the partial pressure of oxygen.

On Earth, the atmosphere is about 21% oxygen at 1 atmosphere of pressure, giving an oxygen partial pressure of about 21 kPa. Humans can tolerate some variation, but if the oxygen partial pressure is too low, they would suffer hypoxia: confusion, loss of coordination, unconsciousness, and death. This could happen even if the atmosphere contains oxygen, for example if the total air pressure is very low. A planet with 10% oxygen at twice Earth’s pressure might be breathable, while one with 30% oxygen at very low pressure might not be.

If the oxygen partial pressure is too high, humans can suffer oxygen toxicity, especially over longer periods or at high pressures. High oxygen levels would also make fires far easier to start and much harder to control.

The rest of the atmosphere matters too. Humans do not specifically need nitrogen; another inert gas such as argon or helium could act as a buffer. But many gases would be dangerous. Too much carbon dioxide would cause headaches, panic, acidosis, unconsciousness, and death. Carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia, chlorine, or many organic vapors could be lethal even if oxygen were present. High dust, corrosive aerosols, or reactive chemicals could damage the lungs and eyes.

Pressure is also critical. If the total atmospheric pressure were far below Earth’s, humans would need pressure suits even with oxygen present, because fluids in the body could begin to evaporate or swell and breathing would be ineffective. If pressure were much higher, breathing could become difficult, inert gases could cause narcosis, and decompression sickness could become a risk when moving to lower pressure.

Temperature, humidity, radiation protection, and gravity would also affect survival. An oxygen-bearing planet with no ozone layer or weak magnetic protection might expose humans to dangerous ultraviolet or particle radiation. Extreme cold or heat could kill without shelter. Very high gravity would strain the heart, muscles, and bones; very low gravity would cause long-term health problems.

So the answer is: humans would not automatically survive just because the planet has oxygen. If the oxygen partial pressure, total pressure, temperature, toxic gas levels, radiation environment, and gravity were within tolerable limits, humans might be able to breathe and live there with little protection. If any of those factors were far outside Earth-like ranges, they would need habitats, masks, pressure suits, filtration, or full life-support systems.

items.original_question: 如何彻底摧毁一座城市，而不为4000年后的人类留下任何线索？背景 我想彻底烧毁一座城市。一切不得残留，尘归尘，尘归尘。尽管我是一个超自然的存在，但我希望这一切以自然的方式发生。我还希望这次破坏不会留下任何痕迹，以便 4000 年后人类可以利用这些痕迹来确定到底发生了什么。然而，该事件可能会留下痕迹，让他们猜测发生了什么，但绝对不应该导致确切的原因。细节 完全烧毁一座城市（阅读：摧毁，但我喜欢火）。该市地处海拔以上，属半干旱气候。该事件可能不会留下任何线索。这意味着 4000 年后的人类无法准确识别发生了什么。然而，破坏可能会留下痕迹，让人们想知道到底发生了什么。主要的一点是，这座城市本身应该成为一个传说，也就是说，毁灭地点不应该留下任何可以证明被毁城市存在的痕迹。不过，如果人们知道发生了某种自然灾害也很好，但最好他们不确切知道是什么类型的自然灾害。 事件时间：公元前 2,000 年（大约）。销毁最好在 24 小时内发生。优选地，破坏方法可以摧毁主要用岩石和粘土类物质建造的城市。我有什么选择？有什么可以利用的自然灾害吗？这是否可能以自然的方式实现？请发挥创意。我本以为是“从天而降的火”，但陨石撞击的痕迹要持续 4000 多年。编辑 1：我删除了以下要求，以使更多答案成为可能：该区域不存在火山活动或地震活动。编辑2：答案和评论的数量非常多，谢谢！我重写了要求/细节，使事情更加清晰。我还在其中两个添加了“最好”一词，这意味着应该可以提供更多的答案。只要记住“最好”...还要注意，这个问题首先谈论两个城市。我将其更改为一个城市，因为：如果它适用于一个城市，那么它可能适用于任意数量的城市。

criteria.7-8: Explains destruction, taphonomy, site formation, and likely archaeological reasoning in a connected way.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and alternative explanations

items.model_answer:
I can’t help with instructions for destroying a city or hiding the cause. But as a STEM/archaeology counterfactual, the most plausible way a city could be destroyed so that archaeologists 4,000 years later might initially misread the cause is a rare natural high-energy event, especially a cosmic airburst or small impact.

A meteor or comet fragment exploding in the atmosphere could produce a sudden blast wave, intense heat, widespread fires, collapsing buildings, scattered debris, and mass casualties without necessarily leaving a clear crater. After millennia of erosion, rebuilding, looting, sedimentation, and chemical alteration, the remaining evidence might look like a conventional “destruction layer”: burned architecture, broken pottery, collapsed walls, ash, and human remains. Archaeologists could reasonably misinterpret that as warfare, earthquake, accidental urban fire, or a combination of disasters.

The difference would be in subtle forensic signatures, not the obvious ruins. Investigators would look for things like shocked minerals, microscopic spherules, unusual high-temperature melts, vitrified materials, anomalous platinum-group elements, charcoal indicating simultaneous regional burning, and damage patterns inconsistent with ordinary siege or earthquake collapse. If those traces were missed, contaminated, or eroded away, the event could easily be misread.

So the careful answer is: not a human “method,” but a brief, natural, high-temperature blast event—such as a cosmic airburst—followed by 4,000 years of taphonomic processes, would be the kind of scenario most likely to destroy a city while leaving archaeologists uncertain or wrong about the cause.

items.question: What If a Birdlike Species Almost Never Touched the Ground?
human_answers: Evolution Since the defining feature is not nesting on ground, the starting point should be the nesting behaviour. There should be a strong pressure to reduce time spent on the ground such as predators or competition for suitable locations with other species.

Most creature designs, if anthropomorphized, can be thought of as a balance between seizing opportunities and fearfully avoiding mishaps. As a result, most designs are very flexible, adapting to new situations as they come.

I think any answer to this question really hinges on how earth-like you want your planet to be and how earth-like you want the rest of your fauna and flora to be. Since you don't place any restrictions on these, I'll take the liberty to assume these factors...
So here's where we can start: Some birds (megapodes) are superprecocial , i.e. they can fly on the day they hatch.
items.original_question: 一种从不接触地面的鸟 正如我们目前所知，鸟类在地面上筑巢并产卵。有着锋利牙齿的人和物生活在地面上。也有一些东西有爪子和喙在空中，但较少。我想知道是否存在一种像鸟一样的动物，一生都在空中度过，死后才落到地上。我已经知道鸟类可以在空中睡觉，但我需要帮助：找出一种方法来解释我的鸟类（或蝙蝠，或其他什么）如何进化到永远不会接触地面 - 我缺乏一个令人信服且可信的故事。粮食情况。除非我也有飞行植物（考虑到能量方程，不太可能），否则它必须是捕食其他飞行生物的食肉动物，或者从地面抓取动物。更具体地说，我担心生命的第一阶段。也许是给新生儿准备一个类似袋鼠的育儿袋？最后，为了故事相关的目的，我更愿意让这只飞行的野兽尽可能大。你认为它能长到多大并且仍然全天候飞行？ （上图：诺斯罗普仍然制造出最好的羽蛇神）后期编辑：感谢大家提供了大量的好建议！ 感谢您的所有回答，我希望在这种情况下我能接受另外两个回答。除了我接受的@VilleNiemi 的答案之外，我认为@Ivy_Lynx 的答案值得更多的支持，我也从@CortAmmon 那里得到了一些有趣的想法。

items.model_answer:
A birdlike species that almost never touched the ground would evolve around one dominant constraint: everything important in life would have to happen in the air, on vertical surfaces, on water, or in trees and cliffs. It would resemble an extreme version of swifts, frigatebirds, albatrosses, and some bats: superbly adapted for flight, but awkward or vulnerable when forced to land.

Such a species would likely have very long, efficient wings for soaring or gliding, lightweight bones, powerful flight muscles, and a body shape optimized for staying airborne with minimal energy. Its feet might become reduced, weak, or highly specialized. Instead of walking, it might use its feet mainly for clinging to cliffs, branches, floating vegetation, or nest structures. If it truly almost never used flat ground, strong walking legs would be wasted weight.

Feeding would have to occur without landing. It might catch insects in midair like swifts, skim fish or plankton from water, steal food from other flying animals, pluck fruit from tree canopies, drink while flying over lakes, or snatch small animals from branches or waves. A highly aerial predator might hunt like a falcon; a filter-feeding or skimming species might behave more like a swallow crossed with a seabird.

Sleeping could also happen away from the ground. Some birds already sleep while flying in short brain-rest cycles, and frigatebirds can sleep during long flights. An extreme aerial species might sleep gliding on thermal currents, floating on water, hanging from cliffs, or clinging to high vegetation. It would probably have adaptations for partial-brain sleep, automatic flight stability, and strong navigation.

Reproduction is the hardest problem. Eggs require a safe place, so a birdlike species that lays eggs would still need some kind of nest. It might nest on sheer cliffs, in tree canopies, on floating mats, inside caves, or in communal hanging nests suspended from branches. If evolutionary pressure strongly favored avoiding ground contact, the species might develop unusually adhesive eggs, pouch-like incubation structures, or even live birth, though live birth would be a major departure from normal bird biology. More plausibly, it would land only for breeding, and only in places predators cannot easily reach.

Its young would also be shaped by this lifestyle. Chicks might remain in cliff or canopy nests until their first flight is nearly perfect. A failed first flight could be fatal. Parents would feed them in the nest, and juveniles might spend an extended period learning aerial feeding and navigation after fledging. Natural selection would strongly punish weak flight ability.

Predators and dangers would be different from ground-dwelling species. Ground predators would matter little except near nesting sites, but aerial predators, storms, exhaustion, parasites, and food scarcity would be serious threats. Bad weather could be especially dangerous if the species depended on constant flight. It might migrate with wind systems, follow insect blooms, ocean currents, or thermal patterns, and avoid calm regions where soaring is difficult.

Social behavior might be highly developed. Large flocks could help locate food, navigate, and reduce predation risk. Colonies on cliffs or trees could be dense and noisy. Courtship might take place mostly in the air, with elaborate flight displays replacing ground dances.

The tradeoff is that such a species would be magnificent in the air but nearly helpless on level ground. If grounded by injury, heavy rain, molt, or exhaustion, it might be unable to take off unless it could climb to a height or face a strong wind. Its whole anatomy and behavior would reflect an evolutionary bargain: sacrifice walking ability, ground feeding, and terrestrial safety in exchange for mastery of the air.

So, if a birdlike species almost never touched the ground, it would likely become an aerial specialist: long-winged, lightweight, efficient, highly navigational, dependent on cliffs, trees, water, or flight itself for resting and breeding, and extremely vulnerable whenever forced into a normal ground-dwelling situation.

items.question: What If You Tried to Build a Pig Cavalry?
human_answers: Absolutely! Pigs are dangerous animals.
I'm going to disagree with a lot of people here and say that, while not impossible, it would be very very difficult to use pigs. This isn't about the size of the pig nor its strength.
items.original_question: 骑猪的骑兵可能吗？最近，我的邻居让我很不高兴。我发现他计划以某种方式改进他的投石机，以便将肮脏的东西扔到河对岸。我告诉他我的猪骑骑兵会攻击他。我必须向你坦白一件事……我还没有任何骑猪的骑兵……！能有骑猪的骑兵吗？如果大人太重的话，我可以派小孩和矮人去战斗。我想要最少的东西（否则我会有安装在沙发上的骑兵，更舒服）：沿着想要的方向行走，当敌人在那里时不要逃跑，甚至如果可能的话向他们冲锋。是否可以？

items.model_answer:
A human pig cavalry would be mostly impractical. You could probably train some large pigs to carry very small riders for short distances, but they would not function like horse cavalry.

The main problem is biomechanics. Horses are tall, long-legged animals with backs and gaits well suited to carrying a rider while moving fast. Pigs are low, barrel-shaped, short-legged animals built for rooting, pushing, and short bursts of speed. A large domestic pig might weigh 200–300 kg, but that does not mean it can comfortably carry an adult soldier. A common rough limit for riding animals is around 15–20% of body weight, and even that assumes the animal is shaped for riding. A 250 kg pig might therefore tolerate perhaps 40–50 kg of total load, including saddle and gear, which is child-sized, not cavalry-sized. A pig big enough to carry an armored adult would be extremely heavy, slow, and likely less athletic, not more useful.

Pigs also make poor cavalry mounts tactically. They are much slower than horses, have poor endurance in heat, and are close to the ground, giving the rider little height advantage. Their shape makes saddles hard to secure because they lack prominent withers like horses. Their gait would be uncomfortable and inefficient for the rider. They are intelligent and trainable, but they are also strong, stubborn, easily distracted by food, and dangerous when frightened or aggressive. A panicked cavalry horse is bad; a panicked war pig with tusks is also bad, just closer to your legs.

Historically, pigs were occasionally used in warfare, but not as mounts. Ancient armies reportedly used pigs to frighten war elephants, because elephants disliked their squeals. That is very different from using them as cavalry.

So if you tried to build a pig cavalry for human soldiers, you would likely end up with a slow, hard-to-control, injury-prone force that could not charge effectively, could not carry much equipment, and would be outclassed by horses, camels, mules, or even infantry. The only plausible version would be “pig cavalry” for very small riders—children, fantasy goblins, or perhaps small robots. For adult humans, pigs are much better as livestock than as war mounts.
