I had a rather lengthy idea I've been toying around with for a party system for a work of fiction written in my Power Without Knowledge setting that I might write out today but on an unrelated note I've been mulling over the impact of a more successful Joseph Smith presidential run . I'm not suggesting that he win, or even that he not be assassinated, I'm just trying to puzzle out the consequences of his electoral platform surviving his death. Perhaps some sort of alliance with the Liberty Party ? Smith's platform included provisions shrinking the size of Congress and docking their pay, along with the elimination of courts martial and instituting the death penalty for public officials that didn't defend their constituents' constitutional rights, but what suggests at least some buy-in from the Liberty Party was a program of complete emancipation by 1850, with at least some degree of compensation financed by the sale of public land. Smith also argued for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. I understand it's a gamble of long odds (especially regarding constitutional changes and territorial expansion) but perhaps a pragmatic move to adopt compensation as a way to attract votes in slave states that would otherwise dig in their heels at any mention of abolition? It would also almost certainly require butterflying away the LDS move to Utah, leaving them a powerful swing constituency in Illinois. The idea of an openly abolitionist party arising in and surviving the 19th century and explicitly focused on the rights of minority religious and ethnic groups has a lot of promise. *EDIT- In keeping with my new Strange Bedfellows idea for an alternate American history in party systems here's my reinterpretation of the Second Party System: Federalist Party - The sole survivor of the First Party System and the Era of Good Feelings, the Federalist Party was able to claw its way back from the brink in the wake of the shattering of the National Republican Party following the much maligned 1824 election. Advocating a strong central government, Hamiltonian economics and infrastructure spending, the party was aided in its recovery by the influx of anti-Jacksonians leaving the disintegrating National Republicans. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. While in office Jackson tended to side with Southern interests against abolitionism, opposed (but could not dismantle) the Bank of the United States and defied the Supreme Court in the lead up to the Trail of Tears. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. The Federalists would side with northern industrial interests in opposition to the spread of the Peculiar Institution, while Nullifiers, viewing such attempts as federal overreach, became adamant defenders of it. Despite this focus on the issue it wouldn't be until the 1850's that the Liberty Party, the only explicitly abolitionist party in the Union, would gain traction beyond the local level. A party of minority rights and abolitionism, the Libertarians would lead a coalition of freedmen, Mormons and Owenite socialists of all stripes to political action, parlaying a pivotal influence in several midwestern states into a coalition with the Federalists in 1860.
failures.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Create an exotic party system

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Divergence Logic
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer establishes a clear alternate-history or institutional premise that plausibly produces an exotic party system rather than merely listing random parties.
criteria.1-2: No clear divergence point or premise; parties appear arbitrary or unrelated to the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a premise, but the link to party formation is weak, vague, or mostly asserted.
criteria.5-6: Provides a recognizable divergence and explains some direct effects on party development.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible divergence with clear causal links to multiple party origins and alignments.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, internally grounded counterfactual premise whose institutional, social, and historical consequences strongly explain the whole party system.

criteria.name: Party System Breadth and Distinctiveness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer creates a varied, exotic, and politically meaningful set of parties with distinct identities, constituencies, ideologies, and roles.
criteria.1-2: Provides too few parties or parties are generic labels with little differentiation.
criteria.3-4: Includes several parties, but many overlap ideologically or lack clear bases of support.
criteria.5-6: Creates a functional multiparty system with some distinct platforms and voter blocs.
criteria.7-8: Offers a diverse party ecology with clear ideological niches, regional bases, factions, and political functions.
criteria.9-10: Presents a vivid, memorable, and exotic party system where each party has a distinctive history, constituency, symbolism, and strategic role.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms by which the new parties emerge, compete, evolve, and affect governance over time.
criteria.1-2: Little or no explanation of how parties form, gain support, or influence politics.
criteria.3-4: Gives limited mechanisms, mostly party platforms without electoral or social dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic formation causes, voter bases, and some electoral consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers party origins, coalitions, regional strength, factional drift, electoral incentives, and policy effects.
criteria.9-10: Traces long-range dynamics across generations, including realignments, splinters, alliances, media framing, institutional pressures, and governing consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the created party system remains coherent across time, geography, ideology, and institutions without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible timelines, or mutually incompatible party claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent elements but frequent inconsistencies in ideology, chronology, or influence.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor unexplained jumps or tensions between party traits and outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains strong consistency across party histories, platforms, regions, and electoral status.
criteria.9-10: Shows excellent systemic coherence, with tensions explicitly explained as factions, compromises, historical legacies, or strategic adaptations.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Constraint Awareness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer balances imaginative exoticism with plausible political sociology and acknowledges uncertainty where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Wildly implausible or deterministic; ignores political constraints and social realities.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible ideas, but relies heavily on unsupported leaps or overconfident claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, though some assumptions or long-range outcomes are underjustified.
criteria.7-8: Balances creativity with realistic voter behavior, institutions, regional interests, and contingency.
criteria.9-10: Highly imaginative yet disciplined; clearly distinguishes likely outcomes from speculative ones and explains constraints, tradeoffs, and alternative possibilities.

failures.question: What If one people, two nation-states
human_answers: Italy would be easy to do, even with a recent-ish POD: there were proposals floating around in the mid-19th century, concerning Victor Emmanuel II crowning himself king of the Two Sicilies rather than annexing the place outright, while keeping the local government around; since Cavour himself was hesitant to annex the South, and only did so because Garibaldi was becoming too much of a loose cannon, if things had gone slightly differently, this could've happened, and since the South had its own distinct identity and history (even though it used Tuscan as its own official language, as every other state in the peninsula did), this could've stuck, with northern and southern Italy becoming kind of like Australia and New Zealand, independent countries closely tied to each other and under the same monarch. Ironically, the Third War of Independence could've gone better for northern Italy, since northern and southern troops couldn't integrate well IRL, and Italy could've gained Trento and Trieste before World War I, butterflying away the need for intervention; the Two Sicilies could have eventually gained a protectorate of sorts over Albania (history would rhyme there, since Skanderbeg had ties to the Neapolitan royals of his era and fled to Naples when his anti-Turkish uprising failed) and would've surely annexed the Papal enclaves once the north annexes Rome. Garibaldi's OTL expedition to Trento might instead take place in Pola or even Fiume but, as I stated earlier, northern Italy could be more willing to just accept territorial bribes from Austria here, since most of the Irredenta would've been gained already.

Faroese should linguistic be seen as a dialect of Western Norwegian. You could pretty much write Faroese with Nynorsk (the written standard the dialects in this region use) and vice versa. Where Faroese differ from Icelandic is that like Norwegian it have seen near complete replacement of vocabulary with Danish vocabulary thanks to the use of Danish Bibles, while on Iceland the Bible was translated into Icelandic early on and the Danish state supported the existence of a distinct Icelandic language for ideological reasons.. The main reason why Danes and Norwegians have trouble reading Faroese is because it use a it own variation of the Latin alphabet which is different from the one Danes and Norwegians use, while even if Icelandic was written using Danish or the different Norwegian written standards, it would be hard to understand it because of the difference in vocabulary. If the Danish-Norwegian Union had survived the Faroese Island would simply have been seen as part of Western Norway.

If the Prussians had done a better job containing the Great Northern War plague, then there might have been far more Prussian Lithuanians, who differ from Lithuanians in that they are Lutheran, strongly influenced by German culture, and speak a Germanized register of Lithuanian. While they kept the Lithuanian language alive during the Russian repression, the Prussian Lithuanians actually opposed Lithuaniation nationalism and explicitly refused to live in an independent Lithuanian state, accepting nothing else than German rule. Thus, when the Memel Territory was established, the Prussian Lithuanians declared themselves to be "Memellanders". Subsequently, after WW2, the Soviets saw them as Germans and expelled them from East Prussia. IOTL, the GNW plague absolutely decimated the Prussian Lithuanians, who comprised nearly 90% of its victims. Had it been contained effectively, and a butterfly net used afterwards, there would've been far more Prussian Lithuanians in East Prussia, perhaps enough to cause a national awakening. The Soviets likely would've propped up "Prussia" as a separate SSR from Lithuania while still expelling the Germans, and supported Prussian Lithuanian nationalism to divide and conquer (having just annexed resistive Lithuania). Basically Moldovenism, though in this case with genuine religious and cultural differences (plus a very different standard language).
failures.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?

rubrics.question_focus: What If one people, two nation-states

criteria.name: Premise Fit and Plausible Point of Divergence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer directly addresses the scenario of one culturally or ethnolinguistically related people plausibly ending up with two distinct nation-states, using a historically grounded divergence rather than an arbitrary split.
criteria.1-2: Does not clearly identify a shared people or two nation-states; divergence is absent, magical, or unrelated to the question.
criteria.3-4: Identifies a possible people-state split, but the point of divergence is vague, anachronistic, or weakly tied to real historical options.
criteria.5-6: Provides a recognizable shared people and two-state outcome with a somewhat plausible historical divergence, though key feasibility issues are underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Uses a well-chosen divergence rooted in real political, dynastic, linguistic, regional, or diplomatic possibilities and clearly links it to two nation-states.
criteria.9-10: Presents a highly plausible, specific divergence that exploits known historical contingencies and makes the two-state outcome feel like a credible near-miss or robust alternate path.

criteria.name: Mechanism of Shared Peoplehood versus Separate Statehood
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains why the population remains meaningfully one people while developing two durable national-state identities, as in north/south Italians, Faroese-Western Norwegians, or Prussian/Lithuanian variants.
criteria.1-2: Treats peoplehood and statehood as interchangeable; gives no mechanism for either shared identity or political separation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions common ancestry, language, or culture, but does not explain how separate institutions or identities persist.
criteria.5-6: Explains either the shared identity or the separate state identity reasonably, but the interaction between the two is thin.
criteria.7-8: Shows how language, religion, dynasty, regional institutions, class interests, or administrative traditions sustain both kinship and separation.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of overlapping identities, showing why people can see themselves as related while accepting or preferring separate national states.

criteria.name: State-Formation and Geopolitical Causal Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the causal pathway from the divergence to durable statehood, including wars, diplomacy, monarchs, borders, great-power reactions, local elites, and institutional continuity.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly from divergence to final map with little or no causal explanation.
criteria.3-4: Provides a few events but relies on handwaving, implausible concessions, or unexplained survival of the new state arrangement.
criteria.5-6: Offers a basic sequence of political and military developments, though some links are compressed or fragile.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain involving relevant actors, incentives, conflicts, treaties, and administrative choices that plausibly preserve the two states.
criteria.9-10: Integrates domestic politics and international constraints into a strong long-range chain where each stage follows credibly from prior conditions.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces important long-range consequences of the two-state arrangement rather than stopping at the initial split, including nationalism, alliances, wars, language policy, minority status, colonization, or 20th-century outcomes where relevant.
criteria.1-2: Gives only the initial counterfactual outcome with almost no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences, but they are generic or disconnected from the two-state premise.
criteria.5-6: Covers several plausible effects, such as altered wars, border claims, language policy, or national movements, but omits major likely pressures.
criteria.7-8: Explores multiple downstream domains and shows how the two-state structure changes later conflicts, identities, institutions, and foreign policy.
criteria.9-10: Provides rich long-range ramifications across domestic, regional, and international history while keeping them causally tied to the original one-people/two-states premise.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids contradictions with established history, acknowledges uncertainty, and distinguishes likely outcomes from speculative butterflies.
criteria.1-2: Contains major factual errors, internal contradictions, or deterministic claims that ignore obvious historical obstacles.
criteria.3-4: Has some accurate elements but also notable contradictions, overconfident leaps, or neglected constraints.
criteria.5-6: Mostly avoids direct contradictions and signals some uncertainty, though several causal claims remain overstated or insufficiently bounded.
criteria.7-8: Handles uncertainty well, notes contingency and alternative paths, and avoids conflicts with known political, linguistic, or demographic facts.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates firm implications from speculation, anticipates objections, and maintains strong consistency with real-world constraints throughout the counterfactual chain.

failures.question: What If Reverse Cuba and the Philippines
human_answers: American interest in Cuban had been more or less secured after the Span-Am War, so it'll be difficult for them to justify annexation, which could earn the ire of the Cuban independentists and the Southern States. But the Philippines presented some once in a lifetime opportunity for the US to finally gain their own foothold in the China market, instead of lurking around ports under the jurisdiction of other great powers. In a relatively practical POV, the US didn't need to annex the whole islands. Why waste men and money against the people that's prepared to fight to the last man to preserve their freedom (some historians even claimed that the Fil-Am War was the US first taste of a Vietnam scenario)? They could just let them be, make some economic agreements with them, get some ports, etc. and voila, they've got themselves a permanent presence in the Pacific without too much blood. Heck they could even convince the Brits to recognize the Republic and establish relations hoping to have Germany (or Japan) to back down from doing anything funny (although that may be a long shot).

Well, these few regions can try to secede. The issue is if they can maintain status quo. Malolos Republic controlled the navy or whatsoever left of the Spanish Navy. The government also controlled majority of the population of the Philippines. The Malolos republic can raise 100k men while your local provinces seceding have that same or lower population than the opposing army with your army having no or minimal rifles whatsoever. Your opponents have also better and well educated generals compared to you. You got also the issue of loyalty of your populace if they are more loyal to your seceding province or Malolos Republic. It is simple reality of warfare, you can try but the question is if you can succeed. It is pure imagination that civil war is because some or one provinces seceded. The only way that Civil war will happen is if Luna or Aguinaldo or anyone in the army fights among themselves. Or if you got a PoD that will butterfly away anything the resembles OTL 1890s Philippines.

Not really. The mood in the US was generally fairly pro-Cuban, and many of the Yellow Journalists of the time were agitating for Cuban independence. Plus, the labor unions in the US were also tied pretty closely to the Cubans. The whole reason the Maine was in Cuba was because the US had much more vested in what happened there than in the Philippines, due to the proximity to Florida. They were very concerned that the violence in the island might damage US investments further, and they were determined that either Cuba would remain Spanish or that Cuba would be in the US sphere somehow. Given that 6 decades later, human civilization nearly ended with a foreign threat got a foothold on that island, that was a fairly prescient concern. The US didn't care much about the Philippines until they managed to sink the Spanish fleet and realized that nothing was stopping them from taking the islands, so they did. So, in summation, if you want the US to annex Cuba and liberate the Philippines, you'd have to change things much earlier than the war.
failures.original_question:
AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.

failures.question: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)
human_answers: The problem is that everything becomes possible with enough wankium, hence the implied 'it would be best achieved by starting very early on, as per the other thread'; otherwise it's not a Challenge, an exploration of history and factors, rather an exercise in taking OTL and changing it all to successful/lucky/positive events while applying a large butterfly net. No assassination of AII; so he gets scared and Stolypin's reforms are implemented earlier and more decisively; but then, Japan still lucks out in War and so people are angry; WWI however you like, except with less Russian losses; Revolution happens later so Russia wins or at least doesn't lose as much, so the Mensheviks come into power and start building a social democracy in Russia; a couple decades of luck preventing any bad luck until the Nazis go West, while Russia prepares herself for being attacked; so when they come they are pushed back faster and with less losses, leading to a well-integrated post-WWII Russia that can enjoy a few decades of growth, has larger borders, and as a result reaches 300M by 2000 as you asked. But somehow, I don't think that's really what you are after, are you?

I do think early PoDs (which naturally make our world unrecognisable and certainly butterfly the birth of Lenin) are more plausible if you want Russia thoroughly similar to Scandinavia. But the 20th century is a good time for catching up, for radical jumps, for deep transformations, as OTL has also shown, only not in the way the OP desires. Steering a course between Bolshevik tyranny of OTL and its most likely counterpart, continuation of a relatively autocratic tsardom, is not impossible. Neither are the population numbers. A solid multi-party democracy, well, if it works in India, why not in Russia. But you could call what is required for it a good run of sixes, or a healthy dose of wankium. I've dabbled in that in Feeble Constitution , so I'll not dwell on the path of February 1917 consolidating with different policies after the April Days. Instead, I can see both earlier and later PoDs. For a good planning thread on a later PoD (basically SR victory in the Civil War), you could have a look at @galileo-034 's Century of the Common Man . Though this may not entirely fulfill your OP challenge - Lenin would not be an obscure footnote here, and instead die in 1918. So maybe let's go with the one big earlier opportunity - a successful revolution of 1905. @Powdermonkey started a TL on this last year. I'd be thrilled to see where this could go. One could argue that the path towards what the OP describes is still stony and uphill. How one would tackle the Great War problem is still up in the air, among other things. But still probably one path worth exploring more here since it hasn't been done often, I think.
failures.original_question:
AHC: A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

The goal is simple - we want to have a 20th century in which Russia avoids the interlocked chain of events leading to a century of trumas as IOTL. In this world, Russia becomes a vibrant multi party democracy, heavily integrated with the rest of Europe and with its intellectual and cultural elites intact. It follows an economic model analogous to the Social Market Economy of post ww2 Germany or even the Nordic Model if things go very positively. Its population is over 300 mln people by 1991 (the year the USSR collapsed IOTL). In this world, Vladimir Lenin is still born (despite the butterfly effect) and still becomes a revolutionary but he dies as an obscure, disillusioned theoretician. His last work, Delusions of the Proletariat , is a scathing critique of the supposed naivety of the working class, lured into capitalism through voting rights and social safety nets. It sells less than 500 copies. When the internet era arrives (either sooner or later than IOTL), Lenin is included in various "10 Failed Radicals You Have Never Heard of" type of articles on various history-related websited but is otherwise a forgotten figure.

rubrics.question_focus: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

criteria.name: Plausible point of divergence and counterfactual discipline
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer chooses a believable divergence capable of producing a drastically better 20th-century Russia without relying on arbitrary good luck, excessive 'wankium,' or implausible suppression of butterflies.
criteria.1-2: Uses vague wish-fulfillment or many unexplained positive changes with no credible point of divergence.
criteria.3-4: Names a divergence, but it is too late, too weak, or requires repeated lucky overrides to work.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible divergence such as altered 1905, Alexander II surviving, or different 1917 dynamics, but with limited justification.
criteria.7-8: Selects a strong divergence and explains why it could plausibly redirect Russian institutions and later crises.
criteria.9-10: Clearly frames the divergence, its limits, butterfly effects, and why it is one of the few credible routes to a much better Russian century.

criteria.name: Domestic political and institutional mechanism depth
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains Russia's transition away from autocracy, Bolshevik dictatorship, or failed liberalism toward a stable and comparatively humane political order.
criteria.1-2: Simply asserts Russia becomes democratic or prosperous without explaining institutions or social forces.
criteria.3-4: Mentions reforms or democracy but ignores resistance from the Tsar, elites, radicals, peasants, army, or national minorities.
criteria.5-6: Sketches a reformist path involving Duma power, 1905 success, Stolypin-style reforms, Menshevik/SR victory, or February consolidation.
criteria.7-8: Explains party politics, land reform, constitutional constraints, military loyalty, labor unrest, and minority management in a coherent sequence.
criteria.9-10: Shows a robust institutional pathway balancing monarchy/republic, socialism/liberalism, federalism, land hunger, and mass politics without assuming automatic Scandinavianization.

criteria.name: Handling of major wars and geopolitical shocks
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer coherently addresses the Russo-Japanese War, World War I, revolution/civil war risks, the rise of Nazi Germany, World War II, and Russia's postwar position.
criteria.1-2: Ignores major wars or assumes Russia effortlessly avoids or wins them.
criteria.3-4: Mentions wars but treats them as background events with little causal impact.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Japan, WWI, revolution, and WWII are key stress tests, though outcomes are only partly explained.
criteria.7-8: Gives plausible military, diplomatic, and domestic consequences for each major conflict and avoids easy total victories.
criteria.9-10: Integrates wars as central causal bottlenecks, explaining how a better Russia survives them with realistic tradeoffs, losses, alliances, and postwar borders.

criteria.name: Long-range socioeconomic and demographic plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly connects reforms and avoided catastrophes to higher living standards, industrialization, public health, migration, fertility, and possible population targets such as roughly 300 million by 2000.
criteria.1-2: States Russia becomes rich or populous without mechanisms or numbers.
criteria.3-4: Provides optimistic outcomes but ignores famine, repression, war deaths, urbanization, or demographic transition.
criteria.5-6: Links reduced civil war, famine, terror, and WWII losses to better population and development, but only broadly.
criteria.7-8: Explains industrial growth, agrarian reform, education, health, infrastructure, and demographic effects over decades.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively and causally grounds the improved outcome, showing which deaths are avoided, how growth compounds, and what limits remain.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, tradeoffs, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer acknowledges uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and distinguishes plausible causal chains from speculative or authorially forced outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Presents a deterministic fantasy timeline with contradictions or impossible coexistence of events.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of difficulty but still stacks convenient outcomes or contradicts known constraints.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that the scenario requires luck and identifies some fragile links.
criteria.7-8: Clearly marks uncertain junctures, offers alternatives, and explains why the selected path is plausible but not guaranteed.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight causal consistency across decades, openly flags low-probability assumptions, and avoids both excessive optimism and cynical inevitability.

failures.question: What If A Danish-Speaking Country with at least 40 million people
human_answers: As other people have said the low hanging fruit would be a Danish settler colony in the America. The next easiest one would be a Danish colony, where Danish end up Lingua Franca and becomes widespread adopted. Next one would be a united Scandinavia under Danish rule but with significant population growth (as there are only roughly 22-23 million Scandinavian speakers) The second hardest is a continued Danish-Norwegian union with massive population growth (as there are only 11 million Danish and Norwegian speakers). The hardest one would be Denmark with roughly OTL borders just with insane population growth, it at first look impossible but Denmark is somewhat bigger than Netherlands, and Netherlands have three times the population. But such a Denmark would demand centuries of different policies to enable it to have such a large population. Some would say that Norwegians and Swedes do not speak Danish as such including them in a Danish speaking state would not increase the number of Danish speakers. People are wrong, the three languages are simply written standards of the same language or for several related languages[1], if OTL Kalmar Union had lasted until after the Reformation had been implemented and the Bible had been translated, the Swedes would have used a Danish translation of the Bible for a long time and that would have become the core of what we think of as Swedish. Norwegian as most people think about it as a modern language only truly split from Danish in 1917. [1] if you split East Scandinavian into different languages based on the old dialects, it would not follow the existing language borders. Jutland would be split into three languages (Anglish in the south, Jutish in the west and Danish in the east), Gotlandic would be its own language. Norwegian would only be spoken in the West and North. Viken would speak Danish and so would coastal Southern Sweden, the rest of Sweden would be split between Swedish around Stockholm and in the north and Geatish in the inland south.
failures.original_question:
AHC: A Danish-Speaking Country with at least 40 million people

In real life, the Danish had a few colonies in the Virgin Islands and Ghana, but they didn't invest much in them. Maybe in this timeline, they form a much larger empire overseas since they have more resources or people. Keep in mind that the former Kalmar Union only has a population of 28 million, but if it stayed together longer, maybe it'd dominate the Baltic and absorb more.

rubrics.question_focus: What If A Danish-Speaking Country with at least 40 million people

criteria.name: Counterfactual route plausibility to 40M Danish speakers
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer identifies credible historical pathways by which a Danish-speaking polity could reach at least 40 million people, such as settler colonial expansion, a Danish-language colonial lingua franca, durable Scandinavian union, or extreme demographic divergence in Denmark.
criteria.1-2: Offers an implausible or purely magical scenario with no viable path to 40M Danish speakers.
criteria.3-4: Names a possible route but gives little explanation of why it could produce 40M Danish speakers.
criteria.5-6: Develops one plausible route with some demographic or political logic, but misses major alternatives or constraints.
criteria.7-8: Compares multiple plausible routes and explains why some are easier or harder to reach 40M.
criteria.9-10: Systematically ranks and justifies major routes, including colonies, Scandinavian union, Danish-Norwegian continuity, and high-growth Denmark.

criteria.name: Language formation and Danishness mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains why the population would actually be Danish-speaking rather than merely ruled by Denmark, including standardization, schooling, administration, Bible translation, elite language, dialect continua, and identity formation.
criteria.1-2: Equates Danish political control with Danish speech without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions assimilation or official language use but lacks a mechanism for mass adoption.
criteria.5-6: Explains some mechanisms such as schooling, administration, or settlement, but treats language shift simplistically.
criteria.7-8: Shows how institutions, literacy, religion, migration, and prestige could make Danish a majority language over time.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes Danish/Scandinavian dialect continua, standardization timing, Reformation texts, and how Danish could become the accepted written and spoken standard.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent sequence of political, demographic, colonial, and linguistic developments from the divergence point to a modern 40M-person Danish-speaking country.
criteria.1-2: Jumps from premise to outcome with no causal chain or with obvious historical impossibilities.
criteria.3-4: Provides a rough sequence but leaves major gaps in state survival, population growth, or language spread.
criteria.5-6: Gives a mostly coherent chain but underdevelops key transitions such as union durability, migration, or colonial retention.
criteria.7-8: Connects divergence points to institutions, population growth, territorial control, and language outcomes across centuries.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust long-range chain with credible contingencies, feedback loops, and continuity from early modern divergence to modern demographics.

criteria.name: Demographic and geopolitical constraint handling
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer respects population arithmetic, geographic capacity, historical rivals, colonial competition, and the difficulty of reaching 40 million under different scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Ignores population scale or asserts 40M without demographic or territorial basis.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the 40M target but uses weak or unrealistic population assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Provides some demographic reasoning, though estimates or constraints are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Uses credible comparisons and constraints, such as Scandinavian population limits, Netherlands-like density, or colonial settler growth.
criteria.9-10: Carefully balances population arithmetic, land capacity, migration, fertility, rival powers, and state capacity for each proposed route.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely from unlikely pathways, avoids internal contradictions, and clearly flags speculative claims in this open counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Makes overconfident claims, contradicts itself, or ignores obvious objections.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but contains unsupported assertions or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids contradictions and marks some scenarios as more speculative than others.
criteria.7-8: Clearly calibrates likelihood across scenarios and addresses objections such as whether Swedish/Norwegian count as Danish-speaking.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight consistency, explicitly handles definitional ambiguity around Danish versus Scandinavian languages, and grades all major scenarios by plausibility.
